A review of the watchdog before #54 merged found a hole in the sh version. The PR sat open from mid-August to mid-September, so the fix (166d208) went out with the rest of it in v0.6.0. The sh script matched test children with ps -o comm=. Linux truncates comm to 15 characters (TASK_COMM_LEN is 16 including the NUL). Here’s a binary named permissions.test:
comm=[permissions.tes] args=[./permissions.test] permissions.tes doesn’t match \.test$, so the watchdog never saw it. Same for personaname and containment, which are of course the security-sensitive packages. PowerShell’s Process.Name isn’t truncated, so the Windows script was fine. And I only ever ran the Windows script at my desk.
Here’s the original sh script (from 291f29e) and the fixed one against the same runaway test under WSL2:
# before: matched on comm safe-test: go test -count=1 ./permissions/... safe-test: cap=300 MB timeout=15 min poll=1 s ------------------------------------------------------------ ok runaway/permissions	6.180s ------------------------------------------------------------ safe-test: per-package peak resident memory (no *.test child observed -- packages may have had no tests, or ran faster than one poll) ------------------------------------------------------------ safe-test: clean pass. A 1.5 GiB test against a 300 MB cap, reported as a clean pass with exit 0. That’s the worst thing a guardrail can do. After the fix:
safe-test: go test -count=1 ./permissions/... safe-test: cap=300 MB timeout=15 min poll=0.5 s ------------------------------------------------------------ ------------------------------------------------------------ safe-test: per-package peak resident memory 229.7 MB permissions ------------------------------------------------------------ WATCHDOG: package 'permissions' (pid 405042) crossed the 300 MB cap at 373 MB resident. WATCHDOG: killed it and the parent 'go' process. This is the runaway -- fix the test before re-running the full suite. (The peak line is the last sample under the cap. The breaching sample is the one in the WATCHDOG line.)
The fix reads args instead, which comes from /proc/<pid>/cmdline and isn’t truncated. It takes argv[0] and basenames it. The whole tree walk and filter is one awk pass:
snapshot() { ps -Ao pid=,ppid=,rss=,args= | awk -v root="$1" ' { pid=$1; ppid=$2; rss=$3; exe=$4; # exe = argv[0], first token of args RSS[pid]=rss; EXE[pid]=exe; kids[ppid] = kids[ppid] " " pid; } END { n=0; queue[n++]=root; for (i=0; i<n; i++) { m=split(kids[queue[i]], a, " "); for (j=1; j<=m; j++) if (a[j] != "") { desc[a[j]]=1; queue[n++]=a[j]; } } for (p in desc) { c=EXE[p]; sub(/.*\//, "", c); if (c ~ /\.test$/) { pkg=c; sub(/\.test$/, "", pkg); print pkg, p, RSS[p]; } } }' } The same commit dropped the default poll from 1 s to 0.5 s to shrink the window between samples.
The lesson is the same one twice. Test the guardrail against a deliberately small cap, and test it on the platform it’s going to run on. The commit message for the fix even says the live Linux ps behavior “can’t be exercised on this Windows dev box”. It could. It just needed WSL and five minutes.
Using it powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\safe-test.ps1 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\safe-test.ps1 -Target ./internal/server/... -CapMB 500 scripts/safe-test.sh scripts/safe-test.sh -t ./internal/server/... -c 500 Both exit non-zero if they kill anything or if go test fails, so they work as a pre-push hook. CI still calls go test directly. The runners are ephemeral VMs, and a runaway there only hurts itself.
How I measured Windows 11 Pro on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X with 128 GB RAM, Windows PowerShell 5.1, Go 1.26. Linux runs were under WSL2 (kernel 6.18.33.2, procps-ng 4.0.4, Go 1.26.0). The runaway module lives in a scratch directory with a single permissions package containing the test above. Commands:
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File safe-test.ps1 -Target ./permissions/... -CapMB 300 sh safe-test-old.sh -t ./permissions/... -c 300 # git show 291f29e:scripts/safe-test.sh sh safe-test-new.sh -t ./permissions/... -c 300 # scripts/safe-test.sh at 166d208 The 104.3 MB healthy peak and 300.2 MB trip are from the PR #54 description, not my runs.
Links shipmates PR #54 (the watchdog) 166d208 (argv[0] instead of comm) scripts/safe-test.ps1 and scripts/safe-test.sh proc(5): /proc/pid/comm

title: Calling Rust From PHP Without a Socket, Part 2: Making Existing Code Use It
description: Thirteen Composer packages let existing Redis and database code in WordPress, Laravel and Symfony use ePHPm's built-in versions. This post covers what's in them and the bugs they turned up.
body:
Part 1 covered the plumbing. ePHPm registers ephpm_kv_* and ephpm_db_* functions that call straight into Rust. A cache read through one costs about a tenth of a microsecond instead of a loopback round trip. That’s nice and also useless on its own. Nobody is going to rewrite their WordPress object cache or their Laravel cache store around a function called ephpm_kv_set(). Applications talk to existing APIs instead:
Redis through phpredis or Predis the cache through PSR-6/16 or wp_cache_* the database through wpdb, mysqli, Eloquent or DBAL So there’s a set of Composer packages in the ephpm org whose whole job is to sit under those APIs and route them to the native functions. This post covers what’s in them and the rule that decides when they switch on. It also covers the bugs that only showed up once real applications ran on top.
The packages There are 13 of them, seven on the KV side and six on the database side:
Package What it stands in for phpredis-shim a userland \Redis class (the phpredis API) predis-connection a Predis Connection, so Predis\Client works with no socket cache-wordpress wp-content/object-cache.php, the WP_Object_Cache drop-in cache PSR-16 SimpleCache and PSR-6 pools cache-laravel a Laravel cache store, auto-discovered cache-symfony a Symfony Cache adapter session-handler a userland SessionHandlerInterface db the base typed wrapper, exception hierarchy and IDE stubs for ephpm_db_* db-wordpress wp-content/db.php, a wpdb with no mysqli mysqli-shim the mysqli API, procedural and OO db-laravel a Laravel database driver ('driver' => 'ephpm') db-doctrine a Doctrine DBAL 4 driver db-codeigniter a CodeIgniter 4 database driver They aren’t on Packagist. You add the GitHub repo as a Composer vcs repository and require it. The Predis one is the easiest to show because it’s the smallest change to an existing app:
use Ephpm\Predis\KvConnection; use Predis\Client; $redis = new Client('ephpm:', [ 'connections' => ['ephpm' => KvConnection::class], ]); $redis->incrby('hits:home', 1); $visits = $redis->get('hits:home'); Everything else in the app keeps calling Predis. KvConnection takes the command objects Predis builds. Instead of serializing them to RESP, it dispatches on the command ID and calls ephpm_kv_*.
When a shim switches on Every package that impersonates a global API follows the same rule: alias the global name only when the real extension isn’t loaded. The namespaced class always works. Here’s the entire activation file for the phpredis shim, loaded through Composer’s autoload.files:
use Ephpm\Phpredis\Redis; use Ephpm\Phpredis\RedisException; if (\extension_loaded('redis')) { return; } if (!\class_exists('Redis', false)) { \class_alias(Redis::class, 'Redis'); } if (!\class_exists('RedisException', false)) { \class_alias(RedisException::class, 'RedisException'); } A userland class can’t replace a loaded extension’s class anyway. Anything cleverer would just fatal on a box that has phpredis. The same rule has a funny consequence for the mysqli shim. The ePHPm SDK compiles mysqli in, so under ePHPm the global mysqli is always the real extension. Only the namespaced shim API is active. The global surface is for plain PHP builds without ext-mysqli. For WordPress that doesn’t matter, because the db.php drop-in replaces $wpdb instead of replacing mysqli.
The WordPress drop-ins also have to survive being copied to a host that isn’t ePHPm. db.php checks for ephpm_db_query() first. If it’s missing, it logs a notice and returns without setting $wpdb. WordPress then builds the stock mysqli wpdb exactly as if the drop-in weren’t there. object-cache.php does the same when it can’t load its classes. A drop-in that fatals your site when you move hosts is worse than no drop-in.
Throwing beats a wrong answer The KV store behind ephpm_kv_* models strings, counters and TTLs. It doesn’t have pipelines, MULTI, Lua, pub/sub or key iteration. Through the native functions it doesn’t have hashes, lists and sets either. The obvious way to write a compatibility shim is to fake those. Run a “pipeline” as a sequence of calls, implement SCAN by returning nothing, and so on. Every one of those fakes gives callers an answer that’s wrong in a way they can’t detect.
So the phpredis shim throws instead:
public function multi(int $mode = self::MULTI): never { throw NotImplementedException::for('MULTI/transactions', 'the KV store has no transaction/pipeline state'); } public function scan(mixed &$iterator, mixed $pattern = null, int $count = 0, ?string $type = null): never { throw NotImplementedException::for('SCAN', 'the KV store exposes no key iteration'); } NotImplementedException extends BadMethodCallException, deliberately not RedisException. Plenty of application code wraps Redis calls in catch (\RedisException $e) and treats it as “Redis is down, carry on without cache”. Calling a command the shim doesn’t implement is a bug in your setup, not a transient outage. It shouldn’t get swallowed by that catch block. The Predis connection does the same with SET ... XX, GET, KEEPTTL and friends.
The WordPress object cache had the same question with wp_cache_flush_group(). With no key scan there is no way to delete every key in a persistent group. So flush_group() clears the in-request copy and returns false for persistent groups. wp_cache_supports('flush_group') says false. Plugins that check support fall back to their own invalidation.
The semantics fixes These are the ones I’d point at if someone asked “why can’t I just write a quick adapter”.
wp_cache_add() is a mutex. The first version of add() in cache-wordpress checked whether the key existed and then set it. WordPress code uses wp_cache_add() as a cheap mutex. Only the first caller’s add succeeds, so whoever gets true does the work. With check-then-set, two concurrent requests could both see “absent” and both win. 19226c2 routes the persistent path through ephpm_kv_setnx. That’s one insert-if-absent under the store’s per-shard lock:
$inserted = $this->ops->setnx( $this->build_key($key, $group), $this->serialize($data), \max(0, $ttl), ); if (!$inserted) { return false; } (int) false is zero. ephpm_kv_incr_by() returns false when the stored value isn’t an integer. Five of the packages had return (int) \ephpm_kv_incr_by($key, $delta);, which turns that error into 0. A counter that silently resets to zero is worse than one that throws. The same one-line bug got the same fix in each of them in the September audit:
$result = \ephpm_kv_incr_by($key, $delta); if ($result === false) { throw new \RuntimeException( "value at key '{$key}' is not an integer and cannot be incremented" ); } return (int) $result; 'O\'Reilly' broke the installer. wpdb without mysqli has to escape strings itself. The first version did what mysql_real_escape_string() does and backslash-escaped the single quote. litewire’s tenant path rejected \' as malformed SQL while accepting every other backslash escape. So any content with an apostrophe failed. The first place that showed up was the twentytwentyfive theme’s block-pattern transient, which 500’d the installer during its last step. 35db6a8 doubles the quote (''), which both MySQL and SQLite accept. It keeps doubling backslashes so a string still can’t be broken out of. Doctrine’s quote() and the mysqli shim’s real_escape_string() got the same change later.
Native ints printed “0 responses”. The bridge hands back real PHP ints and floats. mysqli doesn’t. Unless MYSQLI_OPT_INT_AND_FLOAT_NATIVE is set, every scalar column comes back as a string, and wpdb never sets it. WordPress core depends on that. The comments-title block does '0' === get_comments_number(). With native ints every post with no comments rendered a “0 responses” heading. I found it by rendering the same pages under stock wpdb and under the drop-in, then diffing the HTML byte for byte. ad746e9 stringifies non-NULL scalars during row hydration. NULL stays null, like mysqli.
Stop guessing from the first keyword. Every adapter that implements a single query() entry point had to pick between ephpm_db_query() (rows) and ephpm_db_execute() (affected rows). They all did it by looking at the first word of the SQL. That breaks on WITH ... INSERT, INSERT ... RETURNING and anything else that doesn’t fit. #357 added ephpm_db_run(). It reports has_rowset from the statement that executed. Doctrine deleted its QueryClassifier class outright (e991c20). db-wordpress and the mysqli shim moved over too.
Known limitations I found two things while writing this up. Both come from the boundary rather than the wrappers’ own logic.
Keys go through the native functions as C strings and must be valid UTF-8, as covered in part 1. In the Predis connection, a plain SET that returns false is reported as Redis’ OOM error. The reasoning is that an overwrite can only fail for memory. But a key that isn’t valid UTF-8 also gets false from the bridge. It surfaces as OOM command not allowed when used memory > maxmemory., which will send you looking in the wrong place.
The WordPress object cache stores integers raw so the native incr keeps working on them. It applies that to integer-looking strings too:
private function serialize(mixed $value): string { if (\is_int($value)) { return (string) $value; } if (\is_string($value) && \preg_match('/^-?\d+$/', $value) === 1) { return $value; } return \serialize($value); } private function unserialize(string $value): mixed { if (\preg_match('/^-?\d+$/', $value) === 1) { return (int) $value; } return \unserialize($value); } On the next request (once it’s past the in-request cache), a string "02134" comes back as the int 2134. "5" comes back as 5. For most WordPress caching nobody notices. A ZIP code or a zero-padded ID cached as a string does notice. Distinguishing the two needs a type tag in the stored value, which is a format change. For now it’s a documented quirk rather than a quick patch.
The Laravel lock acquires atomically with setnx. But it releases by reading the owner and then deleting. That’s the same non-atomic release Laravel’s own Memcached lock has. It was written the day before the store grew a compare-and-delete, so it says “no CAS in the SAPI” in its docblock. That one’s a story of its own.
Trying it The wordpress-sample repo puts most of this together:
WordPress on the embedded database through db-wordpress the object cache on the KV store through cache-wordpress a WebSocket broadcast from PHP through ephpm_ws_broadcast It runs WooCommerce and Elementor, which between them exercise more MySQL-isms than WordPress core does.
The theme across all thirteen packages is the same as part 1. The boundary is the easy part. The work goes into matching what callers already depend on: string typing, atomic add(), errors that are errors.
Links Part 1: The Native Functions KV side: phpredis-shim, predis-connection, cache-wordpress, cache, cache-laravel, cache-symfony, session-handler DB side: db, db-wordpress, mysqli-shim, db-laravel, db-doctrine, db-codeigniter ephpm #357: ephpm_db_run and has_rowset ephpm/wordpress-sample

title: ePHPm Odds and Ends: OOM-Killed Links, Opcode Scanning, WebSockets and a 44 ms Stall
description: Four smaller ePHPm stories that didn't need a post each but were too useful to leave in PR descriptions.
body:
Not every fix in ePHPm earns a full write-up. A few of the smaller ones have stuck with me because the lesson in each was bigger than the diff. Here are four from this summer.
A release build the OOM killer kept eating ePHPm statically links libphp, ICU and a pile of other C libraries into one Rust binary. It ships for four targets. For the v0.4.2 performance release I set the release profile to lto = "fat" with codegen-units = 1 (#171). Fat LTO pulls every crate’s LLVM IR into one module in one process and optimizes it as a unit. One codegen unit removes the parallelism that would otherwise spread that memory out. That’s one very large process at the final link.
The linux-aarch64 legs died first. rustc was killed with (signal: 9, SIGKILL) during the link on three consecutive matrix runs. That included one where the leg had the host to itself. The fix ladder:
Thin LTO for arm64 (#181). Enough for about ten days. LTO off for arm64 and Windows (#198) once the Turso engine landed and grew the IR past what thin LTO fit into. The git history made the tipping point obvious. Windows built fine on fat LTO through v0.5.0 and started OOMing in v0.5.1, the first release with Turso linked in. RUST_MIN_STACK=32MiB on Windows (#199). With LTO off, the Windows build got far enough to hit a different wall. sqlparser’s deeply recursive AST types overflowed rustc’s default thread stack (STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW). Only on MSVC. arm64 compiled it fine. The same fix for nightly (#203), which had failed arm64 for eight straight runs. In most of those the OOM killer took the runner agent too. So GitHub reported “the self-hosted runner lost communication with the server” instead of a build error. Same failure, different hat. That’s exactly why it had been read as flaky infrastructure. One detail from #203 I’ll repeat to anybody who touches a workflow file. The value is quoted, "off". Bare off in YAML is boolean false, and Cargo’s lto = false means thin-local, not off.
Every one of those PRs said codegen-units = 1 was a contributing factor, and nobody had measured it. So instead of changing release CI on reasoning, #249 added an opt-in workflow_dispatch probe. It builds the same commit with lto and codegen_units as inputs and records two numbers:
Total peak memory, which is what the OOM killer acts on. The largest single process, which is what rustc-LLVM ERROR: out of memory is about. The first successful Windows run was LTO off with one codegen unit. It peaked at 5.58 GiB total and 2.66 GiB for rustc alone, with a 1001-second build on a 10 GiB host. That’s the baseline any change to codegen-units now has to beat.
Using the embedded Zend compiler as a static analyzer ephpm analyze (#502) is a fail-closed gate you run before deploying PHP. It has an analyzer framework, a policy engine and SARIF output. Some analyzers shell out to existing tools (composer audit, semgrep, YARA). Any analyzer error, timeout or panic floors the verdict at quarantine. A run where something that should have spoken didn’t can never be an “allow”.
The interesting one is opcode-scan (#509). PHPStan, Psalm and semgrep all re-implement PHP parsing. ePHPm already has PHP’s actual compiler linked in. So opcode-scan compiles each file with zend_compile_file under ZEND_COMPILE_WITHOUT_EXECUTION, the opcache_compile_file() model. Then it walks the opcode stream for dangerous calls. Nothing executes. It looks for two things:
ZEND_INCLUDE_OR_EVAL with ZEND_EVAL. Statically named calls through the INIT_FCALL family to system, exec, shell_exec, passthru, proc_open, popen, create_function, assert and unserialize. It checks every op_array. That means functions, methods, closures, arrow functions and conditional declarations.
Asking the compiler beats a text scan in both directions. Opcodes have no comments and no strings-as-code, so system in a docblock produces nothing. And the compiler lowers things a text scan can’t see. Backticks arrive as a genuine shell_exec call. So findings are reported as confirmed rather than suspected. Some boring details matter for a scanner that runs inside a server process:
The whole compile-and-walk runs inside zend_try/zend_catch so a fatal never longjmps into Rust. A file that doesn’t compile is a gating error. Code that can’t compile can’t be vouched for. Class and function table registrations get pruned after each file, so two files declaring the same symbol both scan. My favorite footnote is in #502’s review notes. The test fixtures assemble webshell-shaped strings at runtime. Windows Defender had quarantined earlier fixture source files as Backdoor:PHP/*. If your security scanner’s tests don’t trip the antivirus at least once, are they even testing anything?
WebSockets where PHP never holds the socket #304 added native WebSockets, but not the Swoole or ReactPHP way. Rust owns the socket and PHP runs once per event. That’s the API Gateway ($connect/$disconnect/message) shape. An idle connection costs a registry entry and some reactor memory, not a PHP process. So ten thousand idle connections cost no PHP at all. You do have to raise max_connections_per_site first. It defaults to 1,000 and counts a single-site server as one site. Every event goes through the same handle_php path as an HTTP request. The per-site database, KV keyspace, open_basedir sandbox and crash guard all apply without a parallel implementation to keep in sync.
One script, websocket.php at the vhost’s document root, routes on $_SERVER['WS_EVENT']:
<?php $event = $_SERVER['WS_EVENT']; $conn = $_SERVER['WS_CONNECTION_ID']; switch ($event) { case 'connect': // a non-2xx response refuses the upgrade, verbatim if (verify_token($_GET['token'] ?? '') === null) { http_response_code(401); return; } ephpm_ws_subscribe('lobby'); http_response_code(200); return; case 'message': $payload = json_decode(file_get_contents('php://input'), true); ephpm_ws_broadcast('lobby', json_encode(['text' => $payload['text'] ?? ''])); return; } The connect event runs on the real upgrade request, before the handshake completes. So it sees the cookies and query string that auth needs, and it can refuse with a real 401. There are two decisions I’d copy elsewhere. First, the implicit ephpm_ws_send() called from an ordinary HTTP request throws rather than returning false. A push API that silently succeeds is the worst possible failure mode. Second, every bound is a bound. Each connection has a fixed outbound queue, and on overflow the socket closes with 1013 instead of buffering. One slow reader costs one connection, never the server’s memory.
The 44 ms stall, and the fix that got reverted The single most productive class of performance bug in ePHPm has been TCP_NODELAY on small-response paths. The worst case was the MySQL wire frontend in litewire. PHP talks to the in-process SQLite over pdo_mysql. Single-row INSERTs took about a millisecond and SELECTs were pinned at a fixed ~44 ms. That asymmetry is the fingerprint of Nagle plus delayed ACK. A one-packet response (INSERT OK) can’t trigger it, but a multi-packet result set can. A fixed timer value is a timer, not a slow query.
The non-obvious part is that setting TCP_NODELAY on the server side alone did not fix it. The mysqlnd client’s side of the exchange mattered too. The real fix was coalescing the whole result set into a single write. Here’s the lab’s v0.4.1 retest, with ten sequential PDO queries per request:
That’s 444.0 ms p50 down to 4.4 ms at c=1, and 35 to 106 requests per second at c=16. The same audit found the main HTTP listener didn’t set nodelay either, on the assumption that hyper does it. It doesn’t.
This next part changed how I release things. A rebase conflict during a stacked-PR merge silently dropped the litewire set_nodelay lines. The commit was in history, but its changes had been overwritten by a --theirs resolution. CI was green. The DB benchmark on the release candidate still showed the full 44 ms stall. That’s the only reason it didn’t ship as a headline that was false on the flagship path. “The code merged and CI is green” isn’t the same claim as “the fix is in the binary”. Measure the release candidate.
Links LTO and the arm64/Windows OOMs: #171, #181, #198, #199, #203, #249 ephpm analyze and opcode-scan: #502, #509 Native WebSockets: #304 TCP_NODELAY findings: site/content/benchmarking/findings.md in the ePHPm repo; v0.4.1 retest numbers from the ePHPm lab’s docs/ephpm-0.4.1-retest.md

title: os/exec's StdoutPipe Footgun: How cmd.Wait() Ate My Last Frame (Twice)
description: Calling Wait while a StdoutPipe reader is still draining throws away the child's last output. I shipped this bug twice in shipmates.
body:
shipmates spends most of its life spawning claude (and codex) processes and reading newline-delimited JSON off their stdout. The last frame of a turn is the important one. It’s a result frame with the cost, the model and the final text. Stderr matters too, because that’s where Claude Code tells you Invalid API key · Please run /login. For a while I was throwing both away under load. The cause is documented right there in the os/exec godoc. I fixed it in one package and then found the exact same bug again a month later in another.
The symptoms It started as a flaky test. TestSpawnCapturesChildStderr failed on the linux-arm64 CI leg with a terminal event that had no stderr in it, just exited exit status 1. It passed 20 times in a row locally. The issue I filed blamed a 2 second drain grace:
if ok && p.stderrDone != nil { select { case <-p.stderrDone: case <-time.After(stderrDrainGrace): // = 2 * time.Second } } The theory was that on a loaded runner the stderr reader didn’t finish inside 2 seconds. So the terminal event went out with an empty tail. That’s plausible, and it’s wrong. Raising the timeout would have made the flake rarer and fixed nothing.
There was a second symptom that looked unrelated. Every so often the stdout scanner died with read |0: file already closed, which the read loop reported as a framing failure. That meant the terminal event got published as a string instead of the Terminal struct consumers expected. Anything type-switching on the payload quietly took a different branch. A third test in the codex adapter reported unexpected_eof for a frame the child had definitely written.
Same race, three different losers.
What the docs actually say Both packages read the child with cmd.StdoutPipe() and cmd.StderrPipe(). The supervisor called cmd.Wait() on its own goroutine, concurrently with the readers. Here’s the StdoutPipe doc:
Wait will close the pipe after seeing the command exit, so most callers need not close it themselves. It is thus incorrect to call Wait before all reads from the pipe have completed.
os/exec owns the parent’s end of any pipe it creates for you. Wait closes it the moment the child is reaped. Whatever the kernel still had buffered in that pipe goes with it. The child’s last words weren’t late. They were gone. io.Copy had already returned with os.ErrClosed before the drain grace was even consulted. That’s why a longer timeout couldn’t help. stderrDone was closing early, with nothing in it.
It’s very easy to write. You start the process and kick off a goroutine per pipe. Somebody has to call Wait eventually so you don’t leak a zombie. If that somebody isn’t sequenced after the readers, you have this bug.
A reproducer you can run I wanted to see it fail on demand, not once a week on an arm64 runner. The child writes 200 JSON lines with a result frame last and exits immediately. The parent reads slowly, at 1 ms per frame, standing in for real work. It calls Wait concurrently, the same shape shipmates had.
// go run . stdoutpipe # the footgun // go run . ospipe # own the pipe, drain, then Wait package main import ( "bufio" "fmt" "os" "os/exec" "time" ) const frames = 200 func child() { w := bufio.NewWriter(os.Stdout) for i := 0; i < frames-1; i++ { fmt.Fprintf(w, `{"type":"assistant","seq":%d}`+"\n", i) } fmt.Fprintln(w, `{"type":"result","cost_usd":0.42}`) w.Flush() os.Exit(0) // everything is sitting in the pipe buffer now } func consume(sc *bufio.Scanner) (n int, sawResult bool, err error) { for sc.Scan() { time.Sleep(time.Millisecond) // a consumer that does real work per frame n++ if sc.Text() == `{"type":"result","cost_usd":0.42}` { sawResult = true } } return n, sawResult, sc.Err() } func main() { if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "child" { child() } mode := "stdoutpipe" if len(os.Args) > 1 { mode = os.Args[1] } cmd := exec.Command(os.Args[0], "child") type result struct { n int ok bool err error } done := make(chan result, 1) switch mode { case "stdoutpipe": out, _ := cmd.StdoutPipe() if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil { panic(err) } go func() { n, ok, err := consume(bufio.NewScanner(out)) done <- result{n, ok, err} }() werr := cmd.Wait() // concurrent with the reader: documented as incorrect r := <-done fmt.Printf("%-10s wait=%v frames=%d/%d result=%v scanErr=%v\n", mode, werr, r.n, frames, r.ok, r.err) case "ospipe": pr, pw, _ := os.Pipe() cmd.Stdout = pw // an *os.File goes straight to the child; os/exec never closes our end if err := cmd.Start(); err != nil { panic(err) } pw.Close() // the child has its own copy; ours must go or we never see EOF go func() { n, ok, err := consume(bufio.NewScanner(pr)) done <- result{n, ok, err} }() werr := cmd.Wait() // reaping no longer touches the read end r := <-done // the reader ends at a clean EOF pr.Close() // closed by us, after the drain fmt.Printf("%-10s wait=%v frames=%d/%d result=%v scanErr=%v\n", mode, werr, r.n, frames, r.ok, r.err) } } On Linux (WSL2, kernel 6.18, built with Go 1.26.5):
stdoutpipe wait=<nil> frames=136/200 result=false scanErr=read |0: file already closed stdoutpipe wait=<nil> frames=136/200 result=false scanErr=read |0: file already closed stdoutpipe wait=<nil> frames=136/200 result=false scanErr=read |0: file already closed ospipe wait=<nil> frames=200/200 result=true scanErr=<nil> ospipe wait=<nil> frames=200/200 result=true scanErr=<nil> ospipe wait=<nil> frames=200/200 result=true scanErr=<nil> The reader gets whatever the scanner had already pulled into its buffer before Wait closed the pipe. Then it gets file already closed. The result frame, the one with the cost in it, never arrives. Note that Wait returns nil because the child exited 0. Nothing at the process level tells you anything went wrong.
One thing surprised me. The PR that fixed this in shipmates says the flakes were Linux-only. The reasoning was that on Windows internal/poll defers CloseHandle until a blocked read returns. That holds when the reader is parked inside Read at the moment of the close. In this reproducer the reader is sleeping between frames. There’s no read in flight to protect it, and Windows 11 with Go 1.26.5 loses the same frames:
stdoutpipe wait=<nil> frames=136/200 result=false scanErr=read |0: file already closed ospipe wait=<nil> frames=200/200 result=true scanErr=<nil> So don’t count on the platform to save you. A reader that does any work between reads is exposed everywhere.
The fix: own the pipes, one reaper closes them The fix in PR #44 is the ospipe branch above, grown up. Create the pipes with os.Pipe() and wire the write ends onto cmd.Stdout and cmd.Stderr. When you hand os/exec an *os.File, it passes it straight to the child and never tracks it. So Wait can’t close it. Close your copies of the write ends right after Start. The read ends hit a clean EOF once every writer is gone.
From internal/runtime/claude/claude.go:
stdoutR, stdoutW, err := os.Pipe() if err != nil { return nil, err } stderrR, stderrW, err := os.Pipe() if err != nil { closeFiles(stdoutR, stdoutW) return nil, err } cmd.Stdout = stdoutW cmd.Stderr = stderrW handle, err := r.supervise.Start(cmd) if err != nil { closeFiles(stdoutR, stdoutW, stderrR, stderrW) return nil, err } // The child holds its own duplicates of the write ends now; ours have to go // or the read ends would never reach EOF. closeFiles(stdoutW, stderrW) Then exactly one goroutine is allowed to close the read ends, and only after both readers say they’re done:
func (r *Runtime) reapPipes(p *proc) { select { case <-p.termDone: // The process is gone. Anything still holding a write end is a // descendant that inherited it, not the child, so bound the wait. t := time.NewTimer(readerDrainGrace) defer t.Stop() waitClosed(p.stdoutDone, t.C, r.stopFan) waitClosed(p.stderrDone, t.C, r.stopFan) case <-r.stopFan: // Explicit shutdown: Close must not sit through a drain window. } p.closePipes() } There’s a cost, and it’s the reason StderrPipe gets picked in the first place. With your own pipe, EOF needs every writer gone. A grandchild that inherited the child’s stdout can hold it open long after the child is dead. readerDrainGrace is 10 seconds and exists only for that case. In the normal path the child has been reaped and the pipe is already at EOF. Draining takes microseconds. If the backstop does fire, the terminal event now says “stderr not collected” instead of implying the child said nothing. Those used to be spelled the same way.
Two smaller pieces finished it off:
A scan error that is os.ErrClosed or io.ErrClosedPipe is classified as EOF, not a malformed stream. A genuinely broken stream still shows up as bufio.ErrTooLong or a real I/O error. The read loop waits on stderrDone unconditionally once the terminal event arrives. The leftover timeout is a deadlock guard, not a budget. Each symptom got a test with the timing forced instead of hoped for. TestReadLoopWaitsForTheStderrDrainBeforePublishing holds the stderr reader past the old 2 s bound. TestReapDoesNotDiscardFramesTheChildAlreadyWrote puts the frame in the pipe and completes the reap. Only then does it start the read loop. Both fail on the old code.
Twice That was mid-August and went out in v0.5.0. Then a cross-platform sweep after v0.6.0 turned up PR #60. The server’s own spawn path for live crew members, spawnCrewLive, still used StdoutPipe/StderrPipe with a concurrent Wait. Same bug, different file. On the resume path a claude -p that exited would lose its final result frame and the tail of its stderr.
It had a second bug riding along. Wait was only called on the resume path. Every fresh spawn was never reaped. That’s a zombie per mate on Unix and a leaked process handle on Windows, piling up for the life of a long-running ship. The fix mirrors reapPipes. A single reapLive goroutine is the only caller of cmd.Wait() and the only closer of the read ends. It starts unconditionally so both paths get reaped.
// The single reaper: the ONLY caller of cmd.Wait() and the ONLY closer of // the pipe read ends. Started here so it runs on BOTH the fresh and resume // paths. go s.reapLive(lp) The test for that one uses a fake claude (via TestMain) that writes a terminal result frame and exits immediately. It asserts the frame arrives on both paths and that the fresh child gets reaped.
What I took away from it If you call Wait from anywhere other than “after every reader returned”, don’t use StdoutPipe/StderrPipe. Use os.Pipe or cmd.Stdout = someWriter and let os/exec do the copying. One goroutine owns Wait and one goroutine owns closing the read ends. Ideally the same one. A timeout around a drain is a deadlock guard. If it’s the thing that decides whether you have the data, you have a race, not a slow reader. When you fix a bug class, grep for the rest of it. I fixed internal/runtime/claude and internal/codexapp. I didn’t look at internal/server, which had been doing the same thing the whole time. How I measured I built the reproducer above with Go 1.26.5 on Windows 11 Pro (AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, 128 GB). I also cross-compiled it for Linux and ran it under WSL2 (kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2). That was three runs of each mode on Linux and one of each on Windows. Every run produced the same numbers shown above.
Links shipmates issue #41 and PR #44 (the first fix) shipmates PR #60 (the twin in spawnCrewLive) os/exec Cmd.StdoutPipe docs

title: The Bugs Were Our Own Linker Wraps: Making a PHP Timeout Actually Time Out
description: max_execution_time did nothing in ePHPm because we had wrapped zend_set_timeout to a no-op. The SDK already had per-thread timers. We just had to stop switching them off.
body:
In the stack guard post the villain was a -Wl,--wrap linker flag that turned off PHP’s C-stack overflow guard. It wasn’t the only one. Until August, max_execution_time did nothing in ePHPm on Linux, for the same reason. We had wrapped the function that arms it to a no-op. A runaway script ran until the HTTP layer’s request timeout gave up on it and sent a 504. The PHP thread kept burning CPU after that.
This one is shorter, and it’s really about a habit. A setting you parse and don’t enforce is worse than a setting you don’t have.
Why the wrap existed in the first place When you embed PHP, you inherit its global side effects, and signals are the worst of them. PHP’s classic timeout uses setitimer(ITIMER_PROF), which delivers SIGPROF to the process. The kernel then hands it to whatever thread it likes. In php-fpm that’s fine, since each process has one PHP thread. In ePHPm, SIGPROF could land on a tokio worker thread with no PHP state at all. PHP’s handler would dereference per-request globals that don’t exist there and segfault.
So early in the project, build.rs wrapped PHP’s signal plumbing and the timeout functions. The C wrapper replaced them with no-ops:
void __wrap_zend_set_timeout(long seconds, int reset_signals) { (void)seconds; (void)reset_signals; /* no-op: ePHPm manages request timeouts at the HTTP server level */ } void __wrap_zend_unset_timeout(void) { /* no-op */ } --wrap=zend_set_timeout makes GNU ld resolve every call to zend_set_timeout inside libphp.a to __wrap_zend_set_timeout instead. It’s a clean way to override a function in a static archive you didn’t compile. At the time it was the correct call. But it meant [php] max_execution_time was parsed, documented and ignored. A docs audit landing the same week had it marked “parsed but not enforced”.
The SDK already had the fix compiled in PHP added --enable-zend-max-execution-timers partway through the 8.1 line (8.1.18 and 8.2.5, April 2023). It replaces the process-wide itimer with a per-thread POSIX timer. The question was whether our SDK had it. php-fpm users never think about this flag, and the docs for it are thin. So I checked the artifacts directly:
php_config.h in the Linux ZTS SDK has #define ZEND_MAX_EXECUTION_TIMERS 1. libphp.a defines zend_max_execution_timer_init, _settime and _shutdown, and they reference timer_create and timer_settime. Disassembling zend_max_execution_timer_init shows the important part: timer_create(CLOCK_BOOTTIME, SIGEV_THREAD_ID -> gettid(), SIGRTMIN). The handler is installed through a raw sigaction, not through the zend_signal_* functions we also wrap. That last point matters. SIGEV_THREAD_ID means the kernel delivers the signal to one specific thread. That’s the PHP thread that armed it. The whole reason for the wrap was gone. The source in Zend/zend_max_execution_timer.c matches what the disassembly shows:
sev.sigev_notify = SIGEV_THREAD_ID; sev.sigev_signo = SIGRTMIN; ... if (timer_create(ZEND_MAX_EXECUTION_TIMERS_CLOCK, &sev, &EG(max_execution_timer_timer)) != 0) { and zend_set_timeout() calls into zend_max_execution_timer_settime() when that’s compiled in. So the only thing standing between ePHPm and a working timeout was our own linker flag.
Probe, don’t assume The fix in ephpm#277 doesn’t just delete the wrap. Not every SDK we build against has per-thread timers. macOS doesn’t, for one. Both build scripts read php_config.h and only drop the wrap when the define is present:
let has_exec_timers = php_config_has_max_exec_timers(&sdk_path.join("include").join("php")); if has_exec_timers { println!("cargo::rustc-cfg=php_max_exec_timers"); } let mut wrap_funcs: Vec<&str> = vec![ "zend_signal_startup", "zend_signal_init", "zend_signal_deactivate", "zend_signal_activate", "zend_signal_handler_unblock", // still wrapped at the time; #360 (the stack guard post) removed it "zend_call_stack_init", ]; if !has_exec_timers { // No per-thread timers: zend_set_timeout() arms a process-wide // setitimer(ITIMER_PROF) + SIGPROF handler, which crashes when the // signal lands on a tokio worker thread. wrap_funcs.push("zend_set_timeout"); wrap_funcs.push("zend_unset_timeout"); } The C side gets the matching EPHPM_NATIVE_EXEC_TIMER define, and the no-op stubs only compile when it’s absent. On builds without the timers nothing changes. The HTTP request timeout is the only ceiling, and startup warns.
The second thing turning it off: the embed SAPI Dropping the wrap wasn’t enough on its own. The timer got created and stayed disarmed. The embed SAPI ships its own defaults, and max_execution_time=0 is one of them:
static const char HARDCODED_INI[] = "html_errors=0\n" "implicit_flush=1\n" "output_buffering=0\n" "max_execution_time=0\n" "max_input_time=-1\n\0"; In our setup, by the time a script ran, both the ini entry and EG(timeout_seconds) read 0. PHP’s own ini-to-timer chain armed nothing. Instead of fighting that, ePHPm records the configured value once from Rust after php_embed_init(). Then it arms the timer explicitly per request, right before executing the script:
#ifdef EPHPM_NATIVE_EXEC_TIMER /* php_request_startup above already created the timer but armed it from * EG(timeout_seconds), which the embed SAPI has reset to 0, so we arm * explicitly from the configured value here. reset_signals = 1 also * (re)installs the SIGRTMIN disposition. */ zend_set_timeout(g_configured_max_exec_secs, 1); #endif Arming from a process-wide configured value has a nice side effect. A previous request’s set_time_limit(0) changes the ini entry at runtime, but it can’t leak into the next request on the same thread. set_time_limit() during a request still re-arms the timer live on top of it, the same as in php-fpm.
The result also needed its own status code. A timeout unwinds through zend_bailout() like an out-of-memory fatal. Since ephpm#255 a bailout’s partial output gets discarded. But a timeout’s output is a legitimate php-fpm-style error page. So it’s told apart by PHP’s own message and delivered:
if (PG(last_error_message) && strncmp(ZSTR_VAL(PG(last_error_message)), "Maximum execution time of", 25) == 0) { result = EPHPM_EXEC_TIMEOUT; } else { result = EPHPM_EXEC_BAILOUT; } What it does now From the PR, on a PHP-linked build of PHP 8.5.7 with max_execution_time = 2 and a 30-second request timeout:
case result CPU busy loop 500 at 2.004 s, buffered output flushed, shutdown function ran sleep(5) 500 at 2.002 s (CLOCK_BOOTTIME is wall clock, so sleeping counts) set_time_limit(10) 500 at 10.002 s set_time_limit(0) 504 at 30.002 s, only the outer request timeout fires blocking fread on an empty FIFO 500 at 2.004 s normal request afterwards 200, same thread, no poisoning The FIFO row is my favorite. The timer interrupts a read that’s blocked in the kernel. The HTTP-layer timeout could never do that. It could only stop waiting for the thread, not stop the thread. Worker mode got the same treatment. It also got disarm-on-idle, so a worker sitting in take_request() for longer than the limit doesn’t fatal itself. A cross-request test proves a set_time_limit(0) in one request doesn’t leave the next one unlimited.
So there are two layers now, and the docs say so. max_execution_time is PHP’s own wall-clock limit that answers 500. It’s catchable and set_time_limit-able. [server.timeouts] request is the outer 504 backstop. Startup warns when max_execution_time >= request, since the inner limit could then never fire first.
The wider pattern: silent settings Two linker wraps in this project switched off a PHP feature and left the config pretending otherwise. Once I started looking, the same thing turned up without any linker involved.
An idle timeout that was parsed and thrown away. [server.timeouts] idle was read into a variable and dropped. The documented 60-second default did nothing. ephpm#106 implemented it. An I/O adapter stamps activity on every byte. A re-arming watchdog triggers hyper’s graceful shutdown after a quiet window. In the same pass it turned every other silent no-op it found into either a working knob or a loud startup warning.
Typos and knobs from newer versions. A config key the binary didn’t know was silently ignored. This bit for real. per_site = true on a binary that predated the knob parsed fine and got dropped on the floor. The node came up with every tenant sharing one database, with every health check green. ephpm#434 made every config section deny_unknown_fields. An unknown key is now a startup error that names the key. The top-level struct deliberately stays lenient. figment maps every EPHPM_* environment variable to a top-level key, and ePHPm sets one itself when it runs as a Windows service. The migration note in that PR has my favorite sentence of the year: if startup fails naming a key, that key was already doing nothing.
Estimates nobody measured. Two old perf issues estimated the cost of two things. Rebuilding $_SERVER per request was put at about 0.15 ms. Round-tripping response headers as text was put at 0.05 ms. When ephpm#457 measured them, they were about 4 µs and 1 µs. That’s off by roughly 40x. The fix still went in, and it also closed a header-injection gap on the worker path. But it’s a few microseconds per request, not the 20% the estimates implied.
The common thread is a knob that’s parsed but doesn’t do anything, a feature compiled in and wrapped out, a number nobody measured. Each one looks fine from the outside. For the linker case specifically, every --wrap in an embedder’s build is a runtime feature you’ve switched off. It should have a test that fails the day its reason stops being true. The stack-guard regression tests do that now. If the guard ever goes away again, they fail with a transport error, not a status mismatch. The timeout matrix above was still run by hand when it merged. Turning it into an automated e2e test is on the follow-up list. Writing this post is a decent reminder to go do it.
Links ephpm#277 - natively enforce max_execution_time via per-thread timers ephpm#360 - the other wrap: re-arming PHP’s C-stack guard ephpm#106 - make silent no-op config knobs real or loud ephpm#434 - reject unknown keys in every config section ephpm#457 - the $_SERVER and header round-trip, measured php-src: Zend/zend_max_execution_timer.c, sapi/embed/php_embed.c GNU ld --wrap

title: Clustered SQLite in ePHPm, Part 3: CDC Over the Cluster Channel
description: ePHPm ships Turso's change data capture stream between nodes over one authenticated, multiplexed TCP connection. This covers how that works and the two failover bugs that showed up when the e2e suite killed the primary.
body:
By the end of Part 2 ePHPm v0.7.0 ran exactly one SQLite engine in process. That was Turso, for single-node and clustered mode alike. The sidecar was gone. What I skipped over is how a replica actually gets the primary’s writes, and what happens when the primary dies with data on it. That’s this post.
Part 1: Replication by sidecar with sqld Part 2: Adding Turso Part 3: CDC over the cluster channel (this post) CDC from the engine itself Turso has change data capture built in. Turn it on for a connection and every committed change lands in a turso_cdc table. Each row has a monotonically increasing change_id, the table, the rowid, and before/after images of the record. The primary tails that table and ships transaction batches. Replicas apply them. That’s the whole design. It landed as an experimental path in #186 at the end of July. The tailer and applier live in litewire (litewire#10).
The best surprise of the whole series came out of the first integration test: Turso’s CDC captures DDL. CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN and DROP TABLE all show up in the same turso_cdc stream as the row changes. They appear as mutations on sqlite_schema. The after-image’s sql column carries the CREATE text, so the replica just runs it. That means replication is one ordered stream. There’s no separate schema sync channel to keep in step with it. WordPress creates and alters tables at runtime (plugins do it all the time) and that flows through the normal path.
That convenience is also an injection point, since the replica runs SQL text a peer sent it. Replayed DDL is parsed and allowlisted before it runs (litewire#17, in v0.6.2). It has to be exactly one CREATE TABLE, CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX, CREATE VIEW or CREATE TRIGGER. That’s everything sqlite_schema.sql can legitimately hold. ATTACH and PRAGMA don’t get through.
The primary side of the stream is a loop per subscriber. Each replica gets its own CdcTailer starting at the watermark the replica announced:
let mut tailer = CdcTailer::new(mgmt, from); loop { let batch = match tailer.poll_batch().await { Ok(batch) => batch, Err(e) => { // Drop the stream rather than skip past the failure -- // the replica reconnects with the same watermark and we // retry from the identical cursor. cdc_metrics::record_tail_poll_error(); anyhow::bail!("CDC tail poll error: {e:#}"); } }; // ... match shippable { Some((batch, commit_change_id)) => { let frame = Frame::Batch { rows: batch.rows.iter().map(WireCdcRow::from).collect() }; write_frame(&mut stream, &frame).await?; subscriber.record_batch_shipped(commit_change_id, rows); } None => { if idle_since.elapsed() >= HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL { write_frame(&mut stream, &Frame::Ping).await?; } tokio::time::sleep(POLL_INTERVAL).await; } } } Turso has no wakeup signal for CDC inserts, so it polls. POLL_INTERVAL is 25 ms. Keep that number in mind for the benchmark below.
v1 was a third protocol The first version of #186 had its own port (cdc_listen, 5015), length-prefixed JSON frames, and no encryption. It worked. It was also the third separate inter-node protocol after gossip and the KV data plane. I was going to need snapshot bootstrap next, and probably more after that. Each one wasn’t going to get its own port. So before #186 merged, the transport became the cluster channel. cdc_listen was deleted before it ever shipped in a release (#219).
The rule the channel makes explicit is: gossip carries names, the channel carries payloads.
Gossip (chitchat, UDP 7946) is the control plane only. Membership, phi-accrual failure detection, elections, small KV values. It has to stay small no matter how many writes you do. The cluster channel (TCP 7948) is the data plane for logs: CDC batches and snapshot bootstrap. Gossip says “node A is primary for sqlite:default”. The channel is what moves the transactions from A to its replicas.
Why 7948 and not 7947? Because the KV data plane already took gossip + 1:
// gossip_port + 2, NOT + 1: the KV data plane's default port (7947) is // already gossip-default (7946) + 1, so deriving +1 would collide with // it on any default-ported cluster. +2 lands on 7948 with defaults. let port = gossip .port() .checked_add(2) .context("gossip port is >= u16::MAX - 1; cannot derive cluster channel port")?; Only bound when something asks A config that doesn’t use a channel feature gets no socket, no task, and no log line above debug!. The only way to turn it on is a field in one struct:
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default)] pub struct FeatureFlags { /// Turso CDC replication. pub cdc: bool, } impl FeatureFlags { #[must_use] pub fn any_enabled(&self) -> bool { let Self { cdc } = *self; cdc } } The destructuring in any_enabled is on purpose. Add a field and that line stops compiling until you decide whether the new feature needs the channel. A feature that forgets its flag gets no channel, rather than a half-wired one. There’s a unit test that runs with every flag off. It then binds the derived port itself to prove nothing else did.
One connection, many streams After the handshake (next section) both sides speak yamux over the encrypted socket. Every stream starts with a length-prefixed type string, and that string is the dispatch key. The types are cdc/<site>, snapshot/<site>, and later sql/<site>. An unknown type gets a WARN and the stream is closed. The connection stays up. New features can ship without a protocol version bump, because old nodes just refuse the stream they don’t know.
Backpressure was the part I worried about. yamux has per-stream flow control (256 KiB window). Every subscriber owns a private CdcTailer, so a stalled replica pauses its own stream and nothing else. The tailer just stops advancing while its write is blocked. An earlier design broadcast one shared cursor to everyone. There a slow subscriber got RecvError::Lagged and permanently lost batches. Now the failure mode for a slow replica is lag, not loss.
Snapshot bootstrap rides the same connection. An empty replica pulls a logical dump on snapshot/<site>, captured under one read view along with its watermark. The dump is validated against a CREATE/INSERT allowlist. Then the replica subscribes to the tail from exactly that watermark.
The handshake The first channel handshake was one round trip. The initiator sent a sealed challenge, and the responder opened it and echoed it back. That proves the responder has the secret. It does not prove anything about the initiator. The responder only ever echoes what it’s handed. So anyone who recorded one legitimate setup could replay those bytes verbatim and get through the accept path without the secret.
v2 is a mutual challenge/response, three messages before any yamux frame:
The important line is in the responder. It mixes in a challenge of its own, which a replayer has never seen and can’t open:
let challenge_r = fresh_challenge(); let session_transcript = transcript(&challenge_i, &challenge_r); // Message 2 seals the transcript itself: the echo of C_i (which // proves we opened it) followed by our own fresh C_r. tcp.write_all(&[HANDSHAKE_VERSION]).await?; let sealed = keys.handshake.seal(&session_transcript).context("seal handshake reply")?; write_handshake_body(tcp, &sealed).await?; // Message 3 must be the responder challenge, sealed by a peer that // holds the secret. A replayer cannot get here. let confirm = read_handshake_body(tcp, &keys.handshake).await.context("read handshake confirmation")?; anyhow::ensure!( constant_time_eq(&confirm, &challenge_r), "handshake confirmation did not echo our challenge (replay attempt)" ); Ok(keys.session(&session_transcript)) The rest of it:
Both echo comparisons are constant time. The handshake key comes from its own HKDF domain, so a stray gossip datagram or KV frame can never authenticate here. After the handshake, both sides derive a per-connection session key from the secret salted with C_i || C_r. Every byte yamux writes goes out as a length-prefixed ChaCha20-Poly1305 frame. Frames can’t be spliced between connections, and a frame that fails authentication drops the connection. The source IP has to be a live gossip member before the handshake even starts. That’s coarse. It’s per host, and it trusts the TCP source address. But it means a leaked secret alone doesn’t let an arbitrary host pull a database snapshot. At most 64 concurrent handshakes in flight, a 10 second deadline on each. It refuses to bind at all if a channel feature is on and there’s no secret. Authenticated or absent. There’s a test that does exactly what the v1 attack did. It records a real initiator’s first message and replays it on a new connection. It echoes back whatever the responder says. Then it asserts nothing ever reaches the dispatch table.
Then the e2e suite killed the primary Everything above passed its tests. The two-node path had been validated by hand during benchmarking. What hadn’t happened was a test that started three real ephpm processes, wrote data, and killed the elected primary. #310 added that suite, and it found two defects on its first run. Both were filed as #[ignore]d tests carrying the log evidence. That way the intended behavior was written down and executable before anyone touched the fix.
1. A joining node stole the primary role.
21:41:58 cdc-node-2 elected as SQLite primary (holds the data) 21:42:04 cdc-node-3 elected as SQLite primary (empty, just booted) 21:42:08 cdc-node-2 role changed Primary -> Replica{ primary: node-3 } The initial role was decided before gossip converged. A freshly booted node saw a member list containing only itself. It concluded it was the lowest-ordinal alive node and published a claim. Gossip KV is last-write-wins, so the incumbent demoted. The cluster re-rooted onto an empty database. The joiner believed it was primary, so it never bootstrapped.
2. Writes after a failover were silently never replicated.
cdc-node-1 CDC replica: subscribed from_change_id=5 (watermark from the dead node-2) cdc-node-0 CDC: subscriber attached from_change_id=5 (tailer over node-0's own log) change_id is a per-database sequence. The subscribe watermark was being treated as cluster-wide. A promoted replica’s own CDC log starts empty, because applied batches bypass capture. Its first new writes landed at change_id 1 and 2. That’s below the inherited cursor of 5, so the tailer never yielded them. No error, no metric moved, and the replica reported itself connected and caught up. That’s unbounded silent write loss after any failover.
The fixes are in #346:
Election: a fresh node can’t publish its first claim until a 15 second startup grace has passed. That’s the claim TTL plus one heartbeat. A live incumbent republishes every 5 seconds, so its claim always arrives first. A restarting incumbent whose own claim is still unexpired can reclaim right away. A primary that sees a live foreign claim breaks the tie by lowest node id, the documented rule, instead of yielding to whoever wrote last. The cost is that a brand new cluster elects its first primary 15-20 seconds after boot. Watermarks: every database file gets a random 128-bit log identity. The first frame on every CDC stream is now a Hello naming the log the primary is about to serve. The replica keeps a cursor per log: enum Frame { /// Primary -> replica, first frame on every stream. Identifies /// which CDC log the primary is about to serve. Hello { log_id: String }, /// Replica -> primary, sent after Hello. The applied watermark /// in the log the Hello named. Subscribe { from_change_id: i64 }, Batch { rows: Vec<WireCdcRow> }, Ping, } On a source switch the replica does three things:
Saves the old log’s cursor. Restores the new log’s cursor (0 if it has never followed it). Re-seeds litewire’s watermark table so the applier’s idempotency guard follows along. Primary to replica to primary again resolves correctly.
Removing the #[ignore] was the verification step. Then each fix was verified the other direction. I reverted just that fix, kept the other, and watched its test fail again with the original symptom. The joining-node test failed with the joiner taking the role. The failover test failed with the survivor stuck at its pre-failover rows until a 90 second timeout. Then both went back in. The full e2e run was 55 suites, 236 tests, zero failures. Proving a test fails without the fix is the only way I know to be sure it’s testing the fix.
The audit of #346 turned up one more, narrower door (#353). The fast-restart reclaim matched on node id. But “same node id” isn’t “same data”. A node redeployed onto an empty volume comes back with its old id and a fresh log identity. It could win the reclaim inside the 10 second TTL and re-root the cluster onto nothing again. The claim is now node_id|addr|log_id, and the fast path only fires when both match.
Worth saying plainly: none of these bugs were Turso’s. All three lived in ePHPm’s election and watermark logic layered on top. Turso’s CDC stream did exactly what it said the whole time. One ordered stream, monotonic ids, and DDL included. If you’re wondering whether to trust the beta engine, under failover testing the beta wasn’t what broke.
How far behind is a replica? ePHPm doesn’t export a replication lag gauge yet, so I measured it from the outside. I ran two v0.8.7 nodes on one machine with the real cluster channel between them. The primary was on 127.0.0.1 and the replica on 127.0.0.2. A small Go probe inserts a row through PHP on the primary. It takes the time when the HTTP response comes back, since the write is committed at that point. Then it polls a PHP page on the replica every ~2.4 ms until the row shows up. I took 150 samples per step, with a random pause between samples so they don’t line up with the tailer’s 25 ms poll. In the background, a separate open-loop writer puts a steady rate of single-row INSERTs on the primary.
background writes p50 p90 p99 idle 16.2 ms 26.5 ms 44.9 ms 100/s 17.7 ms 30.0 ms 34.6 ms 250/s 21.3 ms 30.2 ms 51.6 ms 500/s 26.9 ms 37.1 ms 57.9 ms That’s what a 25 ms poll looks like. On an idle primary the median is a bit over half the interval plus the apply. It creeps up as the stream gets busier. For a PHP app, a replica that’s 20-30 ms behind is fine.
At 1,000 writes/s it stopped being fine. The replica fell behind and kept falling. Five probes in a row timed out at 5 seconds, and the ten that did land had a median of 1.7 seconds. So I went looking for the ceiling. I hit the primary with closed-loop writers for 17 seconds and didn’t touch the replica. Then I timed how long it took to catch up:
burst primary inserts/s single node inserts/s replica drain rate 1 writer 2,288 2,740 757 rows/s (25,161 rows in 33.2 s) 4 writers 5,154 6,372 810 rows/s (76,383 rows in 94.3 s) Two things come out of that. First, capturing CDC on the primary costs 16-19% of write throughput. That’s against the same binary with no [cluster] at all. It’s in the same range as the 12-13% the lab measured on its podman rig. Second, the replica applies about 750-830 transactions per second. It’s a straight line no matter how hard the primary is pushed. The reason is in the tailer. poll_batch cuts at the first COMMIT record. So every primary transaction becomes its own poll, its own frame and its own transaction on the replica. The 25 ms sleep only happens when there’s nothing to send, so it isn’t the bottleneck here. The per-transaction round trip is. The obvious next step is batching several source transactions per frame and per apply transaction. Now there’s a number to beat.
During those bursts the replica also logged SQLITE_BUSY from apply_batch twice. Both were an apply colliding with my read probe on the replica. Both times it dropped the stream and resubscribed two seconds later from its watermark, then carried on. The final count on both nodes was 179,369 rows. That’s the “lag, not loss” property from the backpressure section doing its job. A busy timeout on the apply connection would make it a lot less noisy, though.
How I measured AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 cores / 32 threads), 128 GB (62 GiB visible to WSL2), Windows 11 with WSL2 (kernel 6.18.33.2), everything on the WSL ext4 filesystem. No CPU limits on either node, so both ePHPm processes and the load generator share the same 32 threads. ePHPm v0.8.7, the php8.4.23-linux-x86_64 release build, [db.sqlite.replication] role = "primary" / "replica" pinned, [php] mode = "fpm", rate limiting off, query stats off. PHP fixtures use ephpm_db_execute / ephpm_db_query, one statement each. The lag probe and open-loop writer are a ~150 line Go program. The burst writers are closed loop over keep-alive connections. One-machine loopback numbers. They say how the replication path behaves, not what a real network between two hosts adds. Absolute inserts/s won’t transfer to your hardware. The shape should: lag tracks the poll interval, and apply has a ceiling around one transaction per round trip. One database per site Multi-tenant ePHPm (a sites_dir with a database per vhost) and clustering didn’t coexist until #416. Before it, enabling [cluster] collapsed every vhost onto one shared clustered database. With [db.sqlite.replication] per_site = true:
Each vhost gets its own cdc/<site> and snapshot/<site> streams over the same channel connection. Ownership is rendezvous-hashed over the alive nodes. A node death moves only that node’s sites, each to a node that already has a warm replica. A new sql/<site> stream forwards writes from a non-owner to the owner, so they get captured into that site’s CDC log. A review of the PR listed its own blockers, and they were closed before merge. The worst was data loss when a site got re-homed onto a node that never had it. A node joining was enough to trigger it. Two more silent ones came after:
A node that only forwarded a site never replicated it (#429). Stock pdo_mysql writes on a non-owner committed locally and were never shipped (#432). Every health check was green in both cases. The lab’s cluster suite puts the forward hop at about 255-275 µs per statement. It’s paid per statement, so a ten-query page on a non-owner pays it ten times.
Counting protocols Here’s the closing argument for the series. In the sqld era, two nodes talked over four things:
Gossip. The KV data plane. sqld gRPC. Hrana HTTP to a child process on each side. Now it’s gossip, the KV data plane, and one multiplexed, authenticated cluster channel, all in one process.
ePHPm’s docs still label clustered mode experimental, and I think that’s right. That label is about ePHPm’s replication layer, not about Turso. The layer is a couple of months old and has had real bugs in its election and watermark logic. The fixes for those bugs came with tests that fail without them. That’s the best I can offer until it has more time behind it.
Links #186 Phase 2 CDC-native replication, litewire#10 #219 cdc_listen removal, cluster channel docs #310 clustered Turso CDC e2e, #346 election and log identity fixes, #353 log id in the claim #416 per-site clustered replication, #429, #432 Cluster channel design: ephpm.dev/roadmap/cluster-channel Lab cluster suite results: cluster-persite-v087.md

title: Calling Rust From PHP Without a Socket, Part 1: The Native Functions
description: How ePHPm exposes its in-process KV store and SQLite bridge to PHP as plain functions, and what it took to make that safe under ZTS.
body:
ePHPm is a single Rust binary that embeds PHP. It carries its own KV store and its own SQLite-backed database in the same process. For a long time PHP code could only reach that KV store the same way it reaches Redis. It opened a TCP socket to the RESP listener ePHPm runs on localhost, encoded a command and waited for the reply. That works, and every PHP Redis client in existence already speaks it. But it is a strange thing to do when the hash map you’re talking to lives a few pointers away in the same address space.
So ePHPm registers its own PHP functions: ephpm_kv_get(), ephpm_kv_set(), ephpm_db_query() and friends. Calling one is a C function call that hops through a function pointer into Rust and back. This is part one of two. This post is the plumbing:
how the functions get registered how C and Rust share a table of function pointers who owns which bytes the thread-teardown bugs that came with it Part 2 is the 13 Composer packages that let phpredis, Predis, WordPress and Laravel code use them without being rewritten.
Is it worth it? Before writing a post about avoiding a socket I wanted my own numbers, not the ones in the docs. I took the ephpm-lab KV harness and ran it against the v0.10.6 release. The harness is one PHP request that loops over the operation and times it with hrtime(). I pointed the same raw-socket RESP client at two servers. One was ePHPm’s own RESP listener and the other was a stock Redis 7 in a container.
Medians of three interleaved runs:
64 B 4 KB 64 KB ephpm_kv_get() 0.105 µs 0.176 µs 2.04 µs ephpm_kv_set() 0.165 µs 0.210 µs 1.19 µs GET over RESP to ePHPm 83.0 µs 86.7 µs 117.8 µs GET over RESP to Redis 7.4 86.8 µs 88.9 µs 123.3 µs A small get through the native function is about 105 ns. The same get over a socket is about 83 µs. That’s roughly 790 times slower, and it barely matters which server is on the other end. Real Redis comes in within 5% of ePHPm’s own listener. That’s the useful result. The cost isn’t the server, it’s the round trip.
I’d be careful with the absolute socket number. It’s high because this is WSL2, where a loopback round trip is expensive. To check it wasn’t my PHP client, I ran redis-benchmark -c 1 inside the Redis container. That’s plain C with no PHP involved, and it got a p50 of 79 µs. On bare-metal Linux loopback is a lot cheaper, so expect the gap to shrink by some factor there. It doesn’t go away, though. A native call doesn’t have a round trip at all.
The other thing the table shows is that “no serialization” isn’t “no copy”. At 64 KB the native get is memcpy-bound at about 2 µs. The value is copied out of the store and then copied again into a PHP string.
What PHP sees Everything is registered from one macro in ephpm_wrapper.c. The server and the CLI mode, ephpm php, get the same list:
#define EPHPM_COMMON_FUNCTION_ENTRIES \ PHP_FE(ephpm_kv_get, arginfo_ephpm_kv_get) \ PHP_FE(ephpm_kv_set, arginfo_ephpm_kv_set) \ PHP_FE(ephpm_kv_setnx, arginfo_ephpm_kv_setnx) \ PHP_FE(ephpm_kv_del, arginfo_ephpm_kv_del) \ PHP_FE(ephpm_kv_del_if_eq, arginfo_ephpm_kv_del_if_eq) \ /* ... exists, incr, decr, incr_by, expire, ttl, pttl, flush_all, wait */ \ PHP_FE(ephpm_db_query, arginfo_ephpm_db_query) \ PHP_FE(ephpm_db_execute, arginfo_ephpm_db_execute) \ PHP_FE(ephpm_db_run, arginfo_ephpm_db_run) \ /* ... columns, in_transaction, available, errno, error */ \ PHP_FE(ephpm_ws_send, arginfo_ephpm_ws_send) \ /* ... eight more ephpm_ws_* */ \ PHP_FE(ephpm_middleware_config, arginfo_ephpm_middleware_config) That’s 14 KV functions, 8 database functions, 9 WebSocket functions and the middleware config accessor. On top of those there’s a small module with the \Ephpm\Worker\* functions for worker mode. There’s also a native session save handler you turn on with session.save_handler = ephpm. Every one of them follows the same pattern, so I’ll stick to the KV and DB side.
One function worth calling out is ephpm_kv_wait(). It blocks until a key’s version changes. You can’t do that over RESP without pub/sub. It replaced a poll-and-usleep loop in the Datastar demo. In #184 eight idle SSE clients went from 0.35% of a core to 0.02%. Event latency went from a p50 of 100 ms, the poll interval, to 1.2 ms.
Getting the functions registered at all This took three tries. The first two looked fine in the code and failed in the e2e suite.
The obvious move is to set additional_functions on the SAPI module struct before calling php_embed_init(). That does nothing. php_embed_init() overwrites php_embed_module.additional_functions with its own one-entry array, just dl(). That happens at sapi/embed/php_embed.c:219, after sapi_startup() and before module startup. Every request died with “Call to undefined function ephpm_kv_get()”.
The second attempt (752890eb) called zend_register_functions() right after php_embed_init() returned. On a non-ZTS build that’s fine. But ePHPm runs PHP threaded (ZTS). In ZTS, zend_post_startup() runs at the tail of php_module_startup(). It copies the main thread’s CG(function_table) into a static GLOBAL_FUNCTION_TABLE and frees the original. Every new PHP thread builds its function table by copying from GLOBAL_FUNCTION_TABLE in compiler_globals_ctor. Register a function after that point and it lands in a table no worker thread will ever look at.
The window that works is “after the embed SAPI wipes additional_functions, before php_module_startup() reads it”. php_embed_init() rewrites additional_functions but leaves the startup hook alone. So the fix (a50a69ba) swaps the startup hook for a shim:
static int ephpm_module_startup(sapi_module_struct *sm) { sm->additional_functions = g_cli_mode ? ephpm_cli_functions : ephpm_kv_functions; /* worker module goes in as php_module_startup's additional_module so its * functions land in CG(function_table) DURING zend_startup */ int ret = php_module_startup(sm, &ephpm_worker_module_entry); /* after: ext/session's MINIT has to have run. Before the embed init * returns: under ZTS that is the last moment new threads will see it */ if (ret == SUCCESS) { (void)php_session_register_module(&ps_mod_ephpm); } return ret; } void ephpm_pre_init(void) { php_embed_module.startup = ephpm_module_startup; } The same window turned out to be the right place for several later things. The CLI’s -d directives and PHP_BINARY are spliced in there too. That says something about how much of the embed SAPI’s setup happens in that one call.
The ops table The C side doesn’t know anything about Rust types. It declares a struct of function pointers and keeps one static copy:
typedef struct { int (*get)(const char *key); void (*get_result)(const char **ptr, size_t *len); int (*set)(const char *key, const char *val, size_t val_len, long long ttl_ms); int (*set_nx)(const char *key, const char *val, size_t val_len, long long ttl_ms); long (*del)(const char *key); /* ... exists, incr_by, expire, pttl, flush_all, wait ... */ /* Must stay LAST-appended: the layout mirrors kv_bridge.rs. */ int (*del_if_eq)(const char *key, const char *token, size_t token_len); } EphpmKvOps; static EphpmKvOps g_kv_ops = {0}; void ephpm_set_kv_ops(const EphpmKvOps *ops) { if (ops) { g_kv_ops = *ops; } } Rust mirrors it field for field as a #[repr(C)] struct of Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(...)> and fills in a static. An Option of a function pointer has the same layout as a nullable C pointer:
#[repr(C)] pub struct EphpmKvOps { pub get: Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(key: *const c_char) -> c_int>, pub get_result: Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(ptr: *mut *const c_char, len: *mut usize)>, // ... pub del_if_eq: Option<unsafe extern "C" fn(key: *const c_char, token: *const c_char, token_len: usize) -> c_int>, } pub static KV_OPS: EphpmKvOps = EphpmKvOps { get: Some(kv_get), get_result: Some(kv_get_result), // ... del_if_eq: Some(kv_del_if_eq), }; // at startup, before any PHP thread runs a script unsafe { ffi::ephpm_set_kv_ops(&kv_bridge::KV_OPS) }; The table is copied into the C global once, before any PHP thread runs. It’s never written again. That’s the entire thread-safety story. A struct that’s read-only after startup needs no lock, no atomics, nothing. Each PHP_FUNCTION checks its pointer for NULL first. A build where the KV store isn’t wired returns a miss instead of crashing.
C and Rust each declare the layout by hand, so the rule is append-only. New operations go at the end. The last field carries a “must stay LAST-appended” comment on both sides. wait was added after flush_all, and del_if_eq after wait. The DB table has the same comment on available. It’s the same discipline as ePHPm’s native middleware ABI. It’s boring on purpose.
No malloc crosses the boundary This is the rule I care about most. Memory allocated by Rust is freed by Rust. Memory allocated by PHP is freed by PHP. Nothing crosses.
For a get, Rust copies the value into a thread-local buffer and returns 1. C then asks for a pointer and length into that buffer and copies the bytes into a PHP string:
PHP_FUNCTION(ephpm_kv_get) { char *key; size_t key_len; ZEND_PARSE_PARAMETERS_START(1, 1) Z_PARAM_STRING(key, key_len) ZEND_PARSE_PARAMETERS_END(); if (!g_kv_ops.get) { RETURN_NULL(); } if (!g_kv_ops.get(key)) { RETURN_NULL(); } const char *ptr; size_t len; g_kv_ops.get_result(&ptr, &len); RETURN_STRINGL(ptr, len); } The borrowed pointer is valid until the next get on the same thread. PHP is single-threaded per request, so there is no next get until this one returns. That’s one copy out of the store into the buffer and one copy into the zval. It’s why a 64 KB value costs a couple of microseconds and a 64-byte value doesn’t.
The DB side stages more. A statement’s rows go in one thread-local. finish() releases them as soon as C has turned them into zvals. The metadata goes in a separate “last call” record that survives finish(). That covers whether it returned rows, the column names and declared types, affected rows and last insert id. Any error goes in that record too. That split is what made #357 possible. ephpm_db_errno() still works after the exception was caught. ephpm_db_columns() can describe a SELECT that matched zero rows.
Errors stay on the C side Rust callbacks never call into Zend. That’s deliberate. A PHP fatal unwinds with longjmp. A longjmp through Rust frames skips their destructors, which is undefined behavior. So errors come back as return codes and C decides what to do with them. For the DB functions that means throwing an exception, which doesn’t longjmp:
int rc = g_db_ops.run(sql, sql_len); if (rc == -2) { zend_throw_exception(zend_ce_exception, EPHPM_DB_UNAVAILABLE_MSG, EPHPM_DB_ERR_UNAVAILABLE); return EPHPM_DB_THREW; } if (rc < 0) { g_db_ops.error_info(&code, &sqlstate, &msg, &msg_len); zend_throw_exception_ex(zend_ce_exception, (zend_long)code, "SQLSTATE[%.5s]: %.*s", sqlstate ? sqlstate : "HY000", (int)msg_len, msg ? msg : ""); g_db_ops.finish(); return EPHPM_DB_THREW; } SQL errors carry the MySQL server error code litewire mapped them to. That’s 1062 for a duplicate key and 1064 for a syntax error. Infrastructure failures use 2000 through 2004:
no database configured no site context can’t connect unbindable parameter thread shutting down Those sit in MySQL’s client-error range, which a server never sends. An adapter can tell “your SQL is wrong” from “the bridge isn’t there” by number instead of by matching message text.
Which keyspace? ePHPm can serve many sites from one process, and each site gets its own KV store. The C side never sees that. Before PHP runs, the router calls set_site_store() for the request. Every Rust callback resolves its store through a thread-local:
fn effective_store() -> Option<Arc<Store>> { KV_SITE_STORE .try_with(|s| { let site = s.borrow(); if let Some(ref store) = *site { Some(Arc::clone(store)) } else { KV_STORE.get().cloned() } }) .unwrap_or(None) } The DB bridge does the same with the site key. In per-site mode a query with no site context fails instead of falling back to a shared database.
This had a bug that’s worth knowing about if you build something similar. #208 found two separate MultiTenantStore instances. The router built one for the PHP path and the RESP listener built the other. Each lazily created its own per-hostname Store. So in vhost mode ephpm_kv_set() from PHP and a Predis SET for the same site landed in different keyspaces. Neither could see the other’s writes. Single-site mode was fine, which is why it lived for a while. The fix is the obvious one: build it once and hand the same instance to both.
Thread teardown The nastiest bugs in the bridge weren’t in calls. They were in thread exit.
The DB bridge keeps one litewire session per PHP thread, in a thread_local!. When tokio retired an idle blocking thread, that thread-local’s destructor set off a chain of drops:
it dropped the session the session dropped the Turso connection the connection dropped pager buffers Buffer::drop recycles into Turso’s own thread-local buffer cache TLS destructors run in reverse registration order. Turso’s cache was registered after ours, inside our first query. So it was already gone. LocalKey::with on a destroyed thread-local panics. A panic in a TLS destructor aborts the process, and every tenant on the box went down. #300 was found by an overload test where 3 of 10 flooded instances died this way. They died at different points: mid-flood, during the post-flood cooldown and at SIGTERM.
There’s no try_with I can add to fix that. The panicking with is several frames down inside Turso. What I can do is not run that drop on a dying thread. The session is parked in a process-wide “graveyard” instead. The next request on any live thread drains and drops it. In steady state the graveyard is empty and the drain is a single relaxed atomic load.
