#269 is the mirror image. Thread exit runs php_request_shutdown(). That runs register_shutdown_function() callbacks and destructors. Those can call ephpm_kv_* or ephpm_db_* after the bridge’s own thread-locals are destroyed. Every access reachable from PHP now uses try_with and degrades. A KV call reports a miss. A DB call returns -3 and C throws a distinctly worded exception. And it fails closed. When the per-site slot is gone, effective_store() returns None, not the global store. Falling back to the global store would let one tenant’s shutdown function write into another tenant’s keyspace.
The DB bridge ephpm_db_* goes through the same litewire Session the MySQL wire frontend uses. The same MySQL-dialect translation, SHOW/DESCRIBE emulation and transaction tracking apply. There’s one session per PHP thread per site. A thread that moves to a different site gets a new session.
Session::query is async and PHP callbacks are synchronous. So the bridge pins the server’s tokio Handle and uses block_on. That’s only legal because these callbacks always run on PHP OS threads, never inside an async task. If one ever did, tokio would panic. That’s a much better failure than a deadlock.
Thread-scoped sessions have one obvious trap, and I fell into it. The session outlives the request. A script that ran BEGIN and then fataled left the transaction open on that thread. So did one that just forgot to COMMIT. The next unrelated request on the same thread silently joined it. Its writes could later be rolled back with someone else’s. #258 added on_request_end(). It runs at request teardown in both execution modes and rolls back whatever is still open, with a warning in the log.
A worked example: the session handler The native session handler (17493149) shows the whole thing end to end. It’s written in C against the ops table directly, with no PHP in between. Sessions live at session:<sid>. The TTL comes from session.gc_maxlifetime. GC is a no-op because the store expires keys itself.
Two details took real debugging. session.lazy_write is on by default. With it on, PHP calls update_timestamp instead of write when the data didn’t change. The handler refreshes the TTL with expire instead of rewriting the blob. And open has to set *mod_data to something non-NULL:
static int ephpm_session_mod_data_marker = 0; PS_OPEN_FUNC(ephpm) { (void)save_path; (void)session_name; *mod_data = (void *)&ephpm_session_mod_data_marker; return SUCCESS; } ext/session only calls a handler’s write and close when PS(mod_data) is set. A native handler that keeps no state and leaves it NULL never gets written. There’s no error. You get a warning that it failed to write session data, and nothing persisted. The marker is never dereferenced. It just has to exist.
Known limitations Keys cross the boundary as C strings. PHP_FUNCTION parses the key with Z_PARAM_STRING, which gives a pointer and a length. But only the pointer goes through the ops table. Rust reads it with CStr::from_ptr and then requires valid UTF-8:
let key_str = unsafe { CStr::from_ptr(key) }; let Ok(key_str) = key_str.to_str() else { return 0; }; So a key with an embedded NUL byte ("a\0b") addresses the key "a". A key that isn’t valid UTF-8 comes back as a miss or a failed write with no error. Values are binary-safe, since they go through as pointer and length. Real application keys are almost always ASCII. But if you hash something into a raw binary key, hex it first.
How I measured Hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, WSL2 on Windows 11 (kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2, 32 vCPU, 62 GiB). ePHPm: the published v0.10.6 release, ephpm-v0.10.6+php8.5.7-linux-x86_64. It ran as a bare process in per_request mode, with [kv.redis_compat] listening on 127.0.0.1 and no AUTH or compression. Redis: redis:7-alpine (7.4.11) under Podman with --network host, persistence off. Harness: the kv/fixtures/kv_sapi.php and kv_resp.php scripts from ephpm/lab. The native lane is 200,000 ops per loop, timed with hrtime() inside a single request. It’s a bare-loop number with no request dispatch in it. The socket lanes are 20,000 strict ping-pong round trips over one raw PHP stream socket with tcp_nodelay. The same fixture is pointed at each port. Client libraries like Predis add their own overhead on top. Each fixture checks the value it read back. A loop that got optimized into nothing would fail instead of looking fast. Three reps, lanes interleaved, median reported. What’s next The functions are only half of it. Nobody wants to rewrite their WordPress object cache or their Laravel cache store around ephpm_kv_set(). Part 2 covers the wrapper packages. They make existing phpredis, Predis, WP_Object_Cache and wpdb code use the native path unmodified. It also covers the semantics bugs that showed up once real applications ran on them.
Links ephpm/ephpm, crates/ephpm-php/ephpm_wrapper.c, kv_bridge.rs and db_bridge.rs #184 ephpm_kv_wait() #208 the vhost keyspace split #258 rollback at request end #300 SIGABRT on thread retirement and #269 try_with at teardown #357 bridge API for adapters ephpm/lab kv-micro harness

title: Every Way a Tenant Escaped: A Cross-Tenant Breakout Field Guide
description: Eight ways one site broke out of its sandbox on a multi-tenant PHP server, all found by attacking it on purpose, all fixed.
body:
ePHPm can serve a directory full of sites out of one process. Point sites_dir at a folder and every subdirectory is a virtual host. The Host header decides which one you get. That’s how the PR preview environment runs. Every pull request gets a subdomain, and the code behind it is whatever somebody pushed. One process holding many tenants means ePHPm enforces every per-tenant boundary itself, in-process. There’s no container wall between site A and site B unless you add one.
So I spent a couple of weeks attacking it. Every item below was found by deliberately trying to break out. Each one was reproduced against a real PHP-linked binary, and each one is fixed. I’m writing them up together because they’re a better checklist than any I could have written from scratch. They also cluster into a handful of patterns that apply to any multi-tenant runtime.
One note before the list. ePHPm’s own docs say plainly that open_basedir is an in-process boundary, not a container boundary. Untrusted per-PR code still deserves real per-preview isolation. None of what follows changes that advice. It’s about making the in-process boundary hold.
1. The Host header was a path In sites_dir mode the document root was sites_dir.join(raw_host), with no sanitization of the Host header. The downstream containment checks were anchored to that root. So they canonicalized to the escaped directory and passed. Pre-auth, no tenant code needed:
Request Result before the fix Host: ../../../../../etc, GET /passwd 200, served /etc/passwd Host: ../../../../../ETC. (trailing dot + case) 200, served /etc/passwd Host: ../single, GET /pwn.php 200, executed PHP from an arbitrary docroot The only prior mitigation was trusted_hosts. It’s empty by default and exact-match only, so it’s unusable for per-PR hostnames.
The fix (#280) validates the normalized host as a strict DNS-label allowlist: [a-z0-9._-], and no empty label. That one “no empty label” rule rejects ., .., a..b, and leading or trailing dots in a single test. /, \ and NUL fall outside the charset. After that, sites_dir.join(key) can only ever name a direct child. A malformed host is a 404 before any filesystem join.
The fix is lexical on purpose. The obvious alternative is canonicalize().starts_with(sites_dir). But the router deliberately supports a site directory that’s a symlink to a release tree outside sites_dir. That’s the atomic-deploy layout. A canonical containment check would break that. Once the label can’t contain traversal primitives, a direct child is all you need.
2. The suffix that collapsed every tenant into one Preview hosts look like pr-123.preview.example.com. sites_domain_suffix strips the shared suffix to get the site key. The validation from #1 ran on the host before stripping. The stripped result was used without being checked again. Take a dotless suffix like localhost. The request Host: localhost stripped to the empty string, and sites_dir.join("") is sites_dir itself. That’s one virtual host whose document root and open_basedir are the entire tenant fleet, with read and write to every site. The empty key also selected DB file .db, KV keyspace "" and the override lookup. The whole tenant identity collapsed.
#401 re-validates the stripped key. An empty or invalid key falls through to the default site, never to a sites_dir-rooted basedir. It also rejects a suffix without a leading dot at config load. A legitimate suffix always starts with ., so a dotless one has no valid use.
3. Swapping your own web root for a symlink Sites can declare a document root override. document_root = "web" serves <site>/web while PHP can still require upward into the site’s container. The override was validated with starts_with(container) once, at load. But the resolved root got re-canonicalized every couple of seconds, following symlinks, with no containment re-check. And the static file path’s only boundary is that root. It has no open_basedir backstop.
The tenant can’t plant the link from PHP. symlink() checks both the link path and its target against open_basedir. So symlink('/', 'web') from a tenant script just fails with an open_basedir warning. But PHP isn’t the only thing that writes into a site directory. On the preview environment the site is a checkout of whatever somebody pushed. Git stores symlinks as symlinks:
git rm -r web ln -s / web git add web && git commit -m 'tidy' && git push The same goes for an archive the deploy unpacks, SFTP or a shell on the box. Once a link like that exists after the override was validated, nothing looked at it again. The test for the fix plants it from outside PHP the same way. On a Windows test box the next static requests looked like this:
Request (static) Before After GET /Windows/win.ini 200, ; for 16-bit app support 404 GET /.../sites/victim.test/secret.db 200, the other tenant’s DB 404 GET /index.txt (legit) 200 200 #398 re-asserts canonical_document_root.starts_with(canonical_container) on every resolve. It checks against the operator-chosen container that no override can change. It fails closed with a static 404 or a PHP 403. When no override is in play the second canonicalize is skipped, so it costs nothing on normal sites. This one never shipped in a release. It was caught between the override feature merging and the next tag.
4. Everybody’s /tmp Every vhost’s open_basedir included the same system temp directory. session.save_path, sys_temp_dir and upload_tmp_dir were never set per tenant. So every site’s sessions sat in one shared directory that was inside every site’s sandbox:
# from site-b: CROSS_READ_site_a_session_file (/tmp/sess_bb469cd9...) => READ: 'site_a_session_secret|s:20:"SITE_A_SESSION_VALUE";' sess_glob_own_tmp=[7 other tenants' sess_* files] That’s session hijack and tamper across tenants. #285 gives each vhost a private state root, <temp>/ephpm-vhosts/<label>-<digest>. It’s derived from the already-validated document root, with tmp/ and sessions/ underneath at 0700. open_basedir becomes the document root plus that state root only.
Fixing it exposed a second bug. Per-request ini overrides were applied after php_request_startup(). But php_request_startup() is where the multipart parser writes uploaded files. It uses upload_tmp_dir as it is at that moment. Uploads kept landing in shared /tmp, now outside open_basedir, so move_uploaded_file() failed. The ini replay now runs both before and after startup.
5. ATTACH DATABASE as a filesystem primitive This was the worst one, filed as #274 after live exploitation. The embedded SQLite engine runs inside the ePHPm process, not under any tenant’s open_basedir. In multi-site mode every vhost shared one database. From a hostile vhost:
mysqli_connect with junk credentials connected (the proxy didn’t validate them) and read another site’s wp_users.user_pass. ATTACH DATABASE '.../site-b.db' read and wrote another tenant’s database. ATTACH DATABASE '.../sites/site-a/shell2.php' wrote a PHP file into another tenant’s docroot, where PHP’s own file_put_contents had been correctly denied. GET /shell2.php with that tenant’s Host executed it as them. Full cross-tenant RCE. The same ATTACH worked through the always-on native ephpm_db_* bridge, so firewalling the TCP proxy wouldn’t have closed it. #284 made the database file the tenant boundary, since the engine has no per-schema ACLs. [db.sqlite] dir gives every site its own <key>.db, required and fail-closed in multi-site mode. The shared wire listeners don’t start in multi-site mode at all. One listener for all tenants is the original bug. ATTACH, DETACH, VACUUM and path PRAGMAs are rejected on the tenant path with ePHPm’s own error, independent of the engine’s defaults. #351 pins it with an end-to-end test from real PHP userland on both the native and wire paths.
The follow-up pentest found the screen matched on a statement’s leading keyword. So EXPLAIN ATTACH DATABASE '...' sailed past it. Only the engine’s “ATTACH is experimental” default stopped it. #287 peels EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before checking the verb. That handles them stacked and with comments in between. A denylist has to see the statement the way the engine will see it.
6. Two names, one docroot, two databases The same pentest round found the derivations disagreeing with each other. Docroot lookup stripped the domain suffix and the DB key didn’t. So Host: shop.local and Host: shop shared a document root and a session directory but wrote to different databases. The KV keyspace used the raw Host, so ALICE and alice were different keyspaces on the same site. #293 didn’t patch the DB key. It made resolve_site return the key it matched. Everything else is derived from that one value: DB file, wire credential, KV keyspace, OPcache vhost and temp root. A host that matches no site mints no identity at all.
7. Loopback has more than one address The per-vhost eBPF policy lets a tenant run a sidecar on localhost. It stops other tenants from connecting to its ports. The cgroup/connect classifier recognized exactly 127.0.0.1 and ::1 as loopback. Linux treats all of 127.0.0.0/8 as loopback. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address reaches the same IPv4 stack. Anything the classifier didn’t call loopback skipped the port-ownership check:
Vector (Bob to Alice’s sidecar) Before After 127.0.0.1:port EPERM EPERM ::ffff:127.0.0.1:port connected, read Alice’s secret EPERM 127.0.0.2:port (Alice on 0.0.0.0) connected EPERM ::ffff:127.0.0.2:port connected EPERM #489 puts one shared classifier behind both connect4 and connect6:
static __always_inline int is_loopback4_be(__u32 ip_be) { return (ip_be & bpf_htonl(0xff000000)) == bpf_htonl(0x7f000000); } static __always_inline int is_loopback6(const __u32 ip6[4]) { // ::1 (network order: high 96 bits zero, low word == 1). if (ip6[0] == 0 && ip6[1] == 0 && ip6[2] == 0 && ip6[3] == bpf_htonl(1)) return 1; // ::ffff:0:0/96 — IPv4-mapped: first 80 bits zero, next 16 bits 0xffff. if (ip6[0] == 0 && ip6[1] == 0 && ip6[2] == bpf_htonl(0x0000ffff)) return is_loopback4_be(ip6[3]); return 0; } Deprecated IPv4-compatible addresses (::a.b.c.d) are deliberately not folded in. Linux doesn’t route them onto v4 loopback. Treating that prefix as “classify by embedded v4” would misclassify ::1 itself.
8. A login cookie that worked on every site Previews sit behind a GitHub OAuth gate. One module does the OAuth round trip at login and mints an HS256 session with a site claim. A second module verifies that session on every request. The issuer always set site. The verifier never checked it, so a session for preview A verified on every preview on the node. #488 passes the request’s canonical site key into the verifier as expected_site. A missing, non-string or mismatched claim fails closed. The issuer now takes its site from the same canonical key instead of re-normalizing the raw Host. The two agree by construction.
The patterns Looking back at the list, almost none of these were exotic. They fall into four groups:
The identity of a tenant was derived more than once. Host to docroot, host to DB file, host to KV keyspace, issuer versus verifier. Every time two pieces of code derived “which tenant is this” separately, they eventually disagreed (#1, #2, #6, #8). The fix that stuck was one derivation, passed to every consumer. A check ran once and the thing it checked kept changing. Validate-at-load with live symlink resolution (#3), and validate-before-strip (#2). If a value can change after you check it, check it where you use it. The boundary was in the wrong layer. open_basedir doesn’t cover the SQLite engine (#5) or the static file path (#3). Any component running inside the process but outside PHP needs its own boundary. “Loopback” and “keyword” aren’t single values. Address families and statement prefixes (#5, #7). Match the way the kernel or the engine will interpret it, not the way you’d write it. The other habit that paid off was writing each fix with a test that fails on the old code. Several of the PRs above say exactly that in their test sections. Some temporarily reverted the fix to watch the test go red. When the subject is security, a test you’ve never seen fail isn’t telling you much.
Links Host header traversal: #280 Suffix-stripped empty key: #401 Document-root symlink swap: #398 Per-vhost temp and sessions: #285 Per-site databases and the ATTACH screen: #284, #287, #351 One canonical site key: #293 eBPF loopback classifier: #489 Preview session bound to its site: #488

title: shipmates Short Ones: 8 Minutes Extracting Go, and Three Voice-Loop Bugs
description: Four small stories from shipmates, starting with setup-go stuck extracting on Windows CI and Cloudflare's 100 second timeout. The other two are a voice loop that transcribed itself and events lost to a timestamp watermark.
body:
A few shipmates bugs don’t need a whole post each. They were too good to leave in commit messages, though.
setup-go spends 8 minutes extracting Go on Windows CI shipmates CI runs on my own ephemerd runners. On Windows those jobs run inside a Hyper-V utility VM. The windows-x64 leg kept timing out in actions/setup-go. Here’s the log from PR #48:
20:58:46 Setup go version spec 1.26.6 20:58:46 Attempting to download 1.26.6... <- tool-cache MISS 20:58:48 Acquiring 1.26.6 from ...zip 20:58:53 Extracting Go... 21:06:46 ERROR: The action 'Run actions/setup-go@v5' has timed out after 8 minutes Seven seconds from the start of the step to Extracting Go.... Then almost eight minutes extracting until the step timeout killed it.
(Durations computed from the timestamps in the PR #48 job log above.)
The Go toolchain is about 15,000 small files. Every write under _work crosses a VSMB share from the VM to the host. Small-file metadata over that share is brutally slow, and no timeout or retry in the workflow fixes it. The toolchain has to stop being installed per job.
The plan was to take Go from the job’s container image instead. ephemerd intercepts container: on every platform. On Linux it’s an ordinary container. On Windows and macOS the image layers are extracted onto the VM disk. GitHub’s own runner only supports it on Linux. Here’s what changed:
Linux x64 and arm64 got container: golang:1.26.6-bookworm. library/golang is a real multi-arch manifest, so the same tag resolves natively on the arm64 runner. Windows x64 got container: golang:1.26.6-windowsservercore-ltsc2025. macOS keeps setup-go. There’s no upstream image, and it wasn’t the problem leg. setup-go is skipped on the containerized legs, not left to no-op. It never looks at PATH. It probes RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE and installs on a miss, so a toolchain already in the image wouldn’t have stopped it. A nice side effect is that the race job lost its ~30 line “Ensure a C toolchain” step. golang:*-bookworm is built on buildpack-deps and already has gcc. No more run-time apt-get. No more negotiating whether the runner came up as root, a sudo user, or neither.
Keep the image tag in lockstep with go.mod, by the way. The Linux images set GOTOOLCHAIN=local. A go.mod bump past the image fails loudly instead of quietly downloading a toolchain, which is what you want.
Now the honest part. The Linux legs went green. The Windows leg didn’t get Go from the image. It failed at Initialize containers in 13 seconds:
##[error]Container operations are only supported on Linux runners That message is the actions runner’s own Linux-only check. On that leg the job never got as far as the image. The 8 minute timeout became a 13 second failure. That’s better for the queue and still not a passing build. The fix belongs on the ephemerd side, not in the shipmates workflow.
PR #26 also has a note worth repeating if you’re thinking about self-hosted runners. A public repo on self-hosted runners lets a fork PR run code on your hardware. I did it on purpose. ephemerd exists to make that safe and shipmates is part of testing that. But it’s a decision and it’s written down as one.
Surviving Cloudflare’s 100 second edge timeout Fleet Command sits behind cloudflared. The Commodore’s conversation endpoint runs an LLM tool-calling loop. A multi-tool turn on a CPU model can take longer than Cloudflare’s 100 second proxy limit. The operator got a raw 524 HTML page dumped into a chat bubble.
The fix (bb93111) streams whitespace while the model thinks. Bytes on the wire reset the edge timer, and JSON.parse ignores leading whitespace. So the client didn’t change at all:
w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json") w.Header().Set("X-Accel-Buffering", "no") fl, canFlush := w.(http.Flusher) heartbeat := make(chan struct{}) go func() { ticker := time.NewTicker(15 * time.Second) defer ticker.Stop() for { select { case <-heartbeat: return case <-ticker.C: if canFlush { _, _ = w.Write([]byte(" ")) fl.Flush() } } } }() finish := func(v conversationResponse) { close(heartbeat) _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) } The catch is that once the first space goes out, the headers are committed with a 200. An http.Error(w, …, 502) later does nothing useful. So errors moved into the JSON body ("error": "llm: …") and ride the 200. In the same commit the client started sending only the last 12 history messages. The prompt was growing every turn and making the slow turns slower.
The voice loop that transcribed itself In hands-free mode the browser runs a loop:
listen with a voice activity detector send your speech to STT send the transcript to the Commodore play the reply through TTS Then it listens again. Except it started transcribing its own replies back as my input. One of them came back as “I’m always here ready to exist”, which is a better line than anything I wrote that week.
speak() was fire-and-forget. The loop checked if (audioEl.paused || audioEl.ended) resumeListening() right after sending. Playback hadn’t started yet, so the element was still paused. The mic reopened immediately and caught the assistant’s voice from the speakers. 9350c68 made speak() resolve when playback finishes. That’s on ended, error, or pause, since an interrupted reply counts as done. sendMessage awaits it, and the loop resumes 350 ms later to let the speaker tail die out.
Same-second events, gone The bridge streams each captain’s event log to the browser over server-sent events. It deduplicated with a watermark on the event timestamp. That timestamp was a string at one second resolution:
for _, e := range events { if e.Time <= high { continue } // send e high = e.Time } Any batch of events in the same second delivered only the first one. That’s exactly what a broadcast produces. Tell three mates something and you saw one tell and one reply. The log is append-only, so 2e317d5 switched to an index watermark, which is exact. It resets when the log shrinks, which means the lead restarted:
if len(events) < sent { sent = 0 // lead restarted and its log reset; replay from the top } for _, e := range events[sent:] { // send e } sent = len(events) If your log is append-only, the position is the cursor. Timestamps are for humans.
Links shipmates PR #48 (Go from the job image) and PR #26 (CI on ephemerd) bb93111, 9350c68, 2e317d5 Cloudflare error 524

title: Making ephpm php Byte-for-Byte Indistinguishable From php-cli
description: A differential test harness against upstream php, and the bugs it found in an embedded PHP CLI on day one.
body:
ePHPm embeds PHP into a single Rust binary. The obvious follow-up question from anybody deploying it is “do I still need a php on the box?” Composer, WP-CLI, artisan, PHPUnit and every build script in the world call php. If ephpm php can stand in for it then the answer is no. The single binary really means a single binary. “Mostly works” isn’t good enough for that though. These tools parse PHP’s output, check its exit codes and re-invoke it. So the goal was simple to state: ephpm php should be indistinguishable from php-cli.
Getting to “drop-in” the first time The first pass (#306) made ephpm php do six things:
report PHP_SAPI === "cli", set before php_embed_init() so OPcache’s startup verdict sees it read programs from stdin honor -d, -c and -n support line mode (-B, -R, -F, -E) define the STDIN/STDOUT/STDERR constants WP-CLI needs implement the --rf/--rc/--re/--rz/--ri reflection flags, which had been declared and silently did nothing composer.phar create-project laravel/laravel completed clean. wp-cli.phar --version was byte-identical to the system php.
A couple of things are honest errors rather than fakes. -S isn’t aliased to ephpm serve. The embedded libphp.a contains zero php_cli_server_* symbols, and pretending otherwise would just move the surprise. -a says “not supported” because the interactive shell isn’t linked into the embed build.
The second pass (#317) was the tedious one. It checked every rule against sapi/cli/php_cli.c and every output against a real php 8.5.4. It fixed these:
stdin programs with -- args $argv[0] being "Standard input code", not "-". Our docs had claimed the dash matched php-cli, and it never did. exit codes taken from EG(exit_status) unconditionally. Before that, exit(3), fatals and uncaught exceptions all reported 0. -w and -s reading stdin instead of silently executing a piped program $argi being 1-based That PR was verified with a throwaway diff script over 55 cases. Throwaway is the problem. The next regression wouldn’t get caught by anything.
The differential harness #342 turned that into a real harness. tests/cli-conformance/ holds the corpus. The 0xx cases cover the language and runtime surface. That’s var_dump of every type, float formatting, INF/NAN, sprintf, mbstring, sort stability, JSON edge cases, serialize, preg backtrack limits, uncaught exception format, shutdown and destructor ordering, enums, readonly and so on. The 1xx cases cover CLI behavior. That’s exit codes, -r with and without --, -l, -d, $argv/$argc/$_SERVER in every mode, PHP_BINARY, shebang stripping, line mode, -w, -s, -v and --rf. A case is a .php file or an .args file, optionally with .stdin and .meta:
# 115-php-binary.args -r echo PHP_BINARY === '' ? "(empty)" : PHP_BINARY, "\n"; var_dump(is_string(PHP_BINARY)); The runner is cargo xtask cli-conformance --php <upstream> --ephpm <bin>. It runs each case against both binaries with an identical minimal environment: TZ=UTC, LC_ALL=C and a per-side scratch directory. Then it compares stdout, stderr and exit code byte for byte. Any unexplained mismatch prints a unified diff and fails the run. A nightly workflow runs it over PHP 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5 against the matching upstream php from the ondrej PPA.
Three design choices in the runner are the reason I trust it.
It checks the binary’s identity before running anything. <ephpm> php -n -v has to print a PHP banner first. Handing a plain php to --ephpm fails immediately. This isn’t paranoia. A $VAR expansion bug in the WSL bridge had repeatedly made earlier harnesses test the system php against itself. That passes beautifully.
Expected failures are marked, and a stale marker fails the run. A known divergence gets an xfail with a reason and an issue number. If an xfail case starts matching, the runner reports XPASS. It goes red until somebody deletes the marker. Markers can’t quietly rot into lies.
Normalization is a tiny, justified registry. There are exactly four normalizers: strip-versions, strip-zts-marker, strip-distro-banner and strip-binary-path. Every use has to explain itself in the .meta file:
# 115-php-binary.meta # strip-binary-path: the two sides are different executables by definition, # so each side's own binary path is folded to <BINARY>; the case then proves # PHP_BINARY is a non-empty string naming the invoked binary on BOTH sides. normalize = ["strip-binary-path"] Some things are packaging facts rather than behavior. The -m extension list of a static SDK versus a distro php is one. --ini search paths are another. Those get skip with a reason.
What it found on day one Against a build of main, the first real run was total 77: 65 pass, 0 fail, 2 skip, 10 xfail. Seven of those xfails were new, real divergences, all filed as issues:
Issue Divergence #334 register_shutdown_function callbacks and end-of-script destructors never ran #335 --rf on a missing symbol exited 0 (php-cli: 1) #336 an unknown option (-Z) was silently ignored, exit 0 #337 -d of unregistered ini entries invisible to get_cfg_var() #338 CLI $_SERVER lacked environment variables and DOCUMENT_ROOT #339 PHP_BINARY was "" #340 STDIN/STDOUT/STDERR lacked php:// wrapper metadata The first one is the scary one. A CLI that never runs shutdown functions or destructors breaks every tool that flushes a buffer or writes a lock file on the way out. The root cause (#347) was that ephpm_cli_main never called php_request_shutdown(). Teardown ran invisibly at process exit. Its output went into the discarded HTTP capture buffer, after the exit code had already been taken. The fix runs shutdown in php-cli’s exact order, with nested-bailout protection. It takes the exit status afterwards, so exit() inside a shutdown function works.
The fixes, checked against php_cli.c #356 took the next five. A few of them are worth the detail.
-Z was accepted silently. The flag fell through both getopt passes and no mode got selected. The CLI read empty stdin as a program. A typo’d flag ran nothing and reported success. Now php_getopt is called with show_err = 1 like php-cli’s main(). Stderr gets the exact Error in argument 2, char 2: option not found Z and the exit is 1. That had a consequence. The option table is now load-bearing. Any option php-cli accepts that the table lacks turns a working command line into a failure. So the table was diffed against php-src’s OPTIONS[]. The one missing entry was added. That’s --syntax-highlighting, the long spelling of -s. The one deliberate gap is php-cli’s internal --repeat, which php-src itself labels a testing option. Accepting and ignoring it would silently run a script once when the caller asked for N times.
PHP_BINARY was empty on Unix. On Windows php_binary_init() asks the OS, which is why it looked fine there. On every other platform it reads sapi_module.executable_location. php_embed_init() assigns that argv[0], which ePHPm passes as the bare string "ephpm". PHP then searches PATH for something named ephpm, finds nothing and leaves it NULL. The trap is where to set it. Set it before php_embed_init() and it gets overwritten. Set it after php_module_startup() and it’s too late. The only window is inside ePHPm’s startup shim, right before it hands off:
static int ephpm_module_startup(sapi_module_struct *sm) { sm->additional_functions = g_cli_mode ? ephpm_cli_functions : ephpm_kv_functions; /* PHP_BINARY: php_embed_init() has just overwritten executable_location * with argv[0] ("ephpm"), and php_module_startup() below both copies *sm * into sapi_module and calls php_binary_init(). NULL outside `ephpm php`, * so the server's PHP_BINARY is unchanged. */ if (cli_executable_location) { sm->executable_location = cli_executable_location; } /* ... -d splice, worker module ... */ } The first cut set the field pre-init and built clean. It passed on Windows while staying broken on every other platform. The Linux binary is what caught it. That’s a good argument for running the harness on the platform where the code path differs. The value recorded is std::env::current_exe(). It names this binary rather than whatever ephpm is first on PATH.
That same ephpm_module_startup() window is where -d now goes too (#341). OPcache decides once, at module startup, whether it will ever be active in the CLI. We were applying -d after php_embed_init(). So ini_get('opcache.enable_cli') said 1 while opcache_get_status() said false. The fix splices the -d entries into ini_entries right there, after the embed SAPI’s hardcoded block. That gives php-cli’s exact precedence. It also means -d extension= and -d zend_extension= genuinely load now.
$_SERVER in the CLI lacked the environment. php-cli imports the process environment into $_SERVER. The “S” of EGPCS in a CLI process is its environment. It also registers an empty DOCUMENT_ROOT. That’s now done, but only on the CLI path. ephpm serve is multi-tenant and the process environment holds cross-tenant material. It must never reach a web request’s $_SERVER. That was verified by starting the server with a probe variable in its environment. No request could see it. Being byte-compatible doesn’t mean copying every php-cli behavior into the server.
After #356 the run was total 78: 75 pass, 0 fail, 2 skip, 1 xfail. The remaining xfail is permanent and intentional. The usage screen says Usage: ephpm php and omits flags this build doesn’t implement. The part that matters is the stderr diagnostic and exit status. An e2e test pins those byte-for-byte from the ePHPm side.
The last mile: reflection flags The most recent fix (#481) is a good example of how literal “byte for byte” gets. --rf ArrayObject::count was printing Exception: Function ArrayObject::count() does not exist and exiting
php-cli prints the method and exits 0. On 8.5 it also prints this first, on stdout: Deprecated: Calling ReflectionMethod::__construct() with 1 argument is deprecated, use ReflectionMethod::createFromMethodName() instead in Unknown on line 0 That’s php-cli’s own deprecation, from php-cli’s own code. Matching it meant giving up on evaluating an echo new ReflectionX($name) snippet. php-cli constructs the reflection object under a zeroed execute-data frame. That frame is exactly what produces in Unknown on line 0. Evaluated code stamps the eval’s filename and line. So no zend_eval_string shape can produce those bytes. The five reflection flags now run php_cli.c’s algorithm in C. That includes --ri main printing the core ini table and --ri nosuchext exiting 1. The corpus is at 83 cases: 79 pass, 3 skip, 1 xfail.
What’s still open PHP_BINARY now names the ephpm executable. That’s correct, and it creates the next problem. Some tools re-invoke PHP through it, like PHPUnit process isolation, Symfony’s PhpExecutableFinder and Composer @php scripts. They run PHP_BINARY script.php, and ephpm script.php isn’t a PHP CLI. For now that’s documented with a wrapper-script workaround. Making ephpm answer as php when it’s re-invoked that way is next on the list.
The harness is the part I’d reuse on any project that claims compatibility with something else:
diff against the real thing compare bytes, not vibes make the binary prove its identity make every exception to the rule explain itself in a file that fails the build when it stops being true Links ephpm php drop-in: #306, #317 Conformance harness: #342 Shutdown functions and destructors: #347 -d at startup, process titles: #341 Exit codes, unknown options, $_SERVER, PHP_BINARY, stdio metadata: #356 Reflection flags: #481 php-src sapi/cli/php_cli.c

title: Building k9s for Linode With Bubble Tea
description: A k9s-style terminal app for managing Linode. Search for any resource, browse it, and jump straight into k9s, a database shell or SSH.
body:
A lot of my day is spent in k9s. Sometimes I need something from the Linode side of the house. Maybe it’s a node that won’t boot, a volume nobody cleaned up or the kubeconfig for a cluster I just made. Then I’m back in a browser tab or typing linode-cli incantations. I wanted the k9s workflow for the Linode API itself:
: to jump to a resource type / to filter single-key actions on the selected row Enter to go deeper That turned into linode-tui. It’s a Go TUI built on Bubble Tea, linodego and urfave/cli v3.
It started as a private repo in May. In June it got restructured for open source. I flattened internal/, slimmed the CLI down and moved to linodego v2. It went public with v0.1.0 at the end of August. Everything here is as of v0.2.1.
One list view, thirteen resources There are 13 resource views: Linodes, Volumes, NodeBalancers, Firewalls, Images, Domains, LKE clusters, VPCs, Placement Groups, StackScripts, Object Storage, databases and Events. Writing 13 Bubble Tea models by hand would have been a lot of copy and paste. So there’s one generic listView[T], and every resource is a set of options handed to it. This is most of the Linodes view:
func init() { Register("instances", []string{"linodes", "inst", "li"}, newInstances) } func newInstances(d Deps) View { return newListView(listOpts[linodego.Instance]{ Deps: d, Title: "Linodes", Columns: []Col{ {Title: "ID", Width: 10, MinWidth: 6, Priority: PriPinned}, {Title: "LABEL", Width: 28, MinWidth: 12, Priority: PriPinned, Flex: true}, {Title: "REGION", Width: 14, MinWidth: 8, Priority: PriMed}, {Title: "TYPE", Width: 18, MinWidth: 10, Priority: PriMed}, {Title: "STATUS", Width: 12, MinWidth: 8, Priority: PriHigh}, {Title: "IPv4", Width: 16, MinWidth: 12, Priority: PriLow}, {Title: "TAGS", Width: 24, MinWidth: 8, Priority: PriLowest}, }, Lister: func(ctx context.Context, c *linode.Client) ([]linodego.Instance, error) { return c.Raw().ListInstances(ctx, nil) }, // Rower, Matcher, Sort, Actions, KeyHandlers ... }) } The list view owns polling, filtering, selection, bookmarks, the confirm modal and the status line. A view supplies four things:
a lister a function that turns one item into a table row a matcher for / its actions Reboot, for example, is just a key, a label, a prompt and a Run that calls linodego:
{ Key: "R", Label: "reboot", Prompt: func(it linodego.Instance) string { return fmt.Sprintf("Reboot %s (id %d)?", it.Label, it.ID) }, Run: func(ctx context.Context, c *linode.Client, it linodego.Instance) error { return c.Raw().RebootInstance(ctx, it.ID, linodego.InstanceRebootOptions{}) }, }, Register puts the view in a registry with its aliases. The command bar resolves against that registry. Exact names and aliases win, then prefix matches. That’s why :lk in the screenshot above offers lke on Tab. Some drill-in views only make sense with a parent, like a NodeBalancer’s configs or a Domain’s records. Those register with RegisterChild so they never show up as top-level verbs.
Drill-ins: hand the terminal to the real tool I didn’t want to rebuild k9s inside linode-tui. Press c on an LKE cluster and it fetches the kubeconfig from the API. It writes it to a 0600 temp file and runs k9s against it. For DBaaS it builds a connection URL and runs lazysql. On a Linode, c is ssh root@<ip>. C is lish through Linode’s bastion. That works even when the box has no public IP.
Bubble Tea has exactly the primitive for this. tea.ExecProcess releases the terminal and runs the child process attached to it. It resumes the TUI when the child exits:
case config.ModeTUI, "": c := exec.CommandContext(ctx, bin, args...) c.Stdin = os.Stdin c.Stdout = os.Stdout c.Stderr = os.Stderr prepare(c) return tea.ExecProcess(c, func(err error) tea.Msg { return ExitMsg{Kind: kind, Err: err} }), nil Every tool is configurable (tools.kubernetes.exec, tools.mysql.exec and so on). You can point it at Lens or MySQL Workbench with mode: gui and it launches detached instead. If k9s or lazysql isn’t installed, linode-tui offers to download a pinned release. It verifies the checksum and puts the binary in an install dir you pick on first run.
The kubeconfig temp file was also the subject of the first bug report from somebody other than me (#2). c from the LKE list worked. But c from the cluster’s detail page launched k9s, which immediately died with Watcher failed for contexts -- stat .... The detail view was cleaning up the kubeconfig like this:
return tea.Sequence(exec, func() tea.Msg { if cleanup != nil { cleanup() } // runs immediately return lkeDetailDrillDoneMsg{} }) tea.Sequence runs the commands in order. But ExecProcess’s command isn’t blocking. It just returns a message asking the program to run the process. So the cleanup closure ran as soon as that message was handed back. The file was gone before k9s had even started. The list view didn’t have the bug. Its closure only returned a done message. It ran the cleanup when that message came back through Update, which happens after k9s exits. #3 moved the detail view to the same pattern. #16 collapsed both paths into one shared function so it can’t drift again:
func RunDrillIn(deps Deps, msg DrillInMsg, done func(cleanup func()) tea.Msg) (tea.Cmd, error) { runner := tools.New(deps.Cfg) exec, err := runner.RunWithEnv(context.Background(), msg.Tool, msg.Vars, msg.Env) if err != nil { if missing, ok := tools.IsToolMissing(err); ok { return func() tea.Msg { return InstallNeededMsg{Kind: missing.Kind, Drill: msg} }, nil } if msg.Cleanup != nil { msg.Cleanup() } return nil, err } cleanup := msg.Cleanup return tea.Sequence(exec, func() tea.Msg { return done(cleanup) }), nil } If you write Bubble Tea apps that shell out, that one is worth remembering.
Hardening for release This tool holds API tokens. It has a :clear-account command that deletes everything in an account. That deserves a hard look before other people run it. Most of what went into v0.2.0 was that pass, done as a handful of large PRs.
Config persistence (#12). This was the worst one. A --token flag or LINODE_TOKEN got stored in memory as a synthetic __cli__ account. Then the first incidental Save() wrote your environment token into config.yaml in plain text. Starring a row or installing a tool was enough to trigger it. Save now marshals a scrubbed copy. It also stopped truncating the file in place, because a crash between truncate and write lost every account:
// Write-then-rename: os.WriteFile truncates in place, so a crash (or a // full disk) between truncate and write left every account and token // gone. Rename is atomic on POSIX and on Windows (MoveFileEx). tmp := c.path + ".tmp" if err := os.WriteFile(tmp, data, 0o600); err != nil { return err } if err := os.Rename(tmp, c.path); err != nil { _ = os.Remove(tmp) return err } Saves are behind a mutex, since background tool installs save from goroutines. The config dir went from 0755 to 0700. refresh: 1ms gets clamped to 1s instead of becoming a self-inflicted 429 generator. The same PR fixed :clear-account, which only guarded on the name of the local account. accounts: {dev: {token: <prod token>}} is one bad paste away. So it now resolves /profile and refuses to delete anything if the token belongs to a different user than the one you confirmed. It also deletes LKE clusters before instances now. Otherwise the node pools recreate the workers you just deleted.
App state (#13). Opening a modal swallowed the list’s tick message. That quietly ended the pane’s refresh loop for the rest of the session. Switching accounts rebuilt only the focused pane. Split panes kept polling the old account with the old token. A bare :export panicked on args[1:] of an empty slice. A new test now dispatches every command-bar verb and alias. It fails if any of them comes back as unknown command. That test is what found the :export panic.
Responsive columns (#16). The Linodes table wants about 140 cells. On a narrower terminal the bubbles table wrapped every row into garbage. Columns now carry a width, a minimum and a priority. The list drops the lowest-priority column until the minimums fit. Then it spends the leftover space growing the survivors and the Flex column. ID and LABEL are pinned and never dropped. The status line tells you »3 cols hidden — widen terminal.
The yaml tag (#23). #13 made audit_retention_days: 0 mean “keep forever”, like the docs always said. Then the review caught that the field still had omitempty. An explicit 0 got dropped on save, and the next load re-seeded the 90-day default. Users who opted out of pruning would have been opted back in by any unrelated save. The fix was deleting ,omitempty and adding a Save→Load round-trip test. omitempty on an int where zero means something is a bug that’s easy to write.
Tokens The config doesn’t have to hold a token. A literal token: works but isn’t recommended. Accounts can point at a 1Password reference. linode-tui shells out to op to resolve it:
default_account: dev accounts: dev: op_ref: "op://Private/linode-dev/token" e2e: op_ref: "op://Private/linode-test/token" :account e2e switches live. There’s also an audit log of every mutating action (~/.cache/linode-tui/audit.log). That log is what powers :undo and the ctrl+y replay.
How the screenshots were made I didn’t want a real account in a blog post, so the screenshots run against a fake API. linodego honors LINODE_URL. I wrote a small Go server that returns canned JSON for /v4/profile, /v4/linode/instances and /v4/lke/clusters, with IPs from the documentation ranges. Then I ran linode-tui v0.2.1 in a 118x16 tmux pane with LINODE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18080, a dummy token and an empty HOME. The server log shows the polling doing what it should, a list refetch every 2 seconds:
GET /v4/linode/instances GET /v4/profile GET /v4/linode/instances GET /v4/linode/instances GET /v4/linode/instances GET /v4/lke/clusters GET /v4/lke/clusters The images are tmux capture-pane -e output converted to SVG with the colors exactly as tmux reported them.
Install go install github.com/luthermonson/linode-tui/cmd/linode-tui@latest export LINODE_TOKEN=... linode-tui Or grab a binary from the releases page. GoReleaser builds Linux and macOS on amd64 and arm64, and Windows on amd64. If you already live in linode-cli, the README has a five-line shell function. It routes linode tui to this and everything else to the real CLI. A Homebrew tap is next on the list.
Links linode-tui docs/USAGE.md k9s Bubble Tea linodego lazysql

title: Zero-Dependency Deployments - Single Binary for WordPress
description: WordPress with no nginx, no php-fpm, no Redis and no MySQL. It runs from one ePHPm binary, a SQLite file and a distroless container image.
body:
The standard way to run a WordPress site is four services:
nginx for HTTP and TLS php-fpm to run PHP MySQL for data Redis, once the site gets slow enough that someone installs an object cache plugin That’s four processes and four config files. There are three sockets between them and four things to upgrade. For a big site that’s fine. For a brochure site or a staging copy it’s absurd. The same goes for a PR preview, a box at the edge, or a CI job that needs a real WordPress to test a plugin against.
ePHPm is my attempt at making that one thing. This post walks through running stock WordPress from a single binary with no other services. Then it builds a container image that is just that binary and the site. Along the way it covers what’s inside the binary as of v0.8.2.
What’s in the binary The Linux x86_64 build with PHP 8.5.7 is about 132 MB. That one ephpm executable carries:
An HTTP server: hyper with HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, rustls TLS with ACME certificates, static files with ETags and compression, virtual hosts. PHP itself: libphp statically linked and ZTS, with OPcache and the usual extensions compiled in. Those are mysqli, pdo_mysql, pdo_sqlite, gd, intl, mbstring, curl, zip and friends. The same binary is also a PHP CLI: ephpm php -v. A KV store that PHP can call directly through native functions. That’s what the WordPress object cache uses. A database layer: either a pooling proxy in front of a real MySQL, or no database server at all. “Zero dependency” needs one footnote. The Linux release is dynamically linked against glibc, not a static musl binary:
$ ldd ephpm linux-vdso.so.1 libdl.so.2 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libdl.so.2 libm.so.6 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libm.so.6 libpthread.so.0 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libpthread.so.0 librt.so.1 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/librt.so.1 libgcc_s.so.1 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgcc_s.so.1 libutil.so.1 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libutil.so.1 libc.so.6 => /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 $ objdump -T ephpm | grep -o 'GLIBC_[0-9.]*' | sort -uV | tail -1 GLIBC_2.28 Everything above is glibc’s own family plus libgcc_s. Release builds happen in an AlmaLinux 8 container, so the newest symbol version it needs is 2.28. That means it runs on basically any Linux from 2018 onward. I went glibc over musl on purpose. Native middleware modules are loaded with dlopen, and a fully static musl binary can’t do that.
How the binary gets built Building PHP is the slow, fragile part of all of this. So it’s done once per PHP version, not once per ePHPm build. static-php-cli compiles libphp with the embed SAPI and its library dependencies into static archives. ephpm/php-sdk publishes those as release assets per OS, architecture and PHP version. ePHPm’s build is a cargo xtask:
cargo xtask release 8.5 # resolve 8.5 -> pinned 8.5.7, download the SDK, build with PHP linked xtask release does four things:
resolves the PHP minor to a pinned patch version downloads and unpacks the matching SDK points PHP_SDK_PATH at it runs the cargo build with the shipped feature set build.rs compiles the C SAPI wrapper and emits the link flags for libphp.a. A plain cargo build without an SDK builds a stub that answers every PHP request with a “PHP not linked” page. That way the Rust side can be developed and tested without PHP at all.
It’s not a cross-compiler. Each platform’s release is built on that platform, for PHP 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. Linux x86_64 and aarch64 build in the AlmaLinux container. macOS arm64 and Windows x86_64 build natively.
WordPress with nothing else Here’s the whole setup. Grab WordPress and the official SQLite Database Integration drop-in. That drop-in is WordPress’s own project for running on SQLite. Then add the ephpm/cache-wordpress object cache:
curl -sSL https://wordpress.org/wordpress-7.1.tar.gz | tar xz # SQLite instead of MySQL curl -sSLO https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin/sqlite-database-integration.3.0.1.zip unzip -q sqlite-database-integration.3.0.1.zip -d wordpress/wp-content/plugins/ cp wordpress/wp-content/plugins/sqlite-database-integration/db.copy wordpress/wp-content/db.php mkdir -p wordpress/wp-content/database # Persistent object cache backed by ePHPm's in-process KV store git clone https://github.com/ephpm/cache-wordpress wordpress/wp-content/cache-wordpress printf "<?php\nrequire __DIR__ . '/cache-wordpress/dropin/object-cache.php';\n" \ > wordpress/wp-content/object-cache.php Copy wp-config-sample.php to wp-config.php. Leave the DB credentials as placeholders, since the SQLite drop-in ignores them. Add define( 'WP_CACHE', true ); and start it:
ephpm dev --port 8088 --document-root "$(pwd)/wordpress" That’s a working WordPress on http://127.0.0.1:8088, with the installer, admin, themes and plugins. The database is a file at wp-content/database/.ht.sqlite. The object cache lives in the same process as PHP. wp_cache_get() goes straight from the Zend engine into the KV store through ephpm_kv_* native functions. There’s no socket and no Redis.
The container is the binary and the site Since there’s nothing else to run, the image doesn’t need a distro. gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12 is glibc, libssl, CA certificates, tzdata and libgcc. It has no shell and no package manager. That covers exactly what the ldd output above asks for:
# The whole runtime: glibc + libgcc from distroless, one binary, the site. FROM gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot COPY --chmod=755 ephpm /usr/local/bin/ephpm COPY ephpm.toml /etc/ephpm/ephpm.toml COPY --chown=65532:65532 wordpress/ /srv/www/ EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/ephpm", "serve", "--config", "/etc/ephpm/ephpm.toml"] with a config that’s about as small as configs get:
[server] listen = "0.0.0.0:8080" document_root = "/srv/www" [kv] memory_limit = "64MB" I built that with v0.8.2 (PHP 8.5.7), WordPress 7.1, SQLite Database Integration 3.0.1 and cache-wordpress. Then I ran it and installed WordPress by posting the installer form with curl:
$ podman images localhost/blog-wp-zerodep:latest 271 MB gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot 25.1 MB $ podman history --format '{{.Size}} {{.CreatedBy}}' localhost/blog-wp-zerodep | head -5 0B ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/ephpm", ... 0B EXPOSE 8080 114MB COPY dir:... # WordPress 7.1 + plugins 3.07kB COPY file:... # ephpm.toml 132MB COPY file:... # ephpm install step2: 200 <h1>Success!</h1> After that the front page served normally. I wanted to confirm the pieces were really the ones I thought. So I dropped a five-line check.php into the docroot that loads WordPress and prints what it’s running on:
persistent object cache: yes cache class: Ephpm\Cache\WordPress\ObjectCache db driver: WP_SQLite_DB sapi: ephpm After the install and a handful of page views, podman stats had the container at about 76 MB of memory. The whole database was one small SQLite file. Out of 271 MB of image, about half is the WordPress tree and half is the binary. Distroless itself is 25 MB. There’s no shell in the container at all. That’s nice for security and occasionally annoying for debugging. The binary is also a PHP CLI, so podman exec ... /usr/local/bin/ephpm php -r '...' is the escape hatch.
Where this is the right tool, and where it isn’t Where one binary with a SQLite file makes sense:
CI: testing a plugin or theme against a real WordPress without starting MySQL and a web server in the job. PR previews and staging copies, where spinning up and tearing down is the main workload. Edge and small boxes: a Raspberry Pi, a $5 VM, an appliance. Any box where the LEMP stack is most of the resource budget. Low-traffic sites whose real requirement is “it stays up and I don’t have to babysit it.” Where it isn’t:
Write-heavy, multi-writer sites. SQLite is one writer at a time. A busy WooCommerce store with concurrent checkouts wants a real MySQL. ePHPm still helps there. Point [db.mysql] at the MySQL server and its proxy pools connections. You’ve still dropped nginx, php-fpm and Redis. Plugins that assume MySQL-specific SQL in ways the SQLite drop-in can’t translate. WordPress’s SQLite project has come a long way, but test your plugin list before you commit. Setups that need the cache to survive a restart. The KV store is a cache. The object cache starts cold. What’s next The single binary is the easy part to show. The interesting work is behind it. One part is making the embedded engine behave like php-fpm for the apps that assume php-fpm. The other is making the database side do more than SQLite-in-a-file without bringing a server back. That’s where most of the ePHPm commits are going right now.
How I ran it AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, Windows 11 with WSL2 and Podman 5 (rootful machine). I built the image from the files above with podman build and ran it with -p 18300:8080. The installer was posted from the Ubuntu WSL distro with curl. The three GET / timings are the first three requests after install from a cold OPcache, not a benchmark.
Links ePHPm and the v0.8.2 release ephpm/php-sdk, static-php-cli SQLite Database Integration ephpm/cache-wordpress distroless

title: P99 From 280 ms to 58 ms by Making the Queue Fair
description: ePHPm had the best throughput in a Laravel runtime comparison and the worst tail of the fast group. The cause was a bounded channel that let new requests cut in line.
body:
A third-party Laravel runtime comparison put ePHPm’s worker mode at the top on throughput. It was about 19% ahead of FrankenPHP on /api/static. It was also at the bottom of the fast group on tail latency, with a P99 of 157 ms against FrankenPHP’s 57 ms. Best throughput plus the fattest tail is a shape worth chasing, because fast execution can’t produce it. Making requests faster lowers the mean and the tail. Only waiting can pull them apart. Specifically, unfair waiting.
This follows the thread pool post. ePHPm has two pools: the persistent worker pool and the new per-request pool. Both put a bounded queue in front of their threads, and both had the same defect.
What a fair queue should look like The benchmark was wrk with 100 connections against worker_count = 2. At about 2,230 req/s, Little’s law gives the mean time in system for an ideal two-server FIFO queue: 100 / 2,230 ≈ 45 ms. A closed-loop FIFO system at deep saturation is nearly deterministic. Every request waits behind the same ~96 others. So P50, P90 and P99 should all sit close to that 45 ms. FrankenPHP’s numbers looked exactly like that, with P99 at 1.1x its own ideal. ePHPm’s P99 was 3.5x.
I reproduced it on my box with the official v0.8.7 release (PHP 8.4, worker mode, same wrk shape). Three rounds gave this:
round req/s P50 P75 P90 P99 1 2,339 47.5 ms 79.6 ms 131.1 ms 275.9 ms 2 2,331 46.5 ms 80.6 ms 132.9 ms 275.5 ms 3 2,321 47.0 ms 81.0 ms 134.4 ms 285.1 ms P50 is right at the ideal. Then P75, P90 and P99 climb in steps of about 43 ms. Those steps turned out to be the whole story.
The lottery inside send().await The worker pool’s dispatch queue was async_channel::bounded(worker_backlog). worker_backlog defaults to the worker count. So the channel held 2 jobs and 2 more were executing. The other ~96 requests were parked inside the channel’s Sender::send().await. In async-channel 2.5 that future is a try, listen, retry loop:
On first poll it calls try_send before queueing behind the senders already parked. A request that just arrived can grab a freed slot ahead of waiters that have been parked for hundreds of milliseconds. That’s barging. On Full it registers a listener at the back of the waiter list. When a worker pops a job, exactly one waiter is woken. It has to get scheduled by tokio and then retry try_send. If a barging sender got there first, the retry fails. The loser goes to the back of the line again, behind ~95 others. Step 1 is why ePHPm topped the throughput chart. A freed slot never sits idle waiting for a parked task to get scheduled. Step 3 is the tail. Each lost race costs one full lap of the waiter queue. At 2,230 req/s a lap of ~96 waiters is 96 / 2,230 ≈ 43 ms. One lost race lands you at about P75, two at P90, five or six at P99. The defect turns scheduling jitter into whole multiples of 43 ms.
The tell-tale: requests that never waited There’s a histogram for exactly the time a request spends inside dispatch().await. It’s ephpm_worker_request_wait_seconds. Over a 70,083-request run:
wait cumulative ≤ 1 ms 42.7% ≤ 25 ms 47.7% ≤ 50 ms 66.1% ≤ 100 ms 86.1% ≤ 250 ms 98.8% ≤ 500 ms 99.9% Mean wait was 41.2 ms against 1.6 ms of mean execution, so the wait is the latency. And 42.7% of requests got in under a millisecond. In a fair FIFO at this saturation the queue is never empty. Every request should wait about one lap, and sub-millisecond waits should be impossible. Those are the barging winners. The 13.9% that waited 2 to 12 laps are the same thing seen from the other end.
The histogram also ruled out the other suspects:
No per-worker mailboxes. There’s one shared queue, so no head-of-line blocking across workers. No batching sawtooth. The response is a non-blocking oneshot, so a slow client can’t hold a worker. The fix: wait in a fair semaphore, not in the channel tokio::sync::Semaphore is documented as fair. Permits go to waiters in the order they asked. A new acquirer queues behind existing waiters even when a permit is free right now. Those are exactly the two properties send().await lacks. So ephpm#443 moved the waiting out of the channel and into a semaphore with one permit per queue slot:
pub async fn dispatch( &self, request: WorkerRequestOwned, ) -> Result<oneshot::Receiver<WorkerResponse>, DispatchClosed> { // Wait for a queue slot in strict arrival order. Errors only when // `drain()` closed the semaphore. let Ok(permit) = Arc::clone(&self.admission).acquire_owned().await else { return Err(DispatchClosed); }; let (tx, rx) = oneshot::channel(); let job = WorkerJob { request, respond_to: tx, admission: Some(permit) }; // Holding a permit guarantees a free channel slot (capacity == permit // count, and every enqueued job holds one permit until a worker pulls // it), so this `try_send` cannot see `Full`. match self.dispatch_tx.try_send(job) { // ... } } The worker drops the permit the instant it pulls the job off the channel. That’s the same moment a slot freed up under the old scheme, so the refill pipeline and throughput don’t change. The freed slot just goes to the longest-waiting request instead of the luckiest one. A few details fell out of it:
drain() closes the semaphore along with the channel. Parked requests still wake up into the 503 path on shutdown. A request cancelled by the outer timeout while parked leaves no trace, because tokio unlinks the waiter. That also fixed a small existing leak. A request cancelled mid-send().await used to leave the queue-depth gauge permanently high. The shed path maps over one-to-one. A zero grace window is try_acquire, and a non-zero one is timeout(grace, acquire). Shed-mode waiters queue fairly too. A unit test, admission_is_strictly_fifo_and_barge_proof, pins the invariant. Waiters are admitted in arrival order, and a newcomer can’t steal a freshly freed slot. From the PR, same box, parent commit vs fix, four 30-second rounds each:
req/s P50 P75 P90 P99 (per round) max parent (barging) 2,282 49.3 ms 80.2 ms 131 ms 259 / 280 / 303 / 267 ms 1.08 s fix (FIFO) 2,256 43.9 ms 44.4 ms 44.9 ms 46 / 66 / 62 / 62 ms 67 ms P99 went from about 280 ms to about 58 ms at -1.1% throughput. That’s inside the round-to-round spread. P99 landed at 1.3x the ideal sojourn, the same shape as FrankenPHP’s. P50 dropped too, because the median no longer carries lost laps. The uncontended path didn’t move (-c1 P99 1.19 to 1.21 ms). After the fix, 98.5% of waits landed in the 25 to 50 ms bucket and none above 100 ms.
“But barging is more work-conserving” That’s the objection, and it’s a reasonable instinct. If a slot can be filled by whoever is runnable right now, surely you get more done. ephpm#458 added an escape hatch, [php] admission = "fifo" | "barge". It used that to settle the question on the per-request pool with a rotated A/B on the Laravel bench. That was three rounds, with nginx+fpm as an in-session control:
per-request pool, mean of 3 health static cpu db req/s fifo / barge 1030.8 / 1030.1 1018.9 / 1019.1 1008.8 / 1007.7 732.4 / 730.9 P99 ms fifo / barge 105.0 / 354.4 103.0 / 375.0 104.6 / 367.7 152.1 / 425.2 Identical throughput, three times the P99. Here’s why barging buys nothing. At saturation the queue is never empty, so FIFO hands each freed slot to a waiter that’s already parked. There’s no idle window. Both disciplines are equally work-conserving. Barging’s only theoretical edge is filling a slot during a wakeup gap. That’s microseconds against a service time measured in milliseconds.
Re-measuring it on a release binary The knob means the A/B no longer needs two builds. So I re-ran the worker-mode comparison on the v0.9.1 release with nothing but EPHPM_PHP__ADMISSION changing between runs. The worker is a tiny script that boots once and renders about half a millisecond of PHP per request (400 rows, md5, usort, htmlspecialchars). It ran with concurrency = 2. wrk used 10 threads, 100 connections and 30 seconds, for three rounds alternating arms.
mean of 3 rounds req/s P50 P75 P90 P99 fifo (default) 4,917 20.2 ms 20.5 ms 20.8 ms 28.9 ms barge 4,907 19.6 ms 29.3 ms 40.8 ms 77.3 ms Same picture at a different service time. Throughput is a wash (0.2%), and so is the median. Everything above the median spreads out under barging, while FIFO stays in a 1 ms band up to P90. Per round, barge’s P99 was 77.5, 76.5 and 77.9 ms. FIFO’s was 21.3, 32.5 and 32.9 ms. With one client (-c1) the two are identical: 551 µs and 550 µs at P50, 768 µs and 771 µs at P99. Fairness only costs or saves anything when there’s a queue.
Sidebar: which process actually answered? Halfway through this investigation the A/B numbers stopped making sense. The fix seemed to work only with Prometheus metrics enabled, then only on one port, then on neither. Every one of those phantom correlations had the same cause. The A/B binaries were named ephpm-parent and ephpm-fix. The harness cleaned up with pkill -x ephpm, which matches neither. A stale parent server held port 8000 for an hour. Meanwhile freshly started servers died on Address already in use, and wrk kept measuring the stale process. Fat tail on 8000, tight tail on 8001, no matter which binary the harness thought it was testing.
The rule I took from it: a benchmark number is only attributable to a server after you check which process served it. Look up the listener’s PID, read /proc/<pid>/exe, and fail the run on a bind error instead of carrying on. My own harness for this post does exactly that before every measured window.
How I measured Hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 cores, 32 threads), 62 GiB, WSL2 kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2. Binary: the official ephpm-v0.9.1+php8.4.23-linux-x86_64 release, checksum verified against SHA256SUMS. It ran in worker mode with [php] concurrency = 2 and [php.worker] max_requests = 1000000, so no worker recycled mid-run. Each server was started fresh. Its startup log line confirmed the admission policy. The listening PID’s /proc/<pid>/exe was checked before every measured window. Load: wrk -t10 -c100 -d30s --latency with a 3-second warmup per server. Three rounds alternated fifo and barge, then wrk -t1 -c1 -d10s ran per arm. Nothing else was benchmarking on the box during the window. The PR tables above (#443, #458) are from the PR descriptions and the fairness doc. They were run on the same machine with a Laravel app. Links ephpm#442 - the issue, from the Laravel runtime comparison ephpm#443 - FIFO-fair dispatch admission ephpm#458 - the [php] admission knob and the fifo vs barge A/B docs/architecture/worker-dispatch-fairness.md - the full write-up, including the measurement post-mortem tokio Semaphore (fairness is in the docs) and async-channel

title: We Disabled PHP's Stack Guard Ourselves: Containing Segfaults in a Single-Process PHP Server
description: How ePHPm went from dying silently on a segfault to containing stack overflows per thread. It also covers the linker flag that had turned off PHP's own guard.
body:
php-fpm has a property nobody thinks about until they leave it. When a worker segfaults, you lose one request. The master forks a new child and life goes on. ePHPm runs every tenant’s PHP as threads inside one process. That’s where the memory and latency wins come from. It also means one tenant’s segfault takes down every other tenant on the box.
This is the story of closing that gap in four steps over about two weeks. The last step turned out to be a bug we’d put there ourselves. It’s also the payoff for the thread pool work in the previous post. Everything below that actually shipped depends on ePHPm owning its own PHP threads.
Step 1: at least say something on the way out The first problem wasn’t recovery at all. Kubernetes restarts a crashed pod in well under a second. We measured 61 to 90 ms to respawn. The problem was that ePHPm died with no output. A null dereference in an extension produced total silence. The only things that ever said anything were Rust’s own stack-overflow message and glibc’s malloc checker. An operator got a restarted pod and no way to tell whether an extension, a native middleware or PHP itself did it.
ephpm#253 added a fatal-signal reporter for SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE and SIGABRT. Everything about it is shaped by one fact. It runs inside a process that’s already broken:
Async-signal-safe throughout. Output is a raw write(2) to fd 2. Integers and pointers are formatted by hand into a fixed buffer. Only lock-free atomics are used. tracing, format! and println! all allocate or lock, and the faulting thread might already hold the allocator lock. backtrace() is warmed at startup so its lazy init doesn’t happen in a broken process. Raw addresses are written before symbolization is attempted, because _dl_addr takes the loader lock. sigaltstack + SA_ONSTACK, or a stack overflow can’t be reported at all. The handler would need stack to run on. It chains to the previous handler and dies with the original disposition. Every fault type was run twice on the same binary, with the handler on and off. The exit codes matched: 139 for segfaults and 134 for aborts. Kubernetes and exit-code alerting see exactly what they saw before. And deliberately no recovery. The reasoning from the PR is worth quoting: “a ZMM smash was measured returning HTTP 200 to its own client and killing the process 17 ms later on a different thread serving an unrelated request.” After heap corruption there’s no request to blame and no thread to isolate.
Step 2: the spike, and the wall it hit Then a pentest found the process-killer that made this urgent. It’s ordinary PHP. Build a linked list of around 50,000 plain objects and let it go out of scope. Freeing it recurses in C. zend_object_std_dtor goes into zend_objects_store_del and back, one pair of frames per node, until the thread runs out of stack. Nothing in userland reaches it. Not try/catch, not disable_functions and not memory_limit.
But a stack overflow is a different animal from heap corruption. The fault is in a thread-local resource: the thread’s own stack. The objects being freed live in that thread’s Zend MM heap and EG(objects_store). Zend MM mmaps its own 2 MiB chunks instead of going through glibc malloc. So no process-wide allocator lock is held when it faults. Abandon that one thread and the rest of the process is fine.
The spike was ephpm#294, and it was never merged on purpose. It built that in pure libc. That way it compiles and is unit tested without PHP at all. A per-thread sigsetjmp region wraps each request. The fatal signal handler asks a classifier first:
int ephpm_guard_try_recover(uintptr_t fault_addr) { if (!g_armed) { return 0; } if (g_stack_lo == 0) { return 0; /* bounds unknown on this platform: never contain */ } /* Below the guard window? (written to avoid unsigned underflow) */ if (fault_addr + EPHPM_GUARD_WINDOW < g_stack_lo) { return 0; } /* Well above the low bound: a wild write, not an overflow. */ if (fault_addr > g_stack_lo + EPHPM_GUARD_SLACK) { return 0; } g_armed = 0; siglongjmp(g_recover_buf, 1); return 0; /* unreachable */ } Only a fault at or just below this thread’s own stack low bound gets contained. The window is 64 KiB below it, with one page of slack above. The bounds come from pthread_getattr_np at arm time. They never come from inside the handler, because that call isn’t async-signal-safe. The state lives in __thread variables because a signal handler can read those safely. A wild write lands nowhere near the stack. It isn’t contained and dies with the usual diagnostic and exit code. The cover image above is that function as a picture.
The mechanism worked. The process survived 100 concurrent plus 120 paced crashes. There was zero corruption across 3,591 concurrent requests to a second tenant that round-tripped its own database. It also hit two walls. Both came from running PHP on tokio’s spawn_blocking pool:
A poisoned thread can’t be retired. After a contained crash, that thread’s Zend context is garbage. It has to refuse all further PHP. But tokio owns the thread. There’s no API to say “kill this one and give me a fresh one”. During a 100-crash storm, 17 threads got poisoned and the healthy pool shrank. The co-tenant’s success rate was 13.7%. Graceful shutdown aborted after even one contained crash. php_module_shutdown() walks every TSRM entry, including the abandoned poisoned one. It frees that entry’s corrupt heap from the main thread and gets zend_mm_heap corrupted. Exit 134 on every rolling deploy after any tenant crash. Containment turned “one crash kills every tenant until restart” into “degraded but alive”. That’s better, but it isn’t isolation.
Step 3: ship it on threads we own The fix for both walls was the owned thread pool. Once ePHPm runs PHP on its own std::threads, retiring a poisoned one is a break out of the job loop:
let poisoned = matches!(&out, Err(PhpError::Contained(_))); // The receiver is gone only if the router already timed out this // request (504) and moved on; dropping the response is correct. let _ = respond_to.send(out); if poisoned { counter!("ephpm_fpm_pool_contained_crashes_total").increment(1); exit = ThreadExit::Poisoned; break; } followed by the rule that matters most:
if exit == ThreadExit::Poisoned { // DO NOT run worker_thread_shutdown() here. It is php_request_shutdown() // + ts_free_thread(), and both walk this thread's ZMM free lists and // EG(objects_store), which the contained siglongjmp left mid-mutation. // Running them would free out of a corrupt heap and abort the process, // undoing the containment. counter!("ephpm_fpm_pool_recycles_total", "reason" => "poisoned").increment(1); } else { PhpRuntime::worker_thread_shutdown(); } A poisoned thread is abandoned and never cleaned up. That’s the same trade a hung thread already got. It leads to the process-level invariant from ephpm#302: once any crash has been contained, this process must never call php_embed_shutdown(). That closed the second wall. Consecutive poisons inside a 10-second window also back off 25 ms up to 500 ms before respawning. A client in a crash loop can’t make us spin thread creation and TSRM registration at request rate.
These are the numbers from the PR, on PHP 8.5.7 ZTS with a 4-thread pool. They come from two different storm setups. Read the chart as before and after rather than as a controlled A/B:
Check Result Crashes contained 1,400+, each one a 500, PID never changed Threads retired and replaced live thread count flat at 37 across all 1,400 Co-tenant availability 100 concurrent crashes + 1,500 concurrent requests: 1,500/1,500 OK (spike: 13.7%) RSS +90 MiB over the first ~1,000 crashes, then flat SIGTERM after a contained crash exit 0, module shutdown skipped (was 134) Heap-corruption class tgkill SIGSEGV to a thread inside an armed guard: still exit 139 That last row is the one I care most about. The classifier has to say no just as reliably as it says yes. It’s tested both ways: live, and with a forked-child unit test. In that test a real null-deref write inside an armed guard has to re-raise and die. A later benchmark put the guard’s happy-path cost at +0.4% RPS, inside the noise. It still ships as [php] crash_containment = false by default and labeled experimental. There are two reasons. Each contained crash leaks a Zend context, which is bounded but real. And it only covers one fault class.
Step 4: the twist, it was our linker flag Meanwhile there was a much older open issue, ephpm#116: WordPress block themes crash the worker. do_blocks() on nested block markup took down the resident PHP worker. It had been filed as a WordPress-in-worker-mode problem and sat on the “adapter quirks” pile.
When I went back to it, it still reproduced on main. And not just in worker mode:
depth result worker mode 1,000 200 worker mode 20,000 thread 'ephpm-worker-0' has overflowed its stack, process SIGABRT fpm mode 3,000 process SIGABRT on a tokio-rt-worker thread stock php any Error: Maximum call stack size of 8339456 bytes ... reached Stock PHP throws a catchable error for that. PHP 8.3 added a C-stack guard. At request startup zend_call_stack_init() reads the thread’s real stack bounds into EG(stack_limit). The VM and zend_call_function check it before recursing. Some recursion re-enters the VM through an internal function like array_map, preg_replace_callback or call_user_func_array. That’s exactly what do_blocks() to render_block() to apply_filters() does once per nesting level. That kind of recursion raises an Error instead of running off the end of the stack.
ePHPm had switched it off. build.rs had this, from early in the project:
let mut wrap_funcs: Vec<&str> = vec![ "zend_signal_startup", "zend_signal_init", // ... // zend_call_stack_init probes stack boundaries on each request // startup. Fails on tokio spawn_blocking threads with small/ // non-standard stacks. We disable stack checking anyway. "zend_call_stack_init", ]; for func in &wrap_funcs { println!("cargo::rustc-link-arg=-Wl,--wrap={func}"); } and the C side defined the wrapper as a no-op:
void __wrap_zend_call_stack_init(void) { /* no-op: stack checking is disabled */ } -Wl,--wrap=sym tells GNU ld to send every call to sym to __wrap_sym instead. It’s how you override a function inside a static archive you didn’t compile. The theory in the comment was wrong on both counts. Probing doesn’t fail on tokio threads. PHP reads the bounds with pthread_getattr_np, which is exact on any thread glibc creates. And even a probe that did fail would just leave EG(stack_limit) NULL. That means the guard is off, not a crash. What the wrap actually did was leave EG(stack_limit) NULL forever. So zend_call_stack_overflowed() was permanently false. That was on Linux only. macOS and Windows have no --wrap and kept the guard the whole time.
There was a second layer of the same misunderstanding. The wrapper also set EG(max_allowed_stack_size) = 0 in several places, with comments saying “disable stack size checking”. Zero is PHP’s default and means “auto-detect from the real stack”. The disable value is -1. Those writes never disabled anything. They just made the code look like it was doing something on purpose.
The fix is two parts, and the second one matters ephpm#360 dropped the wrap and the no-op. It also deleted the max_allowed_stack_size writes. But re-arming the guard alone would have swapped a crash for a spurious error at a quarter of php-fpm’s depth. PHP derives the ceiling from the running thread’s stack. Rust and tokio threads default to 2 MiB. php-fpm runs PHP on the process main thread with ulimit -s, which is 8 MiB on every mainstream Linux. So every thread that runs PHP now gets an 8 MiB stack:
pub const PHP_THREAD_STACK: usize = 8 * 1024 * 1024; let builder = std::thread::Builder::new() .name(format!("ephpm-fpm-{thread_id}")) .stack_size(ephpm_php::PHP_THREAD_STACK); That’s applied to the tokio runtime threads, the per-request pool and the worker pool. It’s reserved address space that gets committed a page at a time. There’s no RSS cost. Measured on an 8 MiB stack, the test fixture completes 11,000 levels and fatals at 13,000. That’s the same on PHP 8.3.31 and 8.5.7, about 750 bytes of C stack per level. The e2e test asserts 5,000 levels complete. That’s more than 2x margin. It’s also about twice what a 2 MiB thread would allow. So it’s a real test of the thread stack size and not a tautology.
after depth result worker mode 5,000 200 worker mode 20,000 / 60,000 / 200,000 clean 500, server alive, next request served fpm mode 20,000+ clean 500 with PHP’s own message And because the overflow is now a catchable Error, a worker adapter that catches it keeps serving with no recycle at all. That was #116’s acceptance criterion.
