Both guards stay PHP’s guard and the signal-level containment don’t overlap. Here’s precisely why. PHP’s guard is a checkpoint. It’s tested in the VM and in zend_call_function. Recursion that goes through PHP code or internal callbacks hits a checkpoint and becomes an Error. The destructor cascade from the pentest recurses purely through C destructors and never passes one. PHP can’t see it. The signal handler is still the only thing that catches that one, and crash_containment still needs the owned pool. Worker mode can’t contain that class yet. It owns its OS threads, which is the precondition. So it’s tractable, but it’s a feature-sized change of its own.
Takeaway The uncomfortable part of this story is where the bug lived. The bug that took down every tenant on a block-theme page wasn’t in PHP or WordPress. It was a linker flag with a confident comment. It was written early on, when PHP threads lived on tokio’s blocking pool and “small, weird stacks” seemed like a reasonable thing to defend against. Nobody re-tested the assumption, because nothing ever failed in a way that pointed at it.
--wrap is a powerful tool for embedding a C runtime. ePHPm still uses it for PHP’s process-wide signal handling. Every wrapped symbol is a feature of the runtime you’ve switched off. It deserves the same scrutiny as any other config default. Each one needs a test that would fail if the reason for it stopped being true. As it happens, this wasn’t the only feature we’d turned off this way. zend_set_timeout had been wrapped to a no-op too. That’s why max_execution_time did nothing in ePHPm until August. That one gets its own post.
Links ephpm#253 - report fatal signals instead of dying silently ephpm#294 - the containment spike (not merged, kept as the record) ephpm#302 - contain stack-overflow crashes and retire the poisoned pool thread ephpm#116 / ephpm#360 - re-arm PHP’s C-stack overflow guard ephpm/multitenant-scalebench BEFORE-AFTER.md - the guard’s happy-path cost (point 5) php-src: Zend/zend_call_stack.c GNU ld --wrap

title: Stop Running PHP on tokio's spawn_blocking - Own Your Thread Pool
description: Why ePHPm moved PHP execution off tokio's generic blocking pool onto threads it owns. How the switch rolled out behind a knob and what it did to memory, throughput and overload.
body:
For most of its life, ePHPm ran every PHP request on tokio’s spawn_blocking pool. It works. It passes tests and it serves benchmarks fine. It’s the first thing anybody reaches for when they need to call blocking code from async Rust. It’s also quietly wrong for a language runtime. The problems only show up under overload or after a crash. Over the last three weeks it got replaced with a pool of OS threads that ePHPm owns. That pool shipped first behind a config flag, then as the default. As of v0.9.0 the spawn_blocking engine is gone.
One thing up front, because it’s the first question I get. This is not “drop tokio”. hyper, TLS, the database wire protocols, gossip and every timer still run on tokio. That’s 95% of what tokio does for us. spawn_blocking is tokio’s most generic component, and it’s the only thing that got replaced.
Why spawn_blocking is the wrong home for PHP spawn_blocking is a convenience: “run this sync closure somewhere that isn’t the reactor”. tokio grows the pool on demand up to a ceiling of 512 threads. It reaps threads that sit idle. It shares the pool with everything else that blocks, including static file I/O. For PHP that causes three problems.
You can’t retire a poisoned thread. This is what forced the change. After a contained crash, the segfault containment work needed to abandon the thread with the corrupt Zend context and start a fresh one. tokio owns its blocking threads and recycles them on its own schedule. There’s no “kill this one” API. The containment spike proved the mechanism worked, and the PID survived 220 induced crashes. But a tenant sharing the box saw only 13.7% of its requests succeed during a crash storm, because the poisoned threads couldn’t be replaced. More on that in its own post.
Concurrency is unbounded, so memory is a function of traffic. Every in-flight request gets a blocking thread. Every PHP thread carries its own ZTS context. 512 concurrent requests means roughly 512 PHP contexts. On Kubernetes that’s the OOM-kill-under-flood failure mode. The pod’s memory ceiling is set by how hard you get hit, not by anything you configured.
Two halves of the config disagreed. ePHPm’s memory autotune divides a memory budget by N workers to pick memory_limit. The runtime then happily ran many times N requests at once, since tokio’s blocking pool goes to 512 threads. The sizing logic and the execution engine made different assumptions and nothing reconciled them.
Parity by construction The new engine is a fixed pool of std::threads. Each registers with TSRM once, then loops pulling jobs off a bounded async_channel and answering on a oneshot. Pool size is the concurrency cap. The part I’d recommend to anyone doing a swap like this is how the two engines were wired. The per-request body was factored into one closure. That covers the per-site DB session, KV keyspace, open_basedir and temp-dir INI, OPcache invalidation and the bailout guard. The engines differ only in which thread runs it. This is the dispatch from the router while both engines existed:
} else { // Cap concurrent PHP executions when [php].workers is set. // Once the closure reaches spawn_blocking it is committed to tokio's // unbounded, uncancellable blocking queue, where ePHPm can neither // reject nor withdraw it. let _php_permit = match &self.php_semaphore { /* ... */ }; (tokio::task::spawn_blocking(run_php).await, None) }; and the pool arm:
} = if let Some(pool) = self.fpm_pool.clone() { let recv = match self.overload_policy { OverloadPolicy::Wait => pool.dispatch(Box::new(run_php)).await.map_err(ShedReason::from), OverloadPolicy::Shed => pool .try_dispatch(Box::new(run_php), self.shed_after) .await .map_err(ShedReason::from), }; Same run_php, different thread. That made the code review tractable. It also made the benchmark a true single-variable comparison.
The rollout: a knob, then data, then a default Nothing about this was a big-bang migration:
Opt-in (ephpm#296, August 15th). [php] fpm_engine = "pool", default unchanged. It’s a real enum, so a typo is a startup error. It’s also env-overridable (EPHPM_PHP__FPM_ENGINE=pool). The benchmark lab could flip engines on the same binary with no code changes. Benchmark in the lab, closed-loop and open-loop, and fix what the benchmarks found. Make it the default (ephpm#460, September 2nd). The PR left spawn_blocking in as an opt-out, but it never shipped that way. #462 removed it the same night, before v0.9.0 was tagged. Delete the old engine (ephpm#462, v0.9.0) and rename the concurrency config to match what exists now. That’s [php] concurrency and queue_depth, not workers, worker_count and worker_backlog. What the lab measured The first head-to-head came from the multitenant-scalebench repo. It used the same binary with only the env var changed, on a 32-core WSL2 box with the pool sized to 32. Those runs were later found to have a harness bug that capped the light workload about 4x low. That’s its own post. From those runs I only trust the relative engine comparison and the memory numbers. Real WordPress is CPU-bound and wasn’t affected by the harness bug:
real WordPress, 50 sites, c=128 spawn_blocking pool RPS 262.5 276.5 p99 2,036 ms 1,147 ms RSS steady 2,702 MB 581 MB Better on both axes. With the CPU already saturated, 128 blocking threads just add scheduling contention. 32 pool threads, one per core, run cleaner. The re-run on the fixed harness (BEFORE-AFTER.md) landed in the same place: +7% RPS, p99 -22%, RSS -82% (574 MB vs 3.2 GB).
The honest tradeoff showed up on the light path. When there are more clients than pool threads, the extras queue and the tail stretches. p99 went from 28 ms to 70 ms on a light endpoint at c=128. spawn_blocking buys a tight, uniform tail by running everything at once. It pays for that in RAM.
Measuring it again myself v0.8.9 was the last release with both engines in it. I re-ran the closed-loop comparison on it before the old engine disappeared. The workload is one PHP page that does about 10 ms of CPU work. It builds 4,000 rows, runs usort, renders 1,500 list items and runs hash() on the result. There’s no database, so it’s purely about how the two engines schedule PHP. Every run used the same binary. The only difference is EPHPM_PHP__FPM_ENGINE. The pool autotuned to 32 threads.
clients engine RPS p50 p99 max steady RSS 32 spawn_blocking 2,615 11.6 ms 21.1 ms 34 ms 394 MB 32 pool 2,737 11.3 ms 18.5 ms 28 ms 263 MB 128 spawn_blocking 2,508 43.9 ms 146.7 ms 347 ms 2,179 MB 128 pool 2,963 42.7 ms 57.5 ms 109 ms 265 MB 512 spawn_blocking 2,555 183.1 ms 520.6 ms 864 ms 3,002 MB 512 pool 2,981 170.4 ms 196.0 ms 236 ms 281 MB The memory line is the headline. spawn_blocking grows with the number of clients because it holds one PHP context per in-flight request. The pool stays flat at whatever 32 threads cost. On this CPU-bound page the pool also wins on throughput (+18% at c=128) and on the tail. That’s the same shape as the real WordPress result above. Only when the work is very light does spawn_blocking’s run-everything-at-once approach get its tighter tail back.
Open-loop is where it stops being close Closed-loop benchmarks can’t show you overload. Every client waits for its response before sending another. An overloaded server just makes the clients slower and reports zero errors. In open-loop runs, requests arrive at a fixed rate whether or not earlier ones finished. Those runs are written up in detail in What an Overloaded PHP Server Actually Returns. Here’s the short version for real WordPress at 1.5x capacity. spawn_blocking delivered a burst, then went to zero goodput and never recovered. RSS climbed to 5-6 GB. Its queue is unbounded and uncancellable. Requests whose clients had already given up still ran, ahead of every new arrival. The pool stayed around 0.6 GB and recovered within 30 seconds. It drops a queued-but-unstarted job when its client disconnects.
I ran my own version of that against the same 10 ms page on v0.8.9. The flood was 4,444 requests per second for 40 seconds, which is 1.5x the pool’s measured capacity. Clients had a 10-second timeout. After the flood came a 20-second cooldown and a light probe. There were three arms:
spawn_blocking with the default wait policy the pool with wait the pool with overload_policy = "shed" from #305 arm delivered 2xx/s what the other arrivals got p99 of successes peak RSS spawn_blocking, wait 514 82,184 client timeouts, 75,021 connection errors 9.7 s 4,386 MB pool, wait 1,950 63,694 client timeouts, 36,060 connection errors 10.7 s 1,276 MB pool, shed 2,987 58,261 fast 503s, nothing else 33.8 ms 265 MB spawn_blocking went to zero goodput about 13 seconds in and stayed there until the flood stopped. The pool with wait held capacity for about 15 seconds and then degraded too. Tens of thousands of connections waiting on a queue is its own problem. The shed arm is the one that behaves like a server should. It served right at capacity the whole time and answered everything else with an instant 503. RSS didn’t move.
Two honest caveats. First, the load generator itself was strained on the two wait arms. It had up to 38,000 requests in flight and up to 1.7 s of scheduling lag. The connection errors are client-side too. Read the middle of those two curves as shape, not as precise numbers. Second, unlike the WordPress lab, all three arms recovered once the flood stopped. The spike at 47 seconds is spawn_blocking’s backlog draining all at once. With a 10 ms page the stale queue is seconds of work. With WordPress at 100 to 500 ms a request, it was minutes to hours.
The flood also flushed out three real bugs. That’s a decent argument for open-loop testing all by itself:
The connection limiter wrote a 503 and then served the rejected connection anyway (#299). A thread-local destructor panic took down the whole process when a PHP thread retired (#300). There was no request-level shedding at all (#301). Shedding turned out to be engine-specific too. With the pool, a request that can’t get into the bounded queue gets a 503 and no PHP has run. With spawn_blocking, once the closure is handed over there is nothing to reject from.
The numbers that made it the default The default flip in #460 was decided on a Laravel benchmark. It ran wrk with 10 threads and 100 connections for 30 seconds, three rounds. One binary had the engine flipped by env. nginx+php-fpm ran as an in-session control.
rps, mean of 3 health static cpu db pool 1029.0 1010.5 999.8 724.3 spawn_blocking 928.8 911.3 904.8 670.5 The pool’s worst round beat spawn_blocking’s best round in all 12 endpoint cells. Latency was lower at every percentile. Under a 200-connection overload at default settings, spawn_blocking sat at 486 threads and 1,056 MB. The pool sat at 65 threads and 193 MB, serving more.
What I’d tell someone else embedding a runtime “Own your threads” cost nothing in dispatch overhead. That fear is what kept us on spawn_blocking for months. A bounded channel and a oneshot per request is noise next to a PHP request. What you get for it:
a thread you can retire a concurrency cap that’s the same number your memory sizing uses a queue you can cancel from or reject from One thing the owned pool did not fix by itself was fairness. The bounded channel turned out to let new requests cut in line. That’s the next thing I’ll write up.
How I measured Hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 cores, 32 threads), 62 GiB, WSL2 kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2. Binary: the official ephpm-v0.8.9+php8.5.7-linux-x86_64 release, checksum verified against the release’s SHA256SUMS. PHP 8.5.7 ZTS, [php] mode = "fpm", single site, everything else default. Load: the Go load generator from multitenant-scalebench (-c for closed-loop, -rate for open-loop). Each closed-loop point had a 5 s warmup and 20 s measured, with a fresh server per point. RSS and CPU were sampled from /proc at 1 Hz. The server was started from a WSL-native directory. Before each run the harness checked that the listening PID’s /proc/<pid>/exe was the binary under test. Single run per point on a dev box, so treat differences of a few percent as noise. Scripts and raw JSON are kept with my notes for this post. Links ephpm#296 - opt-in dedicated FPM execution pool ephpm#298 / ephpm#305 - the serve-after-503 fix, the TLS destructor abort, request-level shedding ephpm#460 - pool becomes the default ephpm#462 - remove the spawn_blocking engine, rename the concurrency config multitenant-scalebench reports - ENGINE-COMPARISON, SHEDDING, BEFORE-AFTER tokio spawn_blocking docs

title: Kata Containers for CI: Boot Cost Isn't the Problem, File I/O Is
description: Kata containers are safer for CI, but slower. Starting one takes 12x longer, which is fine. Reading small files is about 40x slower for the entire job, which isn't.
body:
Of the three platforms ephemerd runs jobs on, Linux has the weakest isolation. Windows jobs get a Hyper-V isolated container with its own kernel. macOS jobs get a whole VM. A Linux job is an ordinary runc container sharing the host kernel. A kernel escape from a Linux job is a host compromise. Kata Containers fixes that by putting each container in a lightweight VM with its own kernel. It plugs into containerd as just another runtime handler. So I added it in #155, measured it, and left it off by default. This post is why.
Wiring it in From containerd’s point of view Kata is a different shim, io.containerd.kata.v2. So the change to the runtime is small. The job-container creation site used to hardcode runc. Now it resolves the handler from config:
func resolveRuntimeName(linuxRuntime, goos string) string { if goos == "windows" { return "io.containerd.runhcs.v1" } if linuxRuntime == "" { return "io.containerd.runc.v2" } return linuxRuntime } [runner.linux] runtime = "kata" # "runc" (default) or "kata" The more interesting decision was what happens when Kata is configured but can’t run. ephemerd checks for containerd-shim-kata-v2 on the PATH. It also checks that /dev/kvm exists and opens. If either fails, the daemon refuses to start:
f, err := os.OpenFile("/dev/kvm", os.O_RDWR, 0) if err != nil { hint := "this host has no usable KVM device" if os.IsNotExist(err) { hint = "/dev/kvm does not exist — on a VM this usually means nested " + "virtualization is not enabled for this guest" } else if os.IsPermission(err) { hint = "/dev/kvm exists but is not openable — check that ephemerd runs " + "as root or is in the kvm group" } return fmt.Errorf(`runner.linux.runtime = "kata" but %s: %w`, hint, err) } The tempting alternative is falling back to runc with a warning. But then the config says “VM isolation” while untrusted CI runs on the host kernel. Nobody reads warnings. An outage is a better failure than a silent downgrade of an isolation guarantee.
The numbers I measured on one of my amd64 fleet nodes:
an 8-core Proxmox guest with nested virtualization Kata 4.0.0 with QEMU the same runner image for both runc and Kata runs interleaved so neither got a quieter period The full tables are in #155 and the configuration docs. These charts are straight from them.
Measurement runc Kata Ratio Provision a job container, dind on (median, n=9) 203 ms 2,498 ms 12.3x Create to running, dind off (median, n=18) 140 ms 4,146 ms 30x Host RSS per idle container ~13.6 MB ~313 MB 23x CPU-bound compile (median, n=4) 7.5 s 10.2 s 1.35x Create 3,000 files on the rootfs (median, n=4) 645 ms 5,195 ms 8.1x Read 3,000 files on the rootfs 79 ms 2,890 ms 37x Create 3,000 files on the bind-mounted runner dir 435 ms 4,712 ms 10.8x Read 3,000 files on the bind-mounted runner dir 73 ms 2,984 ms 41x The first thing everyone asks about with VM-per-container is boot time. Yes, it’s there. A job container with dind enabled goes from about 200 ms to about 2.5 seconds. Nearly all of it is guest kernel boot during task create:
But I don’t care much about 2.3 seconds per job. A CI job runs for minutes. The boot is paid once and it’s done.
File I/O is the real cost The file numbers are the ones that matter, because they’re paid for the entire life of the job. Both the guest’s root filesystem and the bind-mounted runner directory reach the host through virtio-fs. Every open() and stat() crosses the VM boundary. Reading 3,000 small files goes from 79 ms to 2.9 seconds:
And small-file I/O is most of what CI does. actions/checkout, npm ci, go mod download, a cargo build walking its target directory, tests that glob fixtures. A CPU-bound compile only lost 35%, which would be an easy trade. A job that installs dependencies and runs a test suite is going to feel the 8-41x on every step.
Memory is the other cost. It’s about 310 MB of host RSS per idle job versus ~14 MB for runc. Most of that is the QEMU process (~267 MB resident). On a node running four jobs at a time, that’s about 1.2 GB of headroom it didn’t need before.
One caveat from the PR is worth repeating. The node kept serving production CI while I measured. The workload and memory runs had stable load. The dind-off start-latency runs saw load climb, so the 4.1 s median there overstates an idle node. That’s part of why I quote the dind-on number for start cost. It’s 2.5 s with a tighter spread of 2,472 to 2,528 ms.
Swapping the hypervisor doesn’t fix it Kata ships Cloud Hypervisor and Firecracker alongside QEMU. You select one by symlinking a different shim (containerd-shim-kata-clh-v2, containerd-shim-kata-fc-v2). I ran all three in the same session:
Firecracker came in about 9% under QEMU. Cloud Hypervisor came in about 8% over. (The repo docs summarize this as “neither beat QEMU”, which isn’t quite what the Firecracker number says.) Either way, every one of them is in the five to six second range against runc’s sub-200 ms. (That session ran slower across the board than the runs in the table above, QEMU included.) I only compared start latency across them. I didn’t re-run the file tests under the other VMMs. With QEMU the file I/O cost comes from virtio-fs. Firecracker’s Kata config uses a block-device rootfs instead, so that comparison is still open. There’s no cheap start-time win here from switching VMMs on stock configs.
It’s not just slower, it’s different A few behavior changes showed up that matter as much as the numbers:
arm64 can’t run it at all on my fleet. The arm64 nodes have no /dev/kvm, so a fleet-wide default was never on the table. AppArmor doesn’t apply inside the guest. There’s no AppArmor in the Kata kernel. The profile ephemerd puts on job containers is gone. You trade in-guest defense-in-depth for the VM boundary. cgroup memory limits don’t translate. The guest reported 2.3 GB MemTotal regardless of a 512 MB limit. The Docker socket can’t cross the boundary. ephemerd normally bind-mounts a host unix socket at /var/run/docker.sock. Under Kata the bind becomes a virtio-fs passthrough. It carries the socket inode into the guest but not its connectability. The socket is there and every connect() gets ECONNREFUSED. Sibling -v mounts from the job’s own filesystem don’t work. docker run -v $GITHUB_WORKSPACE:/x from inside a Kata job used to produce an empty directory with no error. Now it’s an explicit 400. The Docker socket one had a fix sitting right there. Hyper-V isolated Windows containers are VMs with exactly the same constraint. Windows jobs have always gotten the Docker API over TCP on the bridge gateway with DOCKER_HOST=tcp://.... The transport had been chosen by build tag. That was really standing in for “does this container share the host kernel”. Now it’s chosen at runtime: unix socket for runc, TCP for Kata, TCP always on Windows.
Moving it to TCP changes the security story, though. The Docker API authenticates nothing. On Linux every container can address the bridge gateway. So the firewall is now the only thing deciding who can drive which job’s Docker daemon. Each job’s port gets an ACCEPT for that one container’s /32. A DROP for the port from everyone else follows it. Both live in an EPHEMERD-DIND chain jumped from both INPUT and EPHEMERD-FORWARD. The isolation was checked with a negative control:
the probe from a neighbour container times out deleting the DROP makes it connect restoring it blocks it again That INPUT detail also led me to a bigger hole. I wrote it up in My iptables Rule Matched 0 Packets in 9.8 GB.
So, default or not? Not, for now. Kata is the right answer for a node that runs untrusted public-fork PRs and can afford the I/O hit. It’s a one-line config change for those nodes. My own repos on my own hardware are a different story. AppArmor, dropped capabilities and the egress firewall already narrow down the kernel-escape class. A 37x slower checkout isn’t worth it there.
If I come back to this, it’ll be for the file I/O, not the boot. Getting the job’s working directory off virtio-fs and onto something guest-local is where I’d start looking.
How these were measured I didn’t re-run these for this post. Kata isn’t installed on my workstation. I wasn’t going to fake a nested-virt setup to get numbers that would be less representative than the originals. Everything above comes from the measurements recorded with the PR:
an 8-core amd64 Proxmox guest Kata 4.0.0, QEMU, containerd handler io.containerd.kata.v2 runc and Kata interleaved against the same image on the same node sample sizes as listed in the table Links #155 opt-in Kata Containers runtime ephemerd configuration docs, [runner.linux] Kata Containers virtio-fs

title: Clustered ACME in Production: Three Bugs That Took TLS Down
description: Moving wildcard TLS onto a live 3-node ePHPm cluster found a leader election that wasn't, a certificate only two nodes could see, and an HTTP port speaking TLS.
body:
ePHPm gets its own certificates from Let’s Encrypt. In a cluster only one node should be talking to the CA. The nodes elect an ACME leader over the shared KV store. The leader orders the cert, and everybody else installs it from KV. That all had unit tests and had worked on single nodes for months. Then I tried to move wildcard TLS termination for our preview environment off a separate proxy and onto the 3-node cluster itself. In about two days it found three separate bugs that each took TLS down. None of them showed up in a unit test. All of them are the kind of thing you only learn by putting the feature on real machines.
The setup Preview deployments get a subdomain each, something like pr-123.preview.example.com. Issuing a cert per subdomain would burn through Let’s Encrypt’s 50 certificates per registered domain per week in no time. So the plan was one wildcard, *.preview.example.com. TLS-ALPN-01 can’t validate a wildcard, because there’s no single hostname for the CA to connect to. That meant DNS-01:
publish a _acme-challenge TXT record wait for it to propagate tell the CA you’re ready That lane landed first (#411), built on instant-acme. It reused the existing clustered pieces from the TLS-ALPN-01 lane: the acme:leader election and the KV cert distribution. Reusing the hard, correctness-critical parts instead of writing them twice is the right call. It also means you inherit their bugs.
Three nodes, a Linode NodeBalancer in front, Let’s Encrypt staging first to protect the production rate limit.
Bug 1: leader election by start time All three nodes logged that they’d acquired ACME leadership. Then they took it back from each other, over and over:
node-1 acquired ACME leadership node_id="1787985979173-..." node-2 acquired ACME leadership node_id="1787986064600-..." node-3 acquired ACME leadership node_id="1787986130867-..." node-1 taking over ACME leadership (lower node id wins the tie-break) ... node-2 taking over ACME leadership (lower node id wins the tie-break) ... The election’s tie-break is “lowest node id wins”, which is fine. The problem was the id. The ACME code minted its own per-process identity:
1787985979173-22749-173895959 └─ epoch millis ─┘ └pid┘ └random┘ With an epoch-millis prefix, “lowest id wins” really means “whichever process started earliest”. That reshuffles on every restart. While nodes are rolling, leadership bounces around. The cycle on the cluster was roughly 70 seconds. A DNS-01 order spends about 60 seconds just waiting on TXT propagation. So no node held leadership long enough to finish an order, and two of three nodes never got a certificate. The third only had one because it loaded an old cert from its disk cache.
It also finally explained something I’d poked at before and left unexplained: “~7 minute leader flapping” in the logs. The cadence came from restart timing, not from any timer. That’s exactly why looking for a timer never found it.
The fix (#418) uses the configured [cluster] node_id. That’s the same stable identity gossip already advertises. The generated form stays only as a fallback for a node without a configured id. That’s a single-node deployment where there’s nothing to elect against. One subtle bit: a blank or whitespace-only node_id also falls back to the generated form. Otherwise every node would collapse onto the same empty identity, and every node would believe it holds the same claim.
Bug 2: the certificate only two nodes could see With a stable leader, node-1 issued a valid certificate and served it. Nodes 2 and 3 never installed it. Ten minutes later they were still failing handshakes with tlsv1 alert access denied, because they had no certificate at all.
The cert was written with Store::set, which in clustered mode routes by value size. Small values ride the gossip layer to every node. Large values go to a sharded tier and land on replication_factor nodes, which defaults to 2. The issued chain was 5140 bytes and small_key_threshold is 4096. So the certificate got sharded like a cache entry. The read side used the plain, local-only Store::get, which has no “fetch it from the owner” path. On a 3-node cluster with a replication factor of 2, one node could never see the certificate.
The obvious knob is raising small_key_threshold, and it’s the wrong one. The small tier is chitchat gossip over UDP, so a multi-kilobyte payload can’t ride it. That’s the whole reason the threshold exists. The bug wasn’t the threshold. It was the assumption that “too big for gossip” means “shard it”. Sharding is a capacity optimization. It’s the wrong routing for state every node needs locally, and every node terminates TLS with this certificate.
So #417 added two things, and both are load-bearing:
A broadcast write tier (Store::set_broadcast) that writes to every alive node regardless of size. Peer writes are awaited rather than fire-and-forget. A certificate gets written a few times a year, so cluster-wide read-your-writes matters a lot more than write latency. A partial delivery logs a warning instead of failing silently. A fetch-through read (Store::get_cluster). On a local miss, it falls back to the key’s replica set over the data plane. Broadcast only reaches nodes that are alive at write time. Without the read fallback, a node that joined after issuance would wait up to 60 days for the next renewal to get a certificate. The TLS-ALPN-01 lane had the identical defect on its own cert and account cache, so it got the same fix. ACME account material moved to the broadcast tier too. Every node needs the same ACME identity. Otherwise a promoted follower registers a second account with its own rate-limit budget.
The test for this is the one I like best in the batch. It spins up three real gossip nodes on 127.0.0.x with a real TCP data plane. It writes a 5140-byte payload (the size from the incident) through the same Store calls the ACME code uses. Then it asserts the value is in the raw local store of the node the sharded tier would skip. Reverting set_broadcast to the old routing makes it fail with left: None on that node. That’s the live outage reproduced in a test.
The same bug from another direction A follow-up showed up the moment the cluster was restarted as a whole. Lowest node id wins. The leader comes up holding a still-valid cert in its disk cache, seeds from disk, and never orders anything. Broadcasts only happened at issuance, so it never published. Followers found KV empty, and two of three nodes served nothing on :443 again. #420 republishes the cached cert to KV on the leadership-acquisition transition. It’s a no-op when KV already has it. After the redeploy, node-1 logged re-published cached certificate to the cluster on leadership acquisition and all three nodes served the staging wildcard.
That same PR fixed the next landmine before it went off. The DNS-01 cert cache keys in KV and the files on disk were keyed only by domain set, never by ACME directory. Flip staging = false and the staging cert is sitting under the exact key the production reader looks up. The cache is read first and nobody checks the issuer. The nodes would have kept serving an untrusted staging cert forever and never ordered a production one. Every cache entry is now namespaced by a hash of the directory URL.
It wasn’t quite the whole story. When I flipped to production, the cluster still came back with staging certs. The account credentials on disk were a single account.json. After the flip the production KV key missed, so the code fell back to disk and loaded the staging account. instant-acme then reconnected to the directory URL embedded in those credentials. That was #421: account-<directory_hash>.json. It was the third facet of the same bug. The order went to staging, so no production rate limit was spent finding it.
Bug 3: the HTTP port that spoke TLS This one had already been misdiagnosed once. The config was [server] listen = "0.0.0.0:8080" plus [server.tls] listen = "0.0.0.0:443". The NodeBalancer health-checks plain HTTP on 8080, and the health check failed. That pulled nodes out of rotation and sent 503s to users. The earlier write-up called it “port 8080 connection refused”.
It wasn’t refused. Sending a plaintext GET with nc got this back:
15 03 03 00 02 02 32 That’s a TLS alert record. 0x15 is the alert content type and 03 03 is TLS 1.2, then a fatal decode_error. The port was listening and accepting the whole time. It was speaking TLS. Clients reported a connection-level failure, so the port looked dead.
The cause was in dispatch_main_connection. Plain HTTP on the main listener was gated on has_tls_listener && redirect_http, and redirect_http defaults to false. So a separate TLS listener without a redirect fell straight through to the TLS-mode match. That wrapped the main listener in TLS too. The code contradicted its own documented contract (“when set, server.listen serves HTTP and this address serves HTTPS”). That contract was already correct in two places. Now whenever a separate TLS listener is bound, the main listener serves plain HTTP. redirect_http only decides whether that’s a 301 or a normal response. There’s no TLS-mode arm on that path anymore, so manual and ACME modes can’t diverge again.
The tests drive the real dispatch_main_connection over a real socket and assert on the first byte written back. That’s H for HTTP/1.1, or 0x16/0x15 for a TLS record. It’s the same signal the live diagnosis used.
A couple of earlier ones While I was in here, two older TLS bugs belong in the same list.
Once the certs were on the nodes, every browser got a 404 or a redirect loop on multi-tenant sites. curl worked fine. Browsers negotiate HTTP/2 over TLS. HTTP/2 carries the host in the :authority pseudo-header with an absolute-form request URI, not a Host header. ePHPm only looked at Host, which left three problems:
vhost resolution defaulted to localhost $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST'] was empty REQUEST_URI was https://host/path WordPress turned that into a canonical redirect to a URL with the host glued in twice. #414 synthesizes a Host header from the authority at ingress. It also emits REQUEST_URI in origin form for every protocol version.
And earlier in August, manual cert/key TLS panicked at startup in v0.6.0 and v0.6.1 (#243). The workspace pinned rustls to ring. Meanwhile rustls-acme, rcgen and hyper-rustls enabled aws-lc-rs. Cargo unions features, so both providers got compiled in. rustls then refused to pick a process default. Nobody noticed because ACME mode always passes a provider explicitly. Every unit test in tls.rs also called install_default() first, which masked the panic for the whole test binary. That’s since been converged on a single aws-lc-rs provider (#368).
What I took away Every one of these passed its unit tests. The election was “correct” given its inputs. The KV write was “correct” for a cache entry. The listener was “correct” for one config shape. They broke on assumptions that only a real cluster exercises: restart timing, value sizes, a load balancer health check that speaks plain HTTP.
The other takeaway is about staging. Running the whole thing against Let’s Encrypt staging first made it cheap to find the cache-collision bugs. The flip to production was where they’d have burned a week of wildcard rate limit. Do the staging run, and then treat the flip itself as a separate thing to test.
Links DNS-01 wildcard lane: ephpm #411 Leader election on the configured node id: ephpm #418 Plain HTTP listener + broadcast cert distribution: ephpm #417 Republish on promotion + directory namespacing: ephpm #420, #421 HTTP/2 :authority: ephpm #414 Two rustls crypto providers: ephpm #243 Let’s Encrypt rate limits and staging environment

title: Finding a Data Race in rancher/remotedialer, Then Pinning Only Two-Thirds of the Fix
description: Two data races in remotedialer v0.6.1 that upstream's tests never ran with -race, and how my replace directive ended up pinned to the middle commit of my own fix.
body:
shipmates ships connect to Fleet Command over outbound websocket tunnels. That way nothing on the ship side has to be exposed to the internet. I didn’t write that tunnel layer. I used rancher/remotedialer, the same library Rancher uses to reach downstream cluster agents. I spent years around that code at Rancher, so it was the obvious pick. What I didn’t expect was for my CI’s race job to find two data races in it in the first week.
CI was the only place -race could run -race needs cgo, which needs a C compiler. Neither machine I was writing shipmates on had one at the time. Every agent session that tried go test -race hit cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found. So I moved shipmates CI onto my ephemerd runners in PR #26. At the same time I added a dedicated race job on linux-x64. Today it runs in a golang:1.26.6-bookworm container, which ships gcc:
race: name: race (linux-x64) runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64] container: golang:1.26.6-bookworm timeout-minutes: 30 steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # ... - name: Test with race detector run: go test -race -count=1 ./... The shipmates fleet tests open and tear down real tunnels quickly. That job went red inside remotedialer v0.6.1, not in my code.
Race 1: Session.pingCancel ConnectToProxyWithDialer builds the racing pair itself. It runs Serve on a goroutine and defers Close:
go func() { session.Serve(ctx) }() // Serve -> startPings: s.pingCancel = cancel (write, no lock) defer session.Close() // Close -> stopPings: if s.pingCancel == nil (read, no lock) Here’s v0.6.1:
func (s *Session) startPings(rootCtx context.Context) { ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(rootCtx) s.pingCancel = cancel s.pingWait.Add(1) go func() { defer s.pingWait.Done() // ticker loop ... }() } func (s *Session) stopPings() { if s.pingCancel == nil { return } s.pingCancel() s.pingWait.Wait() } Session already embeds a sync.RWMutex and the neighboring fields use it. pingCancel just never got put under it. In production the write and the read are separated by the lifetime of a session. You only see it when sessions open and close quickly, like in a reconnect storm or a test suite driving real tunnels.
Race 2: connection.err doTunnelClose does an unguarded check-then-set on c.err. Three callers can hit it at the same time:
a pipe copy noticing its peer failed Session.Close tearing everything down serveMessage on a protocol error connection had no synchronization at all. The kicker is that remotedialer’s own TestExceedBuffer trips this race as soon as you turn the detector on. Upstream’s Makefile test target didn’t use -race. That’s how both of these survived.
Fork, reproduce first, then fix I forked it and did the red/green thing on purpose. I wanted the detector’s report against unfixed code on record:
cf2b335: add TestSessionCloseDoesNotRaceServeStartup and turn on -race in make test. This commit fails. 7e65b78: lock pingCancel, add an errMu around connection.err. Green. The test does what ConnectToProxyWithDialer does in a loop. That gives the detector repeated shots at the startup window:
func TestSessionCloseDoesNotRaceServeStartup(t *testing.T) { for i := 0; i < 200; i++ { conn := &blockingWSConn{closed: make(chan struct{})} s := newSession(int64(i), "race-probe", conn) s.client = true // only the client side runs startPings ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background()) served := make(chan struct{}) go func() { defer close(served) _, _ = s.Serve(ctx) }() s.Close() // the deferred Close, arriving while Serve is still starting _ = conn.Close() cancel() <-served s.pingWait.Wait() } } The fix for stopPings grabs the cancel func under the lock and releases the lock before cancelling. The ping goroutine’s callees also take that lock (getSessionKeys via sendSyncConnections). So pingWait.Wait() is never awaited while holding it. Nil-ing the field makes a second Close a no-op.
Then in shipmates, 84e0d0e pointed the dependency at the fork:
replace github.com/rancher/remotedialer => github.com/luthermonson/remotedialer v0.2.6-0.20260805014355-7e65b789c524 v0.6.1 and upstream main had zero Go-file difference at that point. So the fork was exactly the pinned version plus these fixes. Upstream PR to follow, drop the replace when it lands. Done, I thought.
The third commit About three hours after those two commits, I opened rancher/remotedialer#265 with them. That was a minute after pinning shipmates to them. Within the hour the new test caught one more thing on a machine with more hardware threads. It failed about half of runs at 32. Look at what 7e65b78 did to startPings:
s.Lock() s.pingCancel = cancel s.Unlock() s.pingWait.Add(1) // still outside the lock stopPings now reads pingCancel under the lock, sees it non-nil and goes on to pingWait.Wait(). But nothing says the Add(1) has happened yet. A Close that lands between the Unlock and the Add calls Wait concurrently with Add on a zero counter. The race detector flags it. At runtime it can panic with sync: WaitGroup misuse: Add called concurrently with Wait. That happens in exactly the reconnect storm the PR was supposed to fix.
The third commit, 00b5151, moves the Add inside the same critical section:
s.Lock() s.pingCancel = cancel s.pingWait.Add(1) s.Unlock() Now observing a non-nil cancel implies the Add happened-before the Wait. I pushed it to the PR branch and moved on.
What I didn’t do was bump the replace. shipmates stayed pinned to 7e65b789, the middle commit of the PR. Its stamp was about three hours before the PR even existed. I had the connection.err fix in full and two-thirds of the pingCancel fix. I didn’t notice until a review pass right before the v0.5.0 release, thirteen days later. PR #50 bumped it to the PR head:
replace github.com/rancher/remotedialer => github.com/luthermonson/remotedialer v0.2.6-0.20260805053951-00b5151280f8 Then I checked that the resolved module carries Add(1) between s.Lock() and s.Unlock(). I didn’t trust the pseudo-version.
Seeing all three states To write this up I ran the same reproducer against all three versions straight out of the module cache. That’s upstream v0.6.1, the middle commit and the PR head. Each got 20 iterations with -race on Linux.
v0.6.1 is race 1, exactly as described. Write in startPings, read in stopPings:
WARNING: DATA RACE Write at 0x00c000416de0 by goroutine 2007: github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).startPings() session.go:173 +0x58 github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).Serve() session.go:223 +0x57 Previous read at 0x00c000416de0 by goroutine 1614: github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).stopPings() session.go:213 +0x31 github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).Close() session.go:314 +0x3b ... --- FAIL: TestSessionCloseDoesNotRaceServeStartup (0.01s) testing.go:1712: race detected during execution of test The middle commit, the one I’d been shipping, still fails. But now it’s the WaitGroup. session.go:231 is s.pingWait.Wait() and session.go:179 is the s.pingWait.Add(1) that sat outside the lock:
WARNING: DATA RACE Write at 0x00c00047e6a0 by goroutine 6057: runtime.racewrite() <autogenerated>:1 +0x1e github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).stopPings() session.go:231 +0xa7 github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).Close() session.go:327 +0x3b Previous read at 0x00c00047e6a0 by goroutine 6276: runtime.raceread() <autogenerated>:1 +0x1e github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).startPings() session.go:179 +0xaf github.com/rancher/remotedialer.(*Session).Serve() session.go:236 +0x57 ... --- FAIL: TestSessionCloseDoesNotRaceServeStartup (0.01s) testing.go:1712: race detected during execution of test And the head is clean:
ok github.com/rancher/remotedialer	1.218s The lesson I keep relearning: a replace to a pseudo-version is a pin to a commit, not to “my fix”. If the branch moves after you pin, you’re on whatever you pinned. Nothing will tell you.
Side effect: go install stops working A replace directive in your go.mod means people can’t go install your module:
$ go install github.com/luthermonson/shipmates@v0.5.0 go: github.com/luthermonson/shipmates@v0.5.0 (in github.com/luthermonson/shipmates@v0.5.0): The go.mod file for the module providing named packages contains one or more replace directives. It must not contain directives that would cause it to be interpreted differently than if it were the main module. Release binaries are fine. goreleaser builds in the module, so it honors the replace. The README and the v0.5.0 release notes (f2c4bdf) say to grab a release binary. The other option is git clone and go build until #265 merges. As of this writing the upstream PR is open with no reviews. It’s showing merge conflicts, so the fork stays for now.
Takeaways If your project depends on something concurrent, run your tests with -race even if upstream doesn’t. A suite that churns real connections finds things code reading won’t. Put the reproducer in its own commit before the fix. It made the upstream PR easy to explain, and it’s how I could rerun all three states here. After you pin a fork, check the pin again when the PR is final. How I measured The race output above came from three steps:
copy each version of the module out of my Go module cache (rancher/remotedialer@v0.6.1, luthermonson/remotedialer@...-7e65b789c524 and @...-00b5151280f8) drop the fork’s session_close_race_test.go into the two that didn’t have it run go test -race -count=20 -run TestSessionCloseDoesNotRaceServeStartup . in each That ran under WSL2 with Go 1.26.0, gcc 15.2 and 32 hardware threads on a Ryzen 9 5950X. Paths in the output are trimmed.
Links rancher/remotedialer#265 (the upstream PR, three commits) shipmates PR #26 (CI on ephemerd, the race job) shipmates PR #50 (bumping the pin to the complete fix) go.mod reference: replace directive

title: Middleware in PHP: Compiling It With elephc, Then Not Needing To
description: Fitting PHP into ePHPm's native middleware ABI with an ahead-of-time compiler, and what that experiment said about where PHP middleware should actually run.
body:
ePHPm middleware runs before PHP. It’s a small versioned C ABI, loaded with dlopen, that gets to look at a request and reject it before PHP boots or the request body is read. That’s the right shape for a gateway. It’s the wrong shape for most PHP shops, who want to write their middleware in PHP. This is the story of compiling PHP into a native .so to fit that ABI and finding exactly where it broke. Then I built the lane that should have existed in the first place.
The native middleware ABI A module is a shared library (.so, .dylib or .dll) that exports four symbols. A fifth, optional response-phase hook arrived in v0.8.0:
int32_t ephpm_middleware_init(uint32_t abi_version, const char *config_json, const ephpm_host_v1 *host); int32_t ephpm_middleware_invoke(const ephpm_request_t *req, ephpm_response_t *out); void ephpm_middleware_shutdown(void); const char *ephpm_middleware_describe(void); /* optional */ The host hands the module a callback table at init. It holds request accessors, the tracing logger and the cluster-replicated KV store. The module never dlsyms host symbols. That would need -rdynamic on Linux and has no clean equivalent on Windows. The top byte of abi_version is the major and gates compatibility. The lower bytes are a minor that only ever grows the table by appending. A module built against a shorter table stays correct on a newer host. It just can’t see the slots it didn’t declare.
invoke returns one of three verdicts: CONTINUE, RESPOND or REWRITE. RESPOND short-circuits, so PHP never runs. The contract is plain C, so ePHPm doesn’t care what language produced the .so. That’s the opening an ahead-of-time PHP compiler walks through.
The elephc experiment elephc is a real, MIT-licensed, ahead-of-time PHP-to-native compiler. It parses PHP, type-checks it, lowers it through its own SSA IR and emits assembly. There’s no Zend Engine involved. --emit cdylib turns functions marked #[Export] into C exports. So the question was simple. Can I write ePHPm middleware in PHP, compile it and load it into a stock ePHPm release?
The answer, verified on 2026-08-20 against elephc 0.26.4 and the published ePHPm v0.7.3 Linux binary, was yes. This PHP ran as native code before PHP dispatch:
<?php extern function mw_set_header(string $name, string $value): void; extern function mw_log(string $msg): void; #[Export] function mw_invoke(string $method, string $path): int { mw_log("elephc-mw: " . $method . " " . $path); mw_set_header("X-Elephc", "1"); mw_set_header("X-Route", classify($path)); return 0; // ACTION_CONTINUE } function classify(string $path): string { if (strlen($path) >= 5 && substr($path, 0, 5) === "/api/") { return "api"; } return "web"; } And the headers showed up on live responses. The log lines landed in ePHPm’s own tracing output:
$ curl -sS -D- -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8299/api/users.php HTTP/1.1 200 OK x-elephc: 1 x-route: api INFO ephpm_server::middleware: middleware initialised module=/root/mwx/libelephc_mw.so describe=elephc-php-middleware (experimental adapter) INFO ephpm_middleware: elephc-mw: GET /api/users.php The catch: a mandatory C shim elephc’s cdylib marshaller only handles int, float, bool and string in exported signatures. ePHPm’s ABI is built on struct pointers. Trying to export the entry points straight from PHP fails at compile time:
$ elephc --emit cdylib abi_probe.php error[abi_probe.php:11:1]: exported function 'ephpm_middleware_init' parameter #3 has unsupported type for --emit cdylib v1; supported: int, float, bool, string So there’s a ~180 line C shim that’s not optional. It does five jobs:
exports the four ABI symbols dereferences the host table and request struct flattens the request into strings calls the PHP mw_invoke provides mw_set_header and mw_log The PHP side’s extern declarations are left as undefined symbols in the elephc output. They get resolved against the shim at dlopen:
ePHPm --dlopen--> libelephc_mw.so (C shim, exports ephpm_middleware_*) | +--NEEDED--> libmw_php.so (elephc output, exports mw_invoke) $ nm -D libmw_php.so | grep -E ' T | U ' T mw_invoke U mw_log <-- resolved from the shim at dlopen U mw_set_header A couple of small gotchas came up along the way. The shim needs -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN' or ePHPm fails at startup with cannot open shared object file. And elephc exports can’t return strings, so headers go out through callbacks instead of return values.
Do your Composer libraries work? No. This was the claim most worth being careful about, so I tested it instead of assuming it. I installed three real packages with Composer and fed them to the compiler:
Package Result Root cause Composer’s own vendor/autoload.php fails assignment inside a while condition, typed static properties nikic/fast-route fails new $options['routeCollector'] (dynamic class name after new) firebase/php-jwt fails (object) cast, #[\SensitiveParameter] parameter attribute The first row is the important one. Composer’s generated class loader doesn’t compile. So require 'vendor/autoload.php' is a hard stop for basically every modern PHP project. The failing files are kept in the repo as regression tests for when elephc’s coverage improves. elephc’s own README is candid about this: “not a drop-in replacement for an entire dynamic framework today”. Its stdlib coverage is broad. The gap is parser and feature coverage on real-world library code. What works today is first-party PHP: functions, string and array builtins, control flow, regex. That’s a useful subset for middleware. But it’s your code, not your dependency tree.
More hard limits came out of the run:
elephc’s cdylib runtime has no locking around its heap, and ePHPm invokes middleware concurrently. So the shim wraps every call in a global mutex, and every middleware call runs one at a time. No Windows target, even though ePHPm’s middleware lane loads .dlls fine. A PHP fatal inside the cdylib terminates the process. The headline RESPOND path, rejecting a request before PHP boots, was never exercised. Only CONTINUE was. The contrast case: the same ABI from Rust After publishing the elephc repo it bothered me that our only worked example of the ABI needed a hand-written C shim. That makes the ABI look harder than it is. So I added an in-tree Rust example (#375) called api-gate. It’s an API key check with a fixed-window rate limit on kv_incr_ttl and runtime revocation through KV. It’s ~200 lines of ordinary safe Rust with zero unsafe in the module itself. The declare! macro supplies the rest:
the four exports the version handshake config parsing panic containment response marshaling fn invoke(&self, req: &Request<'_>) -> Response { if !req.path().starts_with(&self.prefix) { return Response::cont().response_header("X-Api-Gate", "bypass"); } let host = req.host(); let Some(tenant) = req.header("X-Api-Key").and_then(|key| self.keys.get(key)) else { return Self::reject(401, "missing or unknown X-Api-Key") .header("WWW-Authenticate", "ApiKey realm=\"api-gate\""); }; // ... revocation via host.kv_get(), rate limit via host.kv_incr_ttl() ... } ephpm_middleware::declare!(ApiGate); It exercises RESPOND three ways (401, 403, 429). The missing x-powered-by header on those responses proves PHP never ran:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized www-authenticate: ApiKey realm="api-gate" {"error":"missing or unknown X-Api-Key"} The shim was elephc’s limitation, not the ABI’s. Don’t let your first example make your ABI look harder than it is.
What PHP developers actually wanted: the php: lane Here’s the thing the elephc run made obvious. Nobody asking for “middleware in PHP” was asking for PHP compiled to native code. They wanted to write a PHP file, point config at it and have it run before their app. So that’s what #382 built:
[[middleware]] library = "php:middleware.php" # relative to the request's document root match = "/api/*" order = 30 config = { realm = "admin" } <?php $cfg = json_decode(ephpm_middleware_config() ?? '{}', true); $auth = $_SERVER['HTTP_AUTHORIZATION'] ?? ''; if (!str_starts_with($auth, 'Bearer ')) { http_response_code(401); header('WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="' . $cfg['realm'] . '"'); echo 'missing bearer token'; exit; // RESPOND, the app never runs } $_SERVER['HTTP_X_TOKEN'] = substr($auth, 7); // REWRITE header('X-Auth-Checked: 1'); // response header // falling off the end = CONTINUE A php: mount runs in the same PHP request as the application, immediately before it. That’s where auto_prepend_file runs, except a mount is scoped by path pattern, supports multiple files and carries config. That position is the whole design. The middleware inherits the superglobals, open_basedir, the OPcache vhost, the per-site DB session, the KV keyspace, the execution timer and the crash guard because it’s the same request. There’s no second PHP context to configure, so there’s none to get wrong.
Three things only running it revealed You can’t use php_execute_script(). PHP 8 implements exit() as an unwind-exit exception. Both php_execute_script() and zend_execute_scripts() hand every pending exception to zend_exception_error(). That clears EG(exception) and returns FAILURE. It does that whether the script called exit(), threw or failed to parse. On return there’s nothing left to tell “called exit()” apart from “blew up”. The first cut didn’t look at the return value at all. So the short-circuit tests failed with the app’s output appended after the middleware’s 401. The chain now runs PHP’s own loop body inline with that one case split out.
An uncaught Throwable fails open. zend_exception_error reports it with E_DONT_BAIL, so execution returns normally. Inside the inline loop, PG(last_error_type) is what’s left to record it. Without an explicit check the app runs anyway. For an auth middleware that’s an auth bypass. It’s checked after every mount now. Every failure mode is a 500 where the application script does not run. That covers a missing file, a parse error, an uncaught exception and a fatal.
The chdir had to go. Matching auto_prepend_file exactly meant a getcwd, chdir and restore around the chain. That measured ~55 µs per request on Windows, about 5x everything else the lane does. I removed it and the docs say to use __DIR__.
What it costs These numbers are from the PR’s benchmark. It used a release build with OPcache on. Each run was 1000 sequential keep-alive requests to <?php echo 'ok';, best of 11. Each middleware set three response headers. The baseline with no middleware was 365.7 µs per request.
In isolation the Rust builtin’s marginal cost is 476 ns. So a php: mount is ~25x a Rust builtin’s isolated cost. Over HTTP the gap shrinks to ~3x, as the chart shows. It’s also ~3% of a trivial PHP request. Both framings are true, so pick the honest one for your audience. An empty middleware file costs the same as a working one. The cost is engaging the lane, not your PHP.
The tradeoff to own Native modules run before the body is read. The exception is if you opt into buffering a bounded body for them with middleware_body_limit. php: mounts run after. A PHP middleware can’t reject an upload before it’s transferred, and no order value changes that. So startup logs the resolved plan and it’s never a surprise.
For multi-tenancy, mount paths resolve against the request’s document root. Each tenant brings their own file, and it has no more reach than their index.php. Absolute paths are rejected at startup in every mode. Sharing one operator file across tenants would need a hole in every vhost’s open_basedir. Worker mode is a startup error rather than a warning. There’s no per-request point to run a mount, so it would silently never run.
Takeaway The elephc run answered the feasibility question. A stale tracking note in the ePHPm repo still listed “native middleware via elephc cdylib” as planned, spec only, no code. It’s now verified working with known limits. It also showed what the real request was. So both lanes stay: native for “reject before the body”, PHP for everything else.
The other thing I’d repeat is how that README was written. Every claim is marked Verified or Not verified. That’s what made the follow-up decision easy. It’s very tempting to write up a prototype as if everything you designed also ran. It’s much more useful to write down exactly which parts did.
Links ephpm/elephc-middleware-example elephc and its cdylib docs Rust api-gate example: ephpm #375 php: middleware lane: ephpm #382 Guide: site/content/guides/native-middleware.md in the ePHPm repo

title: OPcache on Windows: Two Silent Failures
description: An ASLR fatal on Windows looked like a memory-size lottery. Separately, Windows PHP 8.3 builds never had an opcode cache, and the fix sat unpicked for three weeks.
body:
Windows is the platform where ePHPm gets the least traffic and the most surprises. Last week closed out two OPcache bugs that only exist there. Both were quiet in their own way. One killed the server at startup with nothing in our own logs. The other didn’t kill anything. It just ran PHP 8.3 with no opcode cache at all. For three weeks after a fixed SDK was published, every check stayed green.
For context, ePHPm is a Rust server with PHP embedded as a static library. On Windows that’s a ZTS php8embed.lib built by our php-sdk pipeline and linked into ephpm.exe. The versions here are PHP 8.5.7 ZTS on Windows 11, plus the 8.3 and 8.4 SDK pins we ship.
“Opcode handlers are unusable due to ASLR” The report was that an ephpm.exe sometimes dies at launch with the message below. PHP writes it to stderr and to the Windows Event Log. Then the process calls exit(-2) from inside php_module_startup:
Fatal Error Opcode handlers are unusable due to ASLR. Please setup opcache.file_cache and opcache.file_cache_fallback directives for more convenient Opcache usage ePHPm’s own log shows the autotune lines and then nothing. And it looked like a size problem, which sent the first round of debugging in the wrong direction. opcache.memory_consumption = 512 died. 256, 333 and 400 all worked. Turning the JIT off “fixed” it too. That reads like “512 MB is too big to reserve contiguously once ASLR has scattered things around”. It isn’t.
The segment has a name, and the size is part of it On Windows, OPcache’s shared memory is a named, session-global section object. The name comes from create_name_with_username() in ext/opcache/shared_alloc_win32.c:
ZendOPcache.SharedMemoryArea@<md5(username + opcache.cache_id)>@<sapi_name>@<zend_system_id><requested_size_hex> A second process that computes the same name doesn’t create its own segment. It reattaches to the first one’s. That’s how PHP on Windows shares an opcode cache across php-cgi processes. Reattaching is only legal if the VM’s opcode handlers sit at the same address in both processes. Cached op_arrays hold absolute pointers to handlers inside the loaded image. zend_shared_alloc_reattach() checks exactly that:
wanted_mapping_base = ((void**)mapping_base)[0]; execute_ex_base = ((void**)mapping_base)[1]; ... execute_ex_moved = (void *)execute_ex != execute_ex_base; When it has moved, it logs at ACCEL_LOG_FATAL. Whatever the name suggests, that isn’t a log level. zend_accelerator_debug.c handles it outside the verbosity check:
/* perform error handling even without logging the error */ switch (type) { case ACCEL_LOG_ERROR: zend_bailout(); break; case ACCEL_LOG_FATAL: exit(-2); break; } So opcache.log_verbosity_level can’t suppress it. zend_try can’t catch it either, because it’s exit() rather than a bailout. Two details then explain every symptom:
The requested size is in the name (memory_consumption plus the page-aligned jit_buffer_size). Whether two processes collide depends on configured size. That’s why it presented as a size lottery. It’s also why turning the JIT off “fixed” it, since that removes the JIT buffer from the size. Windows picks a randomized image base per file and keeps reusing it, in practice until reboot. Run the same ephpm.exe twice and both processes get the same base, so the reattach check passes. Copy the exact same bytes to a different path and the copy gets a different base. That’s why it was deterministic per binary and not random. Autotune derived 512 MB on any host with more than about 2.8 GB of RAM. In practice every Windows box was one renamed binary away from this. The reproduction is three commands, with instance A still running:
ephpm.exe serve --config a.toml # creates the 512 MB-named segment, OK ephpm.exe serve --config b.toml # same binary, same base: reattach OK copy ephpm.exe ephpm-call.exe ephpm-call.exe serve --config c.toml # same bytes, new path, new base: dies The controls that confirmed it, all with instance A holding the segment:
Variant Result copy, default 512 MB dies with the ASLR fatal copy, opcache_memory_consumption = 256 starts (different size, different name) copy, still 512 MB, opcache.cache_id set via ini_overrides starts and serves PHP same binary, same path, 512 MB starts (same image base) The third row is the one that settles it. Same bytes, same 512 MB, same concurrent instance, and the only change is the namespace.
The fix: never reattach ePHPm is one multi-threaded ZTS process that never forks workers. It has no use for a segment shared with an unrelated process. On Linux and macOS PHP doesn’t support cross-process reattachment at all. The ZEND_OPCACHE_SHM_REATTACHMENT define in zend_portability.h is literally “Currently only possible on Windows.” So the fix gives every process its own namespace:
opcache.cache_id = ephpm-<pid> With a private name, ePHPm always takes the create path, which performs no execute_ex check. opcache.cache_id only exists on Windows, so it’s only emitted there. It’s written before the operator’s ini_overrides, so anyone who really wants a shared segment can still pin their own.
The options I rejected are worth listing, because each would have looked like a fix:
Cap the size. That just moves the collision to a different size. Same lottery, different numbers. /DYNAMICBASE:NO. Turning off ASLR in a server process that runs untrusted PHP to work around a startup bug is a bad trade. opcache.file_cache + file_cache_fallback. Turns the fatal into a warning and a much slower file-cache-only mode. It also adds an on-disk cache with its own multi-tenant questions. opcache.mmap_base. Moves the segment, not execute_ex. Doesn’t help. The PR also caps the derived memory_consumption at 256 MB on Windows, for a separate reason. The Windows section is pagefile-backed and charged against the commit limit in full at startup. Linux commits lazily. To be clear, the cap doesn’t fix the ASLR abort. The negative control still dies. That control forced both binaries onto one shared cache_id at 256 MB. An explicit operator value is still honored, with a startup warning. That’s ephpm#363.
PHP 8.3 on Windows ran with no OPcache, and the fix sat unpicked for three weeks The second one turned up while I was verifying the JIT default on Windows. In serve mode on our PHP 8.3 build, opcache_get_status() returned false. The extension was loaded. It just never engaged.
Up through PHP 8.4, OPcache only activates for SAPIs it knows about. There’s a supported_sapis allowlist in ZendAccelerator.c (apache2handler, fpm-fcgi, cli-server, litespeed, frankenphp and so on). An unknown SAPI name quietly gets no opcode cache. ePHPm’s SAPI is named ephpm, so our SDK builds patch the allowlist. PHP 8.5 removed the allowlist upstream, which is why the 8.5 builds were never affected.
To check whether a static library actually carries the patch, you don’t need a debugger. Grep the string table. Use SAPI names you know are in the upstream list as controls, so you know you’re reading the right table:
Windows SDK ephpm in allowlist frankenphp / fuzzer controls 8.3.31 (what we pinned) missing both present 8.3.33 present both present 8.4.23 (what we pin) present both present 8.4.24 present both present So the SDK pipeline was fine. 8.3.33 had carried the patch since August 2nd. We were just pinning an older 8.3 that predates the allowlist patch. That means our Windows 8.3 builds had gone without OPcache since 8.3 joined the release matrix in June. The original report (php-sdk#47) had also blamed 8.4, which was never broken. The fix in ephpm#373 moves one pin, 8.3.31 to 8.3.33. It deliberately leaves 8.4 alone so an OPcache fix doesn’t drag in an unrelated PHP version change.
Why nobody noticed: the bump PR that couldn’t push We have a nightly “SDK Bump” workflow that opens a PR whenever a newer SDK is published. It had been trying to land exactly this 8.3.33 bump every night since it shipped. It kept failing at the push:
! [remote rejected] bump/php-8.3.33 (refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/release.yml` without `workflows` permission) GITHUB_TOKEN can’t modify files under .github/workflows/, and release.yml is one of the pin sites. The failure was in a scheduled workflow, so nobody saw it. Fixing that needs a token with workflow scope. That’s its own decision and got its own follow-up.
Using the bump tool by hand then turned up two more bugs in it. Substitutions that targeted the same file each started from a fresh read of the file, so the last write won. bump-php-pin 8.3 8.3.33 moved three pin sites in release.yml and silently dropped the other two. That would have left the two Linux release legs building the old SDK. Its own --check flagged the result as drift, which is how I caught it. The nightly run had produced the same incomplete diff. Substitutions now compose per file, through a pure function that’s unit tested without touching disk. The second bug was that windows-php-check.yml hard-coded the 8.3 SDK path, so it wasn’t a known pin site at all. It is now.
The pattern The same lesson showed up in July. It turned out SHA-NI had been off in our Linux 8.3 and 8.4 builds for the life of the project. A C++-only compiler flag leaked into the C flags and made an autoconf probe fail. The hardware sha256 path compiled out. sha256 ran at roughly 2.7x its potential cost (benchmarking findings). The fix added a build guard that greps for the SHA256_Transform_shani symbol.
All three bugs have the same shape. A config field existing, or a feature “being enabled”, doesn’t mean the machine code is in the binary. It doesn’t mean the code path runs either. On Windows especially, the cheap check is the artifact itself. Grep the .lib for the string, or nm it for the symbol, with a control you know should be there. For OPcache the runtime check is opcache_get_status() returning an array and not false. That’s the check worth running on every platform you ship, not just the one CI runs on.
Links ephpm#362 / ephpm#363 - the ASLR startup abort and the private opcache.cache_id ephpm#373 - pin 8.3 to 8.3.33; Windows OPcache was silently off ephpm/php-sdk#47 - the original allowlist report ephpm/php-sdk#36 - re-enabling SHA-NI, PCLMUL and AVX2 in the SDK build php-src: ext/opcache/shared_alloc_win32.c, ext/opcache/zend_accelerator_debug.c

title: Per-Tenant Network Policy in One Process: ePHPm's eBPF Thread Tags
description: Every site on an ePHPm server runs inside the same process, so a normal firewall can't tell them apart. A small eBPF program tags each thread with its site. It keeps sites from reaching each other's local ports for under a microsecond per connection.
body:
In multi-tenant mode ePHPm serves every site in sites_dir from one process. Every tenant’s PHP runs as the same OS user on the same pool of ZTS threads. A thread that just served blog.example will serve shop.example a few milliseconds later. That’s the density win. It also means the kernel has no idea which tenant is behind a given connect(). As far as Linux is concerned it’s all ephpm-web.
Most of the isolation work in ePHPm happens above the kernel. That covers open_basedir, the function denylist, per-site databases and KV keyspaces. Network is the one place where that isn’t enough. This week we brought eBPF in to give the kernel a per-tenant identity. It went from a roadmap doc on Wednesday morning to merged that evening (#413, aimed at v0.8.1). v0.8.1 never got a release because its Linux legs failed to link. v0.8.2 shipped with the BPF object silently stubbed out. v0.8.3 was the first release that carried it. This post covers what it enforces and what it costs. It also covers what broke on the way out the door and what it doesn’t do.
Why uid rules can’t see tenants The hardened preview host already had an nftables table scoped to meta skuid ephpm-web. It seals loopback, drops cloud metadata and RFC1918, and pins DNS. That’s a good floor. It also treats every tenant the same, because a uid match is all it has to go on. Two things fall out of that:
No sidecars. Say tenant A wants to run something on 127.0.0.1:8080 for its own PHP to talk to. You either seal loopback for everyone (A can’t reach its own sidecar) or open it for everyone (B can reach A’s sidecar too). No per-tenant ports. Two tenants that both hardcode 127.0.0.1:8080 collide on bind. Network namespaces are the textbook answer, but they’re built for one process per context. For ePHPm that means a setns() per request plus CAP_SYS_ADMIN. It also means a veth, route, NAT and DNS setup per tenant. That doesn’t fit a model where a 1 GB node is supposed to hold a lot of sites. What we needed was a way to attach an identity to a thread for the duration of one request. Then the kernel could read it at bind()/connect() time.
A tag per thread The whole design hangs off one BPF hash map called tag. It’s keyed by thread ID with a numeric vhost ID as the value. Before a request’s PHP runs, the router writes tag[tid] = vhost. It deletes the entry when the request is done. From crates/ephpm-server/src/tenant_ebpf.rs:
pub fn tag_current_thread(self: &Arc<Self>, site_key: &str) -> TagGuard { let vhost = self.site_ids.id_for(site_key); let tid = current_tid(); if let Ok(mut tag) = self.tag.lock() && let Err(e) = tag.insert(tid, vhost, 0) { tracing::warn!(tid, vhost, error = %e, "tenant_ebpf: failed to write tag"); } TagGuard { owner: Arc::clone(self), tid } } impl Drop for TagGuard { fn drop(&mut self) { if let Ok(mut tag) = self.owner.tag.lock() { let _ = tag.remove(&self.tid); } } } The router creates the guard at the top of run_php. That’s the per-request closure both fpm engines run. The guard is dropped on the same pool thread when that closure returns:
// crates/ephpm-server/src/router.rs let run_php = move || -> Result<ephpm_php::response::PhpResponse, ephpm_php::PhpError> { let _ebpf_tag_guard = ebpf_tag.as_ref().map(|(e, key)| e.tag_current_thread(key)); // ... per-site KV, DB, open_basedir, then PhpRuntime::execute ... The one invariant that matters here is that a stale tag must never survive onto the next request. If it did, tenant B would inherit tenant A’s network identity on a reused thread. That’s the exact cross-tenant leak this is supposed to prevent. The Drop is a bpf_map_delete_elem syscall, not a PHP call. It doesn’t cross PHP’s setjmp/longjmp boundary. PhpRuntime::execute catches its own bailout and returns a Result, so the closure always unwinds normally. The shed, 503 and hung-thread paths return before run_php runs at all. They never write a tag in the first place.
A failed tag write logs and lets the request run untagged. Keep that in mind for the limits section.
Which thread is this, really? On the kernel side the obvious helper is bpf_get_current_pid_tgid(). Its low 32 bits are the TID. The catch is that it returns the global TID. That turned up in the proof of concept before any of this was merged. If ePHPm runs inside a PID namespace (a container, Kubernetes, or WSL2), the gettid() ePHPm sees is a different number. The lookup misses and every thread looks untagged. So the loader writes the {dev, ino} of /proc/self/ns/pid into a one-slot nscfg map at startup. The programs then resolve the TID in that namespace:
// crates/ephpm-server/bpf/vhostnet.bpf.c static __always_inline __u32 resolve_tid(void) { __u32 zero = 0; struct nscfg_t *c = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&nscfg, &zero); if (c && c->dev) { struct bpf_pidns_info ns = {}; if (bpf_get_ns_current_pid_tgid(c->dev, c->ino, &ns, sizeof(ns)) == 0) return ns.pid; // .pid == TID in that namespace } return (__u32)bpf_get_current_pid_tgid(); // global TID (low 32 bits) } I got to re-learn this one personally while benchmarking for this post. I loaded the object with bpftool instead of ePHPm’s loader and forgot to fill nscfg. Inside WSL2 the tagged bind came back on the port I asked for. A tagged connect to a port nobody owned got Connection refused from the network stack instead of EPERM from the hook. The hooks were attached and doing nothing. Filling nscfg the way the loader does fixed it immediately:
## nscfg left empty tagged -> unowned 127.0.0.1:3307 r=-1 errno=Connection refused tagged bind 127.0.0.1:8080 -> real port 8080 ## nscfg = {dev, ino} of /proc/self/ns/pid tagged -> unowned 127.0.0.1:3307 r=-1 errno=Operation not permitted tagged bind 127.0.0.1:8080 -> real port 20000 That’s the failure mode in a nutshell. A mismatch doesn’t error out. It looks like a working box with no policy.
What connect4 decides Four programs attach to ePHPm’s own cgroup: cgroup/bind4, bind6, connect4 and connect6. They only touch the UAPI fields of struct bpf_sock_addr (user_ip4, user_ip6, user_port). That means no CO-RE relocation and no vmlinux.h. connect4 calls it loopback when the destination is 127.0.0.1, and connect6 when it’s ::1. Both then hand off to the same function. It’s short enough to show whole:
static __always_inline int do_connect(struct bpf_sock_addr *ctx, int is_loopback) { __u32 *vhostp = current_vhost(); if (!vhostp) return 1; // untagged: connect unchanged __u32 vhost = *vhostp; if (!is_loopback) return 1; // non-loopback egress handled by the per-vhost allowlist layer __u32 dport = bpf_ntohs(ctx->user_port); // 1) Virtual port for this vhost -> rewrite to its private real port. __u64 key = ((__u64)vhost << 32) | dport; __u32 *rport = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&assigned, &key); if (rport) { ctx->user_port = bpf_htons((__u16)*rport); return 1; } // 2) Shared ePHPm infra port (MySQL wire, KV RESP) -> always allow. if (bpf_map_lookup_elem(&infra_ports, &dport)) return 1; // 3) Direct connect to a real port -> authorize by ownership. struct owner_t *o = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&port_owner, &dport); if (o) return (o->vhost == vhost) ? 1 : 0; // own sidecar allow; cross-vhost DENY // 4) Unowned loopback port: DENY for managed vhosts. This is the loopback // floor that REPLACES the static nft loopback-drop for tagged traffic. return 0; } Returning 0 from a cgroup sockaddr program fails the syscall with EPERM. Step 4 is the important one. It’s the loopback floor. A tagged tenant can’t reach a loopback port that it doesn’t own and that isn’t infra. That includes ePHPm’s own HTTP listener and whatever else the box runs on localhost.
Read that comment on the non-loopback branch carefully, though. It says public egress is “handled by the per-vhost allowlist layer”. There is no per-vhost allowlist layer. The roadmap’s phase 1 described one. What shipped passes every non-loopback connect straight through to whatever the operator’s nftables table does. That table is per-uid. So the eBPF policy is a per-tenant loopback policy. More on that below.
The tag is also only written in fpm mode with sites_dir set. validate() rejects ebpf_policy = true off Linux, without sites_dir, and in worker mode. Worker mode’s persistent loop would need per-event tagging inside the PSR-7 envelope. That isn’t built.
Every tenant gets its own :8080 The bind side is what makes sidecars usable. When a tagged thread binds, bind4 does three things:
pops a free port from a pool ePHPm owns rewrites the bind to it records who owns it The app asked for 127.0.0.1:8080 and the socket really lands on :20000. When the same tenant later connects to :8080, step 1 above rewrites the destination to :20000. Another tenant binding :8080 gets :20001. Neither app knows anything happened.
// Idempotent rebind: same (vhost, vport) reuses its real port. __u32 *ex = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&assigned, &key); if (ex) { ctx->user_port = bpf_htons((__u16)*ex); return 1; } // Per-vhost quota (anti port-bomb), enforced in-kernel on the tag. __u32 *cntp = bpf_map_lookup_elem(&sidecar_count, &vhost); __u32 cnt = cntp ? *cntp : 0; if (cnt >= quota_max()) return 0; // DENY: this vhost is at its sidecar cap __u32 rport = 0; if (bpf_map_pop_elem(&port_pool, &rport) != 0) return 0; // DENY: pool exhausted (box-wide sidecar cap reached) The pool is a BPF_MAP_TYPE_QUEUE. The loader fills it from sidecar_port_range (default 20000-32767) at startup. Allocating is an O(1) pop with no scan. Before filling it, the loader reads net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range and refuses to start if the ranges overlap. Otherwise an outbound connect could get an ephemeral source port that ePHPm also wants to hand out as a sidecar port.
The part that didn’t make it is giving ports back. Returning a port to the pool when a listener closes needs one of two things:
a cgroup/sock_release program that reads the socket’s source port (the verifier rejects that read on 6.18) a BPF_MAP_TYPE_SK_STORAGE map to hang ownership on the socket (aya 0.13 can’t load that map type) So ports and per-vhost counts come back only when the process exits. The assigned map keeps a rebind of the same virtual port idempotent. A sidecar that restarts on :8080 doesn’t burn a second slot. A tenant that cycles through many different ports will hit its max_sidecar_ports_per_vhost cap (default 8) until ePHPm restarts. The code comments and the guide say that’s coming in v0.8.2. v0.8.5 is out and it still isn’t there, because neither blocker has moved.
Watching it work There’s no automated test in the repo yet that loads these programs. They need root and a writable cgroup v2 hierarchy. Nothing in CI has either. So I did it by hand:
