Multiply that by your request rate and MySQL spends a real share of its time authenticating clients it just said goodbye to.
ePHPm puts a pooling proxy in the same process as PHP. PHP connects to 127.0.0.1:3306 exactly like it would to MySQL. The proxy lends it a connection that’s already authenticated. This post covers how that works and what “smart” reset means. It also covers the two bugs that made the default configuration unusable until June, and then again until this month. It ends with some numbers on what it does to the database.
The proxy in 30 seconds Configuration is a URL and a listen address:
[db.mysql] url = "mysql://app:secret@db.internal:3306/app" listen = "127.0.0.1:3306" min_connections = 2 max_connections = 20 reset_strategy = "smart" # or "always" / "never" When PHP connects, the proxy doesn’t touch the backend at all for the handshake. It sends PHP a synthetic HandshakeV10 built from the real server’s saved metadata and a fresh challenge. It reads PHP’s HandshakeResponse41 and answers OK. It doesn’t validate the credentials. The listener is meant for loopback, and the docs say in bold not to bind it anywhere else. The real credentials only ever travel on the pool’s own connections to MySQL. Those support both mysql_native_password and caching_sha2_password, including the RSA full-auth path for MySQL 8’s default plugin.
Then the proxy checks out a pooled backend and relays packets in both directions until PHP’s session ends.
What has to be reset, and when A pooled connection carries session state from whoever used it last. That includes user variables, SET SESSION changes, temp tables and prepared statements. It also includes an open transaction and LAST_INSERT_ID(). Handing that to the next PHP request is how you get the worst kind of bug. That’s the one where request B sees request A’s data. MySQL 5.7 added COM_RESET_CONNECTION for exactly this. It’s one packet (0x1F) and one OK back, and the session is clean without re-authenticating.
/// Resets: transaction state, user variables, prepared statements, temporary /// tables, and `LAST_INSERT_ID()`. Available since MySQL 5.7. async fn reset_connection(mut stream: TcpStream) -> Result<TcpStream, DbError> { // COM_RESET_CONNECTION = 0x1F, sequence = 0. write_packet(&mut stream, 0, &[0x1F]).await?; let (_, resp) = read_packet(&mut stream).await?; if resp.first() != Some(&0x00) { return Err(DbError::Protocol("COM_RESET_CONNECTION did not return OK".into())); } Ok(stream) } That’s a round trip. The three strategies are about when to pay it:
always: reset every connection when the session ends. It’s correct and costs one extra round trip per PHP request. never: park the connection as-is. It’s the fastest, and only safe if you control every query that runs (dev boxes). smart (the default): track a dirty bit per session and reset only if something could have changed state. The dirty tracking happens in the relay loop. That loop already has to parse packet boundaries. More on why below. Each command PHP sends gets classified:
let writeish = match cmd { 0x0E /* COM_PING */ => false, COM_QUERY => { let sql = std::str::from_utf8(&payload[1..]).unwrap_or(""); !matches!(classify_mysql_query(sql), QueryKind::Read) } _ => true, }; if writeish { dirty_w.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed); } and classify_mysql_query looks at the first keyword:
SELECT, SHOW, EXPLAIN and DESCRIBE are reads, unless the statement contains FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE. BEGIN/START and COMMIT/ROLLBACK are transaction boundaries. Everything else is treated as a write, because “unknown” has to mean “dirty.” Any command that isn’t COM_QUERY or COM_PING also marks the session dirty. That includes prepared statements and COM_INIT_DB.
When PHP’s session ends:
match outcome.backend { Some(backend) => match self.reset_strategy { ResetStrategy::Never => checkout.return_to_pool(backend), ResetStrategy::Always => checkout.return_with_reset(backend).await, ResetStrategy::Smart => { if outcome.dirty { checkout.return_with_reset(backend).await; } else { checkout.return_to_pool(backend); } } }, None => checkout.retire(), // backend broke mid-session: never recycle it } The honest limits of “smart” First-keyword classification is cheap, and it’s a heuristic. Two things it can’t see:
A SELECT with side effects. SELECT @x := 1, SELECT GET_LOCK('job', 10), SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID(42) and SELECT ... INTO @var all start with SELECT and all change session state. A session that does only that is “clean” and gets parked without a reset. The named lock case is the nasty one. The lock is held by the connection. So the next PHP request to draw it from the pool inherits a lock it never took. If your code uses GET_LOCK, use always. Most real apps are dirty on connect. WordPress’s wpdb sets the charset on every connection, and mysqlnd sends that as a SET NAMES. On a stock MySQL 8 sql_mode it also runs SET SESSION sql_mode=... to drop the modes it doesn’t support. All of that happens before its first real query. Those are writes by this definition, and correctly so, since they change session state. So for WordPress, smart behaves exactly like always. The win only shows up for code that connects and reads. Neither of these makes smart wrong as a default. But it’s not magic, and the second one is why the numbers below have two workloads.
Bug one: smart reset hung on the first query Until June, smart didn’t use the relay above. It used a per-command routing loop built for read/write splitting. That loop acquired a backend from the pool for every command. Two problems compounded (#97):
Its response forwarder stopped at the first EOF packet. In a MySQL result set that’s the one that ends the column definitions, not the rows. The rows sat unread in the backend’s buffer and the client waited forever. The first query mysql_async sends on every connection is SELECT @@max_allowed_packet,@@wait_timeout. That’s two columns and one row, which was enough. Underneath that, picking a new backend per command destroys session continuity. SET @v = 42 lands on backend A and SELECT @v on backend B. Transactions and prepared statements break the same way. Bug 1 just hid it. The integration tests only exercised always, which used a different path. The WordPress compose example had quietly shipped with reset_strategy = "always" as a workaround. That tells you how it was found. The fix was to use the per-command loop only when read/write splitting is actually on. Otherwise the proxy holds one backend for the whole client session.
Bug two: the pool served corpses on quiet sites The second one is my favorite bug of the year. It got worse the less traffic you had (#221). With the default config, a site would serve a couple of requests and then fail every request after that with MySQL server has gone away. Permanently. The number of successes tracked the pool’s warm connections. Once they were used up, every request drew a corpse.
PHP doesn’t know the proxy pools anything. At the end of every request PDO destroys its handle and mysqlnd sends COM_QUIT, which means “close this connection.” The relay classified COM_QUIT as not-dirty and then forwarded it to the backend anyway. MySQL closed the pooled connection. A clean session then parked that dead socket as healthy. The next request drew it and the write failed with a broken pipe. The error path mapped that to a successful session end and parked the corpse again.
Under load you’d never see it. A connection returned and immediately re-acquired hasn’t been noticed as closed yet. On a quiet site a connection sits idle for a moment between requests, and every one of them is dead. The fix has three parts:
COM_QUIT is intercepted and never forwarded. It ends the client session, full stop. This is also why the relay has to parse packet boundaries. There’s no correct dumb byte-copy for a pooled backend. A connection that has been idle for at least 500ms gets a COM_PING on checkout. Below that it can’t have died for any reason a ping would detect. Busy pools never pay for it. Quiet sites always do, and they’re the ones that expose dead connections. A backend that errors mid-session is retired, never re-parked. What it does to MySQL To put numbers on it I ran MySQL 8.4 in a container with three copies of the ePHPm v0.6.2 proxy in front of it, one per reset strategy. I drove them from PHP itself (ephpm php, PHP 8.4, pdo_mysql). Each “request” is new PDO, the session’s statements, then $pdo = null. There were two session shapes, 2,000 sessions each, run sequentially:
read-only: one primary-key SELECT WordPress-shaped: SET NAMES utf8mb4, SET SESSION sql_mode=..., then the same SELECT Before and after each run I read MySQL’s own counters. That’s Connections from SHOW GLOBAL STATUS, plus the statement/com/Reset Connection and statement/com/Ping counts from performance_schema.
Medians of three runs, 2,000 sessions each:
Target Session µs per session MySQL Connections COM_RESET_CONNECTION COM_PING MySQL directly read-only 479 2,000 0 0 proxy, smart read-only 467 0 0 4 proxy, always read-only 456 0 2,000 4 proxy, never read-only 470 0 0 4 MySQL directly WordPress-shaped 664 2,000 0 0 proxy, smart WordPress-shaped 816 0 2,000 4 proxy, always WordPress-shaped 822 0 2,000 4 proxy, never WordPress-shaped 834 0 0 4 (One of the three smart WordPress-shaped runs saw one new backend connection and 16 pings. The other two saw 0 and 4-5. I didn’t chase it.)
What that says, in order of how much it matters:
MySQL stopped accepting connections. There were 6,000 PHP sessions per strategy and session shape, and one new backend connection in total. That was the one odd run. The pool’s warm connections did all the work. Outside that one run MySQL never ran an authentication exchange after startup. That’s the whole point of the proxy, and it does exactly that. The four or five pings per run are mostly the four warm connections being validated on first checkout. They sat idle between runs, so that’s the quiet-site fix doing its job.
smart is only smart for read-only sessions. Read-only: zero resets. WordPress-shaped: 2,000 resets, identical to always. SET NAMES and SET SESSION sql_mode dirty every session. If you run WordPress through this proxy, smart and always are the same setting.
The reset isn’t on the client’s clock. always was no slower than smart from PHP’s point of view. The proxy sends COM_RESET_CONNECTION after PHP’s session has already ended. So the cost lands on the pool, not on the request. The connection just comes back a round trip later. Under a saturated pool that round trip would start to matter. At this load it didn’t show up at all.
On loopback, pooling doesn’t make PHP faster, and the extra hop can make it slower. This was the one I didn’t expect going in. A direct MySQL connect plus auth on loopback is cheap here. So a read-only session costs about the same either way. The WordPress-shaped session got slower through the proxy, 664 to about 820µs. Each of its three statements now crosses two sockets instead of one. That extra hop costs more than the connect it saved. Across a real network with TLS to the database, a fresh connection is several round trips before the first query. The balance should tip the other way there. But I didn’t measure that here, so I’m not going to claim a number for it.
So the honest pitch for the pool is the database side:
No connection storm when traffic spikes. No per-request auth on MySQL. A hard cap (max_connections) on how many backend connections a fleet of PHP workers can hold. Session state that can’t leak between requests. Lower request latency isn’t on that list unless your database is far away.
How I measured AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, Windows 11 + WSL2. MySQL 8.4 (docker.io/library/mysql:8.4) ran in Podman with host networking on port 3307. ePHPm v0.6.2+php8.4.23 proxies ran on 3311/3312/3313 (smart/always/never, min_connections = 4, max_connections = 20) in the Ubuntu WSL distro. The client is ephpm php bench.php <port> <profile> 2000 from the same binary. Everything is loopback on one machine, so absolute latencies are lower than over a real network. If anything, the difference between direct and pooled connects is understated. Three repetitions per cell, with medians reported. Counter deltas exclude the one connection the script uses to read them. Links ePHPm, the proxy is crates/ephpm-db #97 smart reset hang, #221 COM_QUIT and dead pooled connections MySQL COM_RESET_CONNECTION WordPress wpdb::db_connect(), which sets the charset and sql_mode on every connection

title: Clustered SQLite in ePHPm, Part 1: Replication by Sidecar
description: ePHPm first made SQLite highly available by embedding sqld as a child process. This is how that worked and the list of things that went wrong with it.
body:
Most PHP sites I have run in the last twenty years did not need a MySQL server. They needed a database, and MySQL was the one every framework spoke. With ePHPm I have been trying to get rid of that server for the common case. The piece that makes it possible is litewire. PHP connects with plain pdo_mysql. litewire speaks the MySQL wire protocol, and the queries land in a SQLite file. WordPress and Laravel don’t know the difference. No mysqld, no child processes, just ephpm and a .db file.
That works great until somebody asks the obvious question. What happens when the box dies? SQLite has no replication. This is a three-part series about how ePHPm went from “SQLite file plus a sidecar” to replication done entirely inside the process. The PHP side never changes across all three posts. Everything interesting happens behind litewire.
Part 1: Replication by sidecar with sqld (this post) Part 2: Adding Turso, one engine in-process Part 3: CDC over the cluster channel The first answer: sqld When I wanted HA in March, the shortest path was sqld. That’s libsql-server, Turso’s MIT-licensed SQLite server. It already does primary/replica replication. Replicas pull WAL frames from the primary over gRPC and forward writes back to it. I pinned v0.24.32 and the first wiring landed on 2026-03-30. The initial commit (“single node sqld”) got reverted 17 minutes later. “clustering sqld” landed that night. That should have been a hint about how this was going to go.
The thing I care about most in ePHPm is the single binary, so sqld had to be inside it. The release build downloads the sqld binary. A build.rs copies it into OUT_DIR so include_bytes!() can embed it:
fn main() { println!("cargo::rustc-check-cfg=cfg(sqld_embedded)"); println!("cargo::rerun-if-env-changed=SQLD_BINARY_PATH"); if let Ok(path) = std::env::var("SQLD_BINARY_PATH") { let src = std::path::Path::new(&path); assert!(src.exists(), "SQLD_BINARY_PATH points to non-existent file: {path}"); let out_dir = std::env::var("OUT_DIR").expect("OUT_DIR not set"); let dest = std::path::Path::new(&out_dir).join("sqld"); std::fs::copy(src, &dest).expect("failed to copy sqld binary to OUT_DIR"); println!("cargo::rustc-cfg=sqld_embedded"); println!("cargo::rustc-env=SQLD_BINARY_PATH={}", dest.display()); } } #[cfg(sqld_embedded)] static SQLD_BINARY: &[u8] = include_bytes!(env!("SQLD_BINARY_PATH")); At startup the clustered path does a few steps:
writes those bytes to a temp file and marks it executable spawns it as a child process polls its /health endpoint hands litewire a different backend Single-node mode used rusqlite in-process. Clustered mode swapped litewire’s backend to a Hrana HTTP client pointed at the local sqld:
let mut backend = litewire::backend::HranaClient::new(&sqld_http_url); So “single binary” was technically true. It was a single binary with another binary inside it. There were now two modes running two different engines. rusqlite ran one node and sqld ran a cluster. That split is the seed of everything in Parts 2 and 3.
sqld doesn’t elect anybody sqld knows how to be a primary or a replica. It does not decide which one it is. That is your problem. ePHPm already had a gossip layer for the KV store. That’s chitchat, scuttlebutt-style anti-entropy with a phi-accrual failure detector. The election went on top of it. The lowest-ordinal alive node wins. The winner writes a claim into the gossip KV at sqlite:primary and refreshes it every 5 seconds. The claim has a 10 second TTL.
/// Gossip KV key for the primary node identity. const PRIMARY_KEY: &str = "sqlite:primary"; /// How often the primary refreshes its claim. const HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5); /// TTL for the primary claim. If not refreshed, the key expires and /// triggers re-election. const PRIMARY_TTL: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10); The claim value is just node_id|grpc_addr. When the role changes, a watcher task restarts sqld with new arguments. On Unix that means SIGTERM and a wait of up to 5 seconds. If it’s still there it gets SIGKILL, and then it spawns again:
pub async fn restart(&mut self, new_role: SqldRole) -> anyhow::Result<()> { self.stop_child().await?; self.role = new_role; self.child = spawn_child(&self.temp_path, &self.config, &self.role)?; Ok(()) } That’s a failover. Kill a process and start it again with different flags. It works, in the sense that each piece does what it says. The rest of this post is the list of ways it didn’t work. That list is the reason the next two posts exist.
Failure 1: async replication loses data on failover sqld replicas pull frames from the primary. Say the primary committed a write and acknowledged it to PHP but hadn’t shipped it yet. That write is gone when the primary dies and a replica gets promoted. That’s the nature of async replication. It’s not a sqld bug, but it is a real window and it was mine to document.
Failure 2: no Windows There is no sqld build for Windows. ePHPm runs on Windows (I spend a lot of time making sure it does). Clustered SQLite was simply a startup error there:
#[cfg(target_os = "windows")] { anyhow::bail!( "clustered SQLite (sqld sidecar) is not supported on Windows. \ Use single-node mode (remove [db.sqlite.replication] or set role = \"auto\" \ without clustering), or run on Linux/macOS/WSL." ); } Failure 3: replica mode had never started This one stings. In July I built a two-node comparison fixture to measure sqld against the new Turso path (Part 2). The sqld half wouldn’t come up. sqld’s CLI rejects --grpc-listen-addr combined with --primary-grpc-url, and ePHPm was passing both to replicas. Every two-node bringup had died at spawn. The fix (#189) was a few lines:
match role { SqldRole::Primary => { cmd.arg("--grpc-listen-addr").arg(&config.grpc_listen); } SqldRole::Replica { primary_grpc_url } => { // sqld rejects --grpc-listen-addr when --primary-grpc-url is // set. A replica syncs from the primary and does not serve // WAL frames to further replicas in this topology. cmd.arg("--primary-grpc-url").arg(primary_grpc_url); } } The fix is boring. What it says isn’t. The feature had unit tests, an election, docs, and config. It had never once run with two nodes. “Implemented” and “exercised” are different words. I had been using them as if they were the same.
Failure 4: the control plane was open A security audit pass in late July (#201) found three things. All of them were rooted in the same threat model, a plaintext and unauthenticated cluster control plane:
Empty secret meant plaintext. With [cluster] secret unset, gossip and the KV data plane ran unauthenticated. The only sign was a startup warning. Any host on the network could forge KV writes: sessions, rate-limit counters, ACME keys. Now clustering refuses to start without a secret unless you set allow_insecure_no_auth = true on purpose. Forged primary claims. Replicas dialed whatever grpc_addr was in the gossip claim. Inject a claim and you could point every replica at an attacker’s sqld. Claims are now validated against live gossip membership before anyone dials them. The check is by host, since gossip and gRPC use different ports on the same machine. Predictable extraction path. The embedded binary was written to temp_dir()/ephpm-sqld-<pid>, then chmodded and executed. Classic symlink race on a shared /tmp. It now goes into a fresh 0700 directory from mkdtemp, created with O_EXCL. None of these are sqld’s fault either. They are what happens when you bolt a process manager and an election onto a gossip layer that was designed for cache keys.
Failure 5: the write cliff This is the one that ended it. For v0.6.0 I benchmarked four lanes. They were rusqlite and Turso, each single-node and clustered. Everything ran on one machine with --cpus 1 per node and one autocommit INSERT per request. Here’s what the clustered sqld lane did as concurrent writers went up (issue #217):
writers RPS p50 p99 HTTP 500s 1 458 2.12 ms 2.99 ms 0 2 635 3.04 ms 4.63 ms 0 4 744 (peak) 4.99 ms 12.96 ms 2 8 453 9.6 ms 29.8 ms 8 16 37 20.4 ms 5.04 s 0 It peaked at four writers and dropped to half that at eight. At sixteen it fell over. In the release-build run, the c=16 cell completed zero requests in both 20 second reps. When there was an error, it looked like this:
SQLSTATE[HY000]: General error: 1205 SQLite error: [SQLITE_BUSY] database is locked That is SQLite’s single write lock. Add an HTTP round trip from litewire to sqld for every statement and a busy timeout that runs out. Mostly, though, there were no errors. Look at the 500 column at c=16: zero. The requests hung. The primary logged nothing, with no busy line and no timeout. A health check watching for 5xx would have called that node healthy while it served nobody.
Every other lane got faster with more writers. Single-node rusqlite went 648 to 1130 RPS from c=1 to c=16. The clustered Turso lane went 558 to 876. sqld was the only one that went off a cliff.
The band-aid that proved the point For the 0.6.x line I added write admission control (#222). It’s a semaphore in front of the Hrana backend, [db.sqlite.sqld] write_permits. Reads never take a permit. With the knob unset, c=8 and c=16 completed nothing. With write_permits = 1:
write_permits c=1 c=4 c=8 c=16 0 (default) 442-455 118-552 0 completed 0 completed 1 415-445 561-595 527-593 551-598 8 444-451 232-266 0 completed 0 completed (Ranges are across two reps and two separate cluster bring-ups, from the PR.) One permit fixed it. That means one write at a time. Eight permits sits above the cliff and reproduces it exactly. The best fix I could ship for clustered writes was to stop doing them concurrently. That is a useful knob and a terrible architecture.
Where that left things Count the moving parts in the diagram above. Gossip on UDP 7946. The KV data plane on TCP 7947. sqld gRPC between nodes. Hrana HTTP between litewire and sqld on every node. A child process per node with its own lifecycle, extracted from bytes inside the main binary. Two engines depending on whether the config said [cluster]. No Windows. And concurrent writes needed a semaphore set to 1.
A sidecar means another process, another protocol hop, and another failure domain. WAL plus a busy timeout doesn’t hold up under concurrent writers. The same benchmark that drew the cliff above had a fourth lane in it. That was Turso with in-process change data capture. It sustained 876 RPS at c=16 on the same fixture. That’s Part 2.
Links ePHPm: github.com/ephpm/ephpm, litewire: github.com/ephpm/litewire sqld / libsql-server: github.com/tursodatabase/libsql #189 fix(sqld): omit –grpc-listen-addr for replicas #201 Harden cluster/sqld control plane #216 Turso vs SQLite performance, measured #217 Clustered SQLite (sqld) collapses under concurrent writes #222 sqld write admission control Two-node fixture: github.com/ephpm/turso-cluster-e2e

title: Atomic File Replacement on NTFS Is Not rename + fsync
description: The Unix recipe for durable atomic file replacement doesn't translate to Windows. This is what shipmates uses instead, plus the delete-pending window that made an 8-way test fail only when the whole suite ran.
body:
shipmates writes a lot of small state files that other processes read. Voyage plans and state, tracker files. Each of them has to be replaced atomically, so a reader sees the old file or the new one and never half of each. Each also has to be replaced durably. When the function returns success, a power cut doesn’t take it back. Every Unix programmer knows the recipe for that. It doesn’t work on Windows, and the reasons are more interesting than “Windows is different”.
The Unix recipe Write the new content to a temp file in the same directory, fsync it, rename it over the target, then fsync the directory:
//go:build unix func DurableRename(oldpath, newpath string) error { if err := os.Rename(oldpath, newpath); err != nil { return err } d, err := os.Open(filepath.Clean(filepath.Dir(newpath))) if err != nil { return err } if err := d.Sync(); err != nil { _ = d.Close() return err } return d.Close() } The directory fsync is the step people forget. rename(2) is atomic for other observers. But the new directory entry is just metadata in the page cache until the directory itself is flushed. ext4’s default data=ordered doesn’t promise otherwise. Crash between the rename and the flush and you can lose a file you reported as written.
Neither half translates On Windows, os.Rename is MoveFileEx with MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING and without MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH. It can return before the change reaches the disk. Fine, flush the directory afterwards like on Unix. Except a straight port doesn’t:
1) dir.Sync(): sync .\ntfs-4015850362: Access is denied. That’s os.Open on a directory followed by Sync(), on NTFS, Windows 11, Go 1.26.5. Sync() is FlushFileBuffers, which requires a handle with GENERIC_WRITE. os.Open hands you a read-only one. NTFS itself is fine with flushing a directory. Open it yourself with CreateFile, GENERIC_READ|GENERIC_WRITE and FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS, and FlushFileBuffers on that handle succeeds. I checked both on this box. The read-only handle gets error 5 and the read-write one flushes. So the portable code, as written, has two bad options:
ignore the error and silently drop the durability guarantee return it and report failure for a write that landed The working version is Windows-only code with its own CreateFile call. Once you’re writing Windows-only code there’s a better primitive.
One call instead of two Windows has a primitive that covers both halves. MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH is documented to not return until the move has been flushed to disk. On NTFS a rename is a single logged metadata transaction, so flushing it commits the new directory entry along with it. From 416665e:
//go:build windows func DurableRename(oldpath, newpath string) error { from, err := windows.UTF16PtrFromString(oldpath) if err != nil { return err } to, err := windows.UTF16PtrFromString(newpath) if err != nil { return err } deadline := time.Now().Add(2 * time.Second) for { err = windows.MoveFileEx(from, to, windows.MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING|windows.MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH) if err == nil { return nil } transient := errors.Is(err, windows.ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED) || errors.Is(err, windows.ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION) if !transient || time.Now().After(deadline) { return err } time.Sleep(5 * time.Millisecond) } } Unix needs two ordered operations to make one rename durable. Windows needs one, and no extra handle to the directory. Both paths have to be on the same volume. Across volumes, MoveFileEx degrades to copy-then-delete, which is neither atomic nor what any caller wants. Every caller in shipmates stages its temp file in the destination directory, so that holds.
That retry loop is the second half of the story.
Losing a race on NTFS Voyage state publication in shipmates is deliberately retry-idempotent. It’s legal for several processes to publish the same successor state at once. TestMigrateSuccessorConcurrentPublicationAndAtomicRetry does exactly that, with eight goroutines racing MigrateSuccessor onto the same output path.
On Unix the losers just replace the winner’s file. That’s fine because it has the same content. On NTFS the replace-existing path has to get rid of the old target. While the winner’s replace is in flight the old file sits in a delete-pending state. A loser that shows up during that window doesn’t wait. It fails with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (or ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION).
To see how common that is, I wrote a small experiment. It runs 200 rounds of eight goroutines. Each one has its own staged and fsynced 4 KiB temp file. They’re released at once to MoveFileEx(REPLACE_EXISTING|WRITE_THROUGH) onto the same target, with no retries:
3) 200 rounds x 8 concurrent replacers, no retry: ok 442 (27.6%) ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED 1158 (72.4%) A second run gave 386 ok and 1214 ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (75.9%). So with eight concurrent replacers, roughly three out of four lose. That’s why DurableRename treats exactly those two errors as transient and retries. Anything else is a real error and comes back to the caller. So do the same errors past the deadline. A genuine permission problem still surfaces.
Two seconds wasn’t enough The original deadline in both DurableRename and voyage’s PublishSuccessor was 2 seconds. The 8-way test passed on its own. It failed with Access is denied only when the whole repository’s tests ran at once. 144af92 explains why. The delete-pending window lasts as long as the winner’s fsync-heavy write takes. Under a fully loaded test suite that was observed above 9 seconds. The fix bumped DurableRename to 15 s and PublishSuccessor to 60 s, still only for classified contention errors:
func PublishSuccessor(path string, state *State, plan *Plan, hash string) (*State, error) { deadline := time.Now().Add(60 * time.Second) for { published, err := publishSuccessorOnce(path, state, plan, hash) if err == nil || !transientFSContention(err) || time.Now().After(deadline) { // ... On Unix transientFSContention is simply return false.
I wanted to see the window move with disk load on my own box. The experiment’s last part runs the same 8-way race with the retry loop (15 s deadline, 5 ms sleep). It records how long each process waited before its replace succeeded. I ran fifty rounds on an idle disk. Then I ran fifty more while 16 goroutines write, fsync and delete 1 MiB files in the same directory:
4) retry loop, 0 background fsync writers: n=400 failed=0 p50=14.523ms p99=38.7054ms max=39.3047ms 4) retry loop, 16 background fsync writers: n=400 failed=0 p50=54.2497ms p99=4.4599868s max=5.4956314s and the second run:
4) retry loop, 0 background fsync writers: n=400 failed=0 p50=15.3158ms p99=134.9333ms max=204.3097ms 4) retry loop, 16 background fsync writers: n=400 failed=0 p50=51.0538ms p99=1.7362467s max=4.486713s On an idle disk the worst wait was 39 ms in one run and 204 ms in the other. With the disk busy, the tail went past 4 seconds in both runs. That’s more than double the old 2 second deadline. My 16-writer load is a toy next to a full go test ./... on a big repo. So the 9 second observation from the commit doesn’t surprise me. The median barely moves, which is exactly why this hid. Most of the time the window is short. A deadline sized from “most of the time” fails under load.
What about the cost of write-through? I also timed 500 renames each way with the same staging work. At the median I couldn’t separate them. Both were about 0.52 ms in the first run. The second run’s plain-rename median landed below the timer’s resolution. Write-through had the fatter tail in both runs (p99 1.05 ms vs 0.67 ms, then 19 ms vs 1 ms). At this scale and with this timer that’s not a number I’d hang much on. For small state files that are written once per task, write-through isn’t the thing to optimize.
Takeaways On Windows, durable atomic replace is one call: MoveFileEx(MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING | MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH). Don’t port the directory fsync. os.Open(dir).Sync() fails with Access is denied. Making it work means opening the directory for write with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS, which you don’t need. Concurrent replacers of one file on NTFS see ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED / ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION from the winner’s delete-pending file. Retry those two specifically, and nothing else. Size retry windows for a saturated disk, not an idle one. If a test fails only when the whole suite runs, the suite is the load test you didn’t know you had. How I measured A standalone Go program (Go 1.26.5, golang.org/x/sys/windows) on Windows 11 Pro, AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, 128 GB RAM. The files were on the system NTFS volume (an ADATA LEGEND 860 SSD) under my user temp directory. The program creates a fresh directory, then runs four steps:
os.Open(dir).Sync(). 500 staged 4 KiB replacements each with MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING and with |MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH, timing only the MoveFileEx call. 200 rounds of 8 goroutines replacing the same target with no retry. 50 rounds of the same race with DurableRename’s retry loop. First with no background load, then with 16 goroutines continuously writing, fsyncing and deleting 1 MiB files in the same directory. I ran it twice back to back. Both runs are shown above. Separately, I opened a directory with CreateFileW and FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS twice, once GENERIC_READ and once GENERIC_READ|GENERIC_WRITE. Then I called FlushFileBuffers on each. The first fails with error 5 and the second succeeds.
Links 416665e: DurableRename 144af92: sizing the contention windows for a saturated disk MoveFileExW (Microsoft Learn) FlushFileBuffers (Microsoft Learn)

title: Gossip-Based Clustering for PHP Apps
description: How ePHPm servers find each other, share data and handle a server joining or leaving. It also measures how fast a write reaches the other servers and covers a bug I found while measuring it.
body:
Most PHP developers never touch clustering primitives. That’s by design. PHP is share-nothing. Each request starts from zero, and anything shared lives somewhere else. Sessions go in Redis. Cache goes in Redis or Memcached. Locks go in Redis. When you run two app servers, the “cluster” is really two stateless boxes pointed at the same Redis. That works until Redis is the thing you’re trying not to run.
ePHPm has its own KV store in the same process as PHP. On one node that’s straightforward. On three nodes behind a load balancer, a session written on node 1 has to be readable on node 3. That means the nodes have to know about each other and agree on where data lives. This post is how that works as of v0.5.2, including the parts I’m not happy with yet.
No coordinator The first decision was what not to use. etcd and Consul are the standard answers for membership, and they’re both very good. They’re also another cluster to deploy, secure, back up and upgrade. That’s precisely the operational weight ePHPm exists to remove. Raft-based anything also means a quorum. A two-node ePHPm deployment is common for small sites, and it can’t have a meaningful one.
So membership is gossip. Every node runs Quickwit’s chitchat crate. It’s often lumped in with SWIM, and ePHPm’s own source comments call it that. But it’s actually scuttlebutt-style anti-entropy. Each node owns a small key/value state. Nodes periodically exchange digests of what versions they’ve seen and send each other only the deltas. Liveness comes from a phi-accrual failure detector on heartbeats rather than SWIM’s ping/ping-req probing. For ePHPm’s purposes the important properties are the same:
There’s no leader. Any node can be a seed. A node that disappears gets marked dead without anyone coordinating it. Starting it is a config block:
[cluster] enabled = true bind = "10.0.0.11:7946" join = ["10.0.0.11:7946"] secret = "a-long-random-string" [cluster.kv] small_key_threshold = 512 # bytes: <= rides gossip, > goes to the data plane replication_factor = 2 data_port = 7947 and wrapping chitchat is about thirty lines:
let chitchat_config = ChitchatConfig { chitchat_id: ChitchatId::new(node_id.clone(), generation_id, listen_addr), cluster_id: config.cluster_id.clone(), gossip_interval: Duration::from_secs(1), listen_addr, seed_nodes: config.join.clone(), failure_detector_config: FailureDetectorConfig::default(), marked_for_deletion_grace_period: Duration::from_secs(60), catchup_callback: None, extra_liveness_predicate: None, }; let handle = if encrypted { let transport = EncryptedUdpTransport::new(&config.secret); spawn_chitchat(chitchat_config, vec![], &transport).await } else { spawn_chitchat(chitchat_config, vec![], &UdpTransport).await } .context("failed to spawn chitchat gossip")?; The generation_id is the start time in seconds. A node that restarts with the same node_id is recognized as a new incarnation instead of a zombie.
Gossip is authenticated or it doesn’t start Gossip over plaintext UDP means anyone who can send a packet to port 7946 can join your cluster and write keys into it. When secret is set, both the gossip datagrams and the TCP data plane are sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Each plane gets its own key, derived from the secret via HKDF-SHA256. The info strings are "ephpm-gossip-v1" and "ephpm-kv-data-v1". Datagrams that fail authentication are dropped silently. A node with the wrong secret is simply invisible.
chitchat’s transport trait sends and receives typed messages with serialization inside the socket. There’s no byte-level hook to wrap. So the encrypted transport owns its own UDP socket and mirrors chitchat’s UdpTransport. It seals after serialization and opens before deserialization.
As of late July an empty secret is a hard startup error when clustering is on (#201). You can still opt out with allow_insecure_no_auth = true, and you get a loud warning for it. Failing closed is the right default for something that replicates session data.
Two tiers, because gossip is the wrong place for big values chitchat state is String -> String. Every node gets a copy of every other node’s state. That’s perfect for small things everybody needs. Think sessions, counters, rate-limit buckets and feature flags. It also fits the “this vhost’s OPcache version changed” key that ephpm deploy writes. It’s a terrible place for a 40 KB rendered page fragment. That would be replicated to every node, encoded into gossip deltas and resent to anyone catching up.
So ClusteredStore::set splits on size:
pub async fn set(&self, key: String, value: Vec<u8>, ttl: Option<Duration>) -> bool { if value.len() <= self.config.small_key_threshold { // Gossip tier: replicate to all nodes. self.cluster.gossip_set(&key, &value, ttl).await; if self.config.hot_key_cache { self.maybe_bump_hot_version(&key).await; } return true; } // Large value: write to the replica set (primary + N-1 peers). let ok = self.set_large(&key, &value, ttl).await; if ok && self.config.hot_key_cache { self.maybe_bump_hot_version(&key).await; } ok } The gossip tier stores each value in the writing node’s chitchat state as "{expiry_ms}:{write_ms}:{base64}". A read on any node scans its own state and every live peer’s for that key. It takes the entry with the highest write_ms. If two nodes write the same session at nearly the same time, the later write wins everywhere once gossip settles. Deletes are a tombstone value ("TS:{write_ms}") rather than chitchat’s own delete. chitchat doesn’t fire its change subscription on a real delete, so peers would never hear about it. That was #165 in July. Before it, a delete on one node quietly didn’t propagate.
write_ms is the origin node’s wall clock. That’s a real limitation. With enough clock skew between nodes, “last writer wins” means “writer with the fastest clock wins.” Run NTP. For sessions and caches that’s an acceptable model. It wouldn’t be for a bank ledger, and nobody should put one in a PHP cache.
The data plane is a small length-prefixed TCP protocol on port 7947. Each message is [op][key_len][key], plus [value_len][value] for a SET. Large values are written to an owner node and replicated to replication_factor - 1 more. ClusteredStore::get checks gossip, then the local store, then a local hot-key cache. Finally it asks the owner, falling back to the replicas in order if the owner is down:
for node in self.replica_nodes(key).await { if node.id == self_id { continue; // we'd have served it from the local store already } let Some(addr) = node_data_addr(&node, self.config.data_port) else { continue }; match crate::kv_data_plane::fetch_remote(addr, key, self.cipher.as_deref()).await { Ok(Some(value)) => { self.track_remote_fetch(key, &value); return Some(value); } Ok(None) | Err(_) => continue, } } track_remote_fetch is the hot-key cache. If the same node fetches the same remote key five times in ten seconds, it keeps a local copy for up to 30 seconds. The owner publishes a version counter for hot keys through gossip. A bump invalidates every cached copy. That handles the “every node hammers the owner for the homepage fragment” case without a client-side cache library.
Where a key lives: hash % nodes Here’s the part I’m least happy with. The owner of a large key is:
let start = (key_hash as usize) % n; // n = number of alive nodes, sorted by node id // replicas: the next factor-1 nodes after start, wrapping around The docs and a couple of my own notes call this a “hash ring,” and it isn’t one. It’s modulo over the sorted list of alive nodes. That’s simple and correct while membership is stable. When membership changes, it moves almost everything. I measured how many of 200,000 keys change owner when one node joins. I compared that rule to a textbook consistent-hash ring with 160 virtual nodes per node:
Join hash % n ring, 160 vnodes ideal (1/n) 2 → 3 66.8% 30.8% 33.3% 3 → 4 75.0% 23.0% 25.0% 4 → 5 79.9% 19.7% 20.0% 8 → 9 89.0% 10.0% 11.1% Going from three nodes to four, three quarters of the large keys get a new owner. There’s another honest caveat in the code. Replication happens only at write time, and there’s no anti-entropy or rebalancing for the data plane. Combine the two and a membership change means most large values look like cache misses until they’re rewritten. For a cache that’s a performance event, not data loss. The gossip tier isn’t affected at all, because every node has every small value. But it’s the wrong behavior for a rolling deploy, and a ring is not much code. That one’s on the list.
There’s a second, smaller trap in the same function. hash_key uses Rust’s DefaultHasher. The standard library explicitly doesn’t promise to keep its algorithm stable across releases. Every node in a cluster today runs the same binary, so they agree. Two ePHPm versions built with different Rust toolchains might not agree in the middle of a rolling upgrade. A fixed hash (FNV or xxHash) costs nothing and removes the question.
What a write actually costs The other question everyone asks about gossip is “how long until node 3 sees it?” I ran three nodes from the v0.5.2 release binary on one machine, on separate ports with encryption on. I wrote a 100-byte value with SET on node 1 and polled GET on node 3 every millisecond until it showed up. I did that 60 times, with a random 0.1 to 1.1 second gap between writes:
ms after SET returned fastest 1.7 median 385 p90 789 slowest 833 That’s gossip doing exactly what it’s configured to do. Every node gossips with a peer once per gossip_interval, which is 1 second. A write becomes visible on the next exchange that carries it. That’s anywhere from “right now” to just under a second later. The spread is close to uniform across that window, which is what you’d expect. Eventually consistent, on the order of a second.
The random gap matters, by the way. My first run used a fixed 300ms pause between writes. All but one of 40 samples came back at almost exactly 700ms. The loop period had locked onto the 1 second gossip tick. I was measuring my own benchmark’s phase, not the cluster. If you measure anything that runs on a timer, randomize when you poke it.
In practice, say PHP writes a session on node 1 and the load balancer sends the very next request to node 3. That request can miss it. Sticky sessions on the load balancer are still a good idea for login flows.
The large-value path has a gap I meant to time large values the same way and couldn’t. The reason is worth writing down. Two things got in the way.
The first is my test rig. A node finds a peer’s data plane at the peer’s gossip IP plus its own data_port. So every node in a cluster has to use the same port, which you can’t do with three processes on one IP. That’s a fine assumption for real deployments with one node per host. It’s just not one for a laptop.
The second is not my rig. Reading the code to figure out the first problem, I found that v0.5.2’s RESP listener and PHP’s native ephpm_kv_* functions read the node’s local Store directly. Writes go through a replication hook into ClusteredStore, so large values do get written to their owner and replica. But the read-through above lives in ClusteredStore::get, and neither RESP nor PHP calls it. A large value is readable on the nodes that hold a copy. Everywhere else it’s a cache miss. With replication_factor = 2 on a three-node cluster, that’s one node in three missing every large key it doesn’t own.
For a cache that’s a miss, not corruption. But it means the two-tier picture above is accurate for writes and only half true for reads. Wiring a read-through into Store is the next thing on the clustering list, ahead of the ring. That’s a “fetch from the cluster on miss” hook next to the existing write hook.
Why this is unusual for PHP None of this is new in distributed systems. What’s unusual is having it inside the PHP runtime. As far as I can tell, FrankenPHP, RoadRunner and Swoole all leave anything shared between nodes to an external store like Redis or Memcached. With ePHPm, PHP code calls ephpm_kv_set() and the cluster handles the rest. It can also talk RESP to localhost with an existing Redis client. There’s no extra daemon and no new protocol for the app to learn. The same gossip channel already carries cluster-wide OPcache invalidation for deploys. It’s also what the clustered SQLite work is being built on.
So here’s the list, in order:
A read-through hook so RESP and PHP reads can reach the owner. A real ring and a stable hash. Some form of handoff so a membership change doesn’t look like a cache flush. How I measured Remap numbers: a small Go program with 200,000 keys named session:<i>. Hashing is FNV-1a with a splitmix64 finalizer. Nodes are named node-00 to node-08 and sorted by name, like ePHPm sorts node ids. The modulo rule is ePHPm’s. The ring is a standard 160-vnode ring. The point is the shape, which doesn’t depend on the hash function. Convergence: ePHPm v0.5.2 (linux-x86_64, PHP 8.4.23) as three processes on one Ubuntu WSL2 box (Ryzen 9 5950X). Gossip ran on loopback with secret set and default [cluster.kv] settings. Nodes 2 and 3 were seeded from node 1. A small Go RESP client wrote to node 1 and polled node 3 every millisecond, with a random 100 to 1100ms gap between writes. Loopback has no real network latency, so on a real network add a round trip or two. Links ePHPm, clustering lives in crates/ephpm-cluster chitchat Scuttlebutt paper: Efficient Reconciliation and Flow Control for Anti-Entropy Protocols The φ Accrual Failure Detector #165 replicate deletes and TTL updates, #201 mandatory cluster secret

title: Rescuing a Windows Dynamic Disk Over USB with WSL2 and USB/IP
description: Windows refused to bring an old dynamic disk online over USB. Handing the raw USB device to WSL2's Linux kernel with usbipd-win got every file back.
body:
I pulled a 1 TB NVMe out of an old Windows box, dropped it in a USB enclosure and plugged it in. Windows showed nothing. No drive letter, no “initialize this disk” prompt, nothing in Explorer. Disk Management listed it as Invalid. The enclosure’s booklet said to “bring the disk online”, which silently did nothing. The data was completely intact. Windows was refusing on policy grounds, not because anything was broken. Getting it back meant going around the Windows storage stack entirely. I handed the raw USB device to a Linux kernel that doesn’t share Windows’ opinions.
The setup Drive: WD SN550 1 TB, the old D: from a previous Windows install Enclosure: Sabrent NVMe to USB, Realtek RTL9210 bridge (0bda:9210) Host: Windows 11 build 26200, WSL2 with Ubuntu, usbipd-win 5.3.0 Five tools, four answers The most useful part of the diagnosis was that the Windows storage tools disagree with each other. The disagreement is the clue:
Tool What it says Explorer nothing at all Disk Management present, Invalid, “Online” does nothing, no error dialog Get-Disk / Get-Volume disk not listed at all Get-CimInstance Win32_DiskDrive disk listed, partitions listed, Status OK diskpart → list disk Invalid, and the Dyn column is flagged Win32_DiskDrive is the old WMI view that sits close to the raw device. Get-Disk is the modern Storage Management provider (MSFT_Disk). The disk exists at the bottom of the stack and doesn’t exist at the top. Set-Disk -Number 1 makes the point explicitly:
The requested object could not be found. Any tool built on the modern storage API is structurally blind to this disk. Remember that. It comes back later.
Reading the partition table by hand At this point I stopped guessing. \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE<n> can be opened read-only like a file. A GPT is a simple enough structure to walk in a page of PowerShell:
a protective MBR at LBA 0 (partition type 0xEE) a header at LBA 1 that starts with EFI PART an array of 128-byte partition entries wherever the header says It’s completely non-destructive and it answers the question definitively. Here’s a version of it:
param([string]$Path = '\\.\PHYSICALDRIVE1', [int]$SectorSize = 512) $types = @{ 'C12A7328-F81F-11D2-BA4B-00A0C93EC93B' = 'EFI System' 'E3C9E316-0B5C-4DB8-817D-F92DF00215AE' = 'Microsoft Reserved' 'EBD0A0A2-B9E5-4433-87C0-68B6B72699C7' = 'Basic Data' 'DE94BBA4-06D1-4D40-A16A-BFD50179D6AC' = 'Windows Recovery' '5808C8AA-7E8F-42E0-85D2-E1E90434CFB3' = 'LDM Metadata' 'AF9B60A0-1431-4F62-BC68-3311714A69AD' = 'LDM Data' } $fs = [IO.File]::Open($Path, 'Open', 'Read', 'ReadWrite') function Read-Sectors([long]$lba, [int]$count) { $buf = New-Object byte[] ($SectorSize * $count) $fs.Position = $lba * $SectorSize [void]$fs.Read($buf, 0, $buf.Length) return ,$buf } try { $mbr = Read-Sectors 0 1 '{0,-22} 0x{1:X2}' -f 'LBA0 partition type:', $mbr[450] # 0xEE = protective MBR $hdr = Read-Sectors 1 1 '{0,-22} {1}' -f 'LBA1 signature:', [Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($hdr, 0, 8) $entryLba = [BitConverter]::ToInt64($hdr, 72) $entries = [BitConverter]::ToUInt32($hdr, 80) $entrySize = [BitConverter]::ToUInt32($hdr, 84) $table = Read-Sectors $entryLba ([math]::Ceiling($entries * $entrySize / $SectorSize)) for ($i = 0; $i -lt $entries; $i++) { $o = $i * $entrySize $type = [guid][byte[]]$table[$o..($o + 15)] if ($type -eq [guid]::Empty) { continue } $first = [BitConverter]::ToInt64($table, $o + 32) $last = [BitConverter]::ToInt64($table, $o + 40) $name = [Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetString($table, $o + 56, 72).TrimEnd([char]0) $t = "$type".ToUpper() $label = if ($types.ContainsKey($t)) { $types[$t] } else { $t } # look for a filesystem boot sector at the very start of the partition $boot = Read-Sectors $first 1 $fsNote = '' if ([Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($boot, 3, 8) -eq 'NTFS ') { $ntfsSectors = [BitConverter]::ToInt64($boot, 40) + 1 # +1 for the backup boot sector $fsNote = "NTFS at +0, ntfs=$ntfsSectors part=$($last - $first + 1)" } '{0} {1,-18} start={2,-10} size={3,8:N1} GiB {4} {5}' -f ($i + 1), $label, $first, (($last - $first + 1) * $SectorSize / 1GB), $name, $fsNote } } finally { $fs.Dispose() } It needs an elevated shell. For reference, here’s what it prints against my internal system disk. That’s a normal basic disk:
LBA0 partition type: 0xEE LBA1 signature: EFI PART 1 EFI System start=2048 size= 0.2 GiB Basic data partition 2 Microsoft Reserved start=411648 size= 0.0 GiB Microsoft reserved partition 3 Basic Data start=444416 size= 930.5 GiB Basic data partition NTFS at +0, ntfs=1951346688 part=1951346688 4 Windows Recovery start=1951791104 size= 0.8 GiB NTFS at +0, ntfs=1730560 part=1730560 On the USB drive the partition table was perfectly healthy. The smoking gun was the type GUIDs:
# Type Size 1 EFI System 100 MB 2 LDM Metadata (5808C8AA-7E8F-42E0-85D2-E1E90434CFB3) 1 MB 3 Microsoft Reserved 15 MB 4 LDM Data (AF9B60A0-1431-4F62-BC68-3311714A69AD) 930.3 GiB 5 LDM Data 660 KB 6 Windows Recovery 1.1 GB That’s a dynamic disk. It’s Microsoft’s Logical Disk Manager, the volume manager from before Storage Spaces. And Windows will not bring a dynamic disk online on a USB or other removable bus. Not “can’t”, won’t. There’s no supported override.
I never asked for a dynamic disk. Nobody does. Disk Management offers the conversion in passing when you extend a volume into non-contiguous space. It also offers it when you span or stripe across disks. It’s a one-way trip. Converting back to basic through the UI wants the volumes deleted first. Somewhere along the way, that old D: got converted.
The check that makes it recoverable The LDM metadata is how Windows knows what volumes live in the LDM data partition. A spanned, striped or mirrored volume has its filesystem scattered. You need that metadata to put it back together. But if it’s a simple volume, the filesystem is just sitting in the partition.
The NTFS OEM ID check in the script above settles it. On the USB drive, partition 4 had the NTFS boot sector at offset +0. The NTFS volume size matched the partition size exactly. A simple volume. No LDM database parsing needed. An OS that ignores the type GUID and just mounts the partition gets a perfectly good NTFS filesystem.
That size check is the safety check for this whole post. On a spanned or striped volume the filesystem extends past the partition. Mounting it raw would corrupt it, let alone writing to it. If those numbers don’t match, stop and use ldmtool or one of the alternatives at the end.
Linux ignores the type GUID. Its GPT parser creates /dev/sdX4 regardless of what the partition claims to be. lsblk reports FSTYPE=ntfs. So the plan was to get the disk in front of the Linux kernel inside WSL2.
Dead end #1: wsl –mount wsl --mount exists for exactly this, attaching a physical disk to the WSL2 VM:
> wsl --mount \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE1 Failed to attach disk '\\.\PHYSICALDRIVE1' to WSL2: The system cannot find the file specified. Error code: Wsl/Service/AttachDisk/MountDisk/ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND That looks like a path bug. It isn’t. wsl --mount appears to go through the same Storage Management layer that has no object for this disk. That’s the same one that told Set-Disk it couldn’t find it. Windows can’t hand WSL a disk it refuses to acknowledge. This can never work, so don’t burn time on it. A tool inherits the blind spots of the layer it’s built on. The error message won’t tell you which layer failed.
Dead end #2: the usbipd race The right idea is to pass the USB device through instead of the disk. usbipd-win shares a USB device over USB/IP. WSL2’s kernel has the vhci_hcd client built in. So the enclosure shows up inside Linux as if it were plugged into the VM. Windows never has to understand what’s on it.
First attempt:
WSL usbip: error: Attach Request for 2-7 failed - Device in error state It took a while to see what was going on. The RTL9210 bridge re-enumerates every time its driver is swapped. It flips between two different USB identities:
UAS mode: busid 2-7, “USB Attached SCSI (UAS) Mass Storage Device” BOT mode: busid 2-3, “USB Mass Storage Device” Each has its own instance ID. usbipd bind claims one identity, which swaps the driver. That makes the device reset into the other identity. Then usbipd attach targets the one that’s already gone. Tracking by --hardware-id instead of busid doesn’t help. The flip happens between the two commands regardless.
The fix is dumb and effective: bind in a loop until both identities are registered. Then whichever one is live is already shared, and attach succeeds. Don’t scrape the table usbipd list prints. usbipd state emits JSON, which is the robust thing to script against.
The working recipe From an elevated PowerShell:
# WSL2 must be RUNNING or attach fails outright. This keeps the VM up for 2 hours. Start-Process wsl.exe -ArgumentList '-d','Ubuntu','-u','root','--','sleep','7200' -WindowStyle Hidden # absorb the UAS<->BOT re-enumeration foreach ($i in 1..3) { $d = (usbipd state | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Devices | Where-Object { $_.InstanceId -match '0BDA&PID_9210' } usbipd bind --busid $d.BusId Start-Sleep -Seconds 4 } $d = (usbipd state | Out-String | ConvertFrom-Json).Devices | Where-Object { $_.InstanceId -match '0BDA&PID_9210' } usbipd attach --wsl --busid $d.BusId usbipd list # expect STATE = Attached Then inside WSL. I assumed the in-kernel ntfs3 driver would be there on a 6.18 kernel. It isn’t:
$ zcat /proc/config.gz | grep -E 'NTFS|USBIP_VHCI' CONFIG_USBIP_VHCI_HCD=m CONFIG_USBIP_VHCI_HC_PORTS=8 CONFIG_USBIP_VHCI_NR_HCS=1 # CONFIG_NTFS3_FS is not set # CONFIG_NTFS_FS is not set So it’s ntfs-3g over FUSE. Find the right device with lsblk -p first. It was /dev/sde for me, but that isn’t stable. Look for the 931.5G disk with six partitions:
apt-get install -y ntfs-3g mkdir -p /mnt/old mount -o ro -t ntfs-3g /dev/sde4 /mnt/old And from Windows, the whole old drive is a folder in Explorer:
explorer.exe \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\mnt\old Mount read-only first, always. Prove you can read what you came for before you give yourself the ability to destroy it. When I did need to clean things up, the remount was umount /mnt/old; mount -t ntfs-3g /dev/sde4 /mnt/old. Then I checked that mount shows rw. Close the Explorer window before remounting, because Windows caches the read-only attribute.
Teardown is the reverse, and the order matters:
wsl -d Ubuntu -u root -- umount /mnt/old usbipd detach --busid 2-3 usbipd unbind --all Gotchas While attached over USB/IP the drive disappears from Windows entirely. That’s how USB/IP works, not a bug. There is no Recycle Bin on a \\wsl.localhost path. Deletes are immediate and permanent. The keepalive matters. If the WSL VM shuts down on idle, the USB attachment goes with it. Mid-write, that’s a real problem. The sleep 7200 also runs out, so restart it for long sessions. ntfs-3g buffers writes. umount before usbipd detach. Never just yank it. A dirty NTFS flag blocks a read-write mount. Hibernation or Fast Startup on the old install sets it. No hiberfil.sys on the volume is the quick tell that you’re clean. Copying through \\wsl.localhost goes over WSL’s file sharing, so it’s not fast. Fine for pulling folders out, not what I’d use to move the whole terabyte. Takeaways “Invalid” is a policy verdict, not a health verdict. Windows had a perfectly readable GPT in front of it and chose not to proceed. Nothing in the UI tells you the difference. The “bring the disk online” advice actively misleads. When abstraction layers disagree, drop below all of them. Reading the partition table by hand settled in a few minutes what four tools were giving four different non-answers about. USB/IP is a general escape hatch. A USB device Windows mishandles can be handed to a Linux kernel that doesn’t care. This isn’t really a dynamic disk trick. It’s having a second opinion available on demand. To be honest, there are cheaper options, so nobody over-engineers this:
Put the drive in an internal M.2 slot. Windows imports dynamic disks fine on an internal bus. Zero risk, full speed. Boot a Linux live USB and run ldmtool create all, or mount the partition directly. Use DMDE or R-Studio, which read LDM straight off a raw disk from Windows. The WSL route wins when you don’t want to open a case and you want the files in Explorer.
Links usbipd-win Microsoft: Connect USB devices to WSL Microsoft: Basic and dynamic disks GPT partition type GUIDs libldm / ldmtool, the proper way to assemble LDM volumes on Linux ntfs-3g

title: Building a Custom SAPI - How PHP Actually Talks to the Outside World
description: php-fpm, mod_php and the PHP command line all plug into PHP the same way. Here's how ePHPm does it, and the shortcut that broke WordPress.
body:
If you’ve only ever run PHP behind nginx, you’ve probably never had to think about how echo reaches a socket. When you embed PHP like ePHPm does, it’s the first thing you have to answer. The answer is a SAPI. There is very little written about implementing one. Most of what I know came from reading sapi/cli, sapi/cgi and sapi/embed in php-src. Then I found out which parts I’d misread. This is the write-up I wanted back in March.
What a SAPI is The Server API is PHP’s boundary with whatever is hosting it. In C it’s sapi_module_struct. That’s a name plus a few dozen function pointers that the engine calls whenever it needs something from the outside world. php-fpm is a SAPI. So are Apache’s mod_php, the CLI, the built-in dev server and the embed SAPI. They all run the same engine. What differs is what these callbacks do:
Callback PHP calls it when… ub_write anything is output: echo, print, templates, the error page flush output is flushed send_headers the first output byte is about to go out and headers need to be committed read_post it needs request body bytes ($_POST, $_FILES, php://input) read_cookies it wants the raw Cookie header to build $_COOKIE register_server_variables it’s building $_SERVER log_message error_log() or the engine logs something ePHPm starts from the embed SAPI. php_embed_init() gives you a working engine with stdout-oriented defaults. Then ePHPm overwrites the callbacks with its own:
void ephpm_install_sapi(void) { sapi_module.ub_write = ephpm_sapi_ub_write; sapi_module.flush = ephpm_sapi_flush; sapi_module.send_headers = ephpm_sapi_send_headers; sapi_module.read_post = ephpm_sapi_read_post; sapi_module.read_cookies = ephpm_sapi_read_cookies; sapi_module.register_server_variables = ephpm_sapi_register_server_variables; sapi_module.log_message = ephpm_sapi_log_message; sapi_module.name = "ephpm"; sapi_module.pretty_name = "ePHPm Embedded Server"; } sapi_module.name is what php_sapi_name() returns. Frameworks that branch on cli vs everything else see ephpm and treat it as a web SAPI. All of this is C, not Rust, for the reason I covered in the Rust post. PHP can longjmp out from under any of these callbacks, so they never call into Rust while the engine is live. They read and write thread-local C buffers. Rust copies things in before the script runs and out after it finishes.
Output: ub_write Output is the simplest one. PHP hands over a pointer and a length and expects to be told how many bytes were taken. ePHPm appends to a per-thread buffer that doubles as needed:
static size_t ephpm_sapi_ub_write(const char *str, size_t str_length) { if (output_len + str_length > output_cap) { size_t new_cap = (output_cap == 0) ? 8192 : output_cap; while (new_cap < output_len + str_length) new_cap *= 2; char *new_buf = realloc(output_buf, new_cap); if (!new_buf) return 0; output_buf = new_buf; output_cap = new_cap; } memcpy(output_buf + output_len, str, str_length); output_len += str_length; return str_length; } The buffer is __thread because under ZTS several threads run PHP at once. On MSVC it’s __declspec(thread), behind a macro. It’s never freed between requests, only reset to length zero. So a thread that served one big page keeps that capacity around. That’s a deliberate trade: no allocation on the hot path in exchange for some memory per thread.
Returning 0 from ub_write tells PHP the client went away. If realloc fails, that’s the honest answer.
Headers: send_headers is almost a no-op This one surprised me. send_headers is called once, right before the first byte of output. That’s where a SAPI like php-fpm writes the status line and headers to the FastCGI stream. ePHPm doesn’t stream PHP output in this mode. It buffers the whole response, so its send_headers just says “done”:
static int ephpm_sapi_send_headers(sapi_headers_struct *sapi_headers) { (void)sapi_headers; return SAPI_HEADER_SENT_SUCCESSFULLY; } The real header capture happens after the script finishes, while the request is still alive. It walks SG(sapi_headers).headers, which is the zend_llist that header() appends to. It reads SG(sapi_headers).http_response_code for the status. One subtlety: if a script never outputs anything, the default Content-Type never makes it into that list. PHP adds it as part of sending headers. So when no Content-Type was set, the capture code synthesizes one. It uses SG(sapi_headers).mimetype, or default_mimetype + default_charset.
Input: read_post and read_cookies read_post is a cursor over the request body Rust handed in:
static size_t ephpm_sapi_read_post(char *buffer, size_t count_bytes) { if (!req_post_data || req_post_data_offset >= req_post_data_len) return 0; size_t remaining = req_post_data_len - req_post_data_offset; size_t to_copy = remaining < count_bytes ? remaining : count_bytes; memcpy(buffer, req_post_data + req_post_data_offset, to_copy); req_post_data_offset += to_copy; return to_copy; } and read_cookies returns the raw Cookie header and lets PHP parse it.
Here’s one of the things you only learn by reading main/SAPI.c. sapi_activate() only reads and parses the POST body into $_POST if SG(server_context) is non-NULL. That pointer is how the CGI and built-in server SAPIs say “this is a real request” as opposed to a CLI run. ePHPm’s callbacks don’t use it for anything, so it gets a stable non-NULL sentinel. Without that line $_POST was quietly empty while php://input still worked. Here’s another. PHP 8.4 exports sapi_read_post_data(), but in 8.3 the same function is static inside main/SAPI.c. There’s nothing to call. ePHPm supports 8.3, so for PHP_VERSION_ID < 80400 the wrapper carries a verbatim copy of 8.4’s function.
$_SERVER from a hyper request register_server_variables walks a list of key/value pairs that Rust built from the hyper request. Here’s the original version of that builder. It’s since been reworked to skip the per-header allocations and map names in a single ASCII pass, but the mapping is the same:
let mut vars = vec![ ("REQUEST_METHOD".into(), self.method.clone()), ("REQUEST_URI".into(), self.uri.clone()), ("SCRIPT_FILENAME".into(), self.script_filename.to_string_lossy().into_owned()), ("SCRIPT_NAME".into(), script_name.clone()), ("DOCUMENT_ROOT".into(), self.document_root.to_string_lossy().into_owned()), ("SERVER_NAME".into(), self.server_name.clone()), ("SERVER_PORT".into(), self.server_port.to_string()), ("SERVER_PROTOCOL".into(), self.protocol.clone()), ("GATEWAY_INTERFACE".into(), "CGI/1.1".into()), ("QUERY_STRING".into(), self.query_string.clone()), ("PHP_SELF".into(), script_name), ("REMOTE_ADDR".into(), self.remote_addr.ip().to_string()), ("REMOTE_PORT".into(), self.remote_addr.port().to_string()), ("REDIRECT_STATUS".into(), "200".into()), ]; // Map HTTP headers to $_SERVER variables for (name, value) in &self.headers { let key = match name.to_lowercase().as_str() { "host" => "HTTP_HOST".to_string(), "cookie" => "HTTP_COOKIE".to_string(), "content-type" => "CONTENT_TYPE".to_string(), "content-length" => "CONTENT_LENGTH".to_string(), // "Accept-Encoding" -> "HTTP_ACCEPT_ENCODING" _ => format!("HTTP_{}", name.to_uppercase().replace('-', "_")), }; vars.push((key, value.clone())); } That’s the CGI/1.1 variable set every PHP framework expects. SCRIPT_NAME is derived from the resolved script path relative to the document root, not from the URI. That way it stays right after a front-controller rewrite (/blog/hello → /index.php). HTTPS=on is added for TLS requests. REDIRECT_STATUS=200 keeps code that was written for cgi.force_redirect happy.
Two sharp edges in that header loop, both worth knowing about if you write your own:
httpoxy. A client-sent Proxy: header becomes HTTP_PROXY, which a lot of HTTP client libraries read as “use this proxy for outbound requests.” That’s the 2016 httpoxy bug class, and the generic HTTP_* mapping walks right into it. As of last week ePHPm strips Proxy at request ingest, along with any configured JWT claims header. That happens before middleware runs and before the request crosses into PHP (#200). A fixed-size table. On the C side the server variables live in a __thread array of 128 pairs. ephpm_request_add_server_var() silently drops entries past that. Sixteen-odd CGI variables plus a request with more than about a hundred headers will lose the tail. Nobody has hit it, but “silently” is the word I don’t like there. The shortcut that broke WordPress The interesting part of a SAPI isn’t the callbacks. It’s the lifecycle around them. A normal SAPI does this for every request:
php_request_startup() -> superglobals built, executor fresh php_execute_script() php_request_shutdown() -> user functions, classes, constants, globals, statics destroyed In March, php_request_startup() crashed on tokio’s spawn_blocking threads. The signal and stack-probe functions it calls were the problem, same family as the SIGPROF bug. So the first version of ePHPm took a shortcut. It started one request when the thread was registered with TSRM and reused it forever. Between HTTP requests it only reset the SAPI request info and rebuilt the superglobals by hand:
destroy the PG(http_globals) arrays rebuild $_SERVER through the callback run treat_data over the query string for $_GET call sapi_handle_post() for $_POST/$_FILES parse cookies manually merge $_REQUEST That passed every test I had, because every test was a script that didn’t care what the previous request left behind. WordPress cares. Bryan Spears tracked it down at the end of June (9715d61). User functions, classes, constants, function statics and the global symbol table all survived between requests on the same thread. WordPress’s wp-blog-header.php checks $wp_did_header, a global. It defines WP_USE_THEMES, a constant. So on the second request to a warmed thread it decided it had already bootstrapped and skipped everything. Request #1 on a thread was a full 68KB page. Requests #2 and later were 119-byte blank pages containing a “constant already defined” warning.
By then the functions that made php_request_startup() crash were already --wrap’d to no-ops. So the fix was to do what every other SAPI does:
int ephpm_execute_request(const char *filename) { /* Tear down the previous request and start a fresh one. */ if (request_active) { php_request_shutdown(NULL); request_active = 0; } output_len = 0; headers_buf_len = 0; req_post_data_offset = 0; /* Populate SG(request_info) BEFORE php_request_startup(): PHP builds the * superglobals during startup using our callbacks, which read these. */ SG(request_info).request_method = (char *)req_method; SG(request_info).request_uri = (char *)req_uri; SG(request_info).query_string = (char *)req_query_string; SG(request_info).content_type = req_content_type; SG(request_info).cookie_data = (char *)req_cookie_data; SG(request_info).content_length = (long)req_post_data_len; SG(request_info).path_translated = (char *)req_path_translated; SG(server_context) = &ephpm_server_context_marker; if (php_request_startup() != SUCCESS) { return -1; } request_active = 1; /* startup doesn't reset these on the embed path, so a 201 or 500 from the * previous request on this thread would leak into this one */ SG(sapi_headers).http_response_code = 200; SG(headers_sent) = 0; SG(request_info).no_headers = 0; /* ... replay per-request INI (open_basedir etc.), then execute under SETJMP ... */ } The ordering in there is the lesson. SG(request_info) has to be filled in before php_request_startup(). Startup is what builds the superglobals from those fields, through the callbacks. Once startup owned that job, the old hand-rebuild became actively harmful. It destroyed the arrays startup had just created and re-ran treat_data over them. That was a use-after-free inside php_default_treat_data under load. The correct amount of superglobal code in a SAPI turned out to be none. Set the inputs, let PHP build them.
The cost was about 5% on a trivial no-op script, per the commit’s own measurement. On a real page it’s nothing noticeable. OPcache’s compiled bytecode and the JIT buffer live in shared memory and survive request shutdown. It’s the classic php-fpm + OPcache model, just with threads instead of processes. WordPress went from one good page per warmed thread to 40 out of 40 under concurrency.
The status code reset in that block is the same kind of bug in miniature. http_response_code(201) on one request came back as the status of the next request on that thread. The embed path doesn’t reset it during startup.
What I’d tell someone writing a SAPI Read sapi/cgi/cgi_main.c and sapi/cli/php_cli_server.c before you read the embed SAPI. Embed is the smallest, but it’s built for “run one script and exit.” The gaps are exactly the parts a server needs. Never skip php_request_shutdown(). It is the isolation boundary between requests. If something crashes during request startup, fix that instead of reusing a request. Set SG(request_info) before startup and let PHP build the superglobals. Treat every global in SG()/PG() as suspect between requests and check what startup does and doesn’t reset. Test with WordPress. It relies on more global state than anything else you’re likely to run, and it will find your lifecycle bugs immediately. Links ePHPm, the SAPI lives in crates/ephpm-php/ephpm_wrapper.c 9715d61 per-request shutdown/startup #200 strip Proxy and claims headers at ingest php-src main/SAPI.h for sapi_module_struct php-src sapi/ for every SAPI that ships with PHP httpoxy.org

title: Five Ways to URL-Encode an SSH Key (and Why Proxmox Rejects Them)
description: Proxmox's sshkeys parameter wants Python-style percent encoding that no single Go function produces. This covers a two-year-old issue, its one-line fix, and a related double-encoding bug in guest file writes.
body:
Issue #144 on go-proxmox was opened in April 2024 with the title “Weird sshkeys SSH public key validation error”. It is one of my less proud threads. It’s thirteen comments of people, including me, trying to get a public key into a cloud-init VM through the API. The working answer took more than a year to show up. The fix that finally landed in May is one line. Here’s why it took so long.
What the API wants Setting sshkeys on a VM is how you get a key into cloud-init’s authorized_keys. With qm on the node you can point it at a file (--sshkeys ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub). That’s where the thread started. The reporter passed a path through the API and got 500 SSH public key validation error. Over the API you have to send the key text itself. That part is fair. The confusing part is the next error, once you send the key:
400 Parameter verification failed. - {"sshkeys":"invalid format - invalid urlencoded string: ssh-rsa%20AAAAB ... The schema declares the parameter with format => 'urlencoded'. The format check lives in pve-common’s JSONSchema.pm:
sub pve_verify_urlencoded { my ($text, $noerr) = @_; if ($text !~ /^[-%a-zA-Z0-9_.!~*'()]*\z/) { return undef if $noerr; die "invalid urlencoded string: $text\n"; } return $text; } That’s the entire allowed character set: letters, digits, - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) and %. Everything else has to be percent-encoded, including +, /, =, @ and space. Those are exactly the characters that show up in an OpenSSH public key. There’s the base64 body, the user@host comment, and spaces between the fields. Multiple keys are separated by newlines, so %0A too.
Trying them all The thread worked through url.PathEscape, url.QueryEscape and three flavors of base64. My own contribution was “try url.QueryEscape”, which the reporter had already said didn’t work. A couple of hours later I linked the regex above. That was the right thing to look at, and then nobody, me included, followed it through. So here it is followed through. This program generates a throwaway ed25519 key whose base64 contains both + and /. It runs each candidate through the same regex. Then it checks whether URI-unescaping the result gives the original key back. That’s what Proxmox does with it before handing it to cloud-init:
var pveURLEncoded = regexp.MustCompile(`^[-%a-zA-Z0-9_.!~*'()]*$`) cands := []struct{ name, val string }{ {"raw", key}, {"url.PathEscape", url.PathEscape(key)}, {"url.QueryEscape", url.QueryEscape(key)}, {"base64.StdEncoding", base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(key))}, {"base64.URLEncoding", base64.URLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(key))}, {"base64.RawURLEncoding", base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(key))}, {"EncodeSSHKeys", strings.ReplaceAll(url.QueryEscape(key), "+", "%20")}, } key: ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIJvjKHeVkHgJQH4UQ5/xmNW/x9zm+bx0PLNpFG9hC0gB luther@example raw validator=false roundtrip=true rejected=" /+@" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIJvjKHeVkHgJ... url.PathEscape validator=false roundtrip=true rejected="+@" ssh-ed25519%20AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIJvjKHeVkH... url.QueryEscape validator=false roundtrip=false rejected="+" ssh-ed25519+AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIJvjKHeVkHgJ... base64.StdEncoding validator=false roundtrip=false rejected="=" c3NoLWVkMjU1MTkgQUFBQUMzTnphQzFsWkRJMU5URTVBQUFB... base64.URLEncoding validator=false roundtrip=false rejected="=" c3NoLWVkMjU1MTkgQUFBQUMzTnphQzFsWkRJMU5URTVBQUFB... base64.RawURLEncoding validator=true roundtrip=false rejected="" c3NoLWVkMjU1MTkgQUFBQUMzTnphQzFsWkRJMU5URTVBQUFB... EncodeSSHKeys validator=true roundtrip=true rejected="" ssh-ed25519%20AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIJvjKHeVkH... Going through the failures:
PathEscape is for a single path segment. It encodes the space and the / but leaves + and @ alone because they’re legal in a path. Proxmox doesn’t want them. QueryEscape does HTML form encoding, where a space is +. The validator rejects + outright. Even if it didn’t, a URI unescape that isn’t form-aware turns it back into a literal +. You’d get a corrupted key. Standard and URL-safe base64 end in = padding here, which fails the regex. It doesn’t matter much, because… RawURLEncoding sails through the validator, and it’s the worst one of the bunch. The alphabet is entirely legal characters, so the format check passes and Proxmox stores the base64 text as the key. Then the key check, or cloud-init, gets a string that isn’t an OpenSSH key. What works is RFC 3986 percent encoding with nothing marked safe. That’s what Python’s urllib.parse.quote(key, safe='') does. It’s also what a Proxmox staff member recommended on the forum years ago. Go doesn’t have that as a single function, but QueryEscape is one substitution away from it. It percent-encodes everything except unreserved characters. The only thing it does differently is spaces as +.
The fix @abbaszai posted a working Go version in August 2025. It had some extra trimming and decoding logic around the core idea. #273 reduced it to the core and put it in the library next to MakeTag:
// EncodeSSHKeys returns the given SSH public keys encoded the way Proxmox's // sshkeys parameter requires. Multiple keys are joined with newlines (PVE's // documented separator) before encoding. func EncodeSSHKeys(keys ...string) string { return strings.ReplaceAll(url.QueryEscape(strings.Join(keys, "\n")), "+", "%20") } opts := []proxmox.VirtualMachineOption{ {Name: "sshkeys", Value: proxmox.EncodeSSHKeys(pubKey1, pubKey2)}, } The + to %20 swap is safe because QueryEscape already turned every literal + in the input into %2B. The only + characters left in its output are spaces. The test table includes a key with a literal + to prove that.
It would be easy to do this automatically inside the VM config call, and I deliberately didn’t. Everyone who hit #144 has a workaround in their code that already encodes the key one way or another. Auto-encoding would encode their already-encoded value a second time. %20 becomes %2520 and the validator is perfectly happy with that.
