The key that lands in the guest is garbage with no error anywhere. An opt-in helper and a doc comment on the SSHKeys field is the version that can’t silently break anyone.
The same mistake, in the other direction Encoding flags bit again this month. The QEMU guest agent wrapper has AgentFileWrite, for writing a file into a running VM. The guest agent wants base64 content. The Proxmox endpoint has an encode parameter that the API docs describe like this:
If set, the content will be encoded as base64 (required by QEMU). Otherwise the content needs to be encoded beforehand - defaults to true.
The original wrapper base64-encoded the content itself and also sent encode: 1. It had a confident comment saying that encode=1 “tells PVE the content is already base64”. It means the opposite. Proxmox encoded it again and the guest agent decoded it once. Every file written through that method landed in the guest as base64 text. Someone was writing a TOML config and a PEM file into a guest. They found it when the service inside crash-looped on expected value but found '='. #343 keeps the client-side encoding (binary safe) and sends encode: 0:
body := map[string]interface{}{ "file": file, "content": base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(content), "encode": 0, } Both bugs are the same lesson. When two layers each might encode something, decide which one does it. Write the decision down where the next person will see it. When there’s a flag for it, read the description of the flag on the side that receives it rather than guessing from the name.
Links #144 the original thread and #273 EncodeSSHKeys #343 AgentFileWrite double encoding pve-common JSONSchema.pm Proxmox forum, using pvesh to set sshkeys Python urllib.parse.quote

title: SQLite as a Production Database via Protocol Translation
description: litewire speaks the MySQL wire protocol on one side and SQLite on the other. That lets WordPress and Laravel run against a .db file without a code change.
body:
Most of the PHP sites I’d put on ePHPm don’t need a MySQL server. A brochure WordPress, an internal Laravel tool, a preview environment that lives for an afternoon. What they do need is something that looks like MySQL, because mysqli and pdo_mysql are the only database drivers their code has ever been pointed at. I mentioned this in the ePHPm pragmatism post as a one-paragraph “because”. This is the longer version, now that WordPress 7.0 and Laravel 13 both install and run end to end on it.
The piece doing the work is litewire, a standalone Rust project (MIT) that I started at the end of March. It accepts MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server (TDS) and Hrana HTTP connections. It translates the dialect to SQLite on the fly and runs it against a pluggable backend. ePHPm embeds it as a library.
The challenge to “you need MySQL” The usual objection is that SQLite isn’t a production database. For a lot of workloads that’s just habit. A single-node site with a few writes a second and mostly reads is squarely what SQLite in WAL mode is good at. The operational difference is large:
there’s no server to patch there are no credentials to rotate there’s no connection limit to tune the backup is a file What stops people is the application. WordPress doesn’t have a SQLite driver in core. It has a plugin that rewrites queries inside PHP. Laravel supports SQLite, but every plugin, package and raw query in a real app was written and tested against MySQL. Asking someone to port that is asking them not to use your thing. So the translation has to happen below the app, at the wire.
The shape of it PHP (pdo_mysql, mysqli) | MySQL wire protocol, 127.0.0.1:3306 v litewire-mysql opensrv-mysql shim: handshake, COM_QUERY, prepared statements | litewire-translate metadata emulation, no-ops, text pre-passes, sqlparser AST rewrite | litewire-backend Backend::connect() -> one BackendConn per wire connection | SQLite (rusqlite, WAL) The MySQL frontend is built on opensrv-mysql. It handles the packet framing and the handshake and calls into a shim for each command. PostgreSQL uses pgwire. SQL Server has no Rust server-side TDS crate, since tiberius is client only. So that frontend is hand-rolled and experimental. The Hrana frontend skips translation entirely since the SQL is already SQLite.
The translator is where the real work is. It runs a fixed pipeline on every statement:
Metadata detection before parsing, because some of the input isn’t valid SQL to begin with. Emulation queries against sqlite_master and PRAGMA answer SHOW FULL COLUMNS, DESCRIBE, INFORMATION_SCHEMA.* and SELECT @@vars. Transaction rewrites: START TRANSACTION, BEGIN WORK and friends become BEGIN. No-ops: SET NAMES, SET time_zone, SET sql_mode, isolation level changes. They return OK without touching SQLite. Text pre-passes for MySQL syntax sqlparser-rs can’t represent, like bigint(20) display widths and KEY k (col(191)) index prefix lengths. Parse, rewrite the AST, emit with sqlparser’s Display. Rather than describe the rewrites, here’s what the translator does with real WordPress and Laravel statements. I ran these through litewire_translate::translate(sql, Dialect::MySQL) at litewire 699e634:
IN : CREATE TABLE wp_usermeta ( umeta_id bigint(20) unsigned NOT NULL auto_increment, user_id bigint(20) unsigned NOT NULL default '0', meta_key varchar(255) default NULL, meta_value longtext, PRIMARY KEY (umeta_id), KEY user_id (user_id), KEY meta_key (meta_key(191)) ) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_520_ci OUT: CREATE TABLE wp_usermeta (umeta_id INTEGER NOT NULL, user_id INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT '0', meta_key TEXT DEFAULT NULL, meta_value TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (umeta_id)) IN : INSERT INTO `wp_options` (`option_name`, `option_value`, `autoload`) VALUES ('siteurl', 'http://example.test', 'yes') ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE `option_name` = VALUES(`option_name`), `option_value` = VALUES(`option_value`), `autoload` = VALUES(`autoload`) OUT: INSERT INTO `wp_options` (`option_name`, `option_value`, `autoload`) VALUES ('siteurl', 'http://example.test', 'yes') ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET `option_name` = excluded.`option_name`, `option_value` = excluded.`option_value`, `autoload` = excluded.`autoload` IN : SELECT ... FROM wp_posts WHERE ... ORDER BY wp_posts.post_date DESC LIMIT 10, 10 OUT: SELECT ... FROM wp_posts WHERE ... ORDER BY wp_posts.post_date DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10 IN : alter table `users` add unique `users_email_unique`(`email`) OUT: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX `users_email_unique` ON `users`(`email`) IN : START TRANSACTION OUT: BEGIN IN : SET NAMES utf8mb4 OUT: <noop> IN : SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID() OUT: SELECT last_insert_rowid() IN : SHOW FULL COLUMNS FROM `wp_options` OUT: <metadata ShowColumns { table: "wp_options" }> Two of those are worth a closer look. The wp_usermeta table keeps PRIMARY KEY (umeta_id) on an INTEGER column. SQLite treats that as a rowid alias, so auto_increment behaves the way WordPress expects without the keyword. And the two inline KEY lines are gone. SQLite has no inline secondary index syntax, and the translator drops them rather than failing the whole CREATE TABLE. That’s a deliberate trade. The source calls it “a performance concern, not a correctness one”. I’d like to revisit it by emitting real CREATE INDEX statements, the way the ALTER TABLE ... ADD UNIQUE path already does.
The upsert one is load-bearing. add_option() uses that exact shape, and update_option() falls back to it for a new option. If VALUES(col) doesn’t become excluded.col, WordPress can’t save a setting.
All of that sits behind a bounded LRU cache keyed on the SQL text. The PR that added the cache (litewire#5) measured a WordPress-shaped join in release mode. It took 39 µs per translation cold and 277 ns warm. PHP apps send the same few hundred statement shapes over and over, so the parser runs rarely after warmup.
Wiring it into ePHPm On the ePHPm side the config is a file path. The MySQL listener defaults to 127.0.0.1:3306. You only need the proxy block if you want to move it or add the Hrana listener for external tools:
[db.sqlite] path = "/var/lib/ephpm/myapp.db" [db.sqlite.proxy] mysql_listen = "127.0.0.1:3306" hrana_listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" # optional The app’s config stays the MySQL config it already had. For Laravel that’s the stock .env:
DB_CONNECTION=mysql DB_HOST=127.0.0.1 DB_PORT=3306 DB_DATABASE=laravel DB_USERNAME=ephpm DB_PASSWORD= In single-node mode litewire runs in-process with the rusqlite backend. There’s no child process and nothing else listening. Clustered mode swaps the backend for a client to a replicated SQLite server, which is a separate story. There’s also an experimental engine = "turso" knob. It runs the same frontends over the Turso engine instead of SQLite’s C library. And if you do want a real MySQL, [db.mysql] turns the same listener into a pooling proxy. SQLite drops out of the picture entirely.
What it took to make WordPress actually install For most of litewire’s life, “WordPress works” was a claim in the README that nothing tested. I took it out in July (litewire#4). I replaced it with what the end-to-end tests actually cover. Then I put full installs through it. ePHPm’s Turso evaluation needed a WordPress and Laravel suite run against both engines anyway. So I ran a WordPress 7.0.1 wp core install and a Laravel 13 php artisan migrate through the MySQL frontend. The then-default SQLite engine was the control. Neither got past installation:
Error: Error: WordPress 7.0.1 requires MySQL 5.5.5 or higher opensrv-mysql’s default handshake banner is 5.1.10-alpha-msql-proxy. WordPress 6.5 and later refuse to talk to a server that old. Dropping back to WordPress 6.4.3 got further and then died in dbDelta:
wp_usermeta -> SQL translation error: SQL parse error: sql parser error: Expected: ), found: ( at Line: 9, Column: 24 That’s the meta_key(191) index prefix length, and it hit 7 of the 12 core tables. Laravel failed on the very first statement of migrate. The table options went straight through to SQLite:
SQLSTATE[HY000]: General error: 1105 SQLite error: near "DEFAULT": syntax error in CREATE TABLE `migrations` (...) DEFAULT CHARACTER SET = utf8mb4 COLLATE = 'utf8mb4_unicode_ci' at offset 115 The five WordPress tables that did parse were never actually created. Their inline KEY constraints were emitted verbatim.
The full list came to nine gaps:
the handshake version index prefix lengths table options inline KEY/INDEX ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE ... VALUES(col) a mis-shaped SHOW FULL COLUMNS (WordPress read every core option back as an empty string) SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS information_schema existence probes that Laravel uses before migrating qualified UPDATE t SET t.col = ... references The important thing about the list is that both engines failed it identically. That made it obvious every one of them lived in the wire and translate layer, not the database.
They landed together in litewire#11 with 13 regression tests. After it, both suites went 20/20 green on both engines. The WordPress suite covers install, theme render, posts, comments, a hundred options, generated content, search-replace and plugin DDL. The Laravel suite covers migrate, seed, CRUD, transaction commit and rollback, migrate rollback and re-migrate. ePHPm picked up the pin in ephpm#190.
Two bugs a test suite wouldn’t have found Getting the install green was the visible part. Putting real PHP traffic through it in the same couple of weeks turned up two problems that would have hurt in production.
Transactions weren’t per client. The rusqlite backend held one Arc<Mutex<Connection>> shared by every wire connection. The MySQL handler tracked in_transaction per client in Rust, but the actual BEGIN ran on the shared handle. Client A’s BEGIN meant client B’s next INSERT landed inside A’s transaction. Either one’s COMMIT finalized both. The mutex also serialized every query. That threw away WAL’s concurrent readers before they ever reached SQLite. The fix in litewire#6 turned Backend into a factory:
#[async_trait] pub trait Backend: Send + Sync + 'static { /// Open a new session. Each BackendConn has its own transaction state. async fn connect(&self) -> Result<Box<dyn BackendConn>, BackendError>; // stateless query/execute/describe_columns kept as defaults } Every accepted connection calls connect() once and holds its own rusqlite connection to the same file. SQLite’s file locking coordinates writers. busy_timeout (5 s default) handles SQLITE_BUSY. litewire defaults each session to synchronous=NORMAL, the usual setting for WAL mode. One wrinkle: open_in_memory() gives each connection a different database. The shared-cache URI workaround defeats WAL. So Rusqlite::memory() now quietly backs itself with a temp file.
Every SELECT took 44 ms. This was measured from ePHPm with PHP PDO on loopback. A point SELECT was 44.01 ms p50 and an INSERT was 1.36 ms. The asymmetry is the clue. An INSERT reply is one OK packet. A result set is a column count, column definitions, an EOF, rows and another EOF. opensrv-mysql wrote each of those as its own TCP segment. Something on the loopback path sat on those small segments for about 40 ms. That’s the classic Nagle/delayed-ACK stall. I never got a packet capture inside the test host to prove which side was holding. Setting TCP_NODELAY on the server side (litewire#3) was the right thing to do, but it didn’t cure it on its own. What did was wrapping the write half in a 64 KiB BufWriter, so the whole result set goes out as one write (litewire#7):
op before after point SELECT p50 44.01 ms 0.23 ms INSERT p50 1.36 ms 0.30 ms Those numbers are from the PR, measured on a rebuilt ePHPm image. It only ever reproduced through PHP. mysql_async and the mysql CLI against the same server never showed it. I don’t have a satisfying explanation for the difference yet. mysqlnd sets TCP_NODELAY on its sockets too, so it isn’t that.
Where it doesn’t make sense I’d rather be specific about this than have someone find out the hard way:
One writer at a time. WAL gives you concurrent readers and a single writer. If the app does heavy concurrent writes, run MySQL or Postgres and use ePHPm’s proxy mode instead. One process owns the file. Don’t point a second server or a cron job’s own SQLite client at the live database. Not every MySQL behavior is emulated. SET autocommit = 0 is a no-op with a warning. Half-emulating MySQL’s implicit transactions with a hidden BEGIN would be worse than saying so. LOCK TABLES is also a no-op with a warning, since SQLite only has file-level locking. Inline secondary indexes are dropped, as above. PostgreSQL and TDS are CRUD-level. The MySQL frontend is the one that gets tested against real applications. Inside those lines it’s a good fit for CI and preview environments, a single VPS, edge boxes and small production sites. The same .db file runs under ephpm dev on a laptop and on the server. The app never knows.
Next up is the long tail. Passing an install suite is not the same thing as behaving like MySQL on every query a plugin might send. I expect real traffic to find the next round.
Links litewire ePHPm litewire#11: WordPress and Laravel run over the MySQL frontend litewire#6: per-wire-connection sessions litewire#7: coalescing the result-set write litewire#5: translate cache opensrv-mysql sqlparser-rs

title: Fixing Windows Archive Extraction in SPC
description: wasn't a pipe problem. It was the wrong tar program and Windows symlinks, and fixing one line of static-php-cli took three tries.
body:
One of the first things that broke when I started building PHP on Windows with static-php-cli (SPC) wasn’t PHP at all. It was unpacking the source tarballs. libxml2, xz and a couple of others would die partway through extraction with:
ERROR: The pipe has been ended. Over the last few months I’ve “fixed” this two different ways, and the maintainers fixed it a third. It’s a small piece of code. But it’s a good example of how much Linux assumption hides in a single shell pipeline, so here’s the whole thing.
The pipeline SPC v2 extracted archives on Windows with one line. Here’s the block from FileSystem::extractArchive(). I kept the maintainer’s comments, which tell you how much fun this code has been for everyone:
} elseif (PHP_OS_FAMILY === 'Windows') { // use php-sdk-binary-tools/bin/7za.exe $_7z = self::convertPath(getenv('PHP_SDK_PATH') . '/bin/7za.exe'); // Windows notes: I hate windows tar....... // When extracting .tar.gz like libxml2, it shows a symlink error and returns code[1]. // ... // And MinGW tar.exe cannot work on temporarily storage ??? (GitHub Actions hosted runner) // Yeah, I will be an MS HATER ! match (self::extname($filename)) { 'tar' => f_passthru("tar -xf {$filename} -C {$target} --strip-components 1"), 'xz', 'txz', 'gz', 'tgz', 'bz2' => cmd()->execWithResult( "\"{$_7z}\" x -so {$filename} | tar -f - -x -C \"{$target}\" --strip-components 1"), 'zip' => self::unzipWithStrip($filename, $target), default => throw new FileSystemException("unknown archive format: {$filename}"), }; } 7za decompresses the .xz/.gz/.bz2 layer to stdout (-so). tar reads the inner tarball from stdin and handles --strip-components 1. That flattens the libxml2-2.x.y/ top-level directory into the target directory. On Linux this is the most boring command in the world.
First fix: stop piping I was building on a Windows runner that also has Git for Windows installed. My first read of the error was the obvious one. Windows pipes between processes are flaky with big streams, so don’t stream. Decompress to disk, then extract from disk. That went into my SPC PR #1079 in April:
'xz', 'txz', 'gz', 'tgz', 'bz2' => (function () use ($_7z, $filename, $target) { $dir = dirname($filename); cmd()->execWithResult("\"{$_7z}\" x \"{$filename}\" -o\"{$dir}\" -y"); $tarFile = preg_replace('/\.(xz|txz|gz|tgz|bz2)$/i', '', $filename); if (!file_exists($tarFile)) { $tarFile .= '.tar'; } $winTar = getenv('SystemRoot') . '\System32\tar.exe'; f_passthru("\"{$winTar}\" -xf \"{$tarFile}\" -C \"{$target}\" --strip-components 1"); @unlink($tarFile); })(), It’s two steps. 7za writes foo.tar next to the archive. Then C:\Windows\System32\tar.exe extracts it and the intermediate file gets deleted. It worked. But look at the second-to-last line. That’s the real fix, and the pipe story I told myself was wrong.
What was really happening Notice that the original command says tar, not a path. On a stock Windows box that resolves to C:\Windows\System32\tar.exe. That’s bsdtar from libarchive and it handles Windows paths fine. Some boxes have Git for Windows (or MSYS2) on the PATH ahead of System32. There tar resolves to C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\tar.exe instead. That’s GNU tar built for MSYS, and GNU tar has opinions about colons.
I reproduced it again for this post with a .tar.xz that unpacks to about 67 MB, piping 7za into each tar:
> 7za x -so big.tar.xz | "C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\tar.exe" -f - -x -C "C:\...\out2" --strip-components 1 /usr/bin/tar: C\:\\Users\\...\\out2: Cannot open: No such file or directory /usr/bin/tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now ERROR: The pipe has been ended. > 7za x -so big.tar.xz | C:\Windows\System32\tar.exe -f - -x -C "C:\...\out2" --strip-components 1 (exit 0, files extracted) GNU tar can’t use the C:\... target directory and exits immediately. 7za is still writing decompressed bytes into the pipe, but the reader is gone. So 7za reports the write failure as The pipe has been ended. The error everyone sees is printed by the writer, about the reader dying. Nothing is wrong with the pipe.
The same tar without the pipe gets a different and even stranger error. To GNU tar, -f C:\foo.tar means “a tape on the remote host named C”:
> "C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\tar.exe" -xf C:\...\pkg.tar -C C:\...\out --strip-components 1 /usr/bin/tar: Cannot connect to C: resolve failed So my two-step fix worked for the boring reason that it hardcoded System32\tar.exe. The decompress-to-disk part only added an extra copy of every tarball on disk. Lesson learned. When a pipeline fails, check that each side of it is the binary you think it is before blaming the pipe.
Second fix: v3 and the symlink problem That PR didn’t merge. SPC was in the middle of a ground-up v3 rewrite, and v3’s shell layer already pinned the binary:
$tar = SystemTarget::isUnix() ? 'tar' : '"C:\Windows\system32\tar.exe"'; So in v3 the PATH problem was gone, and the pipe was fine. What was left was the other thing in the maintainer’s comment: symlinks. Some upstream tarballs ship symbolic links. zstd ships tests/cli-tests/bin/unzstd -> zstd, for example. Windows only lets a process create symlinks with admin rights or Developer Mode turned on. bsdtar fails each one with Can't create '...': Invalid argument and exits non-zero. On a CI runner without those rights, the extraction fails and leaves a half-written source tree behind.
My answer in May was #1175. Drop tar.exe entirely and let 7za do both layers. 7za doesn’t fail the extraction on symlinks the way bsdtar does. 7za has no --strip-components, so that moved into PHP. The version below is lightly trimmed, with the logging taken out and comments added:
private function extract7zWithStripComponents(string $archive_path, string $target_path, string $_7z, int $strip = 1): void { $temp_dir = sys_get_temp_dir() . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . 'spc_' . bin2hex(random_bytes(8)); FileSystem::createDir($temp_dir); $archive_arg = escapeshellarg(FileSystem::convertPath($archive_path)); $temp_arg = escapeshellarg($temp_dir); // pass 1: .tar.xz -> .tar $this->passthru("{$_7z} x {$archive_arg} -o{$temp_arg} -y", $this->console_putput); // pass 2: .tar -> files $inner_tar = glob($temp_dir . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . '*.tar'); if ($inner_tar !== []) { $tar_arg = escapeshellarg($inner_tar[0]); $this->passthru("{$_7z} x {$tar_arg} -o{$temp_arg} -y", $this->console_putput); @unlink($inner_tar[0]); } // emulate --strip-components 1: a single top-level dir gets its contents copied up if ($strip > 0) { $entries = array_diff(scandir($temp_dir), ['.', '..']); if (count($entries) === 1) { $inner = $temp_dir . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . reset($entries); if (is_dir($inner)) { FileSystem::copyDir($inner, $target_path); FileSystem::removeDir($temp_dir); return; } } } FileSystem::copyDir($temp_dir, $target_path); FileSystem::removeDir($temp_dir); } It worked in my fork and that’s what my Windows builds ran on for the next couple of months.
What upstream did instead The review feedback was fair. crazywhalecc said a full 7za path was a reasonable direction. But FileSystem::copyDir is slow, and my version copies every extracted source tree a second time to fake --strip-components. It also only approximates it. If an archive has more than one top-level entry, nothing gets stripped.
Then two things landed in v3. In June, PHP’s old php-sdk-binary-tools were replaced with MSYS2 plus a standalone 7za-win tool package (#1193). And the shell layer grew passthruTolerateSymlinks(). It does three things:
keeps the 7za-into-System32\tar.exe pipe captures tar’s output if the only errors are symlinks Windows refused to create, logs a warning and keeps going Anything else still throws.
private function passthruTolerateSymlinks(string $cmd): void { // Symlink creation only fails on a Windows host; elsewhere extraction handles symlinks fine. if (PHP_OS_FAMILY !== 'Windows') { $this->passthru($cmd, $this->console_putput); return; } $result = $this->passthru($cmd, $this->console_putput, capture_output: true, throw_on_error: false); if ($result['code'] === 0) { return; } if ($this->isSymlinkOnlyExtractFailure($result['output'])) { logger()->warning('Some symbolic links could not be created during extraction and were skipped ...'); return; } throw new ExecutionException(/* ... */); } That keeps the single streaming pass and real --strip-components. It only forgives the one failure mode we know is harmless. #1175 was closed as superseded on July 13th, which is the right call. Their version is better than mine.
Takeaways Pin the binary. tar in a command string means “whatever is first on the PATH”. On Windows developer machines and CI runners that’s frequently GNU tar from Git or MSYS2, which reads C: as a hostname. “The pipe has been ended” means the other side died. Go look at what the reader printed before it exited. Tolerate narrowly. Skipping symlinks wholesale (7za) and failing on them wholesale (tar) are both wrong. Matching the specific error and letting everything else fail is the version that survives. Links crazywhalecc/static-php-cli#1079 - the v2 PR with the two-step extraction crazywhalecc/static-php-cli#1175 - the v3 7za-only PR crazywhalecc/static-php-cli#1193 - MSYS2 + 7za-win replacing php-sdk-binary-tools libarchive (bsdtar), which is what ships as C:\Windows\System32\tar.exe Create symbolic links - the Windows privilege behind the symlink failures

title: Two Small go-proxmox Fixes: A Watch Channel That Never Closed, and WithRetry
description: go-proxmox had a task log channel that only closed on the happy path. It also gained a composable RoundTripper that retries the 502s and 503s Proxmox throws during cluster transitions.
body:
Here are two changes from the v0.5 to v0.7 stretch of go-proxmox. They’re too small for a post each. They’re worth knowing about if you write long-running tooling against Proxmox. One is a bug in code I wrote about in 2022. The other is a feature that replaces a retry loop everybody was writing for themselves.
The channel that only closed when things went well In 2022 I wrote up how tasks and Watch work. Watch returns a channel of log lines. A goroutine tails the task log until the task stops. Then it closes the channel so you can range over it. Here is the tail loop from that post:
func tasktail(start int, watch chan string, task *Task) error { for { if err := task.Ping(); err != nil { return err } if task.Status != TaskRunning { close(watch) return nil } logs, err := task.Log(start, 50) if err != nil { return err } // ... } } The channel is closed in exactly one place: when the task is no longer running. Every return err leaves it open. Since context support was added in 2023 there’s a new way to hit those error paths. You cancel the context. @aisbergg reported precisely that in #254:
logChan, err := task.Watch(ctx, 0) if err != nil { return err } for line := range logChan { logLine(line) } Here’s what happens when you cancel ctx:
the next Ping fails and tasktail returns the error the goroutine logs it and exits the range waits forever on a channel nobody will ever write to or close A network blip did the same thing. It was just rarer.
The fix, #255, also came from @aisbergg. It’s the rule I should have followed in the first place. The goroutine that owns the sends owns the close. It does it with defer so every exit path is covered.
-	watch := make(chan string) - log, err := t.Log(ctx, start, 50) if err != nil { -	return watch, err +	return nil, err } ... +	watch := make(chan string) + go func() { +	defer close(watch) t.client.log.Debugf("logs found for task %s", t.UPID) for _, ln := range log { watch <- ln ... if task.Status != TaskRunning { task.client.log.Debugf("task %s is no longer running, closing down watcher", task.UPID) -	close(watch) return nil } The other half of the diff is quieter but matters too. The error returns before the goroutine starts used to hand back a real, unclosed channel alongside the error. Anyone who ranged over it without checking err first would block forever. Now they get nil, and the channel is only created once there’s a goroutine that will close it.
Both halves are @aisbergg’s work: the diagnosis, the diff and the PR. My part was reviewing it and merging it. I tagged v0.5.0 that evening so it shipped. The bug itself is mine, from 2022.
What the caller loses is the reason the stream ended. A closed channel looks the same whether the task finished or the context was cancelled. Check ctx.Err() after the loop, or Ping the task and look at ExitStatus.
WithRetry Proxmox returns 502 and 503 while a cluster is doing something to itself. That could be pveproxy restarting after an update, a node rejoining, or a quorum change. Every tool I’ve seen built on the client wraps its calls in the same three-line retry loop. #326 moves that into the client as an option:
client := proxmox.NewClient(url, proxmox.WithAPIToken(tokenID, secret), proxmox.WithRetry(), // 3 attempts, 200ms-5s backoff, retries 502/503/504/429 and network errors ) It’s an http.RoundTripper wrapped around whatever transport the client ends up with, rather than logic inside Client.Req. That’s what lets it compose with the other transport options in any order. Those are WithInsecureSkipVerify, WithRootCAs, WithProxy and WithRequestInterceptor. It’s installed in a finalize step after all the options have run. So WithRetry() before or after WithHTTPClient(custom) both end up wrapping the custom client’s transport.
The loop itself is the standard shape with a few details I care about:
for attempt := 0; attempt < r.policy.maxAttempts; attempt++ { // Reset the body before every attempt after the first. if attempt > 0 && rewind != nil { req.Body = rewind() } res, err := r.base.RoundTrip(req) // Honor user-initiated cancellation immediately — never retry it. if err != nil && ctxErr(ctx) != nil { return nil, ctx.Err() } lastRes, lastErr = res, err if !r.policy.condition(res, err) { return res, err } // ... non-idempotent check, last-attempt check ... delay := r.computeBackoff(attempt, res) // Drain and close the body so the underlying connection can be // reused on the next attempt. drainResponse(res) if err := r.policy.sleep(ctx, delay); err != nil { return nil, err } } Full jitter. The wait is a random duration in [0, min(5s, 200ms * 2^attempt)). A dozen workers that all got a 503 at the same moment don’t all come back at the same moment. Retry-After wins whenever the server sends one, in both the seconds and HTTP-date forms. It’s capped at the configured max so a misconfigured proxy can’t park the client for an hour. Cancellation is final. A cancelled context is never retried. The sleep between attempts is a select on ctx.Done(), so cancelling during a backoff returns immediately. The body is replayable. The request body is buffered once and a fresh reader is handed to each attempt. In this client every body is already a []byte, so that costs nothing. 4xx other than 429 fails fast. A 400 isn’t going to get better on attempt two. The knobs are WithRetryMax(n), WithRetryBackoff(initial, max) and WithRetryCondition(func(*http.Response, error) bool).
One thing to think about before turning it on. Because the body is replayable, POST is retried along with the idempotent verbs. That’s the right call for a 503 from pveproxy itself. That means the request never reached the API handler. A 502 from a reverse proxy in front of Proxmox is less clear-cut. The proxy may have given up after the backend already accepted the request. A retried POST /nodes/{node}/qemu could then try to create the VM twice. With a fixed VMID the second attempt fails because the ID is already taken. That’s noisy but safe. If you create things without pinning IDs, pass a WithRetryCondition that leaves 502 alone. Or only enable retry on read-heavy clients.
Links #254 Watch channel not closed and #255 the fix, both by @aisbergg #326 WithRetry and retry.go Waiting on Proxmox: UPIDs, Tasks and WaitFor in Go (2022) AWS Architecture Blog, Exponential Backoff And Jitter

title: Maintaining an Open-Source Library With AI Agents: AGENTS.md and the Rule They Kept Breaking
description: Six weeks of go-proxmox with coding agents doing most of the typing taught me what belongs in AGENTS.md. Five parallel agents got the same API shape wrong, and a coverage metric bent the code around it.
body:
On May 9th I merged #264. It added an AGENTS.md to go-proxmox and a stub CLAUDE.md that just points at it. The next six weeks ran through the v0.8.0 migration guide on June 15th. In that time main took 77 commits and +31,794 / -1,144 lines. The repo went from 84 to 186 .go files. Endpoint coverage went from 30% to 100% of the Proxmox API. Most of that code was typed by coding agents, a lot of it by several at once. This is what that looked like from the maintainer’s chair. It’s mostly the parts that went wrong, because that’s where AGENTS.md got its content.
What’s in the file The first version was boring on purpose. It covered:
How to build and test (Mage targets, which env vars the integration suite reads, that CI only runs unit tests). How a request flows through Client.Req. The client.Node(ctx, name) to node.VirtualMachine(ctx, id) to *Task traversal. A handful of gotchas like the ~16 KB upload cap. The one required section was about tests. Any PR that adds or changes an endpoint ships a gock mock in tests/mocks/pve9x/<resource>.go. It also ships a unit test with a happy path and at least one error path. Integration tests need a live cluster and CI doesn’t have one. Without that rule an agent can write a wrapper that has never executed, and the green check means nothing.
Everything else in the file today was added after something went wrong.
Five agents, one rule, five times The coverage push went area by area. The big areas were split into groups and handed to sub-agents in parallel. For qemu that was five PRs, #301 through #305, each one fine on its own. They all appended to the same virtual_machine.go, types.go and mock file. Merging them one at a time meant a four-way rebase. I closed all five and cherry-picked them into #306 with the per-feature commits kept. That became the pattern: parallel branches, one combined PR.
Ceph (#307) was five agents on 41 endpoints. The combined PR needed a cleanup commit for placement alone. Two groups put their mocks in the existing ceph.go, and two appended them to nodes.go. One created a new nodes_ceph.go and registered a second, duplicate loader for it. Three of them wrote the identical func cephNode() *Node test helper in three files. None of that is wrong code. It’s five people who didn’t talk to each other, which is exactly what it was.
The bigger problem showed up in the method signatures. Several agents independently produced this:
node.CephOSDScrub(ctx, id, deep) node.DeleteCephOSD(ctx, id, cleanup) node.CephOSDLVInfo(ctx, id, ...) Every OSD operation hung off *Node with the OSD id threaded through as an argument. It compiles and it works. But it’s not the shape the rest of the library uses. Storage, VMs, containers and network interfaces all have a getter that returns a handle, and the operations live on the handle. The Proxmox schema even tells you which one to use. The path is /nodes/{node}/ceph/osd/{osdid}/scrub, and the {osdid} segment says “this is one of many”. Once I looked, the same thing had happened to node services, node replication jobs and snapshots. It had also happened to firewall rules on nodes, VMs and containers. Fixing it took a refactor commit inside #307 plus four PRs, #308 to #311. The last two were breaking changes to methods that had already shipped.
The fix that matters is #312, which turned it into a rule with no judgement call in it:
// Getter: no API call, just constructs the handle. func (n *Node) CephOSD(id int) *CephOSD { return &CephOSD{client: n.client, Node: n.Name, ID: id} } // Operations live on the instance, not the parent. func (o *CephOSD) Scrub(ctx context.Context, deep bool) error { … } func (o *CephOSD) Delete(ctx context.Context, cleanup bool) (*Task, error) { … } The rule comes with three more things:
An explicit anti-pattern line naming node.CephOSDScrub(ctx, id, ...). A note that creation stays on the parent, because there’s no instance yet. A list of every existing handle type to copy. The cluster SDN sweep that came after it (#320) has handle types throughout: *SDNController, *VNet, *VNetSubnet and friends. The lesson I took: “follow the existing patterns” is not an instruction. An agent sees one file at a time, and the pattern isn’t in that file. “Look at the upstream path, if it has /{id}/ write a getter” is an instruction.
They optimize for the gauge you give them Coverage was the scoreboard for this work. The scanner that computes it is a set of regexes looking for client.Get(ctx, fmt.Sprintf("/nodes/%s/...", ...)). Agents read the scanner’s output after every change. Twice they changed the code so the scanner would count it:
The Ceph group writing start/stop/restart first built them through a shared cephServiceAction(action, ...) helper. Then it inlined three copies. The path normalizer turned fmt.Sprintf("/nodes/%s/ceph/%s", node, "start") into /nodes/{}/ceph/{}, which doesn’t match /nodes/{node}/ceph/start. Another group rewrote a GetWithParams call into the url.URL{Path: ...} form because the scanner understood one and not the other. Both were noted honestly in the PR bodies, which is the only reason I know. Neither is terrible code. But the duplication in the first one exists only to satisfy a tool. The right response was to fix the tool, and #313 taught the scanner about *WithParams. That went into AGENTS.md too. If a wrapper is invisible to the scanner, prefer teaching the scanner over contorting the code or adding to the exclusion list. If you hand an agent a number to move, decide in advance what it’s allowed to change to move it.
Rules written after the second time The rest of the file reads like a list of reviews I didn’t want to write again:
Pointer fields for non-zero Proxmox defaults (#271). The decision procedure is spelled out: look up the default, use a pointer if it differs from Go’s zero, and regression test both ways. Comment every pointer field with the default it protects. That one exists because of a large wrapper PR (#274). It did the pointer conversion correctly and deleted the FIXME comments explaining why. That left bare *int fields that look like noise. #268 put the explanations back. Directory-index endpoints are named Subdirs and their helpers keep a Diridx suffix, because the scanner keys off that suffix. A rename for style would silently drop coverage. Comma-joined fields use the CSV type. That came after []string fields that Proxmox returns as "a,b,c" broke the SDN round trip. Every release with an apidiff incompatible change ships migration/vX.Y.Z.md (#335). It includes the exact apidiff commands and “themed sections with before/after code, not a flat dump”. The pattern for all of them is the same. The first time I correct something it’s a review comment. The second time it’s a line in AGENTS.md.
The file rots like any other file AGENTS.md is documentation that gets executed, and it goes stale. Right now its “Repo-specific gotchas” section warns about a replace directive in go.mod pointing at a local go-diskfs checkout. That replace only ever existed in my working copy. It has never been in a commit, and the file tells every agent to tiptoe around it anyway. It’s harmless, but it’s the same failure as a stale comment. The difference is that the reader takes it literally every single time.
Was it worth it The numbers above happened, and 100% of the schema is wrapped with a mock and a unit test per endpoint. I would never have typed that by hand in six weeks of evenings. But the interesting work moved. I typed very little of the code and a lot of rules. I did a lot of cherry-picking. I spent my review time on shape rather than syntax: is this the right type, the right receiver, the right place for this mock. Every change still went through a PR and CI. The agents are fast and literal. So the quality of what comes out is about the quality of what’s written down. The cheapest time to write it down is the second time you see the mistake.
Links AGENTS.md #264 AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, #312 singleton vs instance rule #306 combined qemu sweep, #307 combined Ceph sweep #308, #309, #310, #311 the refactors agents.md

title: Proxmox JSON, Part 2: Three More Surprises
description: The Proxmox API found three more ways to trip up Go's JSON decoding. Here's what broke and how I fixed it.
body:
In 2023 I wrote about why go-proxmox has StringOrInt and friends. Proxmox sends the same number quoted in one place and bare in another, so the client has types that accept both. That post ended on a pretty confident note. Since then three more shapes of “the JSON is valid and Go still won’t take it” have come in. One of them is a bug I’d already fixed once and then reintroduced myself.
null, twice #198, June 2025: listing VMs on a node fails with
failed to match ^[0-9.]*$: null if any of the VMs is a template. Templates never run, so /nodes/{node}/qemu sends "pid": null for them. A running VM on the same list gets "pid": "14558", a quoted string. PID is a StringOrUint64. Its unmarshaller strips quotes and requires what’s left to match ^[0-9.]*$. null doesn’t.
The embarrassing part is that this worked in May 2023. A contributor had sent a fix for stopped VMs returning null. It had the unmarshaller treat anything without a digit in it as zero:
numeric := numericRegex.MatchString(str) // `\d` if !numeric { *d = StringOrUint64(0) return nil } Three months later I rewrote all the StringOr types to parse floats and truncate. That’s the version in the 2023 post. “Non-numeric means zero” became “non-numeric is an error, except the empty string”. I wanted garbage to fail loudly. null is not garbage. It’s Proxmox saying the field doesn’t apply. No test fixture had a null in it, so nothing noticed for two years. The fix in #265 is one condition on each of the three types:
str := strings.ReplaceAll(string(b), "\"", "") // Empty string and JSON null both yield the zero value. Proxmox returns // null for fields that are simply absent on the resource (e.g. PID on a // stopped VM template — see issue #198). if str == "" || str == "null" { *d = StringOrInt(0) return nil } Note that encoding/json calls UnmarshalJSON with the literal bytes null for a custom type rather than skipping it. That’s why this has to be handled in the type at all.
A petabyte in scientific notation #191: a directory storage backed by a MinIO bucket over a FUSE mount. The FUSE driver can’t tell how big the bucket is, so it reports 1 PiB. pvesh shows exactly that:
content storage type active avail enabled shared total used backup minio_backup dir 1 1125899906842624 1 0 1125899906842624 0 The API sends something else:
json: cannot unmarshal number 1.12589990684262e+15 into Go struct field Storage.Total of type uint64 Somewhere in Proxmox’s storage code that value became a Perl floating point number. A float that big gets printed with 15 significant digits in exponent form. It’s valid JSON. It’s not a valid uint64, and json.Number.Int64() won’t parse it either:
uint64: json: cannot unmarshal number 1.12589990684262e+15 into Go struct field .total of type uint64 json.Number Int64 err: strconv.ParseInt: parsing "1.12589990684262e+15": invalid syntax json.Number Float64 -> uint64: 1125899906842620 actual bytes (2^50): 1125899906842624 The fix (#237, from a contributor’s earlier attempt in #195) is a custom UnmarshalJSON on Storage. It decodes the numeric fields as json.Number. It tries Int64 first and falls back to Float64:
if aux.Total != "" { // Try int64 first, then fall back to float64 for scientific notation if val, err := aux.Total.Int64(); err == nil { s.Total = uint64(val) } else if val, err := aux.Total.Float64(); err == nil { s.Total = uint64(val) } } Look at the last two lines of that output though. The client now reads 1,125,899,906,842,620 for a storage that is 1,125,899,906,842,624 bytes. Those four bytes were gone before the response left the server. They went when the number was printed with 15 digits. No amount of client-side parsing brings them back. For a fake petabyte nobody cares. It’s worth knowing that Proxmox capacity numbers above 10^15 are approximate.
That fix then broke something else in a way I would not have guessed. #241 came from running the cluster-api-provider-proxmox test suite against main. Marshal a Storage, unmarshal it again, and Name comes back empty. The struct had two fields that map to the same key. That’s easy to miss until you remember encoding/json matches keys case-insensitively:
Name string `json:"storage"` // marshals as "storage" Storage string // marshals as "Storage" Marshal writes both "storage":"local" and "Storage":"". On the way back in, the new unmarshaller’s aux struct has a single json:"storage" field. Both keys match it and the later one wins. It’s the empty one. The old Storage field was a leftover from before Name existed. #243 tagged it json:"-" and marked it deprecated. The round trip works again.
net10 and the fields that weren’t there #211: a VM with eleven or more network interfaces only shows the first ten. VirtualMachineConfig had explicit fields for indexed devices. Those were Net0 through Net9, SCSI0 through SCSI30, Unused0 through Unused9 and so on. It also had helper maps (Nets, SCSIs, …) that a custom UnmarshalJSON filled in by reflecting over those fields. Proxmox allows net0 to net31, unused0 to unused255, and so on. encoding/json throws away any key that doesn’t match a struct field before your code ever gets a look at it. So net10 was dropped on the floor, silently.
The fix in #260 unmarshals the body a second time into map[string]json.RawMessage. Then it routes every <prefix><digits> key into the matching map:
routes := vmc.indexedDeviceMaps() // "net" -> &vmc.Nets, "scsi" -> &vmc.SCSIs, ... for k, v := range raw { prefix, ok := indexedDeviceKey(k) if !ok { continue } target, ok := routes[prefix] if !ok { continue } var s string if err := json.Unmarshal(v, &s); err != nil { // non-string indexed value — skip rather than fail the whole config continue } if *target == nil { *target = make(map[string]string) } (*target)[k] = s } The obvious version of this is strings.HasPrefix(k, "scsi"). An earlier PR for the same issue did exactly that. It’s wrong, because scsihw (the SCSI controller type) starts with scsi. The VM config also has a plain numa flag next to numa0..numa9. So the key parser requires the prefix to be followed by digits and only digits:
// indexedDeviceKey returns ("net", true) for "net10" and ("", false) for keys // like "scsihw" or "numa" that share a prefix but lack a pure-digit suffix. func indexedDeviceKey(k string) (prefix string, ok bool) { for i := 0; i < len(k); i++ { c := k[i] if c >= '0' && c <= '9' { if i == 0 { return "", false } // rest of the string must be all digits for j := i + 1; j < len(k); j++ { if k[j] < '0' || k[j] > '9' { return "", false } } return k[:i], true } } return "", false } There are unit tests for exactly those two collisions. #260 kept the explicit Net0..Net9 fields populated for compatibility. v0.7.0 (#261) removed them. The maps are now the only shape: cfg.Nets["net10"]. It’s one of the bigger sections of the v0.7.0 migration guide because a lot of code reads cfg.Net0.
The pattern All three of these are the same bug as the 2023 post wearing a different hat. The JSON is fine. The Go type was written from the docs or from one sample response. The real API sends a shape nobody put in a test fixture: a null, a float, an eleventh NIC. Each fix is small. Finding them is the hard part. That’s why I’m now more interested in testing against recorded responses from a real cluster than in typing more fixtures by hand.
Links Part 1: Proxmox Doesn’t Know What Type a Number Is #198 null PID and #265 #191 large storage, #237, #241, #243 #211 indexed devices, #260, #261 encoding/json Unmarshal (case-insensitive key matching)

title: The Pragmatism of ePHPm - Every Decision Has a
Behind It
description: ePHPm hit v0.1.0 this week. It isn't a rewrite-it-in-Rust project. Here's what I built, what I borrowed, what I sent upstream, and what I deliberately haven't built.
body:
ePHPm tagged v0.1.0 this week, three months after the first commit. Before the feature list grows any further I want to write down how decisions get made on it. This is mostly for myself. The easiest way to ruin a project like this is to let it turn into a checklist of things other projects have.
The pitch is simple. One binary that runs a PHP app with fewer moving parts than nginx + php-fpm + Redis + MySQL. Every feature has to trace back to that. If I can’t finish the sentence “this exists because…” with a real problem from running PHP in production, it doesn’t go in.
Rust, because I measured cgo This isn’t a “rewrite it in Rust” project. I write Go for a living and I’d have been faster in Go. I picked Rust because PHP calls back into its host constantly. Every echo, every header, every cache read once the KV functions exist. I wanted that direction to be a plain function call. When I actually measured it the cgo tax turned out to be a lot smaller than my own design doc claimed. It was about 24ns per call on Go 1.26, not 200, and I said so. The decision survived the correction because the reasons were never only that one number:
One runtime in the process. No GC next to Zend. No second project to upstream into before I can change how a request is dispatched. The part I didn’t get to pick is the C wrapper. PHP’s error handling is setjmp/longjmp, and that has to live in C regardless of what language is on the other side. So the answer to “is it Rust?” is “it’s Rust plus about 1,900 lines of C that I’d rather not have.”
A KV store, because there was nothing to embed I did not want to write a KV store. Building databases isn’t the fun part of this for me. But a PHP app server without a cache just means the user runs Redis next to it. Then the single binary pitch is gone.
So I went looking for something to embed:
Redis isn’t a library. It’s a server that wants to own a process and its event loop. There’s no libredis.a. (Its licensing also changed in 2024, which made me even less interested in building a product on top of it.) Dragonfly is also a standalone server. Its BSL 1.1 license explicitly excludes use in an “in-memory data store product or service.” A PHP server with a built-in clustered cache is close enough to that line that I’m not going near it. KeyDB, Garnet, Valkey: different licenses, same shape. Servers, not libraries. Dragonfly’s shared-nothing model (each thread owns a slice of the keyspace) is also the opposite of what ePHPm needs. Any PHP thread has to be able to read any key. What PHP apps use Redis for is caching, sessions and counters. Strings, a few hashes, TTLs. That’s a DashMap and a RESP2 parser so existing clients work. Add lazy expiry plus a sweeper and an eviction policy. A few thousand lines of Rust instead of a second daemon. It’s not Redis and it doesn’t pretend to be. No lists, no sets, no pub/sub, no persistence. If you need a queue, run a real Redis.
Gossip, because etcd would be a second thing to run Multi-node is where it’d be easiest to reach for etcd or Consul. Both are excellent. Both are also another cluster you have to operate, which defeats the point. I also didn’t write a membership protocol, because that’s a solved problem. Quickwit’s chitchat crate does scuttlebutt gossip with a phi-accrual failure detector. It’s a library and it’s MIT licensed. It runs on tokio, which ePHPm already has. Nodes find each other from a seed list and that’s the entire control plane.
That’s the general rule for what gets borrowed. If a well-maintained crate does the job and fits the runtime and the license, use it. hyper, rustls, tokio and chitchat are all in that bucket.
SQLite behind a MySQL socket, because the code only speaks pdo_mysql A lot of the sites I’d want to run on this don’t need a MySQL server. A brochure WordPress, an internal Laravel tool, something on an edge box. They do need MySQL as far as their code knows. That’s what pdo_mysql and mysqli talk to. litewire speaks the MySQL wire protocol on one side and SQLite on the other. The app’s config says DB_HOST=127.0.0.1 and nothing else changes. It exists because the alternative is asking people to port their database layer, and they won’t. It’s not there because SQLite is fashionable. It’s also optional. Point the proxy at a real MySQL and it pools connections instead.
Upstream, because a fork is forever ePHPm needs a static libphp for every OS and architecture it ships on. static-php-cli is the project that builds those. When it broke for me, the fix went upstream rather than into a private fork:
Test fixes for Windows path separators. A vswhere fix for Windows static builds. Dropping -fno-plt from macOS static CFLAGS. A GNU mirror change. A log filter so GitHub tokens don’t end up in CI logs. A mongodb build fix. Two more Windows build fixes are still open. The Windows embed SAPI work itself moved to php-src, where it’s still under review. Everyone building static PHP hits the same bugs. Every patch I carry privately is a patch I have to rebase forever.
The other half of that is not rebuilding PHP on every CI run. Compiling PHP and its libraries from source on each build was the slowest thing in the pipeline. So the builds moved into a separate repo, ephpm/php-sdk, that publishes prebuilt SDKs per OS/arch/PHP version. ePHPm’s build downloads one and links against it.
So the three-way split I keep coming back to:
Contribute upstream when the thing is shared infrastructure that others are already maintaining (SPC). Use what exists when a library does the job as-is (chitchat, hyper, rustls). Build my own only when nothing can be embedded or the license won’t allow it (the KV store, the C wrapper). What isn’t built The list of things that don’t exist matters as much as the list of things that do. As of v0.1.0:
No admin UI. Early docs listed an embedded dashboard as an advantage over FrankenPHP and RoadRunner. In May I pulled those rows out of the comparison pages. Claiming something you haven’t shipped as a feature is how docs turn into marketing. It’s on the roadmap. It’ll get built when there’s something worth looking at that Prometheus and Grafana don’t already show. No OpenTelemetry. Prometheus metrics exist because I use them. Tracing will come when I need a trace to debug something real. No KV persistence, no lists or sets. It’s a cache. Some knobs are parsed and not implemented, and the config reference says so in bold. That covers auto_explain, the lag-aware read/write split strategy, max_replica_lag, and the Unix socket for the Redis-compatible KV listener. Read/write splitting itself is the one feature I’ll admit went in early on a hunch rather than a need. The half-built strategy options next to it are what that looks like. I’d rather label those honestly than either delete the parsing or pretend they work. That’s the contrast I’m trying to avoid. Some projects chase a competitor’s feature matrix or build the thing that makes a good conference demo. The feature matrix in ePHPm’s docs is there to be honest about status, not to win rows.
Real apps, not hello world The proving ground is my home lab and real applications. WordPress, Laravel, the stuff people deploy. They get installed and clicked through on boxes I can break. That’s on top of the e2e suite that covers the server itself. Synthetic “hello world” benchmarks are good for exactly one thing, which is measuring dispatch overhead. Every interesting bug I’ve hit so far showed up in a real app or under real load, never in a 200-byte PHP file. The SIGPROF crash is the best example.
What’s next The next stretch is about correctness under real apps rather than new boxes on the diagram:
Request isolation. WordPress end to end. Making the KV store fast enough that nobody misses Redis. If something new shows up, it’ll come with its “because.”
Links ePHPm and the v0.1.0 release litewire ephpm/php-sdk chitchat static-php-cli, e.g. #1149 and #1150 Dragonfly’s license

title: Stop Ctrl-C-ing Your tail -f | grep
description: tail-gunner is a drop-in tail that promotes itself mid-stream into a live-filtering Bubble Tea TUI without restarting the stream.
body:
Here’s a loop I end up in all the time:
tail -f app.log something scrolls by that looks wrong, Ctrl-C tail -f app.log | grep ERROR and wait for it to happen again decide I also want to drop the health checks, Ctrl-C | grep -v healthz and wait again Every filter tweak throws away the stream and every line that already went past. I got tired of it and wrote tail-gunner. It’s a tail replacement that you can promote into a filtering TUI with one keystroke. You can drop back out of it without the stream ever stopping.
The tagline in the README is “it’s tail until you need more”. That’s the whole design. Everything below is as of v0.0.1.
Three modes, picked at startup The binary decides what it is based on where stdout goes:
Pipe mode: stdout isn’t a terminal. It behaves byte-for-byte like GNU tail and none of the TUI code runs. Scripts and downstream pipes can’t tell the difference. Plain mode: stdout is a terminal and you’re following (-f). It prints to your scrollback exactly like tail. A listener is waiting on the terminal for a :. Gunner mode: the full-screen Bubble Tea TUI. Filters, stacked searches, scrolling, piping the view through shell commands. q drops you back to plain mode. The check in main.go is short, and it’s the part that makes alias tail=tail-gunner safe:
// Interactive (promotable) only when: following line-oriented output to // a real terminal and not explicitly disabled. Everything else takes the // byte-faithful tailcompat path — that is the drop-in contract. interactive := opts.Follow && !opts.NoPromote && !opts.BytesSet && term.IsTTY(os.Stdout) if !interactive { os.Exit(tailcompat.Run(opts, os.Stdout, os.Stderr)) } os.Exit(app.Run(opts)) The buffer is the product Promotion only works if nothing gets lost while you’re switching. So ingestion is completely decoupled from rendering. A single goroutine drains the source channel into a ring buffer. Only then does it hand the line to whoever is displaying. The ring holds 100k lines by default, and --gun-buffer changes it:
go func() { for ln := range stream.C { ring.Append(ln.File, ln.Text) p.print(ln.File, ln.Text) select { case notify <- struct{}{}: default: } } }() p.print is a no-op while the TUI owns the screen. The notify channel is a coalescing poke the TUI uses to know there’s new data. Lines are addressed by a monotonic sequence number instead of a slice index. That keeps them stable while the ring evicts old entries underneath you:
// Bounds returns the seq range currently retained: [first, next). func (r *Ring) Bounds() (first, next uint64) { r.mu.RLock() defer r.mu.RUnlock() return r.first, r.next } Filters are a view over that buffer, not a stage in a pipeline. When you add :in ERROR, the view gets rebuilt by scanning the whole ring. So you see the errors that scrolled past before you typed the filter. New lines get tested once on the way in. A filter change costs one pass over at most 100k lines. A new line costs one test against the rule stack.
The rule stack itself has three kinds: in (keep), out (drop) and hl (highlight only). Multiple in rules OR together. Any out match drops the line. Most of what I type is a plain word, so there’s a small fast path. If the pattern parses as a regex literal, it uses bytes.Contains instead of the regexp engine.
func isLiteral(pattern string) bool { parsed, err := syntax.Parse(pattern, syntax.Perl) if err != nil { return false } return parsed.Op == syntax.OpLiteral } Promoting without stopping The fiddly part is the keyboard. If you’re doing kubectl logs -f ... | tail-gunner -f, stdin is the log stream. So keystrokes have to come from somewhere else. It’s the same trick fzf uses: open the controlling terminal directly. That’s two five-line files with build tags, one constant each:
//go:build !windows const ttyPath = "/dev/tty" //go:build windows const ttyPath = "CONIN$" In plain mode a goroutine puts that tty into raw mode and reads a byte at a time. A : restores the terminal and signals the main loop. The main loop stops plain printing and hands the same tty to Bubble Tea with tea.WithInput(tty) and the alt screen. Ctrl-C shows up as byte 3 in raw mode, so that gets handled by hand too.
When you press q the TUI exits, and the main loop has to catch you up. Lines that arrived while you were in gunner mode get replayed into the scrollback. The replay is capped at the last 10 lines, with a marker so you know what you skipped. The replay and the switch back to plain printing happen under the same lock. A line can’t sneak in between them:
func replayMissed(ring *buffer.Ring, p *printer, fromSeq uint64) { p.mu.Lock() defer p.mu.Unlock() defer func() { p.plain = true }() _, next := ring.Bounds() missed := next - fromSeq if missed == 0 { return } start := fromSeq if missed > demoteReplayCap { fmt.Fprintf(os.Stdout, "--- tail-gunner: %d lines while in TUI, showing last %d ---\n", missed, demoteReplayCap) start = next - demoteReplayCap } ring.Range(start, func(l buffer.Line) bool { p.printLocked(l.File, l.Text) return true }) } Filters survive the demotion too. If you leave gunner mode with :in ERROR set, plain mode keeps printing only errors until you :clear.
What it looks like These are captures from a real run. A bash loop appended a fake request log every ~50ms, and tail-gunner -f -n 200 app.log followed it in a 100x24 tmux pane. Pressing : opens the palette at the bottom. Lines are already auto-colored by severity:
Then three commands: :in ERROR, :out healthz and :hl dur=[0-9]{3}ms. The status bar shows the filter chips and 21/328. That means 21 of the 328 buffered lines pass. The top of that list is request id=13, which was written long before I typed the filter:
Pressing q from there printed this into the scrollback and kept following:
--- tail-gunner: 98 lines while in TUI, showing last 10 --- 22:22:41 ERROR req id=325 path=/api/users dur=664ms 22:22:44 ERROR req id=365 path=/api/cart dur=834ms 98 lines arrived while I was in the TUI. The last 10 of them got replayed. Only 2 of those 10 were errors that weren’t on /healthz. The filters stuck, which is the behavior I wanted.
Beyond in/out/hl, the palette has a few more tools:
/ searches that stack, each in its own color, with n/N to jump :filters and :searches panels to toggle or edit rules without retyping them :w file to save the current filtered view :| cmd to pipe the view through a shell command (:| jq .msg, :| grep -c ERROR) and look at the output in an overlay Proving it’s still tail None of that matters if the alias breaks a script. tail-gunner doesn’t reuse coreutils source. It’s GPLv3, and tail.c is not a library. So compatibility is pinned by tests instead. test/golden.sh runs 24 scenarios through the real tail and through tail-gunner. It compares the output with git hash-object along with the exit codes. The scenarios cover last-N, +N forms, byte mode, multi-file headers, -q/-v, missing files, stdin, a file with no trailing newline and a follow smoke test.
I built it and ran the suite on Windows from Git Bash, where tail is GNU coreutils:
$ tail --version | head -1 tail (GNU coreutils) 8.32 $ bash test/golden.sh ok default last 10 ok -n 5 ok -n 0 ok -n +15 ... ok explicit - operand ok -f picks up appended lines ---------------------------------------- passed: 24 failed: 0 CI runs the same script on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows runners. macOS ships BSD tail, so the workflow installs coreutils and points GNU_TAIL at gtail. An option tail-gunner doesn’t know gets rejected by the flag parser with an error instead of being quietly ignored. The follow engine itself is nxadm/tail. It already handles rotation, truncation and inotify-with-polling-fallback. I didn’t want to rewrite that part.
Using it inside k9s A k9s plugin with background: false suspends k9s and hands the terminal to the command. So the : promotion works the same way it does in a normal shell. In plugins.yaml:
plugins: tail-gunner: shortCut: Ctrl-L description: tail-gunner logs scopes: - po command: sh background: false args: - -c - kubectl logs -f --tail=500 $NAME -n $NAMESPACE --context $CONTEXT --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG --all-containers=true 2>&1 | tail-gunner -f Select a pod, Ctrl-L, :out healthz, and Ctrl-C to go back to k9s. There are two gotchas. Shortcuts like Ctrl-G are silently shadowed by k9s built-ins, but Ctrl-L is free. And the sh -c wrapper is required, because k9s execs the command directly and the pipe needs a shell. The --kubeconfig $KUBECONFIG pins kubectl to the same config k9s is connected with. 2>&1 puts kubectl’s errors in front of you instead of leaving you staring at a blank screen.
Install Releases are built with goreleaser for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64. Windows gets zip archives instead of tarballs. Or install from source:
go install github.com/luthermonson/tail-gunner/cmd/tail-gunner@latest alias tail=tail-gunner The engine packages are public if you want the follow-into-a-ring-buffer part in your own tool. Those are pkg/source, pkg/buffer, pkg/filter and pkg/tailio. It’s pre-1.0, so the APIs will move. Timestamp parsing and merging multiple files by time are deliberately out of scope. That’s lnav territory, and lnav already does it well.
How I captured the screenshots The two TUI images are tmux capture-pane -e dumps converted to SVG. The colors and text are kept exactly as tmux reported them. The setup was WSL2 Ubuntu, tmux at 100x24, TERM=xterm-256color and tail-gunner v0.0.1 built with Go 1.26. The golden suite output is from Git Bash on Windows 11 with GNU coreutils 8.32.
Links tail-gunner docs/ARCHITECTURE.md nxadm/tail Bubble Tea k9s plugins

title: Escaping WSL: Booting My Own Linux VM Through Hyper-V's HCS API
description: WSL2 refuses to run under LocalSystem, so ephemerd boots an Alpine kernel directly through vmcompute.dll instead.
body:
I’ve been building ephemerd, a daemon that runs self-hosted GitHub Actions runners with a fresh environment per job. On a Windows host, Windows jobs run in Hyper-V isolated containers. Linux jobs still need a Linux kernel from somewhere. The obvious answer on Windows in 2026 is WSL2, and that’s what I used first. It worked great from my terminal and fell over the moment ephemerd became a real Windows service.
WSL2 doesn’t do LocalSystem A Windows service that wants to create containers and Hyper-V VMs runs as LocalSystem. WSL2 doesn’t support that context at all. You get WSL_E_LOCAL_SYSTEM_NOT_SUPPORTED and that’s the end of the conversation. There’s no flag for it. WSL is a per-user feature and a service account isn’t a user.
So there were two options. I could run the service as a real user account and inherit every weird profile-loading problem that comes with it. Or I could skip WSL and talk to Hyper-V directly. I went with Hyper-V. The commit that did it is fa41077, “replace WSL with Hyper-V for Linux VM on Windows”. The rest of this post is what that took.
HCS is the API under all of it Docker, containerd’s Windows shim and WSL itself all end up in the Host Compute Service, exposed through vmcompute.dll. Microsoft’s Go library for it is hcsshim, and hcsshim already knows how to boot a Linux VM. That’s what LCOW (Linux Containers on Windows) does. internal/uvm.makeLCOWDoc builds a JSON document describing a “utility VM” with a kernel, an initrd and some devices, and hands it to HCS.
The catch is the word internal. Go won’t let you import another module’s internal packages, so the code I wanted to reuse was off limits. What I could do is call vmcompute.dll directly, which is exactly what hcsshim does under the covers. Then I defined my own copies of the schema structs:
var ( modvmcompute = windows.NewLazySystemDLL("vmcompute.dll") procHcsCreateComputeSystem = modvmcompute.NewProc("HcsCreateComputeSystem") procHcsStartComputeSystem = modvmcompute.NewProc("HcsStartComputeSystem") procHcsTerminateComputeSystem = modvmcompute.NewProc("HcsTerminateComputeSystem") procHcsEnumerateComputeSystems = modvmcompute.NewProc("HcsEnumerateComputeSystems") // ... ) type hcsLinuxKernelDirect struct { KernelFilePath string `json:"KernelFilePath,omitempty"` InitRdPath string `json:"InitRdPath,omitempty"` KernelCmdLine string `json:"KernelCmdLine,omitempty"` } The whole VM is one document. It uses schema 2.1 and contains:
A LinuxKernelDirect chipset, so there’s no firmware or bootloader. A SCSI controller with the root disk. A network adapter bound to an HCN endpoint on the Default Switch. A COM port mapped to a named pipe. Trimmed down from pkg/vm/linuxvm_windows.go:
doc := &hcsComputeSystem{ Owner: "ephemerd", SchemaVersion: &hcsVersion{Major: 2, Minor: 1}, ShouldTerminateOnLastHandleClosed: true, VirtualMachine: &hcsVM{ StopOnReset: true, Chipset: &hcsChipset{ LinuxKernelDirect: &hcsLinuxKernelDirect{ KernelFilePath: kernelPath, InitRdPath: initrdPath, KernelCmdLine: cmdline, }, }, ComputeTopology: &hcsTopology{ Memory: &hcsMemory{SizeInMB: l.cfg.MemoryMB, AllowOvercommit: true}, Processor: &hcsProcessor{Count: uint32(l.cfg.CPUs)}, }, Devices: &hcsDevices{ Scsi: map[string]hcsScsi{ scsiControllerGUIDs[0]: {Attachments: map[string]hcsAttachment{ "0": {Type_: "VirtualDisk", Path: l.rootVHDXPath()}, }}, }, NetworkAdapters: map[string]hcsNetworkAdapter{"default": {EndpointId: endpointID}}, ComPorts: map[string]hcsComPort{"0": {NamedPipe: consolePipe}}, }, }, } The SCSI controller GUID isn’t arbitrary either. hcsshim derives its controller IDs as v5 UUIDs from a fixed namespace. I copied the first one (df6d0690-79e5-55b6-a5ec-c1e2f77f580a) rather than inventing one and finding out what HCS thought of it.
Calling it is a plain syscall.SyscallN with UTF-16 strings. The one thing that tripped me up is that create and start are asynchronous. A return of HCS_E_OPERATION_PENDING (0xC0370103) isn’t an error. It means the handle is good and HCS is still working:
r0, _, _ := syscall.SyscallN( procHcsCreateComputeSystem.Addr(), uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(idPtr)), uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(configPtr)), 0, // identity uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&handle)), uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&resultPtr)), ) if uint32(r0) == hcsOperationPending { hcsResultString(resultPtr) // free result time.Sleep(3 * time.Second) return handle, nil } The kernel has to be an uncompressed ELF LinuxKernelDirect loads the kernel itself, so it wants a raw vmlinux, not the bzImage every distro ships. I use Alpine’s linux-virt package (6.12 series at the time). The build step pulls the gzip payload out of the bzImage by scanning for gzip magic bytes. It keeps the first stream that decompresses to something starting with \x7fELF:
magic := []byte{0x1f, 0x8b, 0x08} for i := 0; i <= len(data)-3; i++ { if data[i] != magic[0] || data[i+1] != magic[1] || data[i+2] != magic[2] { continue } gr, gzErr := gzip.NewReader(bytes.NewReader(data[i:])) if gzErr != nil { continue } gr.Multistream(false) raw, readErr := io.ReadAll(gr) _ = gr.Close() if readErr != nil || len(raw) < 64 { continue } if raw[0] == 0x7f && raw[1] == 'E' && raw[2] == 'L' && raw[3] == 'F' { return os.WriteFile(dest, raw, 0o644) } } It’s the same trick as the kernel’s own extract-vmlinux script, just without needing a Linux box at build time.
The kernel command line had one trap worth writing down. My first attempt said root=/dev/sda init=/init. That tells the kernel to mount the (still unformatted) disk and look for init there. What I wanted is rdinit=/init. That runs init from the initrd and lets the init script format and mount the disk itself:
cmdline := fmt.Sprintf( "rdinit=/init ephemerd.containerd_port=%d ephemerd.root_disk=/dev/sda%s "+ "pci=off brd.rd_nr=0 pmtmr=0 nr_cpus=%d "+ "8250_core.nr_uarts=1 8250_core.skip_txen_test=1 console=ttyS0,115200", l.cfg.ContainerdPort, dindFlag, l.cfg.CPUs, ) Finding the VM’s IP through the serial console Once the VM is up I need its IP address to dial containerd inside it. There’s no guest agent. Asking the Default Switch for DHCP leases from a service isn’t something I wanted to depend on. The VM already has a serial port wired to a named pipe, though, so the init script just prints its address:
echo "EPHEMERD_IP=$MY_IP" echo "ephemerd-init: gateway=$GW" The host reads the pipe, writes every line to a console.log, and watches for the marker:
scanner := bufio.NewScanner(pipe) for scanner.Scan() { line := scanner.Text() fmt.Fprintf(logFile, "%s\n", line) if strings.HasPrefix(line, "EPHEMERD_IP=") { if ip := strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(line, "EPHEMERD_IP=")); ip != "" { select { case l.ipCh <- ip: default: } } } } Crude, but it has a nice side effect. Every kernel panic and init failure lands in console.log. That’s the first place I look when the VM doesn’t come up. From there it’s a TCP poll until containerd and the dispatch gRPC server answer. The first working version booted in about 20 seconds from service start to containerd ready.
The things HCS didn’t tell me A handful of failures cost me real time. Here they are in case you go down this road too:
The compute system ID has to be a GUID. HCS uses the ID as the identity for GrantVmAccess, and a human-readable name gets rejected. ephemerd generates a v4 UUID for the ID and keeps a friendly name for logs. File ACLs. The VM worker process opens the VHDX as a virtual account. Without an explicit grant on the file, create succeeds and start fails with HCS_E_SYSTEM_ALREADY_STOPPED. That reads like a lifecycle bug and is really a permissions bug (98d786c). ephemerd runs icacls on the VHDX before every boot. Clock drift. Without the hv_utils module the guest has no Hyper-V TimeSync. The clock wanders, and the GitHub runner’s JWTs start getting rejected as expired. That one didn’t look like a VM problem at all (317b92a). Stale VMs. If the service dies hard the VM can outlive it. On startup ephemerd enumerates compute systems owned by ephemerd and terminates them before booting a new one. Stop baking the binary into the initrd The first design was a “fat initrd”. Busybox, the rootfs and the cross-compiled Linux build of ephemerd all went into one cpio at build time. It was about 190 MB, and it had a nasty failure mode. A plain go build of ephemerd.exe didn’t regenerate the initrd. I shipped several rounds of fixes that were running yesterday’s Linux code inside the VM before I noticed.
The fix leans on a kernel feature I’d forgotten about. You can concatenate cpio archives and the kernel unpacks them in order into one initramfs, with later entries overriding earlier ones. So the Linux binary moved into its own go:embed. On every boot ephemerd appends a tiny gzipped cpio tail to the base initrd (fb96345). The build-time initrd dropped from ~190 MB to ~7.6 MB. The VM always runs the binary that’s actually on disk.
That same tail turned out to be the right way to get config into the VM. Every new setting the VM needed used to cost four things:
A struct field. A kernel command line flag. A parser in the init script. A rebuild. #89 puts the host’s config.toml into the tail with mode 0600:
if err := writeCPIOEntry(gw, "assets/ephemerd-linux", 0o100755, binData, ""); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("cpio: ephemerd-linux: %w", err) } if cfgData != nil { if err := writeCPIOEntry(gw, "assets/config.toml", 0o100600, cfgData, ""); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("cpio: config.toml: %w", err) } } The first draft of that feature used a Hyper-V Plan9 share instead, and it failed twice. Starting the VM failed with HRESULT 0xc0370110, HCS_E_SYSTEM_ALREADY_STOPPED again. HCS couldn’t start the Plan9 device document I built. That took Linux CI on my dev rig down for about 100 minutes. And even with the device accepted, Hyper-V serves Plan9 over hvsock, not virtio. Mainline mount -t 9p has no hvsock transport. LCOW gets around that with its own guest agent passing an AF_VSOCK fd to trans=fd. That’s a lot of machinery for one file read once at boot. The details are in docs/arch/host-config-initrd.md.
Running KIND inside it The real test of a homemade VM is whether someone else’s software runs in it. One of my repos runs KIND clusters in CI. That means kube-proxy inside a kindest/node container inside a job container inside this VM. It didn’t work until two kernel modules went into the initrd:
br_netfilter, plus bridge-nf-call-iptables=1. Without it, pod traffic crossing the CNI bridge skips iptables. CoreDNS can’t reach 10.96.0.1:443, and everything downstream times out (fbc1e68). ipt_REJECT (with nf_reject_ipv4 under it). kube-proxy’s first rule is a REJECT for services with no endpoints. Without the module iptables-restore fails on that line and aborts the whole batch. KUBE-SERVICES stays empty (88ebc24). Neither error mentions a missing module unless you go and read kube-proxy’s own logs from inside the node container.
What’s next The boot is still three handoffs: initrd, then a pivot into an Alpine rootfs, then ephemerd. There’s a proposal in the repo (docs/arch/quickboot-image.md) to collapse that into a custom kernel plus an initramfs where ephemerd itself is PID 1. It’s a proposal and nothing more yet. But after this round I’m a lot less scared of owning the whole boot path.
Links ephemerd fa41077 replace WSL with Hyper-V #89 host config via the boot initrd tail microsoft/hcsshim Host Compute Service overview

title: Your Zero Value Just Turned Off My TLS Verification: omitempty, Go Defaults and Proxmox
description: A plain Go field can't tell unset from false. In go-proxmox the fix for one omitempty bug created the opposite bug, until an audit against the Proxmox schema found 75 fields and v0.7.0 moved them to pointers.
body:
Every Go developer knows omitempty drops zero values. What takes longer to sink in is that a plain bool only has two states. A caller filling in an options struct means one of three:
“set it true” “set it false” “I didn’t touch this, do whatever the server does by default” With omitempty you lose “false”. Without it you lose “didn’t touch it”. In go-proxmox we managed to ship both bugs, in that order. The second one quietly turned off TLS certificate verification for anyone downloading ISOs through the API.
Bug one: you can’t say no #209 from @kernel-sanders was a clean report. Create an API token with Privsep: false because you want it to carry the user’s permissions. Proxmox creates a token with privilege separation:
type Token struct { TokenID string `json:"tokenid,omitempty"` Comment string `json:"comment,omitempty"` Expire int `json:"expire,omitempty"` Privsep IntOrBool `json:"privsep,omitempty"` } false is the zero value, so omitempty drops it. Proxmox never sees the field and applies its default, which is 1. It’s the same story for disabling a user, creating an ACL that doesn’t propagate and a handful of others. The issue listed them all.
Bug two: the fix #210 was also from @kernel-sanders. It took option one from the issue and removed omitempty from the affected booleans. I merged it in August 2025, and it went out in v0.2.3:
type StorageDownloadURLOptions struct { ... -	VerifyCertificates IntOrBool `json:"verify-certificates,omitempty"` +	VerifyCertificates IntOrBool `json:"verify-certificates"` } ... type VirtualMachineBackupOptions struct { ... -	Remove bool `json:"remove,omitempty"` +	Remove bool `json:"remove"` ... -	StdExcludes bool `json:"stdexcludes,omitempty"` +	StdExcludes bool `json:"stdexcludes"` Now false can be sent. It’s also sent when you didn’t set anything. Every one of those fields defaults to 1 in Proxmox. Here’s what goes over the wire, from a small program using the same type and tags:
pre-#210 Token{Privsep: false} {"tokenid":"ci"} v0.2.3 StorageDownloadURLOptions{} (unset) {"url":"https://example.com/x.iso","verify-certificates":0} v0.7.0 StorageDownloadURLOptions{} (unset) {"url":"https://example.com/x.iso"} v0.7.0 VerifyCertificates: Ptr(false) {"url":"https://example.com/x.iso","verify-certificates":0} So from v0.2.3 until v0.7.0, node.StorageDownloadURL with a struct that didn’t mention VerifyCertificates told Proxmox to download the file without checking the server’s certificate.
