Every node.Vzdump with default options sent remove: false and stdexcludes: false. Proxmox reads those as 0. So backups stopped pruning old archives per the retention policy and started including /tmp and log files. Nobody filed an issue for either one, which is the scary part. These don’t fail. They just do the wrong thing.
(One more trap while I’m here. IntOrBool’s MarshalJSON has a pointer receiver. Marshal a struct holding one by value and the method isn’t in the method set. You get "verify-certificates":false instead of 0. The client always marshals through a pointer, so it doesn’t bite there. It still surprised me when I wrote the test program.)
The general case The underlying issue was already open. #199 came from @xortim in June 2025. ContainerConfig.Console is an IntOrBool with omitempty, and Proxmox defaults it to 1. The more general problem is any field where Go’s zero value differs from Proxmox’s default. And #178 pointed out that VirtualMachineConfig.OnBoot is an int when the schema says boolean. That’s two classes of bug, both of the form “the Go type doesn’t match what the schema says”. Both had been getting fixed one report at a time.
So instead of waiting for reports I wrote an audit (#266). It loads the Proxmox API schema and walks types.go with go/parser. For each config or options struct, it joins every field’s JSON tag against the parameters of the endpoint that struct is sent to. It prefers the create (POST) endpoint because that’s where Proxmox documents defaults. Indexed parameters like net[n] get matched to net0 and friends. For each match it compares the Go zero value to the schema default and the Go type to the schema type. Then it writes a table:
Field json tag Go type PVE type Go zero PVE default Recommended fix Console console IntOrBool boolean 0 1 *IntOrBool Memory memory int integer 0 512 *int KVM kvm int boolean 0 1 *IntOrBool VerifyCertificates verify-certificates IntOrBool boolean 0 1 *IntOrBool Remove remove bool boolean false 1 *IntOrBool It flagged 75 fields:
38 where the default differs on a non-boolean (needs *T) 9 where the default differs and the schema says boolean (*IntOrBool) 28 that are only the wrong type (IntOrBool, no pointer needed because 0 is the default anyway) That PR only added the tool, the report and a FIXME on each field. That way the breaking change could land as one migration instead of a trickle.
One finding is worth being precise about. The audit’s note on FirewallNodeOption.Enable said an unset value would silently disable the node firewall. That field was still a bool with omitempty on a PUT. Unset is omitted and the firewall stays as it is, so it couldn’t disable it. What it couldn’t do was let you turn the firewall off, which is bug one again. Both are fixed by the same change. But a tool’s description of the failure is a hypothesis until you’ve traced the code path.
The fix: pointers, and a helper so pointers aren’t miserable v0.7.0 changed about 30 fields from T to *T and about 25 from bool/int to IntOrBool. nil means “let Proxmox decide”. Non-nil means “send this”. The cost is that you can’t write Cores: 4 in a struct literal anymore. So there’s a one-line generic helper:
// Ptr returns a pointer to v. It exists so callers can construct optional // fields on config/options structs inline without a temporary local variable. func Ptr[T any](v T) *T { return &v } cfg := &proxmox.VirtualMachineConfig{ Memory: proxmox.Ptr(proxmox.StringOrInt(4096)), Cores: proxmox.Ptr(4), OSType: proxmox.Ptr("l26"), CPUUnits: proxmox.Ptr(1024), } And the regression tests check both directions, because only checking one is how we got here. Unset must be absent. Explicit false or zero must be present:
func TestContainerConfig_DefaultsOmittedWhenUnset(t *testing.T) { // Bare struct — none of the pointer-typed fields should appear. m := marshalToMap(t, ContainerConfig{}) for _, k := range []string{"arch", "cmode", "console", "cpuunits", "memory", "swap", "tty"} { _, present := m[k] assert.Falsef(t, present, "%q should be omitted when unset so PVE applies its default", k) } } func TestContainerConfig_ExplicitValuesAppearOnTheWire(t *testing.T) { cfg := ContainerConfig{ Arch: Ptr("amd64"), CMode: Ptr("tty"), Console: Ptr(IntOrBool(false)), // explicit disable — must reach PVE as 0, not be silently swallowed CPUUnits: Ptr(1024), Memory: Ptr(512), Swap: Ptr(0), // explicit no-swap — must reach PVE as 0, not be omitted TTY: Ptr(2), } m := marshalToMap(t, cfg) assert.Equal(t, float64(0), m["console"]) // IntOrBool false marshals to 0 assert.Equal(t, float64(0), m["swap"]) // ... } Swap is a nice example of why “just use omitempty” doesn’t work even for integers. The Proxmox default is 512. 0 is a perfectly reasonable value meaning “no swap”, and you need to be able to send it.
Making it stick A one-time sweep doesn’t help if the next endpoint wrapper reintroduces it. In v0.7 a lot of new wrappers were being written. So the rule went into AGENTS.md (#271) as a decision procedure:
look up the field’s default in the API viewer use a pointer if it differs from Go’s zero leave it unboxed if it matches add a test that marshals the struct with the field unset The one-line version is the question at the end of that section: if the user never touches this field, will an unintended value reach Proxmox?
There was one more lesson. The sweep that converted the fields stripped the FIXME comments and left nothing in their place. Six months from now someone would see CPUUnits *int and “simplify” it back. #268 put a comment on every pointerized field saying which default it protects:
// Remove — PVE default 1 (remove old backups per retention policy). // Schema is boolean; unset on the wire keeps pruning enabled. See #178 + #199. Remove *IntOrBool `json:"remove,omitempty"` Script string `json:"script,omitempty"` // StdExcludes — PVE default 1 (skip /tmp, /var/log, etc.). Unset on // the wire keeps those default exclusions. See #178 + #199. StdExcludes *IntOrBool `json:"stdexcludes,omitempty"` If you’re on v0.2.3 through v0.6.x and you call StorageDownloadURL or Vzdump, set those fields explicitly or upgrade. The full list of changed fields is in migration/v0.7.0.md.
Links #209, #210, #199, #178 #266 the audit, #268 rationale comments, #271 AGENTS.md rule, #274 cluster wrappers with the pointer rule defaults_omit_test.go golang/go#13284, the long-running omitempty discussion

title: From 52% to 100%: Measuring a Go Client Against the Proxmox API Schema
description: I built a stdlib-only mage target that pulls Proxmox's own API schema and regex-scans go-proxmox for HTTP call sites to report coverage. The tool was wrong more often than the code was.
body:
For five years the honest answer to “how much of the Proxmox API does go-proxmox cover?” was “a lot of it? the parts people asked for?”. Issues would come in for endpoints that didn’t exist in the client. I’d have no idea how many more were missing. At the end of May I finally built the thing that answers the question. Three days after the first run the answer was 100%. The more interesting part is how many times the measuring stick was wrong on the way there.
Proxmox publishes its schema, sort of The API viewer is an ExtJS app. The whole API definition lives in one file next to it: apidoc.js. It’s a JavaScript file, not JSON, but it starts with const apiSchema = [ and the array is valid JSON. Each node in the tree has a path segment (text), an info map keyed by HTTP method, and children. Flatten that and you have every (method, path) pair Proxmox serves.
The first gotcha is getting the array out. The obvious “first [ to last ]” breaks. Below the schema the file has the viewer’s own code, including template literals like ${m2c[method]}. That’s the last ] in the file. The array is pretty-printed with the closing bracket on its own line followed by the semicolon. So that’s the anchor:
// extractSchemaJSON peels the `const apiSchema = [ ... ];` array out of the // upstream JS file. We anchor on `\n]\n;` rather than the last `]` because // the JS handler code below the schema contains template literals like // `${m2c[method]}` whose `]` would be matched first. func extractSchemaJSON(raw []byte) ([]byte, error) { start := bytes.IndexByte(raw, '[') endIdx := bytes.Index(raw, []byte("\n]\n;")) if start < 0 || endIdx <= start { return nil, fmt.Errorf("could not locate JSON array boundaries in apidoc.js") } return raw[start : endIdx+2], nil } On PVE 9.2.1 that’s 675 endpoints across 444 unique paths: 340 GET, 173 POST, 83 PUT and 79 DELETE.
Scanning Go with regular expressions The other side is “which of those does the library call”. Every HTTP call in go-proxmox goes through client.Get/Post/Put/Delete(ctx, path, ...). The path is nearly always a fmt.Sprintf with the Proxmox path as the format string. So it’s a regex per line. Then both sides get normalized so {node}, %s and %d all become {}:
callRE = regexp.MustCompile(`\b\w+\.(Get|Post|Put|Delete)(?:WithParams)?\s*\(\s*ctx\s*,\s*(.*?)$`) func normalizePath(p string) string { if i := strings.IndexByte(p, '?'); i >= 0 { p = p[:i] } p = braceRE.ReplaceAllString(p, "{}") p = fmtVerbRE.ReplaceAllString(p, "{}") p = volidRE.ReplaceAllString(p, "{}") if len(p) > 1 { p = strings.TrimRight(p, "/") } return p } The volidRE is there because storage volumes are a single {volume} segment in the schema. The Go code builds them as %s:%s/%s. I considered walking the AST instead, and didn’t bother. The regex resolved 98.4% of call sites on the first run. The rest were real, just in unusual shapes. The whole thing is mage/endpoints/endpoints.go, standard library only. It has three targets:
endpoints:sync downloads and flattens the schema into .cache/pve-api/ endpoints:extract re-parses offline endpoints:coverage writes the uncovered list and a per-area table The first run (#298) said 353 of 675, 52.3%. The cluster area was at 94 of 259. Ceph, node SDN and node scan were at zero.
The tool was wrong before the code was Then I started using it to decide what to write next. I kept finding that “missing” meant “the scanner can’t see it”.
url.URL{Path: ...}.String() (#300). Calls that need query parameters build a url.URL, set RawQuery, and pass u.String(). The regex matched the call and then found no string literal. Tracking <var> := url.URL{Path: ...} per file uncovered nine endpoints that were already wrapped. One was RRDData, which was next on the list to “add”. Fixing the tool first saved writing a duplicate. Websocket helpers (in #306). VNCWebSocket and TermWebSocket don’t take a context, so ctx, never matched. *WithParams variants (#313). Container.Delete uses DeleteWithParams, so DELETE /lxc/{vmid} showed as missing for a method that has existed for years. Directory-index helpers and uploads (#318, #321). Shared <area>Diridx helpers and client.UploadReader( with the path on the next line both needed their own rules. The upload one needs a little state machine. When the regex matches with nothing after the (, it takes the path from the next non-blank, non-comment line. It gives up after one line so a stray match can’t bind to something far below it. Every one of those made the number go up without a line of library code changing. If you build a coverage tool, the first few days are spent finding out what it can’t see. The only way to find that out is to distrust every “missing” until you’ve looked at it.
Endpoints we skip on purpose A few endpoints don’t fit Get/Post/Put/Delete at all. I didn’t want the number stuck at 99.6% forever. I also didn’t want people writing fake wrappers to make it move. So there is an explicit exclusion map with a reason per entry:
var intentionallyExcluded = map[string]string{ "get /nodes/{}/qemu/{}/mtunnelwebsocket": "URL-builder helper (MigrationTunnelWebSocketPath); caller drives the websocket dialer", "get /nodes/{}/lxc/{}/mtunnelwebsocket": "URL-builder helper (MigrationTunnelWebSocketPath); caller drives the websocket dialer", "get /nodes/{}/storage/{}/file-restore/download": "streaming binary download; needs custom io.Reader plumbing, not the JSON Get helper", } Excluded endpoints come out of the denominator, so the headline is 672, not 675. The important detail is that every coverage run checks the map against the live schema. It fails if an entry no longer exists upstream. An exclusion list that silently outlives the endpoint it excludes is how you end up hiding a regression.
Directory-index endpoints (the ones that return [{"subdir": "x"}, ...]) looked like obvious exclusion candidates. They are deliberately not on the list. They’re real, callable endpoints that any token can hit, and they’re cheap to wrap. Keeping them in the denominator means the scanner’s Diridx rule gets exercised. So they got real wrappers.
May, by commit With the tool trustworthy the rest was work. Ceph went from 0 of 41 to 41 of 41 in one PR. qemu went from 81% to all of it. #322 closed the last 38 cluster endpoints (config, custom CPU models, bulk actions, Ceph flags, HA arm/disarm and friends). That was the final step in taking cluster from 36% at the start of the week to 259 of 259.
I re-ran the final version of the scanner over every commit that landed on main in May to get the curve:
The flat stretch from the 16th to the 24th is a stack of open PRs waiting on review. The jump late on the 24th is them landing. The vertical bits on the 26th and 27th are the Ceph, SDN, node and cluster sweeps. Today, on v0.7.1:
go-proxmox endpoint coverage schema endpoints : 675 call sites scanned : 698 (matched=698, no-match=0 → match rate 100.0%) unique covered : 672 / 672 → 100.0% (excluded by design: 3) area covered total excluded missing pct cluster 259 259 0 0 100.0% nodes/qemu 96 97 1 0 100.0% nodes/lxc 61 62 1 0 100.0% access 45 45 0 0 100.0% nodes/ceph 41 41 0 0 100.0% nodes/storage 19 20 1 0 100.0% nodes/disks 18 18 0 0 100.0% ... Five years of it The scanner only needs a source tree. So I pointed it at every release tag and a few early commits, all against the same 9.2.1 schema:
Here’s how it climbed:
3.9% in August 2021 (26 endpoints, mostly VMs, containers and storage) 11.8% at the first alpha tag in January 2023 24.1% at v0.1.0 in June 2024 29.3% at v0.3.0 on the last day of 2025 30.1% on May 7th of this year Four and a half years to get to 30%, and three weeks for the other 70.
Two caveats on the old points. Code before October 2023 predates context support. For those I relaxed the call regex to make ctx, optional. And the very early code built a few paths with string concatenation, which the scanner can’t resolve. So 2021 and 2022 are probably undercounted by a handful. Also note the first run printed 52.3%. The final scanner over the same week’s code says 52.8%. That difference is the exclusion list plus the blind spots above.
What 100% doesn’t mean It means every endpoint in the schema has at least one Go call site. It says nothing about three other things:
whether the request and response types are right whether a zero value in a struct quietly overrides a Proxmox default whether a JSON tag has a typo in it That’s a different audit and it found plenty, which is its own post. The scanner’s job now is to be a gate. AGENTS.md says new wrappers should move the number in the right direction. If the scanner can’t see a new wrapper, teach the scanner rather than adding to the exclusion list.
How I measured Schema: apidoc.js extracted from the pve-docs_9.2.1_all.deb package on download.proxmox.com (trixie, pve-no-subscription). That’s 675 endpoints. Old and new code are measured against the same API. Scanner: mage/endpoints/endpoints.go copied verbatim from main into a scratch main package. A tiny harness takes a schema path and a source directory. For pre-2023-10 revisions only, the call regex’s ctx\s*, is optional. Revisions: every release tag from v0.0.0-alpha1 to v0.7.1 and five early commits. Those are the last commit before 2021-09-01, 2022-01-01, 2022-04-01, 2022-07-01 and 2023-01-01. I added every first-parent commit on main from May 7 to May 31, 2026. All were extracted with git archive <rev> | tar -x. Machine: Windows 11, Go 1.26. The chart is the “unique covered” line from each run. Links go-proxmox and mage/endpoints/endpoints.go #298 the scanner, fixes in #300, #313, #318, #321 #322 cluster to 100% Proxmox VE API viewer

title: Cloud-Init ISOs in Pure Go with go-proxmox
description: Building nocloud cloud-init ISOs in memory with go-diskfs, uploading them to Proxmox and mounting them on a VM in one call, with no genisoimage.
body:
Proxmox’s built-in cloud-init support is fine for the basics: a user, an SSH key, an IP config. It falls apart the second you want your own user-data, vendor-data or a real network-config. The GUI and the ci* options only expose a handful of fields. The escape hatch is cicustom pointing at snippet files, and that means getting files onto the Proxmox host’s filesystem first. The usual alternative is building a nocloud ISO yourself with genisoimage or mkisofs. That means a system dependency on whatever machine runs your automation. You get a different package name on every OS and a subprocess to babysit.
go-proxmox has done this in Go since early 2023 with vm.CloudInit(). After the Joliet work in go-diskfs last month it works for Windows guests too. v0.6.0 added the ability to choose where the ISO goes. So this seemed like a good time to walk through it.
Prerequisites go-proxmox v0.6.0 or newer (it pulls in go-diskfs v1.9.3) A Proxmox VE API token with rights to upload to a storage and change VM config A storage on the node that accepts iso content (local does by default) A VM template whose image has cloud-init installed (or cloudbase-init for Windows) The nocloud convention cloud-init’s nocloud datasource looks for a filesystem with the volume label cidata and reads up to four files off its root:
meta-data - required, and it must at least carry an instance-id (hostname is optional). user-data - the #cloud-config document, or a script. vendor-data - optional, same format as user-data, merged underneath it. network-config - optional, network config, version 1 or 2. That’s it. No metadata service, no special Proxmox integration. Put a CD-ROM in the VM with a cidata label and those files, and cloud-init picks it up on first boot.
Using it Here’s the whole thing from the consumer side. This compiles and vets against go-proxmox as of v0.6.0:
package main import ( "context" "fmt" "log" "github.com/luthermonson/go-proxmox" ) func main() { client := proxmox.NewClient("https://proxmox.example.com:8006/api2/json", proxmox.WithAPIToken("root@pam!mytoken", "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx"), ) ctx := context.Background() // grab the VM you want to initialize node, err := client.Node(ctx, "pve") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } vm, err := node.VirtualMachine(ctx, 100) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } userdata := `#cloud-config hostname: webserver-01 manage_etc_hosts: true users: - name: deploy ssh_authorized_keys: - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... deploy@workstation sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL shell: /bin/bash packages: - qemu-guest-agent - curl runcmd: - systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent ` metadata := fmt.Sprintf(`instance-id: vm-%d local-hostname: webserver-01 `, vm.VMID) networkconfig := `version: 2 ethernets: eth0: dhcp4: true ` // builds a nocloud ISO, uploads it to Proxmox storage, // and mounts it as a CD-ROM on ide2 - all in one call if err := vm.CloudInit(ctx, "ide2", userdata, metadata, "", networkconfig, proxmox.WithCloudInitStorage("local"), ); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } fmt.Printf("cloud-init ISO mounted on VM %d, boot it up\n", vm.VMID) } Pass an empty string for any of vendordata or networkconfig you don’t need and that file is left off the ISO. Then start the VM.
Building the ISO All the interesting work is in makeCloudInitISO(). go-diskfs needs a backing file, so it creates an empty one in the OS temp dir. It wraps it and creates an ISO 9660 filesystem on it with a 2048-byte block size:
func makeCloudInitISO(filename, userdata, metadata, vendordata, networkconfig string) (isopath string, err error) { isopath = filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), filename) isoFile, err := os.Create(isopath) if err != nil { return "", err } if err := isoFile.Close(); err != nil { return "", err } iso, err := file.OpenFromPath(isopath, false) if err != nil { return "", err } defer func() { if cerr := iso.Close(); cerr != nil && err == nil { err = cerr } }() fs, err := iso9660.Create(iso, 0, 0, blockSize, "") if err != nil { return "", err } if err = fs.Mkdir("/"); err != nil { return "", err } Then it writes whichever files were provided. The Close() inside the loop matters. With Joliet enabled, go-diskfs v1.9 records each file’s size when its handle closes. Writing without closing before Finalize gives you a Joliet tree with the wrong sizes. (I found that one while switching go-proxmox over to Joliet for v0.5.0.)
cifiles := map[string]string{ "user-data": userdata, "meta-data": metadata, } if vendordata != "" { cifiles["vendor-data"] = vendordata } if networkconfig != "" { cifiles["network-config"] = networkconfig } for name, content := range cifiles { rw, err := fs.OpenFile("/"+name, os.O_CREATE|os.O_RDWR) if err != nil { return "", err } if _, err = rw.Write([]byte(content)); err != nil { return "", err } // Joliet finalization in go-diskfs v1.9+ requires the file handle to // be closed before Finalize so its size is recorded correctly. if err = rw.Close(); err != nil { return "", err } } And finalize, which is where the actual ISO layout gets written:
if err = fs.Finalize(iso9660.FinalizeOptions{ RockRidge: true, Joliet: true, VolumeIdentifier: volumeIdentifier, // "cidata" }); err != nil { return "", err } return } Both extensions are on for a reason. Plain ISO 9660 names are 8.3 uppercase, so user-data is stored as USER_DAT.;1. Rock Ridge adds the real name in a way Linux reads, along with POSIX modes and timestamps. That’s what cloud-init on a Linux guest sees. Joliet adds a second directory tree with UCS-2 names. That’s the only thing Windows reads, and it’s what cloudbase-init needs. The go-diskfs post has the full story of getting both right. That includes the bug where the Joliet label came out as 捩摡瑡.
The result is tiny. A three-file ISO like this comes in well under 100 KB.
Uploading and mounting CloudInit() strings the rest together. It builds the ISO and always removes the temp file on the way out. Then it resolves which storage to use, uploads, tags the VM and points a CD-ROM drive at the ISO:
func (v *VirtualMachine) CloudInit(ctx context.Context, device, userdata, metadata, vendordata, networkconfig string, opts ...CloudInitOption) error { var cfg cloudInitConfig for _, opt := range opts { opt(&cfg) } isoName := fmt.Sprintf(UserDataISOFormat, v.VMID) // user-data-<vmid>.iso isofilename, err := makeCloudInitISO(isoName, userdata, metadata, vendordata, networkconfig) if err != nil { return err } defer func() { if rerr := os.Remove(isofilename); rerr != nil { v.client.log.Warnf("failed to remove temp cloud-init iso %s: %v", isofilename, rerr) } }() node, err := v.client.Node(ctx, v.Node) if err != nil { return err } storage, err := resolveCloudInitStorage(ctx, node, &cfg) if err != nil { return err } task, err := storage.Upload("iso", isofilename) if err != nil { return err } // iso should only be < 5mb so wait for it and then mount it if err := task.WaitFor(ctx, 5); err != nil { return err } _, err = v.AddTag(ctx, MakeTag(TagCloudInit)) if err != nil && !IsErrNoop(err) { return err } task, err = v.Config(ctx, VirtualMachineOption{ Name: device, Value: fmt.Sprintf("%s:iso/%s,media=cdrom", storage.Name, isoName), }, VirtualMachineOption{ Name: "boot", Value: fmt.Sprintf("%s;%s", v.VirtualMachineConfig.Boot, device), }) if err != nil { return err } return task.WaitFor(ctx, 2) } The storage selection is the new bit in v0.6.0 (#272). It closes a long-standing #119. Before, the ISO went to the first enabled storage on the node that accepted iso content. That’s non-deterministic when a node has more than one. Now WithCloudInitStorage("name") picks one explicitly and validates that it takes ISOs:
func resolveCloudInitStorage(ctx context.Context, node *Node, cfg *cloudInitConfig) (*Storage, error) { if cfg.storage == "" { return node.StorageISO(ctx) } s, err := node.Storage(ctx, cfg.storage) if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloud-init storage %q: %w", cfg.storage, err) } if !strings.Contains(s.Content, "iso") { return nil, fmt.Errorf("cloud-init storage %q does not accept iso content (got %q)", cfg.storage, s.Content) } return s, nil } Cleaning up after yourself The cloud-init tag is how go-proxmox remembers that a VM has an ISO lying around. Once the guest has booted and cloud-init has done its thing, vm.UnmountCloudInitISO(ctx, "ide2") empties the drive (none,media=cdrom) and deletes the ISO. And vm.Delete() checks for the tag first and removes the ISO before deleting the VM. That way you don’t slowly fill your ISO storage with user-data-1xx.iso files from VMs that no longer exist. Since the storage is now selectable, the delete path scans every enabled ISO-capable storage on the node for the file. It doesn’t assume the default one.
Why not just shell out I like the benefits of keeping this in-process. There’s nothing to install on the machine that runs the automation. The same code works from a Linux CI runner, my Mac and the Windows box I’m writing this on. The ISO is built from strings in memory and a temp file. There’s no templating a directory tree on disk and no parsing a subprocess’s exit code. And it’s easy to test, because the ISO is just bytes you can read back with the same library.
If you want the ISO without the Proxmox part, I have an old standalone CLI called quiso that does the same job from the command line.
Links go-proxmox go-diskfs - the iso9660 implementation under the hood go-diskfs: Getting Rock Ridge Working for Joliet on Windows nocloud datasource docs cloudbase-init quiso

title: Staying Logged In to Proxmox: Ticket Renewal, Expiry and Where API Tokens Stop
description: Proxmox tickets die after two hours. How go-proxmox went from never re-authenticating to renewing tickets in place, plus the one thing API tokens can't do.
body:
Back in 2023 I wrote up how go-proxmox logs in and ended it with a shrug. Once a session existed the client never logged in again. A ticket-based client died at the two hour mark. My advice was “use an API token for anything long running”. It took until this month to fix that properly. It took three PRs from two of us to get there. Here’s the whole arc, plus the one place where an API token isn’t an option at all.
Step one: stop racing yourself The original 401 handler looked like this:
if c.credentials != nil && c.session == nil { // credentials passed but no session started, try a login and retry the request if _, err = c.Ticket(ctx, c.credentials); err != nil { return err } return c.Req(ctx, method, path, data, v) } return ErrNotAuthorized Two problems. The obvious one is c.session == nil, which means “log in once, ever”. The less obvious one is that c.session is read and written by whatever goroutine got the 401. A client is usually shared. Fire ten requests at a fresh client from ten goroutines and you get ten logins writing the same field. #223 from Serge Logvinov put a mutex around it. It also moved the login into CreateSession, which returns ErrSessionExists if somebody else already did the work.
Step two: know when it’s stale That still never re-logged in. #239, also from Serge, added an expiry so CreateSession treats an old session as gone:
if c.session != nil && time.Now().Before(c.sessionExpiresAt) { return ErrSessionExists } // ... c.sessionExpiresAt = time.Now().Add(time.Hour) Proxmox tickets are good for two hours ($ticket_lifetime = 3600 * 2 in PVE::AccessControl). The client calls them stale after one. That leaves plenty of slack for clock skew between you and the cluster. From here a credential-based client survives. The ticket dies at two hours and the next request gets a 401. CreateSession sees a stale session and logs in again with the stored password.
Step three: renew without the password That fixed username and password logins. It didn’t fix two cases people had been asking about since 2024. #181 wanted to renew with the existing ticket instead of keeping the password around. #196 was throwing away the whole *Client on auth failure and building a new one. That orphaned every cached *VirtualMachine and *Node that held a pointer to the old client. And if your login used a TOTP code, re-sending the stored credentials doesn’t work at all. The code is single use.
Proxmox has a documented answer for this: POST /access/ticket with the current ticket as the password. On the server side create_ticket runs verify_ticket on the password field first. It only falls back to a real password check if that fails. #267 wires that up:
func (c *Client) RefreshTicket(ctx context.Context) error { c.sessionMux.Lock() defer c.sessionMux.Unlock() return c.refreshTicketLocked(ctx) } func (c *Client) refreshTicketLocked(ctx context.Context) error { if c.session == nil || c.session.Ticket == "" { return ErrNoSession } if _, err := c.Ticket(ctx, &Credentials{ Username: c.session.Username, Password: c.session.Ticket, }); err != nil { return err } c.sessionExpiresAt = time.Now().Add(time.Hour) return nil } CreateSession now tries a renewal first when it has a session. It only falls back to the full credential login if that fails. The session is replaced on the existing *Client. Every resource handle hanging off it picks up the new ticket without doing anything. That’s the #196 fix: stop rebuilding clients.
Renewal is on you, though Here is the part that I think is easy to get wrong. I had to read the Perl to be sure. Renewal only works with a ticket that is still valid. verify_ticket checks the signature and the age against the same two hour lifetime. An expired ticket is just a wrong password. The client only reacts to a 401, and Proxmox doesn’t send a 401 until the ticket is already past two hours. So the automatic path in CreateSession is mostly going to fall through to the password login. Some clients have no password to fall back to, like an OTP login or one built WithSession from somebody else’s ticket. For those that’s the end of the session.
If you’re in that situation, renew on a timer and stay inside the window:
go func() { t := time.NewTicker(45 * time.Minute) defer t.Stop() for { select { case <-ctx.Done(): return case <-t.C: if err := client.RefreshTicket(ctx); err != nil { log.Printf("proxmox ticket refresh: %v", err) } } } }() One more wart I know about and haven’t fixed yet. Two goroutines can hit a 401 at the same moment. The first one renews. The second one waits on the mutex, finds a fresh session and gets ErrSessionExists. Req turns that into ErrNotAuthorized instead of retrying with the new ticket. It’s a narrow window, and the fix is a retry rather than an error. But it’s there.
The cost of logging in lazily While I was in here the v0.7 work added a few auth options worth knowing about. WithOTP stashes a single TOTP code. It zeroes the code after the first login so a later re-login doesn’t resend a dead code. WithDefaultRealm("pam") turns root into root@pam so you stop getting 401s for forgetting the realm.
WithEagerAuth is the one with a story. The client has always logged in lazily. The first request goes out without auth and gets a 401. Then the client logs in and retries. What I didn’t know in 2023 is that pveproxy deliberately slows down every 401:
if ($res->{status} == HTTP_UNAUTHORIZED) { # always delay unauthorized calls by 3 seconds $delay = 3 - tv_interval($reqstate->{starttime}); So every credential-based client has been paying three seconds on its first call since the beginning. WithEagerAuth logs in inside NewClient instead, so that cost moves to startup. It swallows the error because options can’t return one. If it failed, the lazy path still kicks in on the first request. If you need to know at startup that your password is wrong, call CreateSession yourself.
Where API tokens stop API tokens are still the right answer for most automation. One header, no CSRF token, no two hour clock. Except for terminals. #221 reported that opening a container terminal failed with an opaque failed to create terminal websocket: unexpected EOF. It turned out to be three separate bugs in the websocket handshake (#259).
Two of them were mine, from the 2022 xterm.js post. The UI opens the socket with new WebSocket(url, "binary"). The vncwebsocket handler hangs up on clients that don’t ask for the binary subprotocol. So the dialer now sends Subprotocols: []string{"binary"}. And the resize message is 1:<cols>:<rows>:, width first. I wrote it height first in 2022. It’s right there in that post’s resize code. It took four years for anyone, me included, to notice their terminal coming out transposed.
The third is a Proxmox limitation on older releases. Through PVE 8 and early PVE 9, termproxy verified the VNC ticket through /access/ticket. There verify_username rejects the !tokenname suffix a token user carries. The ticket’s HMAC is bound to that same name, so stripping the suffix on the client side doesn’t work either. Newer PVE 9 ships a /access/vncticket endpoint that accepts a token id. Node shells got it in pve-manager 9.0.13 in November 2025. Guest terminals got it with this spring’s qemu-server and pve-container updates. But go-proxmox doesn’t detect the server version yet. For now the client fails fast with a sentinel instead of the mystery EOF:
// ErrAPITokenWebSocketUnsupported is returned by TermWebSocket and VNCWebSocket var ErrAPITokenWebSocketUnsupported = errors.New("proxmox does not accept API tokens for vncwebsocket; use WithCredentials or WithSession") So if your tool targets PVE 8 and needs both automation and a shell, it needs a ticket for the shell. Now the ticket can stay alive.
Links #223 session race, #239 session expiry, #267 ticket renewal #259 websocket fixes and the API token limit #327 TLS, timeout and auth options pve-access-control, PVE/AccessControl.pm pve-http-server, PVE/APIServer/AnyEvent.pm Logging In to Proxmox From Go (2023)

title: go-diskfs: Getting Rock Ridge Working for Joliet on Windows
description: I fixed Rock Ridge and added Joliet to go-diskfs so a Go-built cloud-init ISO works for cloudbase-init. Then I found out what Windows actually wanted.
body:
go-proxmox has had a CloudInit() helper since 2023. It builds a small nocloud ISO in Go, uploads it to Proxmox and mounts it on the VM as a CD-ROM. It’s always worked fine for Linux guests. It has never worked for Windows guests running cloudbase-init. The reason is a filesystem extension from 1995 called Joliet.
Getting it fixed took three PRs to go-diskfs over about seven weeks. It also took a bug report from a user who ran it on Windows. That turned out to be the most important part.
Why Windows can’t read the ISO Plain ISO 9660 is very strict about names. At interchange level 1 a file name has four parts:
up to 8 characters of uppercase letters, digits and underscore a dot a 3 character extension a ;1 version suffix Here are the three nocloud files as go-diskfs writes them into the primary directory tree:
META_DAT.;1 NETWORK_.;1 USER_DAT.;1 Nobody reads those names. Two extensions layer real filenames on top. Which one an OS uses decides what it sees:
Rock Ridge is for Unix. It hides POSIX metadata inside each directory record’s System Use area using the SUSP framework. The entries are:
PX for mode/uid/gid/links NM for the real name SL for symlink targets TF for timestamps CL/PL/RE for relocating directories nested deeper than ISO 9660’s 8-level limit an ER entry announcing the extension Linux reads it, so Linux sees meta-data.
Joliet is Microsoft’s. It doesn’t touch the primary tree at all. It adds a Supplementary Volume Descriptor, or SVD (sector 17 here, right behind the PVD). The SVD is flagged with an escape sequence (%/@, %/C or %/E for UCS-2 levels 1 to 3). It points at a second directory tree whose names are UCS-2 big-endian, up to 64 characters.
Windows’ CD-ROM filesystem doesn’t do Rock Ridge. Without a Joliet tree it sees META_DAT.;1. cloudbase-init is looking for meta-data, so it finds nothing. Here’s the layout of the ISO that works, with both trees, read out of a real one:
There is no Go library for this I went looking before writing anything. As of March:
kdomanski/iso9660: its README says it plainly, “Joliet extension is NOT supported”. Rock Ridge reading is still experimental. hooklift/iso9660: a reader only, last touched in 2019. bgrewell/iso-kit: new (January 2025) with a couple of stars. It says it does Joliet but calls itself early development. go-diskfs: the serious one, and what go-proxmox already used. It could write Rock Ridge. “Joliet extensions to iso9660” was sitting in the plans section of the README. Issue #73 asking for it had been open since 2020. So, go-diskfs. The two extensions are independent on disk. The maintainer pointed that out in review, and he’s right. But Rock Ridge was already in the tree and half-working. Before bolting a second directory tree onto the finalize code, I wanted the first one to be correct.
Step 1: Rock Ridge up to spec (#353) PR #353 merged April 10th. Most of the fixes were small. Each one is a good example of the spec being specific about something the code had been loose about:
Modes were hardcoded. Mode() returned 0o755 for everything regardless of the PX entry. Now it reads the PX mode. It only falls back to fixed values for non-Rock Ridge images:
func (de *directoryEntry) Mode() os.FileMode { for _, ext := range de.extensions { if px, ok := ext.(rockRidgePosixAttributes); ok { return px.mode } } // Fallback for non-Rock Ridge if de.isSubdirectory { return os.ModeDir | 0o755 } // ... symlink fallback return 0o755 } No way to get at the metadata. Sys() now returns a *RockRidgeInfo with UID, GID, link count, mode and symlink target. That’s the standard Go way to expose filesystem-specific detail through fs.FileInfo:
type RockRidgeInfo struct { UID uint32 GID uint32 Nlink uint32 Mode os.FileMode Symlink string } RE was 8 bytes. The Relocated Directory entry is just a marker. It holds 2 bytes of signature, a length byte and a version byte, so its length is 4. The code allocated 8 and zero-filled the rest. Harmless to most readers, still wrong.
Relocated directories were looked up too late. When a tree is deeper than 8 levels, the deep directory is moved. A CL (child link) entry points at its new home. The reader checked path depth before resolving the CL, so relocated directories didn’t resolve at every level. The lookup moved ahead of the depth check.
Symlinks were treated as files during finalize. A symlink’s target lives inline in the SL entry. It has no data extent. But finalize put symlinks in the list of files to copy. os.Open() would follow the link and either fail on a dangling one or copy the target’s bytes. They’re now excluded from data allocation while still getting directory entries.
Relative symlinks came out absolute. The SL parser glued components together with a leading separator. A relative target.txt came back as /target.txt. The fix only adds a separator once something is already in the path. Review asked for that repeated check to be pulled into a helper:
appendComponent := func(component string) { if name != "" && name != "/" { name += "/" } name += component } The more interesting part was testing. I wanted to check go-diskfs against a reference implementation instead of against itself. The reference for Rock Ridge is xorriso. The PR as first written added Docker-based tests in both directions. One built with go-diskfs and checked with isoinfo. The other built with xorriso and read with go-diskfs. On top of that was a byte-level comparison of the PX and NM entries each one writes.
Getting xorriso into the test image hit a fun Alpine problem. cdrkit (which provides isoinfo) and xorriso both provide mkisofs and refuse to install together. My workaround involved shuffling binaries around and editing /etc/apk/world. That got a well-deserved “why the whole rigamarole” in review. The maintainer dropped cdrkit from the image entirely. I rewrote the test to read back with go-diskfs instead of isoinfo. Much simpler.
Reading the metadata back looks like this:
entries, err := fs.ReadDir(".") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } for _, e := range entries { fi, _ := e.Info() rr, _ := fi.Sys().(*iso9660.RockRidgeInfo) fmt.Printf("%-16s %v size=%d rr=%+v\n", fi.Name(), fi.Mode(), fi.Size(), rr) } meta-data -rw-rw-rw- size=49 rr=&{UID:0 GID:0 Nlink:0 Mode:-rw-rw-rw- Symlink:} network-config -rw-rw-rw- size=46 rr=&{UID:0 GID:0 Nlink:0 Mode:-rw-rw-rw- Symlink:} user-data -rw-rw-rw- size=37 rr=&{UID:0 GID:0 Nlink:0 Mode:-rw-rw-rw- Symlink:} (That ISO was written on Windows, hence 0666. go-diskfs’s Windows stat shim returns zero for link count, UID and GID. That’s on my list.)
Step 2: Joliet (#372) PR #372 went up the day #353 merged and landed April 16th. It closed #73 after more than five years. On the write side it’s a single flag:
err = fs.Finalize(iso9660.FinalizeOptions{ RockRidge: true, Joliet: true, VolumeIdentifier: "cidata", }) Under that flag, finalize does three things:
builds a parallel directory tree with UCS-2 names generates Joliet L and M path tables writes an SVD with the UCS-2 level 3 escape sequence Both trees point at the same file extents, so the data is only on disk once. On the read side go-diskfs detects a Joliet SVD by its escape sequence. It transparently reads the Joliet tree when Rock Ridge isn’t active.
Two review questions are worth repeating. They’re the kind of thing the spec makes easy to get wrong. First, Rock Ridge and Joliet aren’t mutually exclusive. A comment in my code claiming “Joliet entries never have SUSP” read like they were. The flag is per directory entry. Entries in the Joliet tree carry no SUSP. Entries in the primary tree carry the full Rock Ridge set. Second, with both El Torito and Joliet enabled, does the root directory location get bumped twice? Yes. The boot record and the SVD are each their own volume descriptor sector, and that deserved a comment.
go-proxmox switched makeCloudInitISO() over to Joliet: true and shipped it in v0.5.0 on May 7th, pinned to go-diskfs v1.9.2.
Step 3: what Windows actually wanted (#391) A day later go-proxmox#258 came in from rgl, titled “0.5.0 creates an invalid iso file”. On Ubuntu, blkid showed this as the label:
/dev/sr0: BLOCK_SIZE="2048" UUID="2026-05-08-21-11-46-82" LABEL="M-fM-^MM-)M-fM-^QM-!M-gM-^QM-!" TYPE="iso9660" That’s cat -v escaping for 9 bytes of UTF-8. Decode them and you get three CJK characters: 捩摡瑡. That’s what you get when you take the six ASCII bytes of cidata (63 69 64 61 74 61) and read them as UCS-2 big-endian: 0x6369, 0x6461, 0x7461.
$ printf 'cidata' | iconv -f UCS-2BE -t UTF-8 | cat -v M-fM-^MM-)M-fM-^QM-!M-gM-^QM-! The Joliet SVD’s volume identifier is a UCS-2 field like everything else in that descriptor. go-diskfs was copying the ASCII string straight in. Linux preferred the Joliet label and got garbage. cloud-init’s nocloud datasource never found a volume called cidata. So the Joliet work had broken Linux guests too. That’s the opposite of the plan.
Fixing the label got Linux back. On Windows the label now showed correctly and dir D:\ listed the files. But reading one failed with Cannot find path 'D:\meta-data' because it does not exist. An xorriso-built ISO worked. The second bug was in the Joliet path table. Every directory gets a path table record, and the root’s identifier is a single byte. I’d written 0x01. ECMA-119 says the root’s path table identifier is a single 0x00 byte. That applies in the Joliet tables as much as the primary ones. My best read is that Windows resolves paths through the path table. It could enumerate the root through its directory record but couldn’t resolve a file path through the bad table entry.
PR #391 fixes both. The identifier encoding is gated on the escape sequence. Review pointed out that not every SVD is a Joliet SVD:
func (v *supplementaryVolumeDescriptor) toBytes() []byte { b := volumeDescriptorFirstBytes(volumeDescriptorSupplementary) b[7] = v.volumeFlags if isJolietSVD(v) { copy(b[8:40], ucs2StringToBytes(v.systemIdentifier)) copy(b[40:72], ucs2StringToBytes(v.volumeIdentifier)) } else { copy(b[8:40], v.systemIdentifier) copy(b[40:72], v.volumeIdentifier) } // ... } and the path table root becomes "\x00". rgl confirmed it worked against a Windows guest running cloudbase-init. The maintainer tagged go-diskfs v1.9.3 on May 14th, and go-proxmox v0.5.1 pinned it the same day.
Why the tests didn’t catch it I had round-trip tests and xorriso tests, and neither caught a wrong label. The round-trip tests couldn’t. The reader and writer had the same bug in opposite directions. parseSupplementaryVolumeDescriptor() read the identifier as raw bytes. toBytes() wrote raw bytes. So a go-diskfs ISO read back by go-diskfs said cidata every time. A round trip through your own code proves your reader and writer agree with each other. It says nothing about whether either one agrees with the spec.
The thing that caught it was someone booting a real VM. I’d add tests that assert specific bytes against the spec instead of only asserting that what goes in comes back out. The SVD identifier is UCS-2. The root path table entry is 00.
How I tested To check this for the post I built the same three-file ISO (RockRidge: true, Joliet: true, VolumeIdentifier: "cidata") with go-diskfs v1.9.2 and v1.9.3. I compared them on Windows 11 (build 26200) with Mount-DiskImage:
v1.9.2 SVD volume id bytes: 63 69 64 61 74 61 00 00 ... Joliet L path table root: 01 00 1a 00 00 00 01 00 01 00 Get-Volume label: 捩摡瑡 dir D:\ lists 3 files Get-Content D:\meta-data -> Cannot find path v1.9.3 SVD volume id bytes: 00 63 00 69 00 64 00 61 00 74 00 61 ... Joliet L path table root: 01 00 1a 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 Get-Volume label: cidata Get-Content D:\meta-data -> instance-id: vm-100 ... Same symptoms rgl saw in the VM. One extra thing turned up. The raw files are 57,354 bytes, but the primary volume descriptor claims 29 sectors (59,392 bytes). Mount-DiskImage refused both as “corrupted and unreadable” until I padded them to 29 full sectors. Proxmox and QEMU don’t care, but it’s another thing for the list.
Links diskfs/go-diskfs#353 - Rock Ridge support diskfs/go-diskfs#372 - Joliet support diskfs/go-diskfs#391 - Joliet SVD UCS-2 volume identifier and path table root luthermonson/go-proxmox#258 - “0.5.0 creates an invalid iso file” rgl/proxmox-clone-vm-example - rgl’s Windows + cloudbase-init example ECMA-119 - the ISO 9660 standard Rock Ridge Interchange Protocol (IEEE P1282) Joliet Specification

title: PHP Signal Safety - The Init Ordering Bug Nobody Warns You About
description: Embedding PHP in a multithreaded server means PHP's timeout signals can land on any thread. How ePHPm got that under control.
body:
Last week I wrote about why ePHPm embeds PHP from Rust and promised the signal bug its own post. Here it is. It’s the kind of bug where the fix is about ten lines and the explanation is the whole post. Nothing in PHP’s embed documentation (there’s barely any) tells you that initializing PHP has process-wide side effects. Those side effects assume PHP is the only thing in the process.
The setup The first working version of ephpm serve looked like every async Rust program. It was #[tokio::main]-style. Build the runtime, then inside it load config, initialize PHP and start the HTTP server. PHP requests run on spawn_blocking threads. Simplified:
async fn run_serve(command: Option<Commands>) -> anyhow::Result<ExitCode> { let config = load_serve_config(command)?; // tokio's worker threads already exist at this point ephpm_php::PhpRuntime::init().context("failed to initialize PHP runtime")?; ephpm_server::serve(config).await?; // ... } It served pages. It also took a SIGSEGV inside a signal handler, on a thread that had never executed a line of PHP. The stack under the handler was tokio’s, not mine and not Zend’s. That’s a confusing thing to stare at. I blamed PHP’s SIGPROF timer and built the fix around that theory. Going back through php-src to write this up, I found the theory was too simple. Init doesn’t arm that timer at all. The hazard is real, but it’s narrower than I thought. Knowing which builds it applies to is the useful part.
What php_embed_init() does that you didn’t ask for php_embed_init() does module startup and then starts a request. Module startup sets the LC_CTYPE locale. Request startup activates PHP’s zend_signal layer. That installs deferred handlers for SIGPROF, SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGQUIT, SIGTERM, SIGUSR1 and SIGUSR2. Then it calls zend_set_timeout() to enforce max_execution_time. The embed SAPI hard-codes max_execution_time=0 (it overrides whatever php.ini says). So at init that call only installs the timeout handler. The timer gets armed later by the first set_time_limit() or ini_set('max_execution_time', ...) with a non-zero value. That happens from whatever thread is running that script. Here’s the arming path on Linux builds without per-thread execution timers, trimmed down:
/* Zend/zend_execute_API.c, the setitimer branch of zend_set_timeout_ex() */ if (seconds) { t_r.it_value.tv_sec = seconds; t_r.it_value.tv_usec = t_r.it_interval.tv_sec = t_r.it_interval.tv_usec = 0; setitimer(ITIMER_PROF, &t_r, NULL); } signo = SIGPROF; if (reset_signals) { zend_signal(signo, zend_timeout_handler); } Two process-wide things are in play:
Process-wide signal handlers, installed at init: SIGPROF plus the zend_signal list above. Signal dispositions belong to the process, not to the thread that set them. A process-wide CPU timer, once anything sets a non-zero limit. ITIMER_PROF counts CPU time consumed by the whole process. That’s every thread, user and system. With a 30-second limit, it fires after 30 seconds of CPU across all threads. That second point also means the bug is load-dependent. That’s what makes it slippery. An idle server burns almost no CPU, so the timer barely moves. A busy one with 32 threads chewing through requests can burn 30 CPU-seconds in about a second of wall time.
Which thread gets the signal A process-directed signal on Linux is delivered to one thread that doesn’t have it blocked. The kernel picks. It is not “the thread that called setitimer.” PHP was written for two kinds of world. In one the process has one thread (CLI, php-fpm, mod_php prefork). In the other every thread is a PHP thread (ZTS under a threaded Apache MPM). So that distinction never mattered to it.
You can watch the kernel make that choice with a page of C. main() plays the PHP thread. It installs a SIGPROF handler and arms ITIMER_PROF (10ms, repeating, so we get plenty of samples). Then it starts eight threads that burn CPU, like busy tokio workers, and goes to sleep. The handler increments a counter for whatever thread it happens to run on:
static atomic_int hits[WORKERS + 1]; // [0] = main thread static __thread int my_slot = 0; // thread-local, like PHP's TSRM globals static void on_sigprof(int sig) { atomic_fetch_add(&hits[my_slot], 1); } int main(void) { struct sigaction sa = {0}; sa.sa_handler = on_sigprof; sigaction(SIGPROF, &sa, NULL); struct itimerval t = {{0, 10000}, {0, 10000}}; setitimer(ITIMER_PROF, &t, NULL); for (long i = 0; i < WORKERS; i++) pthread_create(&th[i], NULL, worker, (void *)(i + 1)); sleep(3); /* ... stop, join, print the histogram ... */ } $ ./sigprof thread SIGPROF main 0 worker-1 95 worker-2 135 worker-3 120 worker-4 118 worker-5 103 worker-6 109 worker-7 98 worker-8 75 total 853 The thread that installed the handler and armed the timer got none of them. That held in this run and in a second one (the split across workers moved around, main stayed at 0). It was asleep, like a PHP thread waiting on a database. All 853 deliveries landed on threads that had nothing to do with the timer. In this toy the handler only touches a thread-local int, so it’s harmless. PHP’s handler isn’t.
What that does to PHP PHP’s timeout handler isn’t a counter bump. It reaches into engine state. That means the executor globals and the flags that tell the VM to stop at the next opcode. What happens when it runs on the wrong thread depends on how PHP was built.
On the NTS build I started with, the globals are real globals. A handler running on a tokio worker sets the flags just fine. The PHP thread dies with “Maximum execution time exceeded” at its next opcode. The problem is the clock. Under php-fpm a worker blocked on a database query burns no CPU, so ITIMER_PROF stands still while it waits. In ePHPm the other 31 threads keep burning CPU. A script with a 30-second limit can be killed after a second of wall time for CPU it never used. It gets worse. NTS PHP re-arms the same timer for hard_timeout (2 seconds by default). Say it fires again while the PHP thread is still stuck somewhere that doesn’t check the flag. Then the handler calls _exit(124). On a busy box two process CPU-seconds go by in well under a tenth of a second. That _exit takes the whole server down, not one request.
Since last week ePHPm runs ZTS PHP. There the question is whether the handler can find its globals at all. Every “global” lives in a per-thread slot handed out by TSRM. A thread gets a slot when it registers with ts_resource(0). ePHPm does that on the first PHP request a blocking thread runs. A tokio worker that only accepts sockets never registers. PHP 8.2 and earlier went looking for that slot anyway. PHP 8.3 added a tsrm_is_managed_thread() check to both handlers. The deferred signal handler forwards to the original disposition. The timeout handler prints “zend_timeout_handler() called in a thread not managed by PHP” to stderr and returns. So on a current ZTS build the symptom is a timeout that silently never happens, not a crash.
And on Linux, PHP 8.3+ turns on per-thread execution timers for ZTS builds by default (--enable-zend-max-execution-timers). That’s a POSIX timer per thread, aimed at that thread with SIGRTMIN. The kernel isn’t picking a thread at all. The ZTS libphp I switched to last week has them. static-php-cli passes the flag explicitly as well. So the SIGPROF problem is real for three cases:
NTS builds ZTS builds older than 8.3 or built without those timers platforms that don’t have them It is not a problem for the build ePHPm runs today. That matters for the second half of the fix.
The fix, part one: do the global stuff while you’re alone Here’s the first rule I took from this. Anything that touches process-global state (signal dispositions, timers, atexit, locale) has to happen before there’s a second thread. So PHP init moved out of the async world entirely. main is synchronous again. The tokio runtime is built only after PHP is up:
/// PHP must be initialized BEFORE the tokio runtime is created. PHP's /// `php_embed_init()` starts a SIGPROF timer for `max_execution_time`. /// If tokio worker threads exist when the signal fires, it gets delivered /// to a non-PHP thread whose signal handler dereferences NULL → SIGSEGV. /// /// The sequence is: /// 1. Load config + init tracing (no threads) /// 2. Init PHP + disable SIGPROF timer (still single-threaded) /// 3. Create tokio runtime (spawns worker threads — now safe) /// 4. Run HTTP server fn run_serve_sync(command: Option<Commands>) -> anyhow::Result<ExitCode> { let config = load_serve_config(command)?; ephpm_php::PhpRuntime::init().context("failed to initialize PHP runtime")?; ephpm_php::PhpRuntime::finalize_for_http() .context("failed to finalize PHP runtime for HTTP")?; // Now safe to create the multi-threaded tokio runtime let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().context("failed to create tokio runtime")?; rt.block_on(async { ephpm_server::serve(config).await }) } The comment overstates it. With max_execution_time at 0, init installs the handler and leaves the timer alone. I’d lumped init together with the first script that sets a limit. The ordering rule it enforces is still right. Signal dispositions, the locale and the rest of PHP’s process state get set up while nothing else is running. (finalize_for_http() just closes out the embed’s initial request. The linker trick below deals with the timer.)
That fixes init. It isn’t enough on its own, because init isn’t the only time PHP touches the timer. So the same change also took the timer away from PHP entirely.
The fix, part two: take the timer away from PHP Every php_request_startup() calls zend_set_timeout() again. A script’s set_time_limit() does too. So on a SIGPROF build the timer can be re-armed from a worker thread long after main was alone.
ePHPm links libphp.a statically, which means the linker gets a say. GNU ld’s --wrap=symbol rewrites every undefined reference to symbol into __wrap_symbol. If the binary provides __wrap_zend_set_timeout, PHP’s own calls go there instead. That has to go in the binary crate’s build.rs. rustc-link-arg from a library crate doesn’t reach the final link (trimmed):
// crates/ephpm/build.rs if env::var_os("PHP_SDK_PATH").is_some() { for func in &[ "zend_signal_startup", "zend_signal_init", "zend_signal_deactivate", "zend_signal_activate", "zend_signal_handler_unblock", // zend_set_timeout directly calls sigaction(SIGPROF) + // setitimer(ITIMER_PROF), bypassing the zend_signal system. "zend_set_timeout", "zend_unset_timeout", ] { println!("cargo::rustc-link-arg=-Wl,--wrap={func}"); } } And the C wrapper provides the replacements, which do nothing (trimmed, comments shortened):
void __wrap_zend_signal_startup(void) { /* skip process-wide handler install */ } void __wrap_zend_signal_init(void) { /* skip per-request setup + SIGPROF unblock */ } void __wrap_zend_signal_deactivate(void) { } void __wrap_zend_signal_activate(void) { } void __wrap_zend_signal_handler_unblock(void){ } void __wrap_zend_set_timeout(long seconds, int reset_signals) { (void)seconds; (void)reset_signals; /* no-op: ePHPm manages request timeouts at the HTTP server level */ } void __wrap_zend_unset_timeout(void) { } The original definitions are still in the archive under their own names. __real_zend_set_timeout is how you’d reach one if you wanted to. Nothing does.
What that costs Being honest about the trade, because it’s not free:
max_execution_time is not enforced by PHP anymore. ePHPm’s HTTP request timeout bounds a runaway script instead. It returns a 504 to the client. The PHP thread itself keeps running until the script finishes. That’s worse than php-fpm. PHP 8.3+ can use per-thread execution timers instead (--enable-zend-max-execution-timers, POSIX timers aimed at the owning thread via SIGRTMIN). It turns them on by default for ZTS builds on Linux. So the ZTS libphp I switched to last week already has them. The wrap above still covers the NTS build. On the ZTS build it is now throwing away a timer that was already thread-safe. Letting PHP keep it is the real fix and it’s on the list. pcntl_signal() doesn’t do anything useful. I’m fine with this for a web server. FrankenPHP has had to work around the same problem. It blocks the pcntl-style signals on all of Go’s threads and only lets its CLI mode see them. --wrap is a GNU ld feature. macOS’s linker doesn’t have it, so the macOS build will need a different answer. Why nobody warns you The embed SAPI has very few serious users. Most of PHP’s process-level assumptions are documented implicitly by php-fpm’s architecture. One process handles one request at a time, so a process-directed signal can only ever land on the PHP thread. Those assumptions stop holding the moment you put PHP in a process that has its own threads. Nothing in the API tells you which functions carry process-wide side effects. You find out from a crash, or from a timeout that makes no sense.
Here’s the broader lesson, which I’ve now written on a sticky note. When you embed a C runtime in your process, you inherit all of its global side effects. Signal handlers, timers, atexit hooks, setlocale, environment reads, thread-locals it expects someone to initialize. The runtime doesn’t know it’s not alone anymore. Do its global init while your process is still single-threaded. Then go through what it does per-request. Decide which of those global effects you’re willing to let it keep.
How I ran the repro Ubuntu under WSL2 on a Ryzen 9 5950X, gcc 15.2, gcc -O2 -pthread -o sigprof sigprof.c && ./sigprof. The full file is 55 lines including the printing. The excerpt above is the part that matters. Exact counts will differ from run to run and machine to machine. The point is the distribution, not the numbers.
Links ePHPm signal(7), see “Signal disposition” and the note that a process-directed signal may be delivered to any one of the threads that does not have it blocked setitimer(2) for ITIMER_PROF GNU ld --wrap PHP embed SAPI

title: Why Rust for PHP Embedding (Not Go)
description: I'm a Go developer building a PHP application server in Rust. Here's the FFI reasoning, the C wrapper it forced on me, and what cgo actually costs when you measure it.
body:
Go is my primary language and has been for a long time. When I started building ePHPm a few weeks ago the obvious move was to write it in Go. ePHPm is a PHP application server. It’s one binary that embeds the real PHP interpreter (libphp, the Zend engine) and puts an HTTP server, TLS, a KV cache and a database proxy around it. A PHP app doesn’t need nginx + php-fpm + Redis to run. FrankenPHP already proved the “PHP inside a Go web server” idea works, and it works well. I wrote it in Rust anyway. This post covers the reasoning, and the part of the design that Rust made easier and the part it didn’t. It also has some numbers I should have measured before I wrote the design doc instead of after.
What embedding PHP actually means PHP is a C library if you build it with --enable-embed=static. Plain --enable-embed gives you a shared libphp.so. You get libphp.a, a header set, and the embed SAPI (php_embed_init() / php_embed_shutdown()). Everything else is your problem. Where output goes, where the POST body comes from, how $_SERVER gets filled. PHP asks for all of that through the SAPI. That’s a struct of function pointers that the host fills in (ub_write, read_post, send_headers, register_server_variables and friends). php-fpm, Apache’s mod_php and the CLI are all just different implementations of that struct.
So the host language talks to PHP in two directions:
Host calls PHP: start a request, execute a script, read back results. PHP calls host: every echo is a ub_write callback, reading php://input is read_post, building $_SERVER is register_server_variables. The second direction is the one that matters for this comparison. It happens many times per request, and it’s where the language boundary gets crossed from the “wrong” side.
What my design doc said When I sat down to compare runtimes I wrote up FrankenPHP in some detail. I covered its Caddy module, its worker loop, and how it parks a PHP thread on a Go channel. The headline in my own project notes was this line. It’s in AGENTS.md and the architecture doc:
Go’s CGO incurs ~200ns overhead per call. FrankenPHP crosses the CGO boundary 11+ times per request (~2.2μs+ overhead). Rust FFI to libphp is zero overhead.
The 11 crossings came from walking a request through FrankenPHP:
Dispatch to the PHP thread. The SAPI callbacks for superglobals, headers, cookies, body reads and output writes. The trip back to finish the request. The 200ns was a number I’d carried around in my head for years from older Go releases. I didn’t measure it. That’s fine in a design doc and not fine in a blog post, so I measured it.
Measuring the boundary The benchmark is about as small as it gets. Three C functions, compiled with gcc -O2 and marked noinline. They’re linked into both a Go test binary and a Rust binary. Each side gets its own copy of the file, and this is the Go one:
#include <stddef.h> __attribute__((noinline)) void noop(void) {} __attribute__((noinline)) size_t write_buf(char *p, size_t n) { return n + (p != 0); } extern size_t goUbWrite(char *p, size_t n); /* rust_ub_write on the Rust side */ __attribute__((noinline)) size_t c_calls_host(char *p, size_t n) { return goUbWrite(p, n); } write_buf is the shape of ub_write, a pointer and a length. c_calls_host is C calling back into the host language. That’s what every SAPI callback does if the host owns the output buffer. On the Go side it’s a cgo package with an //export’d goUbWrite and a normal testing.B loop. On the Rust side it’s an unsafe extern "C" block and a #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn rust_ub_write. A loop of 200 million calls is timed with Instant, with black_box on the arguments so nothing gets folded away. Each case ran five times and I took the median.
Case Go 1.26 cgo Rust 1.94 Plain function call, no FFI (baseline) 1.20 ns 1.15 ns Empty C call 23.6 ns 1.15 ns C call with pointer + length 29.3 ns 1.39 ns C calls back into the host 61.2 ns 1.60 ns So my doc was wrong, and wrong in Go’s favor. A cgo call on Go 1.26 is about 24ns on this box, not 200. Going the other way, C calling into an exported Go function, is about 61ns. Rust calling C is indistinguishable from Rust calling Rust. It is the same thing. Same calling convention, same stack, a call instruction.
If I redo the napkin math with real numbers, 11 crossings cost somewhere between roughly 0.25µs (all cheap calls) and 0.7µs (all callbacks) per request. That is real and it’s measurable. It is still small next to running a WordPress page. Anyone who tells you cgo overhead alone is what makes Go the wrong choice here is doing what I did in the design doc.
So why Rust anyway The per-call number isn’t the whole cost of putting a Go runtime and the Zend engine in the same process. These are the things that pushed me over.
There’s no second runtime in the way. A cgo call isn’t just a jump. The goroutine has to move onto the system stack and tell the scheduler it’s leaving Go. A callback from C into Go has to get back onto a goroutine. A C thread that Go didn’t create has to be adopted by the runtime first. FrankenPHP creates each PHP thread in C with pthread_create and calls back into Go from it. It parks the thread on a channel select waiting for the next request, so the goroutine scheduler never gets to move it. All of that is well-engineered. All of it is also machinery that exists because there are two runtimes in the process with different ideas about threads and stacks. In Rust a PHP thread is an OS thread. I call ts_resource(0) on it once to register it with PHP’s thread-safe resource manager and that’s the whole story.
No GC sharing the process with Zend. PHP has its own allocator and its own refcounting/GC. Go’s GC doesn’t scan C memory, so it’s not a correctness problem. But it is a second source of pauses in the same process as your PHP requests. Tail latency is one of the numbers I care about for this project.
The scope is bigger than an HTTP front end. ePHPm isn’t only going to serve PHP. The plan includes an in-process KV store that PHP can call into directly, a pooling MySQL/Postgres proxy, and gossip clustering. Most of those are hot paths where PHP calls out of the Zend engine into host code. That is exactly the 61ns-vs-1.6ns row in the table. I’d rather that direction be free from day one than try to batch around it later.
I want to own the binary. FrankenPHP is a Caddy build. That’s a feature for them. For ePHPm I wanted the HTTP stack (hyper), the TLS/ACME stack, and the PHP lifecycle all under my control. Nothing should have to be upstreamed into a second project before I can change how a request is dispatched.
None of that makes Go bad at this. FrankenPHP exists and people run real traffic on it. It’s a trade I’m comfortable with because I’m the one paying the Rust learning tax.
The part Rust doesn’t solve: setjmp/longjmp Here’s the catch that every embedder hits regardless of language. PHP’s error handling is setjmp/longjmp. A fatal error, an exit() in older paths, a memory limit or a timeout all end the same way. The Zend engine calls zend_bailout(), which longjmps back to the nearest zend_try. The zend_try/zend_catch macros expand to a SETJMP on a jump buffer stored in executor globals.
You can’t do that from Rust. setjmp “returns twice,” which Rust’s compiler doesn’t model. A longjmp across Rust frames skips their destructors and is undefined behavior. If PHP longjmps through a Rust frame that holds a MutexGuard or a Vec, you’ve leaked or corrupted something. You won’t find out until later.
The fix is boring and mandatory. Rust never calls into the Zend engine directly for anything that can bail out. It calls a C function, and the C function owns the jump buffer. This is the core of ephpm_execute_request() in crates/ephpm-php/ephpm_wrapper.c (trimmed):
int ephpm_execute_request(const char *filename) { /* ... reset buffers, fill SG(request_info), rebuild superglobals ... */ int result = 0; JMP_BUF *__orig_bailout = EG(bailout); JMP_BUF __bailout; EG(bailout) = &__bailout; if (SETJMP(__bailout) == 0) { zend_file_handle file_handle; zend_stream_init_filename(&file_handle, filename); php_execute_script(&file_handle); /* PHP 8.x: exit()/die() throws an unwind exit exception instead * of calling zend_bailout(). Treat it like the old bailout path. */ if (EG(exception) && zend_is_unwind_exit(EG(exception))) { zend_clear_exception(); result = -2; } } else { /* PHP bailed out (fatal error) */ result = -2; } EG(bailout) = __orig_bailout; capture_response_headers(); response_status_code = SG(sapi_headers).http_response_code; return result; } The longjmp lands in a C frame and the C function returns an int. Rust only ever sees a normal return. The rules the rest of the code follows fall out of that:
Every Rust → PHP entry point goes through a C function that sets up the bailout. SAPI callbacks are C, and they write into thread-local C buffers (output_buf, headers_buf). They don’t call into Rust while PHP might still bail out above them. Rust reads the buffers back after the C function returns. On the Rust side, the call is a handful of CStrings that have to outlive the call. Then it’s a plain function call:
unsafe extern "C" { pub fn ephpm_request_set_info( method: *const c_char, uri: *const c_char, query_string: *const c_char, content_type: *const c_char, cookie: *const c_char, post_data: *const c_char, post_data_len: usize, path_translated: *const c_char, ); pub fn ephpm_execute_request(filename: *const c_char) -> c_int; pub fn ephpm_get_output_buf(out_len: *mut usize) -> *const c_char; } // method, uri, script_filename... are CStrings owned by this stack frame, // so the pointers C holds stay valid until ephpm_execute_request returns. let ret = unsafe { ffi::ephpm_execute_request(script_filename.as_ptr()) }; let body = { let mut len: usize = 0; let ptr = unsafe { ffi::ephpm_get_output_buf(&mut len) }; if ptr.is_null() || len == 0 { Vec::new() } else { unsafe { std::slice::from_raw_parts(ptr.cast::<u8>(), len) }.to_vec() } }; The C wrapper is just under 1,400 lines at this point. Most of it is SAPI plumbing I’ll write up separately. The Rust side is mostly CString conversions and // SAFETY: comments. The split has held up so far. Rust handles everything that’s async or long-lived. C handles anything that touches Zend’s control flow.
Threads The other thing the diagram at the top hides is threading. PHP comes in two flavors:
NTS (non-thread-safe) runs one request at a time per process, which is why php-fpm forks. ZTS (Zend Thread Safety) keeps every global in a per-thread slot managed by TSRM. For the first couple of weeks ePHPm ran NTS PHP behind a mutex. That’s a fine way to get correct output and a terrible way to serve concurrent requests.
As of this week it’s ZTS. hyper and tokio handle connections asynchronously, and each PHP request runs on a tokio spawn_blocking thread. The first time a given thread runs PHP it calls into C to register with TSRM and start a request context. After that it’s a thread-local bool check. All the per-request C state in the wrapper is __thread. Rust’s threads are OS threads, so there’s no question about which thread a piece of code runs on.
One thing is not free, and I learned it the hard way the same week I wrote the code above. PHP’s init installs process-wide signal handlers, including the SIGPROF handler behind max_execution_time. Those do not care that your process has 32 tokio threads in it. That bug gets its own post.
What I’d tell a Go developer considering this If you want PHP inside a Go web server, use FrankenPHP. It’s mature and it’s under the PHP Foundation now. 24ns per crossing is not what’s going to hurt you. Rust fits a different shape of project:
PHP calls back into host code constantly. You want one runtime in the process. You’re willing to write a C shim for Zend’s control flow either way. There, Rust gets out of the way in a way cgo structurally can’t.
And measure your own numbers before you put them in a design doc.
How I measured AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 cores / 32 threads), Ubuntu under WSL2, kernel 6.18, gcc 15.2 Go 1.26.0 (go test -bench, five runs of about 2 seconds each), Rust 1.94.0 (cargo build --release, opt-level 3) The same three C functions are linked into both binaries (two copies differing only in const and the callback name). They are noinline and live in a separate object, so neither compiler can inline across the boundary (no cross-language LTO) Numbers are the median of five runs per case Links ePHPm FrankenPHP and its source cgo documentation The Rustonomicon on FFI, whose section on FFI and unwinding is the reason you don’t let anything unwind or longjmp through a Rust frame PHP embed SAPI source

title: Maintaining a Go Tool That Edits /etc/hosts on Every OS
description: Notes from maintaining goodhosts, the hosts file CLI and Go library behind vagrant-goodhosts and ddev. It covers Windows quirks, a HostsPerLine bug, and making the CLI testable.
body:
Editing the hosts file sounds like the most boring problem in software. Read a text file, add a line, write it back. Then you find out your binary is being shelled out to from a Ruby Vagrant plugin on a Windows laptop with UAC prompts. Your library is being called in a loop by ddev. And every hosts file you parse was hand-edited by somebody at some point. I’ve been maintaining goodhosts for a few years now. I just spent a chunk of the fall and the holidays on it, so here’s what that looks like.
Where it came from I didn’t start it. Lex Toumbourou wrote the original goodhosts CLI in Go in April 2015, and Windows support landed that June. In January 2020 I moved it into the goodhosts org and split it in two:
goodhosts/hostsfile, the Go library that parses a hosts file into structs, indexes it, and flushes it back to disk goodhosts/cli, the goodhosts binary on top of it (add, remove, list, check, clean, backup, restore, edit) The biggest consumer of the CLI is vagrant-goodhosts, which has a longer history than either. It’s descended from vagrant-hostsupdater (first commit April 2013). In May 2020 Daniele Scasciafratte swapped its Ruby hosts file handling for the goodhosts CLI. The gem bundles a prebuilt binary per platform and picks one at runtime. This is trimmed, and the current version also branches on arm64 vs amd64:
def get_os_binary if OS.windows? return 'cli.exe' elsif OS.mac? return 'cli_osx' elsif OS.linux? return 'cli' else raise Error::WebDriverError, "unknown os: #{host_os.inspect}" end end That’s the main reason the CLI is Go. Ruby plugins that edit system files on three operating systems are miserable. A static binary you can drop next to the gem works on all three. ddev uses the library directly.
“Every OS” is two files The OS-specific surface of the library is small, and I want to keep it that way. Unix-likes get this:
//go:build !windows package hostsfile var ( HostsPerLine = -1 // unlimited HostsFilePath = "/etc/hosts" eol = "\n" ) func (h *Hosts) preFlush() error { return nil } func (h *Hosts) postFlush() error { return nil } And Windows gets this:
package hostsfile var ( HostsPerLine = 9 HostsFilePath = "${SystemRoot}/System32/drivers/etc/hosts" eol = "\r\n" ) func (h *Hosts) preFlush() error { // need to force hosts per line always on windows see https://github.com/goodhosts/hostsfile/issues/18 h.HostsPerLine(HostsPerLine) return nil } The HostsPerLine bit came from issue #18. A Vagrant user had 16 hostnames on one 127.0.0.1 line and sites stopped loading. Windows only honours the first 9 names on a hosts line. That’s undocumented, but easy to reproduce. So on Windows every flush splits long lines into chunks of 9. Most of the other platform fixes over the years came from users too:
Till Wegmüller fixed the build tags so it builds on the other POSIX platforms. Guillaume Rose closed a file descriptor that leaked after the writable check. Christophe Fergeau added a missing +build directive. The bug that only shows up in a loop From the end of September through October I did a round of cleanup on the library:
A reindexer for the ip and hostname position lookups. A fix for duplicate removal reordering lines. Keeping comments when cleaning. Moving the build to mage. Coverage reporting. That went out as v0.1.2 through v0.1.4. A few hours after the v0.1.4 release, Randy Fay from ddev opened #51. ddev calls the library once per hostname, roughly like this:
hosts, err := goodhosts.NewCustomHosts(osHostsFilePath) if err != nil { return err } err = hosts.Add(ip, name) if err != nil { return err } hosts.HostsPerLine(8) err = hosts.Flush() Run that 15 times and the first line fills to 8 hosts. Then every new hostname ends up on its own line, newest first. Each test in the suite called Add a bunch of times and then HostsPerLine once, and that was fine. Nothing tested the load, add, split, flush cycle repeated.
I wrote a reproduction that does the same thing as ddev against a scratch file, reloading from disk for every add. I ran it against three tagged versions of the library. This is the real output:
The cause was in Add. When the ip already existed it appended the new hostname to the first line with that ip:
// add new host to the first one we find hostsCopy := h.Lines[position[0]].Hosts After the first split, the first 127.0.0.1 line is always full. So each add pushes it to 9 hosts. HostsPerLine(8) splits off the overflow into a new line directly below it, and the previous overflow lines get pushed down. That’s the reversed staircase in the v0.1.4 output. It also wasn’t copying the slice before appending. That’s asking for trouble once HostsPerLine has handed out subslices of the same backing array to multiple lines.
#52 switched to the last line for that ip and copied the slice properly. It also added a test that does 50 rounds of add plus split and checks the result is identical to adding all 50 and splitting once:
// test if multiple calls to HostsPerLine doesn't create havoc and has identical output as calling it once hosts = newHosts() for i := 1; i <= 50; i++ { assert.Nil(t, hosts.Add("127.0.0.1", fmt.Sprintf("a%d.ddev.site", i))) hosts.HostsPerLine(8) // 8 } hosts2 := newHosts() for i := 1; i <= 50; i++ { assert.Nil(t, hosts2.Add("127.0.0.1", fmt.Sprintf("a%d.ddev.site", i))) } hosts2.HostsPerLine(8) // 8 assert.Equal(t, hosts.String(), hosts2.String()) That went out as v0.1.5, and it had a bug of its own:
loc := position[len(position)-1] // last element hostsCopy := make([]string, len(h.Lines[position[loc]].Hosts)) position is the list of line numbers for that ip, so loc is already a line number. position[loc] indexes the list with a line number.
