In the test fixtures and in Randy’s repro the 127.0.0.1 lines start at line 0 and run consecutively. So position[n] always happened to equal n and every test passed. Put two comments at the top of the file, like a real hosts file has, and the first add panics. That’s the orange box in the image: index out of range [2] with length 1. #53 changed h.Lines[position[loc]] to h.Lines[loc]. v0.1.6 was tagged under an hour after v0.1.5.
The lesson for me was the fixtures. Hosts files in the wild start with comments, and most of the lines are for other ips. A fixture where the line you care about is line 0 hides a whole class of index bugs.
Making the CLI testable The CLI had the opposite problem: it barely had tests. Over the holidays I fixed that in #40 through #43. The main obstacle was that the whole cli.App was built inside main() as a local variable. The commands wrote straight to logrus, which main configured as a fmt.Print replacement. You can’t drive that from a test without running a binary.
So the app moved into the cmd package as an exported App, and main shrank to almost nothing:
func main() { if err := run(os.Args); err != nil { logrus.Fatal(err) } } func run(args []string) error { cmd.Version(version, commit, date) return cmd.App.Run(args) } Errors come back out of App.Run where a test can assert on them, and only main turns them into logrus.Fatal. Output still goes through logrus, which makes capturing it easy. Point logrus at a buffer and run the app with fake args.
// Setup takes args slice and resets logrus and returns args to pass to App.Run func setup(args ...string) ([]string, *bytes.Buffer) { out := &bytes.Buffer{} logrus.SetOutput(out) a := os.Args[0:1] a = append(a, args...) return a, out } With that, list tests are table-driven against hosts files written to disk, including the malformed-line marker:
"malformed comment added to row": { input: `127.x.x.x localhost 127.x.x.x localhost # comment `, expected: `127.x.x.x localhost # <<< Malformed! 127.x.x.x localhost # comment <<< Malformed! `, }, Writing those turned up a real bug right away. list loaded the hosts file in write mode, so it refused to run without elevated privileges just to print the file. It’s read-only now. The tests also have to know which OS they’re on. The error for a missing file is no such file or directory on Linux and macOS and The system cannot find the file specified. on Windows. The --debug and --quiet flags got tests too. Debug switches logrus to its text formatter, and quiet discards output entirely. version is now testable because the version string gets injected instead of read from package globals in main.
The CLI and library both build with mage now instead of a Makefile. Windows is a first-class target for this project. So mage ci working the same in PowerShell and bash is worth more than make’s familiarity. cli v1.1.2 went out last week with all of this and a codecov badge.
What’s next The library’s position indexes are the fragile part. Both bugs in this post were a line number pointing at the wrong place. The next round is testing Remove and HostsPerLine against hosts files that look like real ones, with comments at the top and other ips in between. If you use goodhosts in something, issues with a hosts file attached are the most useful bug reports I get.
Links goodhosts/hostsfile goodhosts/cli goodhosts/vagrant hostsfile#51, #52, #53 ddev

title: Proxmox Doesn't Know What Type a Number Is
description: The Proxmox VE API returns the same field as 1234 in one place and
in another. This is why go-proxmox has StringOrInt, StringOrUint64, StringOrFloat64 and IntOrBool instead of plain Go types.
body:
Every couple of months somebody opens an issue on go-proxmox with a title that starts with json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field. The most recent one was fixed last week. It’s the same root cause every time. The Proxmox VE API is backed by Perl, and Perl doesn’t really care whether a scalar is a number or a string. The JSON encoder on the other end writes whatever the scalar happens to be at the time. So a field that is documented as an integer comes back as 2048 from one endpoint and "2048" from another. Sometimes it changes on the same endpoint depending on how the value got into the config.
Go’s encoding/json does care, a lot. Here’s how the client deals with it.
The cpulimit report The cleanest example is #66 and its follow up #69. CPULimit was an int in VirtualMachineConfig. That’s wrong on its face because the Proxmox docs describe it as a float (1.0 is 100% of a core, 0.4 is 40%). So it became a float32. Then the reporter came back with the actual response from /nodes/{node}/qemu/{vmid}/config:
{ "data": { "cores": 2, "memory": 2048, "cpulimit": "0.4", "scsihw": "virtio-scsi-pci" } } That’s trimmed. The real payload has the rest of the VM config in it. cores and memory are numbers. cpulimit is a string. Same object, same endpoint.
Why not ,string The reporter’s first suggestion was the ,string struct tag option. It tells encoding/json the value is a number wrapped in quotes. That handles exactly one shape. I tried it and it was a mess. Here is the comparison as a little program you can run. It feeds three inputs to a plain float64, a float64 with ,string, and the type we ended up with:
type plain struct { CPULimit float64 `json:"cpulimit"` } type withTag struct { CPULimit float64 `json:"cpulimit,string"` } type withOr struct { CPULimit StringOrFloat64 `json:"cpulimit"` } {"cpulimit":"0.4"} float64: 0 err=json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field plain.cpulimit of type float64 ,string: 0.4 err=<nil> StringOrFloat64: 0.4 err=<nil> {"cpulimit":0.4} float64: 0.4 err=<nil> ,string: 0 err=json: invalid use of ,string struct tag, trying to unmarshal unquoted value into float64 StringOrFloat64: 0.4 err=<nil> {"cpulimit":""} float64: 0 err=json: cannot unmarshal string into Go struct field plain.cpulimit of type float64 ,string: 0 err=json: invalid use of ,string struct tag, trying to unmarshal "" into float64 StringOrFloat64: 0 err=<nil> (Go 1.21.4.) ,string fixes the quoted case and breaks the unquoted one. It also can’t cope with an empty string, which Proxmox also sends. In this client a lot of structs are used for two endpoints that disagree. A tag can’t help you there. You need a type that accepts both.
The StringOr types The idea goes back to the first version of the client. It’s a named numeric type with its own UnmarshalJSON that strips any quotes and parses what’s left. There’s one type per Go numeric kind we need. Here’s the float version I wrote for #69:
var ( isFloat = regexp.MustCompile(`^[0-9.]*$`) ) type StringOrFloat64 float64 func (d *StringOrFloat64) UnmarshalJSON(b []byte) error { str := strings.Replace(string(b), "\"", "", -1) if str == "" { *d = StringOrFloat64(0) return nil } if !isFloat.MatchString(str) { return fmt.Errorf("failed to match %s: %s", isFloat.String(), str) } parsed, err := strconv.ParseFloat(str, 64) if err != nil { return err } *d = StringOrFloat64(parsed) return nil } StringOrInt and StringOrUint64 are the same thing with a math.Trunc before the conversion. So "2048", 2048 and 2048.0 all land as 2048. Before that change the integer versions used strconv.ParseUint, which chokes on a decimal point. Moving everything to ParseFloat and truncating fixed a second class of report for free. The regex is there so garbage fails loudly with the offending value in the error instead of quietly becoming zero.
#59 asked the obvious question back in May. Wouldn’t it be easier to always convert to uint64? My answer then is still my answer now. The API was returning 1234 and "1234" and interchanging them a lot. One unmarshaller on a StringOrUint64 means you don’t write a custom UnmarshalJSON for every struct that has a numeric field which might show up quoted. The cost is that you have to convert at the edges (uint64(vm.VMID)), which I’ll take.
Going the other way is a non-issue. None of these types have a MarshalJSON, so they serialize as plain numbers. Proxmox is perfectly happy to accept a number for a field it would hand back to you as a string.
When upstream changes the type under you #105, merged last week, is the other way this bites. Reading a VM config started failing on memory after a Proxmox update. Johann tracked it down to qemu-server 8.0.8. That release gave memory its own property-string parser ([current=]<integer>) “in preparation to add more properties to the memory configuration”. From then on the API returns it quoted. The fix was one line:
Memory StringOrInt `json:"memory,omitempty"` // See commit 7f8c808772979f274cdfac1dc7264771a3b7a7ae on qemu-server That’s the real argument for the StringOr types over hand-picking int vs string per field. A field can flip between Proxmox point releases. When it does, you want a type that already accepts both rather than a broken release for everyone who upgraded their cluster.
Booleans have the same problem Booleans are their own flavor. Some endpoints return true/false and most return 1/0. The config files on disk are all 1/0. IntOrBool leans on the fact that strconv.ParseBool already accepts 1, 0, true and false:
type IntOrBool bool func (b *IntOrBool) UnmarshalJSON(i []byte) error { parsed, err := strconv.ParseBool(string(i)) if err != nil { return err } *b = IntOrBool(parsed) return nil } func (b *IntOrBool) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) { if *b { return []byte("1"), nil } return []byte("0"), nil } This one does marshal, and always as 1/0, because that’s the form every write endpoint accepts.
I follow one rule now when adding a field. If Proxmox documents it as a number, use the matching StringOr type. The exception is when I’ve seen it come back unquoted from every endpoint that shares the struct. It’s a little uglier in the struct definitions and it means far fewer cannot unmarshal string issues.
Links go-proxmox #69 cpulimit as a string and #71 StringOrFloat64 #59 Use of StringOrUint/64 #105 memory field parsing after qemu-server 8.0.8 encoding/json, the ,string option

title: Logging In to Proxmox From Go: Tickets, CSRF Tokens and API Tokens
description: Proxmox VE has two ways to authenticate against its API. Here's how go-proxmox handles each one and why the client is now configured entirely with functional options.
body:
I just spent a week of evenings on the access side of go-proxmox. Realms, groups, users and roles all landed. Before any of that, I reworked how a client gets its credentials in the first place. Proxmox gives you two different ways to authenticate. They behave differently enough that it’s worth writing down how each one works on the wire and what the client does with it.
Tickets This is what the web UI does. You POST /access/ticket with a username and password and get back a ticket and a CSRF token. Add an otp if the user has TFA, and optionally a realm:
type Credentials struct { Username string `json:"username"` Password string `json:"password"` Otp string `json:"otp,omitempty"` // One-time password for Two-factor authentication. Path string `json:"path,omitempty"` Privs string `json:"privs,omitempty"` Realm string `json:"realm,omitempty"` } type Session struct { Username string `json:"username"` CSRFPreventionToken string `json:"CSRFPreventionToken,omitempty"` // Cap is being returned but not documented in the API docs, likely will get rewritten later with better types Cap map[string]map[string]int `json:"cap,omitempty"` ClusterName string `json:"clustername,omitempty"` Ticket string `json:"ticket,omitempty"` } The ticket goes back to Proxmox as a cookie named PVEAuthCookie. The CSRFPreventionToken goes in a header of the same name. Proxmox requires it on every request that writes (POST, PUT, DELETE). A GET with just the cookie works. A POST with just the cookie gets you a 401, which is a fun one to debug the first time. The client sends both on every request, so you never have to think about it.
The thing to know about tickets is that they expire. Proxmox signs them with a lifetime of two hours ($ticket_lifetime = 3600 * 2 in PVE::AccessControl). That’s great for a browser tab and less great for a daemon.
API tokens Tokens are the better fit for automation. You create one under a user in the UI (Datacenter, Permissions, API Tokens). You get a token ID like root@pam!mytoken and a UUID secret, shown exactly once. There is no login round trip. You send a single header on every request:
Authorization: PVEAPIToken=root@pam!mytoken=<uuid secret> No CSRF token, no cookie, and no two hour expiry. Tokens can have an expiry date but default to none. The one decision you make when creating one is privilege separation. With privsep on, which is the default, the token only gets the permissions you grant to the token itself. With it off, the token has everything the user has. For a CI job or a provisioning tool I always leave it on and grant exactly what the tool needs.
Picking between the two happens in one place in the client:
func (c *Client) authHeaders(header *http.Header) { header.Add("User-Agent", c.userAgent) header.Add("Accept", "application/json") if c.token != "" { header.Add("Authorization", "PVEAPIToken="+c.token) } else if c.session != nil { header.Add("Cookie", "PVEAuthCookie="+c.session.Ticket) header.Add("CSRFPreventionToken", c.session.CSRFPreventionToken) } } Logging in lazily When you give the client credentials, it doesn’t log in when you construct it. The first request goes out with no auth, and Proxmox answers 401. Req notices it has credentials but no session. It grabs a ticket and replays the request:
if res.StatusCode == http.StatusUnauthorized || res.StatusCode == http.StatusForbidden { if path == (c.baseURL + "/access/ticket") { // received an unauthorized while trying to create a session return ErrNotAuthorized } if c.credentials != nil && c.session == nil { // credentials passed but no session started, try a login and retry the request if _, err := c.Ticket(c.credentials); err != nil { return err } return c.Req(method, path, data, v) } return ErrNotAuthorized } NewClient can’t return an error the way it’s built. I didn’t want a constructor that makes network calls anyway, so lazy login keeps it cheap. The /access/ticket check is there so a bad password returns ErrNotAuthorized instead of recursing.
Read that c.session == nil condition again though. Once a session exists, the client never logs in again. So when the ticket hits its two hour limit, every call after that comes back ErrNotAuthorized. For a CLI that runs for ten seconds that’s irrelevant. For something long running, use an API token until I get renewal sorted out.
Everything is an option now The other half of this round of work was getting rid of the setters. The client used to have client.Login(user, pass) and client.APIToken(id, secret) that you called after NewClient. That meant there was a window where you had a client that wasn’t configured yet. Now everything goes through functional options:
type Option func(*Client) func WithCredentials(credentials *Credentials) Option { return func(c *Client) { c.credentials = credentials } } func WithAPIToken(tokenID, secret string) Option { return func(c *Client) { c.token = fmt.Sprintf("%s=%s", tokenID, secret) } } // WithSession experimental func WithSession(ticket, CSRFPreventionToken string) Option { return func(c *Client) { c.session = &Session{ Ticket: ticket, CSRFPreventionToken: CSRFPreventionToken, } } } WithSession is for when something else already did the login, like a web app that is passing through a user’s ticket. The old Login, APIToken, WithLogins and WithClient are still there. They have // Deprecated: comments pointing at the replacements, so nobody’s build breaks on the next alpha.
A token client with a self-signed lab cert looks like this:
insecureHTTPClient := http.Client{ Transport: &http.Transport{ TLSClientConfig: &tls.Config{ InsecureSkipVerify: true, }, }, } client := proxmox.NewClient("https://localhost:8006/api2/json", proxmox.WithHTTPClient(&insecureHTTPClient), proxmox.WithAPIToken("root@pam!mytoken", "somegeneratedapitokenguidefromtheproxmoxui"), ) version, err := client.Version() if err != nil { panic(err) } fmt.Println(version.Release) Users and their tokens are readable from Go now too. The token list comes back on the user. So the next step is the write side: creating a token from a password-based client and handing it to whatever runs unattended. That’s how I want the integration tests to bootstrap themselves.
Links go-proxmox PR #74, deprecate old access funcs in favor of options PR #83, users and tokens Proxmox VE API viewer, /access/ticket Proxmox wiki, Proxmox VE API (authentication)

title: Waiting on Proxmox: UPIDs, Tasks and WaitFor in Go
description: Most Proxmox VE API calls that change something hand you a UPID instead of a result. Here is how go-proxmox turns that string into something you can wait on.
body:
If you start automating Proxmox VE through the API, one thing trips you up first. Almost nothing you ask it to do is finished when the HTTP call returns. Start a VM, clone a template, download an ISO to storage, delete a disk… the response is a single string that looks like a typo. The actual work is happening in a worker process on the node. If your next call depends on that work being done, you have to go find out when it’s done.
I’ve been building that part of go-proxmox over the last couple of months. The xterm.js post covered the shell side. With the simpler WaitFor that just landed, I think the shape is settled enough to write up.
The UPID Here is what a download-url call on my home lab node i7 gave back:
UPID:i7:00303F51:09D93CFE:61CCA568:download:8fd77349e9f6.iso:root@pam: That is a Unique Process ID, and it’s more useful than it looks. It’s colon separated and every field means something:
The middle three are hex:
00303F51 is the PID of the worker on the node (3161937). 09D93CFE is the process start time in clock ticks. Proxmox uses it to tell PIDs apart after they get reused. 61CCA568 is a unix timestamp (1640801640). That’s December 29th 2021 at 18:14 UTC, which is when I was testing this. The rest is plain text. There’s the task type, then an id, then the user that started it. The id is the VMID for VM tasks and the file name for a download.
The important bit is the node. Task status lives at /nodes/{node}/tasks/{upid}/status. If you parse the node out of the UPID, you can poll it without the caller having to remember where the work was scheduled. That’s the entire reason NewTask exists:
func NewTask(upid UPID, client *Client) *Task { if upid == "" { return nil } task := &Task{ UPID: upid, client: client, } sp := strings.Split(string(task.UPID), ":") if len(sp) == 0 || len(sp) < 7 { return task } task.Node = sp[1] task.Type = sp[5] task.ID = sp[6] task.User = sp[7] return task } Every method in the client that kicks off work now returns a *Task built this way instead of the raw string. VM start is the simplest example:
func (v *VirtualMachine) Start() (*Task, error) { var upid UPID if err := v.client.Post(fmt.Sprintf("/nodes/%s/qemu/%d/status/start", v.Node, v.VMID), nil, &upid); err != nil { return nil, err } return NewTask(upid, v.client), nil } The response body for these calls is {"data": "UPID:..."}. A UPID is just a string type, so unmarshalling straight into one works with no special handling.
Ping, Wait and WaitFor Once you have a *Task, Ping refreshes it from the status endpoint. The status payload has status, which is running or stopped. Once it’s stopped it also has exitstatus, which is OK or the error text.
func (t *Task) Ping() error { return t.client.Get(fmt.Sprintf("/nodes/%s/tasks/%s/status", t.Node, t.UPID), t) } Note it unmarshals right back into the task itself. The status response has the same fields the UPID encodes plus the ones that change. So the struct just keeps filling in as you poll it.
Wait is a polling loop with an interval and a max. I went with a plain select on a time.After. I wanted the timeout to be a real error you can check for, not a silent return:
func (t *Task) Wait(interval, max time.Duration) error { // ping it quick to fill in all the details we need in case they're not there t.Ping() t.client.log.Debugf("waiting for %s, checking every %fs for %fs", t.UPID, interval.Seconds(), max.Seconds()) timeout := time.After(max) for { select { case <-timeout: t.client.log.Debugf("timed out waiting for task %s for %fs", t.UPID, max.Seconds()) return ErrTimeout default: if err := t.Ping(); err != nil { return err } if t.Status != TaskRunning { t.client.log.Debugf("task %s has completed with status %s", t.UPID, t.Status) return nil } t.client.log.Debugf("waiting on task %s sleeping for %fs", t.UPID, interval.Seconds()) } time.Sleep(interval) } } After writing task.Wait(1*time.Second, 10*time.Second) twenty times across the integration tests, I added the lazy version. Most of the time you just want “poll every second, give up after N seconds”:
var DefaultWaitInterval = 1 * time.Second func (t *Task) WaitFor(seconds int) error { return t.Wait(DefaultWaitInterval, time.Duration(seconds)*time.Second) } One thing to be aware of: Wait returning nil means the task is no longer running, not that it worked. A clone onto storage that’s full stops just as fast as one that succeeds. Check task.ExitStatus after the wait if you care. You probably do.
Watching the log Some tasks take long enough that you want to see what they’re doing. A big ISO download is the obvious one. Proxmox writes progress lines to the task log as it goes. The log endpoint is paged with start and limit. Watch reads what’s there and hands it back on a channel. Then it tails the log until the task stops:
func tasktail(start int, watch chan string, task *Task) error { for { task.client.log.Debugf("tailing log for task %s", task.UPID) if err := task.Ping(); err != nil { return err } if task.Status != TaskRunning { task.client.log.Debugf("task %s is no longer running, closing down watcher", task.UPID) close(watch) return nil } logs, err := task.Log(start, 50) if err != nil { return err } for _, ln := range logs { watch <- ln } start = start + len(logs) time.Sleep(2 * time.Second) } } There is a small race at the front of this. If you call Watch immediately after starting a task, the log can be empty for a moment. So Watch retries the first read three times with a one second sleep. After that it gives up with no logs available. The channel is closed when the task finishes, so you can just range over it.
Putting it together The integration test fixture for VMs is the best example of all of this in one place. Download a tinycore ISO and wait for it. Create a VM with it attached and wait. Configure it and wait:
isoName := name + ".iso" task, err := td.storage.DownloadURL("iso", isoName, tinycoreURL) assert.Nil(t, err) assert.Nil(t, task.Wait(time.Duration(5*time.Second), time.Duration(5*time.Minute))) iso, err := td.storage.ISO(isoName) assert.Nil(t, err) cluster, err := client.Cluster() require.NoError(t, err) nextid, err := cluster.NextID() require.NoError(t, err) task, err = node.NewVirtualMachine(nextid, VirtualMachineOption{Name: "cdrom", Value: iso.VolID}) require.NoError(t, err) require.NoError(t, task.Wait(1*time.Second, 10*time.Second)) And the task test itself covers the rest:
It downloads an Ubuntu ISO big enough to still be running after 30 seconds. It waits on it in a goroutine with a 30 second max, so it has to hit the timeout. It stops the task with a DELETE on the task path. It reads the Watch channel on the main goroutine until it closes. One test, the whole lifecycle: start, poll, time out, tail, cancel.
That’s the plumbing. Clone landed in February. With tasks working, it and the rest of the VM lifecycle calls are just “post, wrap the UPID, return the task”. The next thing I want on top of it is booting a VM straight from a qcow URL without touching the node’s shell.

title: Recreating Proxmox Ve Xtermjs in Go
description: Proxmox's web console is xterm.js over a websocket. Here's how I reverse engineered that protocol and rebuilt the terminal connection in Go with go-proxmox.
body:
Part of a hobby of mine is running a home lab and using on Proxmox VE to do the virtualization. Since I work in the space I’m slowly trying to build tooling around Proxmox that will let me use the home lab full time for work. Usually my work involves building Kubernetes management tooling. You can imagine waiting for public cloud APIs all day can take away hours of your day. That’s at cost to your employer for both your time and the compute resources.
There’s also a real problem today with cloud offerings of Windows. Booting a Windows 2019 or 2022 server in Amazon EC2 today can take up to 4 or 5 minutes before you are given access to the Administrator password. If you build up and tear down constantly the waiting can get tiring. Proxmox just runs qemu under the hood and with snapshotting I Just get everything working and take a quick snapshot. When I want to roll back a cluster for another provision run I can simply shut down the VMs and restore from backup. I’m up and running again in no time.
go-proxmox To accomplish everything I’ll need I first started out building a Go client for Proxmox. Go is my primary language and gives everything will need to start from a well-built with proper Go types for all responses. This is in comparison to the most popular Go client which uses map[string]interface{} for everything. Beyond mapping REST endpoints to structs, the real power of the client will be to build in functions to more easily automate things. PVE gives you access to these but forces you to the host cli, as they haven’t built the tooling into their API/UI yet.
A great example of this is loading a VM from a qcow disk image. It’s a wonderfully simple image format. The way we want to use them for work is to specify a local network storage URL and tell Proxmox to pull and build a VM from the image. All of that is possible in qemu directly on the host, as per Jamie Phillips’ blog post which outlines the idea.
xterm.js Backwards Engineering I wanted to recreate what the UI was doing to get on to a host. It’s native and works right out of the box with no extra additions to Proxmox after installation. Back tracing how some of this worked I went down some rabbit holes looking into implementing a VNC client in Go. There are some people who have built some packages 1 2. But all I was trying to do is get on the Debian host and make some calls, and this was overkill.
I traced back the xterm.js functionality built into the UI and landed on exactly what I needed. For reference, here is the entire `main.js file I found used. I’ll walk you through how I backwards engineered it in Go and got exactly what I wanted.
Step 1, websocket connection Grab gorilla/websocket and negotiate the connection. While reading the implementation you notice quite quickly they reuse xterm.js for nodes, qemu and lxc. This was huge because it meant I could implement this code once and get triple the usage. There is a limitation to using this with qemu but the host nodes and lxc work right out of the box. I opened the shell to a node and started backwards engineering the UI requests.
You can see in the bottom right there is a call to termproxy then immediately to vncwebsocket. This was easily confirmed by the Proxmox API docs. It validated my suspicion that this code could be reusable, as node (termproxy vncwebsocket), qemu (termproxy vncwebsocket) and lxc (termproxy vncwebsocket) all had duplicate API endpoints. Reading the main.js you can quite clearly see every where socket.send() is called. You can decode the login, ping and data send, along with what looks like a resizer if you make your browser bigger or smaller. This was perfect. It was everything I needed to get into the host and send shell commands!
Step 2, recreating the login Recreating the login was trivial. A call to the termproxy endpoint results in a response which includes a user and a ticket. Call the web socket with those in the get params and the web socket boots right up. Just make sure you pass the PVEAuthCookie header in the dialer.
The socket only sends/receives binary messages. The next step is to start negotiating the web socket to elevate your permissions to send commands to the host. The first thing the Javascript did was login again via the socket. In Go after connecting simply do
err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.BinaryMessage, []byte(vnc.User+":"+vnc.Ticket+"\n")) if err != nil { // handle } Read the next message for OK response from the server…
_, msg, err := conn.ReadMessage() if err != nil || string(msg) != "OK" { // handle } That’s it for connecting and logging into the websocket, you can now start sending commands
Step 3, adding functionality Go lets you effortlessly manage the concurrency of a web socket and give you some standard interfaces for someone implementing the client’s VNC Web Socket feature. To do this I setup standard string channels for send/receive and an additional errors channel. Since you need to close everything when you’re done I also added a helpful closer func to make sure everything is cleaned up and you’re not leaking resources.
The function signature looked like this:
func (c *Client) VNCWebSocket(path string, vnc *VNC) (chan string, chan string, chan error, func() error, error) And this will let the client manage things the consumer doesn’t care about like the keep alive. To interface with the web socket you will need to spin off two go routines, one for reading the web socket and one for writing to the web socket. You can’t concurrently write to a web socket or you’ll panic. So try and make sure you’re keeping a clean select statement, or you will accidentally write to the socket twice.
To perform the keep alive it was quite obvious they’re sending a binary 2 for a ping. To recreate that I simply added a case for a 30s ticker.
case <-ticker.C: c.log.Debugf("sending wss keep alive") if err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.BinaryMessage, []byte("2")); err != nil { errors <- err } You also want to close the socket when you’re done. So another case is a simple CloseMessage with an empty []byte{}, which will only happen when the closer is called by the client implementor.
case <-done: if err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.CloseMessage, []byte{}); err != nil { errors <- err } return To support terminal resizing I decided to add a height/width calculator and implement a watcher to notify the web socket in the event the user resizes the terminal. To get the terminal size I used buger/goterm. I simply captured the height/width when the func is called and pass it to a go routine. It checks every second and notifies a channel if it changes. It also obeys the done channel closed by the closer.
type size struct { height int width int } // start the session by sending user@realm:ticket tsize := size{ height: goterm.Height(), width: goterm.Width(), } resize := make(chan size) go func(tsize size) { ticker := time.NewTicker(1 * time.Second) defer ticker.Stop() for { select { case <-done: return case <-ticker.C: resized := size{ height: goterm.Height(), width: goterm.Width(), } if tsize.height != resized.height || tsize.width != resized.width { tsize = resized resize <- resized } } } }(tsize) And catch the resize in a case in the go routine for the web socket send…
case resized := <-resize: c.log.Debugf("resizing terminal window: %d x %d", resized.height, resized.width) if err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.BinaryMessage, []byte(fmt.Sprintf("1:%d:%d:", resized.height, resized.width))); err != nil { errors <- err } Finally, all we need to do is send/receive messages on the channel. I wanted the implementor to call the VNCWebSocket func and send and receive strings. I added the channels and handled them by converting to a []byte. Then I send the message format as specified in the xterm.js version.
case msg := <-send: m := []byte(msg) send := append([]byte(fmt.Sprintf("0:%d:", len(m))), m...) if err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.BinaryMessage, send); err != nil { errors <- err } if err := conn.WriteMessage(websocket.BinaryMessage, []byte("0:1:\n")); err != nil { errors <- err } The entire receive go routine is pretty easy but has some nice to have added error checking and is as follows…
go func() { for { select { case <-done: return default: _, msg, err := conn.ReadMessage() if err != nil { if strings.Contains(err.Error(), "use of closed network connection") { return } if !websocket.IsUnexpectedCloseError(err, websocket.CloseGoingAway, websocket.CloseAbnormalClosure) { return } errors <- err } recv <- string(msg) } } }() Step 4, using the string channels For simple testing I just tried to gety ls -la, hostname and exit which was basically the following…
vnc, err := node.TermProxy() assert.Nil(t, err) send, recv, errs, close, err := node.VNCWebSocket(vnc) assert.Nil(t, err) defer close() go func() { for { select { case msg := <-recv: if msg != "" { fmt.Println("MSG: " + msg) } case err := <-errs: if err != nil { fmt.Println("ERROR: " + err.Error()) return } } } }() send <- "ls -la" time.Sleep(10 * time.Second) send <- "hostname" time.Sleep(10 * time.Second) send <- "exit" time.Sleep(5 * time.Second) It ends up looking quite easy. Just grab the TermProxy vnc response which includes the ticket and pass it to VNCWebSocket. You get your string channels, error channel and a closer. Start a go routine to watch the receive and error channels and start sending messages to the send channel.
Step 5, testing… The output from my test looked like the following with all debug enabled. You can see you can interact with the host with no restrictions right from Go.
[DEBUG] [WSS] wss://192.168.1.87:8006/api2/json/nodes/i7/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=***** [DEBUG] sending terminal size: 55 x 134 [DEBUG] sending: ls -la MSG: ls -la MSG: Linux i7 5.13.19-2-pve #1 SMP PVE 5.13.19-4 (Mon, 29 Nov 2021 12:10:09 +0100) x86_64 The programs included with the Debian GNU/Linux system are free software; the exact distribution terms for each program are described in the individual files in /usr/share/doc/*/copyright. Debian GNU/Linux comes with ABSOLUTELY NO WARRANTY, to the extent permitted by applicable law. MSG: Last login: Sun Feb 6 18:27:16 MST 2022 on pts/0 MSG: root@i7:~# ls -la MSG: total 49 drwx------ 3 root root 9 Dec 9 12:40 . drwxr-xr-x 18 root root 24 Sep 10 18:30 .. -rw------- 1 root root 2279 Feb 6 18:27 .bash_history -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 571 Apr 10 2021 .bashrc -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 25 Sep 10 18:29 .forward -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 161 Jul 9 2019 .profile -rw------- 1 root root 1024 Sep 10 18:34 .rnd drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 6 Sep 10 18:31 .ssh -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 206 Jan 23 08:41 .wget-hsts MSG: root@i7:~# [DEBUG] sending: hostname MSG: hostname MSG: i7 MSG: root@i7:~# [DEBUG] sending: exit MSG: exit MSG: MSG: logout --- PASS: TestNode_TermProxy (26.17s) Wrap Up Time to build more tooling on top of this which I’m hoping one day will be a terraform provider, a Terminal UI and a Machine Driver.

title: Free Blog Hosting Using Hugo + Github Pages
description: Upgrade your Personal Blog Game with Apex Records for No Cost
body:
Since I just rode this merry-go-round here is a quick overview of how you can get a professional looking personal blog with custom DNS. It takes minimal effort, costs nothing and runs completely out of a single Github Repository.
Prerequisites You’ll need to do your own homework on how to use Hugo. You should have a Github account and a decent understanding of using git and getting changes committed and pushed to a repo. You should also have a domain and know how to do some basic DNS changes. The only thing you likely can’t get for free is a domain name, since registrars charge registration costs. But you can get introductory $0.99USD domains for the first year if you shop around and don’t care what TLD you end up with. For reference, luth.io cost me $30/year to register with CloudFlare.
DNS Do this part first… it can take a while to propagate depending on your provider. Getting it out of the way will just make your life easier. What you are trying to do is use Github Pages with an Apex record for your domain. This will let something like https://luth.io be the place where people find your blog. Apex record support for a hosting service will let you bypass using subdomains like https://blog.luth.io which are called CNAMEs in DNS terms. You’re looking for A, ALIAS or ANAME records. When pointed at the root of your domain they need to be an IP address.
This requires Github Pages to support Apex records and provide IP addresses to point your DNS to. This was easy to find since Github Pages has an entire write-up in its help documentation. Following the advice from the article you will need to configure 4 A records and 4 AAAA records. For validation with Github you should add a CNAME for www pointed to your Github Pages username DNS e.g. luthermonson.github.io.
# A Records 185.199.108.153 185.199.109.153 185.199.110.153 185.199.111.153 # AAAA Records 2606:50c0:8000::153 2606:50c0:8001::153 2606:50c0:8002::153 2606:50c0:8003::153 # CNAME www <githubusername>.github.io When configured through Cloudflare my DNS entries looked like the following. Note that skipping the proxy and doing a grey cloud “DNS Only” was intentional. The proxy with SSL will cause an infinite redirect loop, and Github takes care of SSL for you.
Verifying your Domain with Github You will need to add your domain to Github and add a DNS TXT record to be able to add it to a repository later. Go to your Github Pages settings for your account (not repository) and Click “Add a Domain”. Follow the instructions by typing your domain and clicking next. You’ll get the DNS TXT records to validate your Domain with Github Pages.
Grab the details from the Verification Step, add the TXT record to your DNS Provider and then click Verify.
Github Repository You will need a Github Repository to house your Hugo blog and all the content. This will be where you serve your pages. Play with Hugo and create your blog, pick a theme and get used to the Hugo tool chain. Hugo will create a directory structure. By default when you run the hugo cli command it will generate your blog and place all contents in the ./public directory. Github Pages can NOT serve from anything other than the root ./ and the subdirectory ./docs. For our purposes to serve from one Github Repository we will use ./docs. To fix Hugo to publish to ./docs you can simply add a config line of publishDir = "docs" to the config.toml. When you now run hugo cli it will generate all files to the ./docs directory and prime your repository for serving via Github Pages.
To get Github Pages to serve the contents of your Blog with your domain you will need to configure the Pages settings for the repository. Check all your code into a branch and configure your Pages settings like the following. Summary Configure your DNS properly and use the free Github Pages service. Then you can easily host your personal blog at no cost on your own personal vanity domain name from a single Github Repository. Configure Hugo to use the ./docs directory to adhere to Pages standards and you’ll be able to effortlessly set up your Blog. Go henceforth and buy up some novelty domain names and get to blogging!

title: About the Blogger
body:
Originally born and raised in the Midwest, Luther received a Bachelor of the Arts in Computer Science from Gustavus Adolphus College in Southern Minnesota. After that he moved to the expansive deserts of the American Southwest. In Arizona, Luther spent his career building web APIs and utilities for various industries in PHP and NodeJS. From there he migrated to Open Source DevOps tooling using Containers and Virtualization.
Luther works at Akamai on LKE Enterprise, the enterprise tier of the Linode Kubernetes Engine. Before Akamai he spent years in the Kubernetes space at Rancher Labs and SUSE working on the Multi-Cluster Management tool Rancher. As the Team Lead for Windows on Rancher he specialized in Kubernetes on alternative operating systems and architectures including Windows, arm64 and s390x. After Rancher he worked at Spectro Cloud on Cluster API providers for AWS and Azure. That included OIDC/IRSA support for self-managed clusters on AWS. Working in this unique space and working from home full time has made him a home lab aficionado and consumer of Proxmox VE.
ePHPm ePHPm runs the same PHP app the same way from dev to prod as one Rust binary. It embeds real PHP through a custom SAPI. It bundles a web server with automatic TLS, an embedded SQLite-compatible database, a KV cache, a pooling SQL proxy and gossip clustering. A PHP app runs as a single process with no other services to operate.
ephemerd ephemerd is ephemeral GitHub Actions runners in a single binary for every platform: containers on Linux, Hyper-V on Windows, VMs on macOS. Every job gets an isolated, disposable environment that is thrown away when the job finishes.
litewire litewire speaks the MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server wire protocols in front of SQLite. Point pdo_mysql at :3306 and an unmodified app runs on embedded SQLite. There’s no database server and no code changes. It is the database layer inside ePHPm.
shipmates shipmates gives Claude Code subagents that remember. It provides role-specialized personas with persistent per-project memory. It also has a live lead-and-crew channel for dispatching work, steering an agent mid-task and approving actions with a human in the loop.
go-proxmox go-proxmox is a Go client, with types and tests, for the Proxmox VE REST API. It started in 2021 as a side project for the home lab. It’s now used by projects like the Cluster API provider for Proxmox.
Other Projects tail-gunner: a drop-in tail that promotes mid-stream into a live-filtering TUI linode-tui: a k9s-inspired terminal UI for the Linode API goodhosts: hosts file management from a Go CLI, on every OS quiso: QUickISO builder for cloud-init Open Source Contributions Rancher Machine and the vSphere Node Driver RKE1, RKE2 and remotedialer Cluster API and its providers for AWS (OIDC/IRSA support for self-managed clusters) and Azure, plus Spectro Cloud’s AWS and Azure provider forks sig-windows-dev-tools Flannel govmomi go-diskfs static-php-cli php-src Turso
